What I like most about AN OLD BETRAYAL--and the entire Charles Lenox mystery series--is the seemingly effortless way it immerses the reader in the historical place and time (Victorian England). The story develops unhurriedly (but not too slowly!) at a pace consistent with a simpler, slower-moving society. Historical facts abound, but they are woven seamlessly into the narrative--there are no lengthy descriptive passages, pedagogic history lectures, or jolting anachronisms. To pull this off, a writer like the highly skilled Charles Finch must have a wide knowledge and deep understanding of the historical era in which his characters are placed.

In AN OLD BETRAYAL, Charles Lenox now finds himself fully occupied--too occupied, in fact--with entertaining political figures like Prime Minister Benjamin Disraeli, reading boring technical documents, and otherwise carrying out his duties as an elected Member of Parliament. Charles' influence within the government is on the rise, but he misses his former work as a private detective. So when his protégé in detection, former playboy Lord John Dallington, finds himself too ill to meet with a secretive client, Charles steps in--and botches the assignment. Before Charles can speak with the fearful client, a gentlemanly stalker appears, and she flees. Now it's clear that the client is in danger, but Dallington doesn't know her name. The client must be located.

Charles quickly discovers that the stalker is impersonating another gentleman--a country gentleman who has come to London and been murdered in his quiet hotel room. In making inquiries, Charles is helped along by some of Dallington's private-detective competitors. As the details come out, and the plot thickens, Charles and Dallington realize there is a conspiracy afoot that they must unravel in order to prevent an attempt on the life of Queen Victoria herself. But even as he dabbles in detection, Charles must continue his work in Parliament, making speeches, arranging compromises, and obtaining votes to ensure the passage of important acts that will benefit the working classes. And this necessary work is being compromised by the rumors of influence-peddling for personal gain that are swirling around Charles' trusted political secretary Graham.

This is a novel that is totally enjoyable as a standalone (the first in the series is [[ASIN:0312386079 A Beautiful Blue Death]], which was named one of the Library Journal's best books of 2007). Charles Lenox is currently my favorite Victorian-era detective, but if you enjoy Victorian mysteries, you might also enjoy Lynn Shepherd's much more Dickensian series that features former policeman/detective Charles Maddox (e.g., [[ASIN:0345532430 The Solitary House]]).

Until now, I’ve enjoyed each new entry in the “Ruth Galloway” series. The novels are pleasant “cozy police procedural” mysteries about an archaeologist, now a single mother, who consults with local police whenever bones are discovered in henge sites in England’s North Norfolk salt marshes. However, most of this 11th series entry, THE STONE CIRCLE (RUTH GALLOWAY MYSTERIES), is duplicative of the earlier novels, and the new material about The Great Circle of stones at Stanton Drew is thrown in at the end and almost irrelevant to the solution of the main mystery.

In the novel, a second stone circle is discovered at the marshy henge site explored in the prior novels. This one includes a stone cist (a grave), but Ruth finds, once again, that the bones in it are recent--definitely not Bronze Age like the henge. Ruth’s detective contact (Nelson), her daughter Kate’s father, is once again receiving anonymous letters with literary references that urge him to investigate circumstances related to the child’s bones buried at the henge site.

A prime suspect in the burial is the look-alike son (Leif) of the deceased author of the letters Nelson received in the previous henge investigation. The bones are soon identified as probably belonging to a 12-year-old girl (Margaret) who went missing in 1981. But where were the bones kept, before they were reburied in the newly discovered cist? Who was responsible for Margaret’s death? And who reburied her bones in the cist?

Most of the novel deals with Ruth’s star-crossed relationship with Nelson. Nelson is married with adult daughters, and hasn’t informed his family of Kate’s paternity. He does have a regular visitation arrangement with Kate, so that one wonders why they don’t seem to suspect that he is Kate’s father. The novel also ties up a lot of loose ends from the original henge investigation--it’s basically a reworking of the original henge plot.

The novel does NOT work as a standalone. It’s extremely slow-moving, and the plot and ending are unsatisfying. Read it if you’re interested in following the latest developments in the Ruth/Nelson and Cathbad/Judy relationships.

Cheese balls are for parties--and they really are great when they're decorated to entertain and delight your guests! This book, GREAT BALLS OF CHEESE, is filled with an amazing variety of creative ideas for sculpting the standard party fare into works of art.

My favorite designs are the Wise and Cheesy Owl (shown on the book's cover; decorated with almonds, Ritz bits, black olives, carrot); the Christmas Tree (decorated with chopped parsley, pepper bits, star fruit); the Ham and Cheese Easter Egg (multicolored bell peppers cut into shapes, chives, deli ham); the Pineapple (toasted pecan halves for body, scallions for leaves); the Herbed Turkey (coated with slivered almonds, with almond nose, bell pepper wattle, pretzel stick "tail feathers"); the Sweet Almond Hedgehog (raisin eyes and nose, bristles of toasted slivered almonds), and the Wedding Cake (decorated with beads of cheese mixture circling the "layers").

The recipes themselves have a lot of interesting taste combinations. For example, there is the Mexican Black Bean Ball (canned black beans, cheddar cheese, cream cheese, red onion, cilantro, cumin); Cranberry & Rosemary Christmas Ornament (cream cheese, goat cheese, chopped cranberries, chopped fresh rosemary, garlic); the Spinach Artichoke Ball (frozen chopped spinach, cream cheese, chopped artichoke hearts, Parmesan cheese, garlic, lemon juice, hot sauce); the S.O.S. (cream cheese, cheddar cheese, chopped dried beef, Dijon mustard, Worcestershire sauce, hot sauce); the French Onion Pyramid (unsalted butter, sliced sweet onions, dry white wine, Gruyere cheese, cream cheese, cayenne pepper); and the Orange Creamsicle Cheese Ball (cream cheese, confectioner's sugar, frozen orange juice concentrate, orange marmalade, vanilla extract, graham crackers).

The recipes are introduced with short, often humorous paragraphs. This touch of humor, plus the imaginative designs shown in the photos, make this a fun book to page through. I think that the designs alone--or the recipes alone--are worth the price of this book. It's a terrific idea book!

The factory she worked in in New Jersey moved to Costa Rica and left Cara and many of her friends out of work. Her life had a rhythm and purpose, getting up each day to take the van across the George Washington Bridge for a job she loved. And now, Cara meets each week with the job counselor/social worker and the voice we hear is Cara's throughout, talking about her interests, then opening up little by little till we learn all about Cara, her best friend Lulu, her 96 year old neighbor who she feeds every night, her belief in an email/phone psychic that she pays for help and insight, her much younger sister Angela who became an accountant, is married to a hospital worker and saves her money to move to Long Island. Angela's children, who Cara cares for after school each day. Lulu's distress and breakdown over family concerns. Cara's estrangement from her son, that breaks her heart. Her vicious mother who tried to make Cara stay with her dangerous and abusive husband before she fled for New York. Cara is the one who helps organize neighbors to check on the forty year old daughter of a woman who has to work three jobs, so that this very disabled woman/child can stay with her. Cara is the one who cleans that friend's apartment when the daughter gets very upset in the middle of the night and throws things around, breaking them. She creates a better place for her friend to come home.

The thing is Cara has faced a lot and she cares for people who face a lot. She has done the best she could, sometimes making big mistakes. And she learns from them. There is a TON of humor in this novel because there is a TON of humor in looking at each of our lives and choices and beliefs about what we have done right or wrong. The laugh out loud stuff comes from when Cara takes tests or fills out applications or creates her first password and responds to password recovery questions. She gives full responses to these questions, not understanding the point and it is deeply funny and sweet. Less sweet and also funny is the name of the company that is trying to offload all of the Dominican residents in rent controlled apartments so that they can gentrify the building that is still undeniably in a high crime neighborhood where white people will find more affordable places to live and work in Manhattan. I, of course, read the audio book and cannot tell you the name of the company, so you get to hear or read the joke for yourself.

We, the outsiders to this conversation can see the times that Cara has to come to terms with having done something wrong and her efforts to justify it, because she knows she is fundamentally a good woman. Change comes slowly to Cara. But her humanity and love forces her to see her errors and to make amends, to do the work and to change and embrace change. She also knows what she can do and believes in herself and is proud of her strengths. She can speak English fluently, but if a job requires talking on the phone it will not work because she cannot understand English speaking people on the phone. She cannot take a job with a one hour commute because of the people she takes care of every day. She cannot have an in home daycare because she does not believe in behavior management that never involves the right to use at least a whack across the legs. But she is willing to try new things and learn about other ways of looking at the world. It just takes her some time.

Most of us have probably seen Cara in the store or standing at the bus stop or working as a house cleaner but few in my position in life can know Cara, the human being, the remarkable force, the sympathetic woman. Cruz opens the window and lets me peek in and meet this smart, complex character with a huge heart and a full life we can only wish for. I want to eat at her house. I want to be someone she cares about. I want to learn about her culture. I want her son to forgive her. This book is poignant, loving, funny, all that life should be. Read it. Better yet: Listen to it.

Before reading this book, I had only known cancer of the breast as "breast cancer" and nothing more. I had never heard of Triple Negative Breast Cancer (TNBC) until now. TNBC is a type of breast cancer that lacks receptors for the estrogen (ER) and progesterone (PR) hormones as well as for the human epidermal growth factor receptors (Her2/neu)--meaning all the receptors are negative.

The author is a TNBC survivor and she wrote this book to help others understand this disease. Throughout this text she not only educates her readers but makes the story personal by interweaving her experience and those of a few other breast cancer survivors into the stories.

These are some of the major positives of this book:

- She discusses how age, race, diet, genetic code, chemicals in products we use, etc. play a part in this disease.

- Although this is mostly about TNBC, she discusses the various terminology associated with cancer such as clear margins, lumpectomy, mastectomy, primary tumor, nodes, distant metastasis, poorly differentiated, histologic type such as ductal or lobular, etc.

- She discusses various treatment options and why certain treatments work better than others. For instance Tamoxifen is not for TNBC because it's a drug that blocks the effects of estrogen and with TNBC estrogen is not the problem. In her case brachytherapy, where radiated seeds are implanted in the breast, might have been an option but because none of her doctors mentioned this treatment she became ineligible by the time she inquired as this is generally used early in the postoperative period.

- She provides websites to consult for further information.

- She provides an annotated copy of her pathology report in the Appendix to demonstrate how such a report is interpreted.

- There's also a useful but brief glossary at the end of the book.

Although this book is easy to read, I found it was packed with so much information that I forgot things as soon as I moved on to the next chapter. I had wanted to consult the index but one was not provided with this pre-release version; however, there is a page reference to it in the table of contents for the released version. One caveat is that the treatment information provided is excellent but a book like this will have to be updated frequently since treatments are ever changing.

Overall "Surviving Triple Negative Breast Cancer" is superb and covers many facets of breast cancer with TNBC being the focus. The author also makes this story a very personal one.

After spending around six months scouring various digital camera reviews online and through magazines, I finally decided on the Canon Powershot A95 5 Megapixel camera as offering the perfect marriage of power and portability. My first digital camera, I bought it as a going-away present for myself, since I was spending the summer living and working in Spain and knew that I needed a camera that could keep up with my travels.

It was a snap to take out and set up, and intuitive enough that a couple of cursory glances at the Quick Start guide had me well on my way to pointing and shooting. The camera comes with a USB cable, several software programs, a 16 MB Compact Flash card (of course, you'll want to invest in more memory as soon as possible - with the highest-resolution photos, consider a 512 MB or larger card), batteries, and a wrist strap.

I would rate the camera as mid-sized. It is not wafer-thin, but neither is it absurdly bulky or heavy. For most of my traveling around Spain, I simply slipped it into its bubble wrap and into a soft fabric bag, where it fit comfortably in my purse. The design is comfortable to shoot with over long periods, and I found the layout of the buttons to be intuitive. Less is more: there are few external buttons (shutter, on/off, menu and related buttons), and most controls are carried out through the on-screen menus. The flip-out LCD screen is one reason I decided on this Canon over others in the PowerShot line; it makes previewing photos a snap, and can be swiveled 180 degrees.

The photo quality (I kept it on large superfine) is astonishing: clear, sharp, vibrant photos (check out some of my uploaded photos using the Canon A95) in true-to-life tones with minute detailing. There are various shooting modes, including manual, macro, panoramic (with Stitch Assist software), nighttime, slow shutter, and more, and a movie mode that captures brief (jerky) videos with tinny sound. This isn't a camcorder, so I wasn't surprised that video quality wasn't better, since I bought this primarily for photos.

You will also want to invest in a few basic accessories: rechargeable NiCad batteries and a rapid charger, a sturdy case, and a bigger memory card, for starters. Although the included software is capable enough to get the job done, consider upgrading to Adobe Photoshop Elements (around $90), or if you're a pro, Adobe PhotoShop CS 2 (several hundred dollars). An excellent first camera with plenty of power and a reliable name.

My interest in vegan cooking started because of a friend of mine who adopted a vegan lifestyle for health reasons. I have learned quite a bit about the subject through him, and I look for ideas and recipes with him in mind. The one issue I have had with vegan cooking is that some substitutes for non-vegan ingredients (for example, cheese) are unappetizing at best. This book doesn’t rely on some of the more unusual substitutes and is a very good collection. On top of that, it is full of beautiful pictures.

It’s hard to classify the chapters in a way that is easy to describe. They’re not broken up into topics like “cakes”, “cookies”, and other typical dessert types as you’d expect. Instead, the author organizes them into more purpose-driven categories like “breakfast”, “cafe-style desserts”, “snacks” and “shareables”. There’s certainly nothing wrong with that and finding a recipe isn’t hard due to the well-made table of contents and the index, but it is a slightly unusual organization that will take some time to get used to.

So, I dove into the recipes expecting to find really odd ingredients that I would never buy. I was pleasantly surprised and found things that I can get at my local grocery without having to order online or go to a specialty store. One of the main substitutions that is prevalent in many recipes is “plant-based milk”, such as soy or almond. We always have a carton of almond milk in the refrigerator so this is an easy substitution. Dates are used in some recipes, and chia seeds show up in a few recipes as well. There are a few recipes here and there that call for more unusual ingredients but they are not the norm.

What’s interesting is something else that I discovered. The author shies away from refined sugars and uses maple syrup and similar sweeteners. That alone is a huge plus if you are concerned about highly refined and processed foods in your diet. This is not just a vegan collection for the sake of being vegan, but the emphasis is more on healthy, unrefined ingredients that are just better for you. Had this book not been marketed as a vegan book and instead was marketed as a dessert book using only wholesome, less-refined ingredients, I may not have realized immediately that this is a vegan cookbook.

Some of the recipes are everyday types of foods that you’d expect a home baker to put together, but some are more fancy and will require an investment in time and effort. The author explains that she was once a bakery owner and the types of cakes she lists within this book are evidence of that.

Through the whole book are lots and lots of pictures – gorgeous, full-color pictures that really put the desserts on display. Every recipe has at least one picture. It is said that you eat with your eyes first; this book definitely understands that!

This is not simply a collection of vegan dessert recipes. This goes a little deeper and is a wholesome, healthier foods collection of recipes. If you’re a vegan looking for dessert recipes, or if you just want to avoid highly refined ingredients and still have amazing desserts, give this collection a close look.

PAST TENSE: A JACK REACHER NOVEL solves a mystery surrounding Jack’s parentage--who, exactly, was Jack’s father, a guy who could never remember his birthday? Reacher fans will want to read this novel to find out. But otherwise, except for the dramatic ending scenes, the novel is just plain boring.

In the novel, Jack starts to hitchhike from the East Coast to San Diego, but takes a side trip to Laconia. NH, his father’s birthplace. He visits various public records offices, and gets a lot of help from the locals when dad Stan Reacher doesn't show up right away in the town’s 80-year-old census records.

At the same time, a young Canadian couple has car trouble, and ends up at a remote motel near Laconia. They can’t leave, because the weird motel owners keep making excuses for not calling a mechanic or driving them to town to get a tow truck. Eventually the couple finds themselves imprisoned, because the motel owners have secret plans for them.

SPOILER ALERT: Naturally the two plotlines--Jack’s search for his roots, and the couple’s predicament--merge, but only in a superficial way. The couple’s plotline is basically “Psycho" meets “The Most Dangerous Game", and it isn’t even close to the quality of either one. The motel owners’ intentions are easily guessed, long before the reveal.

This novel is the latest in the long, popular Jack Reacher series, and it works fine as a standalone. It’s well-written, but, as previously mentioned, darned boring.

The book is excellent in showing some major things we kind of take for granted, but really shouldn't, because to come up with dramatic advances in science or in understanding, we have a better chance when pondering these challenges.

There are some things I will never think in quite the same way after reading this book, like:

1. The universe is expanding, but doing so at an ever faster rate. Therefore, we should be ready to alter current science, like our understanding of gravity. The author presents the concepts of dark energy (causing the ever faster expansion) and dark matter (affecting the shape, size and spin of galaxies). Plus, that can lead us to question whether scientific constants, are actually constant or might vary somewhat over millions or billions of years. Then, there is cold fusion and we still can't say it isn't possible.

2. As for 'Life', we still don't know how it began. NASA once claimed they had found life on Mars, through the Viking exploration, but then not sure. In 1977, we received a radio signal from space, and still not sure if it was or wasn't some alien communication. The best hope for some signal would likely be some fundamental mathematical code or a laser beam.
Maybe a virus was the first form of life. There are some indications that this is possible.

3. As for 'Aging' and 'Death', some fish, amphibians and reptiles don't seem to age. Some organisms don't appear to die. There is some thought that death was only introduced to protect against damaged DNA being passed on, so maybe by tinkering with our DNA we can extend life and the vibrancy of life.

4. Why 'Sex', since many living things reproduce assexually? Maybe to purge deleterious mutations or evolve to get rid of parasites and parasites evolve to always be able to find a home. Plus, since female animals don't always select the strongest or most dominant male, maybe something else at work, like what is in the best interest of the whole group. Mathematical Game Theory does seem to indicate that the best solution is when most, in a group, are optimally happy. So, is the reason for sex mathematically based? Interesting.

5. As for 'Free Will', do we really have it? There are some scientific studies which show our actual actions can precede the mind's actual awareness of wanting to start the action. It is noted that most psychological disorders involve people who try to exert maybe too much control over their life. Maybe a better road to sanity is acknowledging we aren't in control. Anyway, it does seem likely we have a lot less free will than we think we have.

6. The 'Placebo Effect' does seem to work, like the drug, Valium, doesn't seem to work unless the patient knows he/she is taking it. But, why the placebo affect works, we still don't know.

7. Homeopathy does seem to work beyond what might be attributed to the placebo effect. But, why? We don't know.

Anyway, this book is really great at making a reader just think a little deeper about some pretty important things.

Though I enjoy reading, it is unusual for me to find a book that interests me enough to burn through the entire thing in less than 24 hours. "Confessions of a Contractor" is one of those rare books that, once I delved into it, I could not put it down until I had digested every page and finished it.

It reads somewhat like a memoir, though it is a work of fiction. The premise is that of a home renovation specialist that has found his niche working on the homes of wealthy women in the Los Angeles area, and though he has a code of conduct he gets involved a bit too deeply with a couple of his clients. The result is a fast-moving account of the subsequent adventure that consumes his summer, bringing tension to other relationships in his life and ultimately helps him to solidify himself in terms of who he is and where he's going.

The author uses a lot of witty humor through the whole book, keeping the reader engaged with not only the base storyline but also with several laughs sprinkled in. It's a fine balance between serious moods and humorous anecdotes.

One paragraph in particular made me howl: "Dancing is great exercise. So is being chased by a mountain lion, except when you're being chased by a mountain lion you're not surrounded by mirrors, looking at yourself being chased by a mountain lion."

Even if you are not into home renovation and construction, "Confessions of a Contractor" presents a tale that will both entertain and engage. This is a book I will likely read again.

In August 1992, a lone, unidentified man was found starved to death inside an abandoned bus, miles from the nearest road, deep in the Alaskan bush. This spawned a small media blitz that eventually identified the man as Christopher McCandless. However this left a bigger mystery of who Christopher McCandless was.

For those who are familiar with Jon Krakauer's Into Thin Air, this is a different book from the start. Into Thin Air was a white-knuckled ride with Krakauer as he attempts to survive Everest. This book is more of a subtle mystery as Krakauer tries to piece together the evidence of the months that led up to the discovery of McCandless' body. The tragedy of his death is established but the suspense is in discovering who Christopher was.

What Krakauer does in this book is fill in the picture by talking to the people who encountered Christopher in his last months. The image that comes out is not a genius or a messiah, but an intelligent young man who is at odds with the society he was raised in. And at the same time Krakauer describes a tribe of men who just don't seem to fit into our society and look for life on the fringes and beyond. The book is brilliant in capturing this spirit, I'm sure in large part because this spirit is shared by the author.

It's not an action adventure like Into Thin Air, but it is just as hard to put down. If you haven't read this one, do yourself and favor and get a copy. Mine is well dog-eared from being passed around.

This is a book of knitting patterns (by well-known knitting author Lucinda Guy). It is not a book about knitting history or the ethnic knitting designs and traditions of Scandinavia, Iceland, and the Shetland Isles.

The cover photo ("Pia Laceweight Pullover") is a good example of the kind of patterns included. The patterns are for "simplified" Scandinavian, Icelandic, and Norwegian garments, in that the designer uses traditional ethnic motifs, designs, and techniques, but makes the garments themselves a little bit easier and faster to knit by choosing less-fine yarns and by limiting the amount of patterning on each garment.

For example, the "Unnur Icelandic Pullover", which uses the classic Icelandic rose motif around the yoke and above the ribbing, looks traditional but lacks fine patterning detail--because the yarn is Lopi and the gauge is 14 stitches and 18 rows to 4 inches.

As another example, the "Effie Fair Isle Pullover" has patterning detail, because the sweater is knit at 30 stitches and 34 rows to 4 inches--but the traditional shifting of background colors beneath the horizontal Fair Isle motifs is kept to a minimum, meaning fewer ends to weave in but a final fabric that is less interesting.

As a third example, the "Crowning Glory Cobweb Shawl", which is knit with cobweb lace yarn at a daunting gauge of 42 stitches and 50 rows to 4 inches, uses three somewhat challenging Shetland lace patterns--but arranges them in horizontal sections on a stole, so that the project is far simpler to knit than a traditional Shetland lace wrap or shawl that combines several lace patterns.

However, there is nothing wrong with a book of "simplified" patterns, if the garments produced by the patterns are attractive and wearable! In fact, there are several patterns that I like quite well, and that justified my purchase (at a brick-and-mortar bookstore) of the book:

(1) "Moth", a pattern for a short-sleeved top knit that uses Jamieson & Smith's shetland wool in dark brown, dark gray, medium gray, light gray, and cream, and produces an intriguing "shaded squares" fabric with a sort of optical effect. (2) "Hulda", a pattern for a pullover with bold but feathered stripes that start wide at the garment hem and narrow until they end just below the armhole. (3) "Ennid", a pattern for a triangular garter-stitch shawl with a simple but interesting little textured edging, done in laceweight yarn and perfect for mindless television knitting. (4) "Annemor", a pullover using a classic Norwegian star or snowflake pattern across the chest, and using traditional "lice" dots on the sweater body. (5) "Iliv", a pattern for elaborately patterned socks using dancing figures, eight-leaf roses, lice stitch, a decorative cuff, and a star toe. (6) "Ola", a pattern for a white placket pullover with minimalist embroidered cross-stitch patterning around the placket and at the tops of the sleeves.

In all, this is a very nice book, which should serve as a great introduction to knitting Scandinavian, Icelandic, and Shetland garments, and which may inspire some knitters to tackle more complicated, more traditional "northern knitting" garments in the future. The book is published by Interweave Press, which means that it has beautiful photos, professional layouts, charts, and well-written patterns. Also, should the patterns turn out to have errors, the publisher will undoubtedly publish corrections on its web site.

However, do take a minute to use Amazon's "Look Inside This Book" feature before you buy--just to make sure that you like at least some of the patterns well enough to want to knit them. Pattern photos are also available on the publisher's web site.

I recently ate dinner at a tiny Italian restaurant in San Francisco. Highly recommended by local residents, the place had a simple charm that was at the same time both inviting and slightly foreign. I ordered the roasted chicken with potatoes, and marveled at how delicious the food was. There was no fancy sauce over the chicken or even an extravagant garnish to dress the plate. Just roasted chicken with a hint of rosemary, and soft, delectable potatoes on the side. I could taste the purity of the food, and was left utterly satisfied, without the feeling of gluttony or eater's remorse.

I make the analogy of food with this website, and so I extend the analogy of this wonderful meal to my review of Kat Ricker's book of poems and short stories, Something Familiar. There is certainly something in this book for everyone - a bit of fantasy, a sample of memory, quiet humor, and even a story "based on actual hearsay." It is a small, simple, appealing, rich, wonderfully executed collection of writing.

The title is entirely appropriate, for what I see as two distinct reasons. On one hand, I believe readers will find something in the stories and poems that is familiar to themselves. In "Ray's Foul Ball," I saw myself as a parent in the juxtaposition of Ray's own individual dreams versus his selfless love for his daughter. In "Remembering Mrs. Little," I saw myself on Mrs. Little's bed, pouring out her tin of buttons (only, in my memory, they are my grandmother's buttons, passed down through generations). And even in the fantastical "The Secret of Lara Lee," I know what it's like to have "something click" and to understand Lara Lee's declaration "Isn't it good just to be!"

The other incarnation of the title is the way in which many of Ricker's characters, when faced with the circumstances of a changing life, retreat to something familiar in their own lives, or in their past. Oftentimes, you can even see it in their eyes. In "Change of Venue," the artisan, faced with harsh financial realities, must turn to different pursuits, and yet you know the "truth - eyes sparkled" of where he would rather be. Old Michael's bent form is transformed in "Walnut Harvest in Newberg," as he remembers his fine accomplishments and "his eyes dawned" through the recollection. And despite Mattie's confused behavior in "Mattie's Orchids," something of her former self slips through when "from the blankets, she turns and winks at you, twinkle of mischief in her eye."

The flowing theme throughout this book of "something familiar" is rounded out by some wonderful phrasing in the poems and stories. In fact, in some cases as I was reading, the title could have just as easily have been something *unexpected,* as Ricker puts images together in beautiful new forms. There are also moments of humor that gratefully caught me off guard. I really enjoyed this smooth book, served up with little flair, relying instead on its own, unpolished beauty to deliver an exceptional reading experience.

Sometimes it is necessary to take a picture of something on a solid background, often white for contrast but also sometimes black for lighter-colored objects. This is especially true when you are creating promotional materials and you want the item in question to stand out in the picture. It’s not always easy to get that kind of background. A light box is a good way to accomplish this. The Purebox is one such light box and I have had the pleasure of working with it for the past week. This is my very first light box so I have been learning as I go.

The whole thing comes in a gray padded fiber sleeve that is about the size of a padded envelope. I was a little surprised at first when I opened the package and this flat cloth envelope was all that I found. Once I opened everything up and started assembling the Purebox it made sense. The sleeve does provide some protection and it is also compact enough that it can travel fairly easily, though I would discourage packing it in luggage. The box itself is made of white vinyl.

When unfolding the box it is fairly straightforward to see how the box assembles. There are lengths of Velcro along the edges of the tabs that hold the box together and retain its shape. Itf you line these up wrong it results in a box that is very unstable and does not stand up right. When finished, the whole box is approximately 12"x”12"x12".

The top of the box has a very bright ring of LED lights, so bright that I was able to illuminate my basement just with the box alone. They cast an almost clinical light that borders on harsh and it makes the entire box (which is opaque) glow.

Included with the box are two long, wide strips of plastic, one white and the other black. By placing these against the back of the box, it is possible to get the solid-colored background desired. It occurred to me that there is no reason that a different color plastic sheet couldn’t be used to make even more color backgrounds, like light blue, pale yellow and more. It would be easy enough to make such a background from construction paper in a pinch.

This is a box suitable for very small items, such as a pair of glasses, a toy car or a small computer peripheral such as a mouse. In testing I photographed several small items such as batteries, my trackball, a small rock and the like. I used the white insert and I noticed that there is very little shadow at all, though if you look hard enough for it you can see shadows on taller items.

I found one thing about this box that gave me a little concern until I spoke to the vendor about it. I had trouble with the sides of the box staying open properly, and as a result I was constantly fiddling with the sides to keep them open. I finally tried a small paperclip on the sides in the upper corners and that seemed to resolve the issue. A better solution will be to add a little more Velcro, a suggestion I offered to the vendor. This is not a huge problem as I think I could resolve it by opening the box and forcing the crease in the sides to open more so they would press against the sides a little more tightly, and it is easy enough to correct if it appears.

This is a nice photo white box for someone who needs a pure, clean background for capturing images of small items. The light is very bright and with changeable backgrounds one can capture the image just as it’s envisioned. I am pleased with this box and I will be working with it often if not daily.

I spend a lot of time in the kitchen and I often find myself tracking down recipes that can be prepared relatively quickly. I also keep watch for healthy recipes that will feed my family. This cookbook seemed like a good bet, and so far I am not unhappy with it.

The subtitle of the book is "100 Simple and Healthy Recipes to Enjoy Together". I think making this a subtitle is a bit of a mistake, in that the healthy aspect of this collection is easily overlooked. If I was looking specifically for a book on healthy cooking, I might miss this one. Though that seems like a nitpick, it's a consideration.

The very first chapter of the book lays down that this is a collection of recipes that can be prepared quickly. I have had some limited success with these types of recipes and generally allocate 45-60 minutes, though so far this collection has been fairly on point. This does assume you work efficiently.

The recipes are divided up into 8 other chapters: ""Breakfast", "Bites and Small Plates", "Salads, Wraps, and Sandwiches", "Vegetarian Entrees", "Poultry and Seafood Entrees", "Beef and Pork Entrees", "Simple Sides", and finally "Speedy Sweets". The breakdown is one of the more logical that I've seen in a while - often it is a loose mix of chapters with lots of recipes that can fit into more than one. The author did a good job of laying this one out.

In digging through the recipes, many call for low-sodium or low-sugar ingredients. They do not shy away from canned vegetables and other ingredients that have been partially processed, but the emphasis seems to be on lower sodium, lower fat and lower sugar. That's a decent combination.

The recipes I have tried have turned out well. I haven't made many yet, but I have several more earmarked.

Overall I am not unhappy with this cookbook. My main criticism is a marketing issue - it should emphasize the healthy aspects of the recipes more - but it's a good book that delivers on the promise of quick, healthy recipes.

I am always looking for good Bibles and I was very interested in the Once a Day Bible which is a Bible designed to be read in a year. Though not a perfect Bible I think it comes fairly close.

I will start with the one major negative I have with this Bible - the typeface is small. It is small enough that people with poor vision or that otherwise need a little assistance to read will struggle with the small font used in this Bible. I have decent vision and I find the typeface to be a little too small for my tastes. There is a note on the spine that says "Standard Print" which suggests that there may be a larger print edition available - if so I would more likely use that version instead.

Otherwise, I have little about with to complain when it comes to this Bible. It is divided up into daily readings, going back and forth between Old and New Testaments. The selections for each day end with a "Daily Reflection" summary that make good springboards for prayer after reading. The NIV translation is very readable and is suitable for most readers which makes this Bible even more effective.

It is important to remember that the format disqualifies this Bible from being a typical study Bible but this should not come as a surprise at all. This isn't marketed as a study Bible but as a reading Bible. There is no easy way to track down a particular verse nor are there bunches of study helps. This is straight Scripture but the chapters in the Bible are divided up according to days and there are places where chapters are divided across days. This is not a fault but it is a point to keep in mind.

If you are looking for a study Bible that will help you dig deeply into the Word and gain a better understanding of some of the more subtle points of Scripture, this is the wrong Bible for you. If you are looking instead for a reading Bible that gives you a good reading plan, though, this very well may be exactly what you're seeking. The print is a little small in the standard print edition but it's not unreadable and it will definitely help you work through the Bible in a measurable time frame.

I love pasta dishes and I wanted to find a book that gave strong guidance on how to actually make the pasta itself, not just provide a series of recipes on how to use pasta in dishes. After doing a good bit of research I selected Making Artisan Pasta with high expectations. This book has not disappointed me.

Many pasta books talk about making a couple of different types of pasta and then present a long list of sauce recipes, recipes for prepared pasta dishes like lasagna, the odd side salad and more. This book is not at all like that - this is a book just about pasta and nothing more. Do not look to this book if you want a recipe for a good tomato sauce or cream sauce as you won’t find it here. Furthermore, do not look to this book if all you want is a quick recipe on making egg pasta. This book goes into very deep detail on the process of making pasta doughs and describes how to choose ingredients, how to handle the doughs as you work the ingredients together, how to shape and press the different types of pasta and so much more. This is more of an in-depth course on the art of making pasta. It even goes into detail on flour grades, grinding your own wheat berries and more.

To give you an idea of what to expect with this book, it presents making egg pasta dough - three times. It presents making the dough by hand, with a stand mixer and with a food processor. Each recipe is a full two pages and is presented with multiple full-color photographs describing each stage of the process. The discussion of each recipe is fairly exhaustive and tries to answer the large majority of questions that arise.

Every single recipe in this book is accompanied by multiple full-color photographs and full discussion on the dough being presented. Not only is this book very thorough but it’s also beautiful. I enjoy leafing through the book just for the scenery as I do for finding recipes and getting ideas.

My favorite recipe in the book [so far] is potato gnocchi. I have a number of other recipes earmarked for trying out but gnocchi is a favorite of mine and this recipe is better than average in my opinion.

I wanted a book that was just about making pasta. I have plenty of other books that describe making spaghetti sauce and lasagna but precious few that describe in detail how to make more than just egg pasta. This book is exactly what I wanted and I could not be happier with it. If you want a good book on actually making pasta, look no further than this book.

I have several of the Jamisons’ other cookbooks (my favorite among them being A Real American Breakfast) and all of them up to this point have followed a very distinct and successful formula - lots of recipes and formulas intermingled with tips and stories that make the overall book a useful and fun read. This book does follow that pattern, though to a smaller degree. This is a good book on grilling and it does accomplish the goal of gathering many good recipes together into one place in a concise and useful “short list” collection.

It should be clear, just from the title, that this is not an exhaustive collection of recipes. It can almost be viewed as a “best of” collection, though that is not entirely accurate as many of the recipes and formulas in this cookbook are not in the authors’ other books. If you’re looking for a complete grilling book, this is not the title you want.

The book starts off early with an explanation of why there are just 100 recipes in the collection, and this explanation does make some sense - this equates to an average of about two meals per week done on the grill in the span of a year and this seems like a reasonable amount for an avid griller. I personally would like more choices but that’s just me.

This book covers the spectrum of foods that can be cooked on a grill - appetizers, grilled pizza, burgers & hot dogs, meats, seafood, vegetables and desserts. There is a bit of overlap between some of the chapters (seafood in the appetizers, for example) which is to be expected but for the most part the recipes are ordered logically.

As always, the results at the grill are excellent. So far I have found no dud recipes in this collection.

In previous works the authors included a lot of anecdotes, stories and helpful tips that were sprinkled all through the pages. This is the case with this book as well. There are some helpful hints that accompany certain recipes and sections and there are a few stories within, though I cannot help but notice that these are markedly fewer than in previous works. This is mildly disappointing to me, though anyone who is not familiar with some of the authors’ previous collections will not really know.

100 Grilling Recipes You Can’t Live Without is a good cookbook for grilled food and it is sure to have recipes that will become lasting favorites in the house. It is not as exhaustive as some other collections available but the quality is high. If you are looking for a book on grilling that includes a better-than-average collection of recipes, this is a title worth owning.

I'll read anything that Patrick Lee publishes, because his novels (e.g., [[ASIN:0061584452 The Breach]]) are all guaranteed page-turners, with intricate plots filled with fascinating future technology (imaginary, at least for now). Lee's latest mystery/thriller, SIGNAL, does not disappoint.

Sam Dryden (introduced in [[ASIN:1250030730 Runner]]) is a highly skilled, retired Special Forces operative. When an old colleague (Claire) calls in the middle of the night, desperately asking him to meet her asap at an isolated location in California's Mojave Desert, he unquestioningly responds. Sam and Claire are able to thwart a horrible crime, because Claire possesses a bleeding-edge, high-tech machine that lets her see into the future. But some very bad people (The Group) who also have access to Claire's technology, have also looked into the future and have sent gunmen to change that future (and secure the technology for themselves alone) by recovering Claire's machine in the present. Sam and Claire are exposed to a sniper attack that nearly kills both of them outright.

Once again, Sam is on the run from unknown people who are equipped with virtually unlimited political, financial, and technical resources. Separated from Claire, Sam must figure out mostly on his own who the players are, and must ensure that The Group is unable to achieve its objectives. The physics of Claire's high-tech machine are convincingly explained, and the time-travel paradox of changing the future by changing the past is handled well in a new and unorthodox fashion.

SIGNAL has a fast-moving plot that is filled with edge-of-the-seat action, that takes many unexpected turns. The characters are memorable (Sam, Claire, Marnie, Curtis, etc.), and the dialogue is excellent. This is an extremely well-written mystery/thriller that also works as a series standalone. Readers who like both thrillers and science fiction should enjoy this novel as much as I did.

So first of all, I must confess that I am from the town of Lovelock NV and have lived here my whole life. I am a native here, by actually being born in this little town. Did she talk to Hospital staff, school employees, homemakers, miners, Paiutes  etc? Or just the bar clientele, coffee shop and restaurant customers? Nonetheless, this book is a good read, and is fun to read for those of us fortunate enough to live here. Yes, some of us feel fortunate to be able to live here. We are capable of leaving if we so choose to. Like the author said, we can always leave. Some of us find living away from the rat race of big city life very comforting and peaceful. The mystery was well worth the wait while developing the characters in a way the reader could try and understand. Lovelock isn’t for everyone, and it’s really gone down hill from it’s Boom days, but there are still so many good and decent people living here that I hope the people reading about Lovelock don’t forget to remember, this is a fictional story. I have a Fuji X-T3 and I have not shied away from third-party lenses at all. I have been looking for good wide-angle lenses and I have been aware of TTArtisan for a while. I was curious how well this lens would perform and I decided to take a chance on it. So far I am very pleased with it though I am still working with it and learning that it can do.

This lens is a brick! Right out of the box I was startled at the overall weight. It has a lot of glass in it, but it also is all metal - very little (if any) plastic. Even the front lens cap is metal. In spite of the price, this is a solid little lens.

It is probably the tightest fit lens I have used. It requires a little pressure to get it to click into place and to remove it later when mounting on the camera body. I was a little concerned at first, thinking I could potentially damage the camera. However, it does fit and does not harm the camera in spite of how tightly it fits.

Optical quality seems to be good, though that varies a little with the aperture setting. At the widest settings (and f/1.4 in particular) there is a little softness in the corners and a slight vignetting. As the aperture is closed more the image gets sharper at the edges. This is not unusual or unexpected for wide-angle large-aperture lenses, and it is actually slightly better than I was expecting.

I have not yet had a chance to get out and determine the coma with this lens. I am waiting for a clear night so I can get a starry sky shot with the aperture wide open, which will highlight not only the coma but also the chromatic characteristics. If it is particularly bad I will come back and update.

As a portrait or landscape lens this one works very well. Initial exposures have worked out well, but I am still learning what this lens can do.

Are there better wide-angle lenses out there? Sure - and they cost a lot more too. For the price this lens is far better than expected and I am looking forward to working with it more. It is good enough that I am staring to look at other TTArtisan offerings.

This is my first exposure to Panasonic Active Noise Canceling (ANC) headphones. This particular model is very inexpensive relative to most ANC phones on the market, and unfortunately the low price is justified. These phones fall short in a couple of important areas.

First and foremost, these are ANC phones and the ANC function does indeed work. That said, the degree to which it works is in line with the pricing. I have a very specific fan in the house that I use as a benchmark, as most ANC phones are able to nearly completely wipe out the white noise that this fan generates when on the lowest speed setting. The Panasonic phones kill a good bit of the fan noise but allow more noise than almost every other ANC set I have tried. In the office I tried these phones in an area serviced by two large air handlers that generate a lot of noise and these headphones did remarkably well though still not as well as most other phones I have tried in the same environment. Now, when compared to the likes of Bose, Panasonic does a very poor job but then again they cost maybe 15% of what Bose costs. When considering this price differential the Panasonic phones do a decent job with their ANC which should be acceptable by most for traveling.

One area where these phones fail, though, is in build quality. These headphones are extremely lightweight and they feel very flimsy and fragile. These are not the headphones to take when traveling frequently. To add insult to injury, they come with a cloth carry bag which offers absolutely no protection at all beyond serving as a dust cover.

Worse, though, is the miserable sound quality. I don't know if my specific headset is the problem but while I have a decent full range of sound, everything across the spectrum sounds slightly tinny and hollow. I was encouraged that Panasonic does not overdrive the bass as many manufacturers tend to do and instead delivers a fairly balanced spectrum, but this does not make up for the poor quality of sound. As these are inexpensive headphones I would never expect them to be audiophile quality, but the sound should absolutely be much better than it is.

I was encouraged to see that Panasonic includes a 2-prong adapter in the package, but then they omit the 1/4" adapter which is something I actually use.

Panasonic has made a very inexpensive ANC headphone and unfortunately the low cost is justified. While the ANC capabilities are within reason for the price range, the sound quality and build quality are severely lacking. If looking for ANC phones for the purpose of using the ANC function, and keeping costs low is important, then these phones may fill that need acceptably. However, if sound quality is in any way important, these are the wrong phones and will sorely disappoint.

It has taken me over three weeks to read this very large guide. The text covers many topics in an easy-to-read format that every employee should be aware of with regard to their rights in the workplace. The topics range from OSHA rules, tobacco smoke in the workplace, 401K and pension plans, privacy rights, pregnancy discrimination, medical insurance and COBRA, whistleblower laws, etc., etc.

There are some interesting case studies that the author uses to make a point. For instance in one case study a company denied workers the use of toilet facilities. Although the employer was following the letter of the law (providing enough facilities but not letting them use it) OSHA's official ruling on the matter stated "Toilets that employees are not allowed to use for extended periods cannot be said to be 'available' to those employees."

The author also provides a list of laws by topic for each state (where applicable) which you can research further.

One thing I felt lacking in the book is an explanation of whether employees have different rights depending on living in one state and working in another. I assume the law associated with the state they work in applies, but I am wondering if there are exceptions to this.

Overall, this guide is good for someone who is unfamiliar with their employee rights. Many of the items covered will be familiar to those who have been in the workforce a while and, except for some nuances of the law, this book will offer just a little bit more knowledge. What I've learned more than anything else is that in many cases you'll need to get a lawyer to protect your rights.

I have been baking bread for my family for over 20 years and I have amassed a good collection of cookbooks on the subject of bread and bread baking. I was interested in this book, with the thought of making more holiday breads (such as stollen, for example). This book delivers and is filled with all kinds of bread recipes for special occasions, but it definitely lacks some pictures that would make it even better.

One of the things I learned a while back is that measuring ingredients by mass instead of volume is important for getting very consistent results in bread baking. Many cookbooks out there have taken the approach of having measures by mass and by volume together, and this cookbook takes that approach which is a good thing. This makes this book more accessible for bakers of different skill levels or have different thoughts on measures. Most recipes in this book follow this format carefully, resorting to only volume measures when it would otherwise be impractical to weigh ingredients (such as 1/8 teaspoon dry measures).

The author presents a good bit of material up front on bread basics as well as some more advanced topics. This includes care and feeding of sourdough starters, which is a topic I did not expect in a general collection. Often, sourdough is covered either separately as a primary topic or in a dedicated work. It’s not unwelcome here at all and is very much relevant – many of the traditional breads presented are typically made with such starters.

The collection is broken up by seasons – Spring, Summer, Fall and Winter, with a final chapter on special occasion breads. The seasonal breads should make sense to most – Christmas stollen, Easter breads, etc. The special occasion breads are suitable for when having special company or celebrating special events, and these generally do not really fit into the other chapters. The categorization is well-defined and there isn’t much overlap which is unusual.

The one main improvement that this book could use is more pictures. There are a few full-color photographs in his book but not many, and as such there is likely going to be occasions when a good recipe is missed because it didn’t catch the attention of the reader. While adding more pictures would drive up the cost and expand the mass of this volume, it would be a big value add too.

This is a nice book on seasonal and special occasion breads that is well written and well organized, with a good selection of bread recipes. It’s a good choice if you’re looking for a broad collection of recipes that cover most occasions and offer some variety beyond typical loaf and artisan loaves.

Ok, I do think it is best in class (a narrowly defined class) but not the best general field guide out there. That bar still stands at [[ASIN:0679451226 The Sibley Guide to Birds]] which has painted illustrations rather than photographs that tend to work better for portraying idealized birds and page layout.

But this guide does stand heads and shoulders above the old [[ASIN:B000K0DPIO Audobon Bird Guide: Eastern Land Birds]] in photo quality as well as layout. Audobon's original attempt really showed just how hard it is to identify birds from photographs due to changes in lighting and feather contours (see kinglet images.) This was improved upon greatly with [[ASIN:0618574239 Kaufman Field Guide to Birds of North America]] Kaufman reattempted a photographic field guide by using a lot of retouching and computer work to make more idealized photographs and was easily the best until this book.

This book succeeds in the most part because the pool of available high quality photographs is much larger than it was when the Audobon series came out. Each species is well represented with striking images. You can never have too many reference books when trying to make a difficult identification and this would augment the Sibley guide very well. However we are still talking about three images to identify a Thayers Gull, where sibley can dedicate 6 or more to a gull species. Also there are family specific guides out there like [[ASIN:0122956400 Gulls: Guide to Identification]], [[ASIN:0618432949 The Shorebird Guide]], [[ASIN:069111644X A Photographic Guide to North American Raptors]] which this book cannot compete with, however it is surprisingly decent for covering these families.

Pros
Great high quality pictures
General design puts all information for a species on one page
Good species coverage
DVD of bird songs is a nice bonus (see caveats below)
Good additional reference for field identification
Size decent (approx the size of Sibley's, but does not fit in pocket)
High Quality construction

Cons
Photos make page design seem a little cluttered
Species information is pretty brief
range maps small somewhat confusing, somewhat optimistic in ranges.
DVD has limited species

Notes on the DVD

Much like this book in general, I would never pass on getting another reference, especially if it is kind of a bonus DVD of bird calls. But I was a little disappointed to find out that the 587 birds songs listed on the front was not 587 species, but only 587 clips of 138 major species. And it is a little strange what species they chose. It appears that they chose the most common species you would find in your backyard. This seems less helpful than choosing confusing sound alike species, or species that are most likely located by calls. It is odd that they don't cover all the epidonax flycatchers which are ID'ed by calls, or the call of the yellow billed cuckoo without the black billed. If you were hoping to learn bird calls from this DVD, think about getting [[ASIN:0618225900 Birding by Ear: Eastern and Central North America (Peterson Field Guides(R))]] or [[ASIN:1570424837 Stokes Field Guide to Bird Songs: Eastern Region (Stokes Field Guide to Bird Songs)]] for a more complete species list.

All in all, if you are getting one field guide get [[ASIN:0679451226 The Sibley Guide to Birds]], if you are getting just two, get this for your second, or if you are like me get this for your 23rd. It is a good but not perfect guide.

The most reliable and solid printer I have ever owned is a Canon Pixma i4500 which sits on my desk and is wired directly to my personal computer. It has been more dependable than any HP or Epson printer I have used and I have used and abused it for years. Because of my experience with my older Pixma, I had very high expectations of the MG5420. For printing, it performs quite well. For scanning, though, it is less than ideal.

Setup of this printer is absurdly easy. I did follow the printed directions, not because I felt like I did not understand the device but because I wanted to determine if the included instructions are useful or if they are somewhat off in their guidance. They took me step by step through configuration, but it could have been summarized as "plug it in, turn it on, follow the instructions on the screen".

This particular printer comes with a black pigment cartridge in addition to 4 color ink tanks. I like this configuration as it means I can print a lot more text pages.

Initial configuration, while straightforward, is lengthy. It takes about 10 minutes of calibration and alignment (during which time it makes all manner of odd noises) before it is ready to go to work. Once it finished configuring itself, I plugged it in to the USB port and Windows 7 loaded drivers from online and it's ready to go. So, if the system has Internet access, the installation media isn't even necessary.

I elected not to set up this printer on wireless, as it will be dedicated to a single machine and as such connected via USB. So, I can't really speak to it's configuration on a wireless LAN.

Print quality is very good. I selected a high-resolution photo and sent it to the printer, and the printer dutifully produced a borderless letter-sized picture with fine detail, even set on regular paper and normal print settings. Color reproduction was slightly dull, though, and I will have to retry with photo paper and photo settings. More astonishing, though, is the print speed - my photo emerged from the printer in roughly 20 seconds, making this one of the fastest color printers I have used for printing photos.

I then decided to scan an image with the printer. The scan was quick and painless. That said, the scan was very banded and the image was marginally acceptable. I tried another scan and got similar results - banding on the image and the overall quality was low. Other reviewers have had good success with the scanning, so I am hopeful that my particular unit is slightly faulty.

I tried using the copy feature using a text-only document and the copy was nearly indistinguishable from the original. Because the copy portion relies on scanning I was unsure if the copy would have the same banding issue - it did not. So, this tells me that in the capacity of a copier this unit is capable of decent OCR work.

My experience with this printer is mostly good. The photo printing and copying is good while the scanning of images leaves something to be desired. Overall, this is a decent printer for moderate use and is worth a look.

The premise of "Afterwards" by Rosamund Lupton is similar to that of "The Lovely Bones": a dead (or nearly dead) person communicates with others in an attempt to uncover a crime. In the case of "Afterwards," the crime is arson, and the beginning of the book is well done--fast-paced, interesting, and engaging. The main character rushes into a burning school to save her teenaged daughter. Both mother and daughter are severely injured in the fire, and their spirits communicate with one another as they lie in comas in the local hospital. Then minor characters (father, son) become involved as Mom tries to discover who set the fire and why.

After this superb beginning, this novel simply bogs down. It is too long in the middle, and there is far too much psychological analysis for my taste. Of course the reader wants to know underlying complexity of motivation, but too much is too much. Mother and daughter communicate, and parts of this section are confusing. It is occasionally difficult to know who is speaking. Mom finds out things she never knew about her family--surprise, surprise--and the incredible and undying love of a mother for her child is repeatedly reinforced.

In the end, the reader discovers who set the fire, and the answer is very unexpected. There are any number of likely suspects, and the motivations of each are explored, but most readers will not guess the identity of the arsonist.

To sum up, this was a good story, but not great. I notice that many other reviewers have mentioned Lupton's other book, "Sister." I plan to read this book to see if I can get a better handle on her storytelling. For now, count me in the ambivalent category.

I selected this title with the expectation of getting an introduction on game design. The title and description suggest that this is a book about designing games (strategy, behind the scenes architecture, etc.) and not a tome full of code and snippets. As it turns out, it is neither.

The book goes into various descriptions of what types of gameplay are out there in popular games, digging in right off the bat with Windows Solitaire and moving on to other games such as Fallout 3, Tetris and other hits. The author lays out not so much game design but playability concepts such as 1st-person shooting, drag-and-drop (such as card games), and other gaming ideas that have captivated audiences. This is true all the way through the book, and I found no instance where the author explains (even in general terms) HOW to implement these concepts.

From a designer's perspective this book will help to identify what kind of game will reach your target audience and will guide the decision process at a very high level. It is a far cry from a book about game design in the sense that it will not provide any guidance on how to get past the concept stage.

I give this book 3 stars based on the fact that it is well written and it does contain some interesting ideas on what kinds of games are out there and what general concepts in usability and playability exist. I cannot recommend this book as a reference for technical game development or design, however, because it really isn't that kind of book .

This is a clamp system that includes a couple of adapters for attaching cameras and accessories so that the camera can be held steady without having to set up a big, bulky tripod or having to hold the camera by hand. It comes with two clamps that can be connected via the ball joint adapter so that the system can convert to an anchor support for a pole as well (not the intended use, but practical nonetheless).

Included in the kit is a 1/4" adapter that connects to a standard camera mount (like my mirrorless), and an adapter for connecting a GoPro. It can be used directly with a cell phone, but it is not ideal for that and does require being creative with the clamps (not recommended); better is using the clamp to hold a selfie stick which in turn holds the camera.

The clamps hold tight as do the ball joints. It takes a little bit of fiddling but getting this set up exactly as desired is possible so that you can get the perfect angle. Further, the system can hold a little weight and has no trouble at all holding my mirrorless camera steady.

It seems to be made well and so far I have not had any issues with loose screws, stripped components, wobbly connectors (when properly tightened) or slipping grips. It's still early on in working with this system but so far I see no red flags.

I am happy with this clamp set-up and I will get some good use out of it. It's a practical solution when a tripod or other mount is not workable. It's not particularly expensive, either.

I ordered this book because the cover contains pictures of healthy ingredients that I am drawn to. I have not been diagnosed with Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) but am wondering if I have it after reading this, especially as it relates to bloating. This diet is suppose to "provide relief from bloating, abdominal pain or discomfort, constipation, and diarrhea in up to three out of four people with IBS."

FODMAP stands for fermentable, oligosaccharide, disaccharide, monosaccharide, and polyol which really describes a "group of rapidly fermenting carbohydrates" that are hard to digest. The idea behind the diet is to be on it for a while and then introduce hi-FODMAP ingredients into the mix to see which produce symptoms. It is not a diet to eat for life.

In the beginning chapters there is a list of low, moderate, and high FODMAP ingredients as well as a four-week meal plan. The recipe section starts a third into the book.

My purpose in ordering this book was to add another cookbook to my library from which I could make some healthy meals. I was correct about my assumption that there are a lot of healthy recipes within and in this regard this book is perfect for me. I do not mind that they are low-FODMAP. There are over 19 recipes I would try. There are 3 recipes I did try in less than 24 hours and they came out excellent. In addition, they were not time consuming to make as most recipes I have made from other books.

I made the Cranberry-Quinoa Salad (w/o the cranberry vinaigrette), the broccoli and cheese frittata, and the olive lover's hummus. My boyfriend ate the first two items with me and loved it as well. He was not around when I made the third. Although the hummus did not look good, the taste was exceptional.

There are only three disappointments I have with this book. First, I was extremely disappointed that the acronym FODMAP was not spelled out until Page 10.  Acronyms should always be spelled out during first use even if one is not likely to understand them.  Second, only the start of each chapter has pictures and no pictues accompany the recipes.  Third, there is some fluff in this book with shopping lists and pantry staples.

In summary, I love this cookbook for the healthy recipes. The three recipes I tried were extremely flavorful and easy to make from start to finish. I do not follow meal plans, so I cannot vouch if this plan works or not. However, for someone who wants to follow this plan, then be prepared to be dedicated.  The four-week meal plan may require you to make most (if not all) of the recipes in this book morning, noon, and night with two snacks. If this had many more pictures and spelled out FODMAP at the beginning, it would have received 5 stars from me.

In Charlaine Harris's seventh Sookie Stackhouse adventure All Together Dead, it's a blend of CSI, 24 and World Trade Center as Sookie is sent to a vampire summit in Rhodes. As a human telepath, she's expected to scan human minds for signs of dishonesty in business dealings. Sounds simple enough, but much is brewing at the summit; Sophie-Anne, the Queen of Louisiana, is recovering from the devastating economic impact of Hurricane Katrina on her state's economy. That, and having her new vampire husband the King of Arkansas murdered. Sophie-Anne will stand trial for his murder at the summit.

Sookie's ex-boyfriend Bill (also of a bloodsucking persuasion) is also at the summit, as is the handsome, ancient Viking Eric. Although Bill's out of the romantic picture, Eric and Sookie once again find time to exchange bodily fluids (in Sookie's case, drinking Eric's blood to gain a powerful edge). Sookie's new flame Quinn the weretiger is also working at the summit. Unlike Harris's previous Sookie books, there is precious little in the way of "fooling around," for which some readers will be grateful.

Instead, Sookie is wrapped up in several ongoing dramas at the summit, including a run-in with Fellowship of the Sun members. Fellowship of the Sun is an anti-vampire group that performs terrorist acts against vampires and their human associates, and Sookie's getting some bad, guilty vibes from werewolf-turned-vamp Jake Purifoy, who hates his new undead existence. Add to that that someone murdered the remaining vamps from Arkansas under Sookie's nose, a crude bomb was planted outside the Queen's hotel room, and several vamps (and people) turning up dead, and you have quite a mystery. A horrific event provides the wrenching climax, although references to 9/11 seemed unnecessarily overstated.

All Together Dead provides more action and interwoven plots than in the last several Southern Vampire novels, making it one of my favorites in the series. If you were looking for more hot undead romance, you'll want to read the earlier books; Sookie's simply too busy in Rhodes for any extracurriculuar activities.

Harris has carefully nurtured Sookie's gift of telepathy across the series, and Sookie is allowed her moment in the sun at Rhodes, where her gift becomes the difference between life and death for survivors of a terrorist attack. Without the romantic baggage of previous novels, Sookie has reverted to her headstrong, confident self, which is a relief after putting up with her lust-and-lovesick preoccupations in earlier novels. Bill fans will be disappointed, as Sookie is clear that she wants him out of her life. Eric hasn't gained much ground with Sookie since his amnesia in [[ASIN:B000PC0SN2 Definitely Dead]], and Sookie discovers some dark, dark secrets about Quinn's past. From the standpoint of action, intrigue, and character development, this may be the best in the series thus far (book eight, [[ASIN:0441015891 From Dead to Worse (Southern Vampire Mysteries, Book 8)]], is due in May 2008).

I am an amateur photographer and I have spent a good bit of time learning to get better, see creatively and improve my skills. I have a number of very good books on the subject, and I am always looking for more. I had the opportunity to review this little book and I got the impression from the description that this book is less technical and more creative, like an idea book. I was close. This is more like a field guide. It has its uses but it is most suited for the creatively inept or the absolute beginner.

There is very little technical information in this book; instead, it is full of ideas and suggestions on things you can do with your camera, creative ideas for interesting photos, and generalities on possible issues and approaches on fixing them. For someone who knows more than nothing about photography, this is going to be really disappointing as there’s no meat. However, for someone just starting down the road of photography beyond the odd selfie and the occasional quick snap of the family cat, these suggestions will get the reader thinking about what to do. There are some good ideas in here, and some of the tips do touch on more technical aspects of photography, an example being a discussion about focal lengths and varying them.

I can’t call this a bad book at all, but it’s beneath the majority of readers. Chances are if someone is buying a book on photography to learn, this is not the one they would choose unless they’re an absolute beginner with extremely limited knowledge. That said, for the right reader, it’s a good starting point and it has some good ideas in it.

But far from a gimmick, "The Literacy Cookbook" has proven to be a lifesaver for a particular student I've been working with.

I have a master's degree in TESOL, but much of my coursework was theoretical (and my bachelor's was in French, Spanish and Japanese, so I don't have an education background to fall back on). Other than some PhD-level classes in reading and vocabulary acquisition theory, I was lost in reaching out to adult second language learners who struggled with reading in English (and for many of our Saudi students, this is a persistent problem).

Although it's aimed at K-12 students, "The Literacy Cookbook" is applicable just as easily to adult learners. I found Sarah's advice on teaching paraphrasing particularly helpful, as that is what my current student was struggling with. I loved her emphasis on building knowledge of word roots; that's something I do frequently in my own EFL/ESP classroom, but many of my students don't have much practice analyzing and breaking down words in English. And for second language learners, having them "draw" idioms is a great tool for visual learners to "lock in" the meaning.

In addition to mini-lessons, along the way there are multiple sample worksheets to help students with inferences, reading from context, transitions, checklists, organizers, citations and more illustrated with cute food-themed line drawings (although I admit the frequent sports analogies went over my head!). You'll find advice on teaching with novels, book talk projects, training students to listen and speak effectively, test prep tips and more that will empower your students to become strong readers and speakers. This is one book I wish I'd had when I started teaching, and all new teachers should have this in their arsenal!!
