I really love this book. It's focused on its theme and does not waste time with introducing the basics of photography, it just gets right to some real life tips and facts about photographing specific climate and natural phenomenas. I recently got a copy of [[ASIN:0240817850 Landscape Photography: Four Seasons]] which I really liked because it culled out what you needed to know now, to shoot the season you are in. This book goes a step further and gives even more granular advice on very specific situations.

The book is full of beautiful illustrations for various conditions from what I traditionally think of the elements, lightning and rain storms, snow, sandstorms etc, to other natural events like Aurora Borealis and Volcanoes. I read through it almost immediately and I'm inspired to try many shots based on ideas put forward in this book. But if you are like me, knowledge is best delivered when it is needed. This book does well at doing that also. Recently we had a few possibilities of Northern lights here so I quickly read through the section on photographing the lights to make a run north away from city lights. Sadly clouds came in and obscured them but I felt a little more prepared.

Sadly, to continue on the example of the aurora, I was only slightly better prepared. Since the book covers so many different "elements" it does not go into great depth for many of the situations. For me it helped to remind me to check the photos and histograms a lot because the lights wax and wane in intensity, and it reminded me to compose the ground into the photo and look for reflective water if possible. There is far more information that could be passed on and many more tips but the scope limits depth. I was kind of disappointed by the two pages on glaciers. I would love to have some better ideas about how to handle the dynamic range of ice fields next to mountains, or how to pull in that beautiful glacier blue (would polarizers help or hurt?)

But despite the shortfalls in depth, I'm leaving it at 5 stars because the inspiration more than makes up for a little depth of technical details. Many of the tips are about setting yourself up for the shots to learn to anticipate possibilities. There is a great overview of clouds and the section on rainbows near the end are great examples of that. It's not a perfect book, but it is a very good book.

I think the author has locked onto the perfect format to teach composition. I learned everything I know about composition from peer reviews in graphic arts classes and photography salons. This book uses hundreds of example photographs, one per page with a short critique of what works and what doesn't work in the photos. It seems like this should be an incredibly effective way of teaching composition by focusing analysis on lots of sample photographs one at a time. Probably the best way to learn is to critically look at thousands of photos, or even better thousands of your own photos. However I feel it needs to be tweaked just a bit to take this book from good to brilliant.

Photos - I didn't find the photograph selections to be the greatest. I do like the mix from classic photos and paintings to snapshots. It is a good idea to show that you should still think composition in point and shoot snapshots, but in general there were a lot of uninspiring photos. Flipping through the photos, there is very little wow factor. While there are a few truly inspiring photos, I think it is possible to create a collection that inspires you so much it literally drives you into the field to start shooting. Also, some of the concepts could be demonstrated with better photos.

Text - The text is very short and concise when getting the point across, however there seems to be a little filler information that seems discordant. Occasionally the narrative is broken to give information on photo content matter like to list the members of the camel family when viewing a photo of a dromedary or the height of Denali. These show up infrequently, just often enough to interrupt the focus.

Exercises - I read the book front to back, but have not done the exercises yet. I really like the suggestions for more classic examples to track down. Also there are some thought provoking questions and some good suggestions to get you shooting and thinking about your compositions.

Overall - I would recommend this book to beginner photographers who are looking for help in crafting their compositions. I would put myself at high intermediate and I don't know how much new information I learned by reading the book, but it was great reinforcement. I would like to see this format revisited again. It is great focusing on so many example photos.

This is one of the more unusual books I have seen and I was not sure what to make of it at first. I wasn’t sure if this was going to be a survival guide, a how-to, a “knowledge-is-power” book or something else. It turns out it is all of those rolled into one book. It is full of interesting information and very practical advice on how to survive in many adverse situations.

To read through the table of contents alone one might believe this book is specifically about surviving natural disasters. That’s true to a point - emphasis is placed on dealing with natural events like tornados, hurricanes, tidal waves and more. However, there is provision in this book for blackouts, nuclear fallout and more.

The book is divided up into a number of logical sections: “Well Before” which covers planning and the what-if’s, “Days Before” which is the point at which the realization that all of the planning in the previous section is likely to be needed, “Just Before” which addresses the time before the event hits bit there is still time for a bit of planning, “Just Before” which covers the last minute stuff, “Suddenly” which addresses the abrupt arrival of the event, “During” which is the shortest section and covers what help you can expect, “Just After” which deals with the needs immediately right after the passing of the event and finally “Well After” which is post-disaster recovery.

Not all of the sections deal with the same things. For example, The “Suddenly” section includes a paragraph on dealing with threatening calls and suspicious packages. These are not things for which you can plan ahead most of the time so you would not find such in the planning sections.

Most of the things presented in this book are all common-sense, though some might consider many of the topics in this book as over-the-top or paranoid. While that could be the case for a few topics in this book, I would rather see these things in here than have an incomplete book. Topics are well-written and are presented in a very matter-of-fact manner that is approachable and does not insult the reader.

What I really appreciate about this book is that it is not just a raw presentation of “If-this-then-do-that” rules and guidelines. The author goes into some detail about the “why” as well and also includes some good information on how certain things can happen so they can be avoided. For example, included is a good explanation on what exactly is an avalanche and under what conditions it can occur, explaining the anatomy of it and where the danger lies. There is information in this write-up that I did not know and found fascinating.

Finally, I think this is not the kind of book you would sit down and read and memorize. This is more the kind of book I would keep somewhere close by as a reference manual to refer to when needed. The planning sections are the exception to this, of course.

Overall, this is a very interesting and approachable book. I can’t just sit down and read it but it does have a lot of interesting information on various topics that, if you know ahead of time, just might be the difference between surviving and struggling.

BOTANICAL KNITS is a pattern collection with 12 knitted garment designs "inspired by trees and foliage." Because I love anything with knitted-in leaf motifs, I ordered this book immediately when I saw an ad from an online yarn shop. Leaf motifs aren't particularly difficult to knit, but they use cables, travelling stitches, and/or yarnovers, and always require the knitter to pay attention. Usually the leaf designs are charted, and this book is no exception. To knit the patterns in this book, a knitter will probably need at least advanced intermediate skills.

I like nearly all of the patterns, but my favorites are "Twigs and Willows" (long-sleeve cardigan with simple curved yoke made from an embossed branch and leaves); "Forest Floor" (slouch hat covered with complex leaf-like cables); "Pressed Leaves" (beret with flat leaf outlines); "Oak Trail" (cloche with wide brow band ending with oak leaf on left side); and "Wrapped in Leaves" (a semi-circular shoulder shawl knit in stockinette with a simple but elegant border of leaves).

The entire BOTANICAL KNITS collection includes: (1) a raglan pullover ("Autumn's End", chest sizes 34-1/2" to 58-1/2"); (2) a wide-collared cardigan ("Buds and Blooms", chest sizes 34" to 62"); (3) a yoked cardigan ("Twigs and Willows", chest sizes 35" to 57-1/2"); (4) a three-quarter-sleeve cardigan with leaf detail down the sleeves ("Entangled Vines", chest sizes 31-3/4" to 58-3/4"); (5) a cable-knit slouch hat ("Forest Floor", head size 20"-22"); (6) ivy-patterned top-down socks ("Ivy Trellis Socks", size women's medium); (7) a leafy cowl ("Twin Leaf Loop"); (8) mittens to match the socks ("Ivy Trellis Mittens", size women's medium); (9) a twisted-stitch leaf-motif beret ("Pressed Leaves", head size 20"-22"); (10) a cloche hat with a leafy band ("Oak Trail", head size 20"-22"); (11) fingerless mitts with asymmetrical leaves ("Spring Foliage", size women's medium); and (2) a leaf-bordered stockinette stitch shawl ("Wrapped in Leaves"). The author notes that "Wrapped in Leaves" is a larger version of her "Cedar Leaf Shawlette" pattern (which is not included in this collection).

This is a large (8.5"x 11") book, printed on heavy stock in full color. The photo layouts are beautiful. A very nice feature is that the charts are large--so you can work directly from the book, or make copies for your personal use without enlarging. The sweater schematics are also large, and are especially attractive because the line figures and measurements are superimposed on photographs of the sweaters. Full-figured women will appreciate the large and extra-large sizes included for the sweaters.

If you like these designs, you might also be interested in [[ASIN:0615529348 Coastal Knits]], another knitted garment pattern collection that is co-authored by designer Alana Dakos.

[[VIDEOID:512ae0995c3d5f536cd724c6f4460732]] GREAT LEGO SETS: A VISUAL HISTORY is a beautifully designed and written coffee-table book that any adult LEGO fan should love. It doesn't include every LEGO set ever released--there are far too many sets--but it does include a great many of the most popular, most famous retired sets (e.g., Grand Carousel, Taj Mahal, Millennium Falcon) from every line (e.g., Friends, Bionicles, Mindstorm) that have become expensive collectors' items. This book allows the average, not-so-well-heeled LEGO fan to closely examine and enjoy these storied creations!

The book is a slip-cased set with two "volumes"--a hardcover GREAT LEGO SETS book, and a cardboard box that contains an exclusive "Mini Space Cruiser" model to build. There are 102 pieces in the model, enough to generate some satisfying building time. The pieces--which show through a window in the slip-case--are in a factory-sealed bag, and come with a standard booklet of LEGO building instructions. The exclusive "Mini Space Cruiser" model is a small version of the Space Cruiser from the 1979 Space Cruiser and Moon Base set.

As an armchair historian, I really love the 6-page, illustrated timeline that traces the development and expansion of LEGO products from the very beginning when the original brick sets were placed on the market, to the present day (2015). The timeline clearly shows the years when each new type of product was introduced and/or renamed (e.g., Elves, Architecture, Technic).

The pages that describe the individual LEGO sets include the set number, product line, year introduced, number of pieces, and number of minifigures. Often there is a text box with a brief biography and photograph of the set's designer. There are closeups of the significant features of the models (e.g., building interiors, underlying story, unusual or collectible minifigs). Each included set has a "Brick by Brick" text box that gives factoids (e.g., first example of minifig printing, description of dropped design elements such as a stormtroopers' bath in the Star Wars Death Star, inclusion of rare bricks like Harry Potter's invisibility cloak).

I was pleased to be able to look closely at the Grand Carousel, Green Grocer, Taj Mahal, and detailed Eiffel Tower, because all of these great collectible sets are now out of my price range. Also, I was pleased to see that my three current personal favorites, the original Haunted House, the Detective's Office (currently available from LEGO stores), and the Emerald Night Train were all featured with full coverage.

I have worked with K&F Concept filters in the past and generally had good experiences with them. They're good, mid-range quality filters at (usually) a budget price. I haven't worked with any black diffusion filters prior to this one so I have no basis against which to compare, but so far it seems to work as designed and seems to be made very well.

In a nutshell, this type of filter softens light a bit, causing some gentle halos around light sources, without impacting image sharpness or detail. Where I have seen the most noticeable impact is in images where there otherwise would be a lot of shadows and contrast; instead of stark contrast and strong shadows, the filter has the effect of brightening up the shadows somewhat and creating smoother color gradients. Sure, this can be done in software after the fact, but it is a lot easier to do this at the time the image is taken and it certainly is a lot less work.

The filter is very easy to install. This is my first magnetic filter and it is as easy to attach to my camera as I could have hoped. The threaded ring attaches to the lens in the same manner as a step ring or another filter, and the filter itself just snaps securely into place due to the magnetics. Removing the filter is just as simple, especially if you choose to leave the magnetic ring in place on the lens.

The assembly seems to be well made. I have had filters in the past that have been poorly constructed and rattle in the frames when shaken, or have been mildly blemished, or just felt cheap. This filter has none of those issues and appears to be well made.

This is a nice black diffusion filter. It's easy to install and use, and it just works. I will be using it more in the coming weeks.

THE NINE-TAILED FOX (A SERGEANTS SUEÑO AND BASCOM NOVEL) is the 12th series novel (but my first), and it works fine as a standalone. It’s a plainly written military police procedural set in 1970s South Korea. Because the author was stationed in Korea for 10 years, the details of the setting ring absolutely true. The novel includes a good portion of entertaining army humor (reminiscent of the M*A*S*H book and TV series).

In the novel, the two military investigators (George and Ernie) are ordered to investigate the unusual disappearances of three GIs from three different bases. They soon learn that the men were last seen in the company of an attractive, respectably attired, older woman. Their informants whisper that the woman may be a fearsome Gumiho, a supernatural being described in Korean folklore as a nine-tailed fox that has taken the form of a siren-like woman.

In the midst of their inquiries, George and Ernie get caught up in a dispute between a pair of feuding officers’ wives that has them removing and reinstalling a PX refrigerator in an unauthorized location, a local “women’s power” center. As enlisted men, they have no choice but to do as they’re told, even though their investigation is of the highest priority (because the Pentagon and U.S. government is demanding answers from top brass about the AWOL soldiers).

Serious George and do-whatever-he-wants Ernie are delightful characters. The novel inserts just the right amount of Korean language and background detail for verisimilitude. The narrative flows smoothly, moves along at a steady clip, and the story is interesting enough to keep the reader reading. The novel is well-written, and perfect for light escape reading. I’m really happy to have discovered this enjoyable mystery/thriller series.

My family loves a good dessert after dinner and we have been looking for more ideas for cakes and pies in particular. Most of the books I have seen and looked at have been for baked goods, though I have a few that hit a variety of dessert types including ice cream, cookies and holiday confections. This is the first book I have seen that has been specifically about non-baked desserts and it is a nice one. It is not all-inclusive, but it has a wide range of ideas and recipes that covers most fancies.

The book is divided up into eight chapters (titles paraphrased): 1. Cakes, 2. Pies, 3. Layered Desserts, 4. Tarts, 5. Ice Cream and Related, 6. Cookies/Bars, 7. Puddings and 8. Helpful Tips. Each of the first seven chapters has a nice collection of desserts, some larger than others but all with a selection for everyone. There is a little bit of overlap between chapters (for example ice cream cakes) which is hard to avoid.

The large majority of recipes come with a full-color photo of a finished dessert, which makes selecting a cake, tart or ice cream dessert very easy.

Some of the recipes call for pre-made ingredients such as Oreo cookies or specific breakfast cereals. This is certainly not an issue, but it should be kept in mind – some of the recipes are designed for quick preparation.

I have not made many of these desserts yet, but I can say two things about the ones I have tried: they're easy to prepare, and they turn out very well. I will come back here and update as I try more. So far, my family is happy with my efforts.

This book is not exhaustive. For example, it has a very limited number of recipes for ice cream, and there are no candy recipes at all. The emphasis is on cakes, pies and tarts. This again is not a problem but it's worth keeping in mind if you are looking for ice cream, frozen yogurt or candies (like buckeyes).

I am pleased with this cookbook and I am looking forward to trying more of the recipes. No baking required, and all of the desserts are easy to put together.

I have worked with numerous pairs of active noise canceling (ANC phones) and I’ve seen a wide variation in sound profiles, features, and the quality of the ANC function. Some are better than others. I was a bit skeptical of these because of the price; most of the ANC phones I have used that were worth anything have a higher price tag. These are better than the price suggests.

Right out of the box, these headphones do not draw much attention to themselves. They’re not flashy and do not have any noticeable markings on them unless you’re looking for them. They are over-the-ear headphones which tend to be more comfortable than on-ear phones, and these have a snug fit without clamping down tightly. They adjust easily to fit almost any size head too. The padding on the cans is soft enough to not pinch, though after extended wear they do start to get a little warm.

Pairing and connection with my computer was a painless affair and these were ready very quickly after they were powered on.

The ANC function is far and away better than any other headphones I have worked with in this price range. They’re almost as aggressive as that of the Bose QC-15’s that I own, without that weird faux pressure sensation when the ANC is turned on. Even with the volume down low, these cancel out enough background noise to make them a serious contender. I have no complaints with the ANC.

The sound quality is very good, though not quite to my tastes. The bass is very strong – much stronger than I like personally, but not out of line with what has been trending in the last decade. Where Skullcandy got it right, though, is in how well they’ve implemented the bass enhancement. Even though the bass is very strong (enough to give me a headache at higher volumes), it does not distort or turn into just low-frequency noise. More importantly, the bass enhancement does not stomp on the midrange which is the usual casualty. The midrange is warm and fairly balanced. The highs are bright and clear without being piercing. The end result is a sound profile that sounds full and rich. So many headphones with enhanced bass I have used have killed the midrange which makes music sound hollow, or distort the bass so much as to make music sound like a low-fidelity render. These are refreshing in that regard.

Some headphones detect when you take them off and pause music or playback when you take them off. These do not.

These come in a carry pouch that offers little in the way of drop and crush protection but it does keep them clean and free of scuffs and scratches. Also included is an audio cable for wired use as well as a USB Type C cable for charging.

Overall, these are far and away better than the price would suggest. They are very comfortable to wear, they have a good sound profile (particularly if you like heavy bass) and the ANC function is better than average and competitive with much more expensive headphones. These are budget-friendly ANC headphones with higher-end performance.

I like America's Test Kitchen (ATK) cookbooks and have had generally positive opinions of their stuff. Their cookbooks follow a consistent format and are almost always full of recipes that are easy to follow and are well-tested so less chance of disappointing results. This cookbook, The Complete Salad Cookbook, is a good one that falls very much in line with their other good cookbooks.

This is a big cookbook with a lot of recipes divided into multiple sections. Sections include "The Salad Bar" (which is a collection of ad-hoc ingredients and assemble-your-own dressings and toppings), "Leafy Salads", "Fruit and Vegetable Salads", "Bean and Grain Salads" and "Pasta and Noodle Salads". These sections are fairly well defined and delineated.

One thing I'd like to mention about the first section, "The Salad Bar". One of my favorite dressings is Green Goddess dressing, and I was encouraged to see it represented here. It seems like a fairly straightforward recipe and though I haven't had the chance to make it yet, it is one my short list.

One of the trademark features of ATK cookbooks is the "Why This Recipe Works" sections with nearly every recipe, and this cookbook follows that formula. These paragraphs describe what worked when developing the recipe, what didn't work, ideas that were tried, differences in ingredients (and sometimes brands of ingredients), and more. While interesting reading, it is most useful in understanding how the recipe was finalized and what pitfalls can be avoided since the ATK testers likely have already tried the variations. The first section, "The Salad Bar", does not include this write-up on the recipes it contains - being simple toppings and relatively straightforward dressings, this omission is not important and isn't really missed.

Many of the recipes have full-color photos along with them. I have heard it said many times that you eat first with your eyes, and this cookbook is a visual feast in that regard. Just paging through you'll find a lot of wonderful pictures that will give you good ideas of what you're actually hungry for.

A few of the recipes in this book represent some old-time dishes you'll find on picnics and at church potluck suppers. Potato salad and macaroni salad are both in this book, though perhaps not the same as you might remember them if you had them a lot 40 years ago. However, some once popular salads and other common salads are not represented at all; Jello salad and Watergate salad are two that come to mind (though to be fair, Jello salad is not one I actually expected to find in this book).

This is a large and fairly comprehensive cookbook for salads in particular, covering a lot of ground and packed full of pictures. I wouldn't call it absolutely complete due to a couple of omissions, but what is there is great and it follows ATK's formula for solid, readable, and well-designed cookbooks. If salads are your thing, this is a very good resource.

This book wonderfully augments the Anne Frank diary by giving another perspective to the events in the Annex. It humanizes the story even more and helps bring the reality to life in the readers mind. However the book is a fictional "best guess" about what is going on in Peter Van Pel's mind during their time in hiding. But historical fiction can have great value. My wife is a middle school history teacher who often uses historical fiction to bring history to life and has added the book to her suggested readings for those who have read Frank's diaries.

The book reads well and quickly. I finished it in just as few days of leisurely reading and it kept me engaged, even in suspense at times, despite knowing the ultimate outcome. If I had any criticism of the book, it would be that Peter's ultimate fear of never making love to a woman seemed a little over the top and used these yearnings a little too hard to connect Peter's story with Anne's. As someone who survived the male teen years, I could see his desires being an issue, but not so singular as it becomes in this book. At times the book seems to be a romance for tweens and young teen-agers.

Those mild criticisms aside, the book stands up fine against Frank's diaries in conveying the claustrophobic confinement in the annex. It was interesting to hear another angle from one of those involved (again with a grain of salt as it is fiction, but valuable in that it helps young minds connect to the historic reality.) But where I felt the book truly shone was the section that started after they were discovered. The concentration camp section of the book was a great synthesis of survivor experiences. It covers life in the camps very well for a juvenile fiction audience and even better then the section in the annex, it brought me into the world of the characters.

Great Juvenile Historic Fiction.

I don't golf as much as I'd like these days, but for the couple of games I participated in recently I decided to bring this along. I've never used a rangefinder before, so using this was a nascent experience, to say the least!

Another reviewer here mentioned watching the introductory video offered on the company’s website. I did so, though I used the instructions as well. The video I watched before my first use, and kept the instructions with me during the games.
The video was far more helpful than I initially thought as it went into the gadget's features into great detail without being exhaustive (they even put a Table of Contents at the beginning of the video so you can jump around). Even though it made using the device far more intuitive, I found that, when it came time to actually use the device, I still fumbled through the screens; I often had the button configurations mixed, and so many times I’d enter screens which I didn’t intend. I’m uncertain if this is something to do with the design of the gizmo or if they all are like this. I s’pose I’ll just have to become accustomed to it.

During one of my games, I had a friend of mine use it with me, and he got the hang of it faster than I did; his experience with other golf GPS devices was minimal, but it still was more than what I had. He was able to memorize the shortcuts better than me, and that helped me while I watched him navigate.

While it’s a great learning experience for me considering I've used it only a couple of times, it was very nifty to have and helped a ton. The backlit feature is nice, but if you’re golfing early in the day you probably won’t need it much. It’s light in its weight, no doubt, and convenient to stash in any pocket. The dot-matrix display makes the experience much easier to read and manipulate; truthfully, I did think that most of the screens are organized very well from screen to screen, image to text. The company seems to have excelled in this area.

I realize I became far more serious in my game with this than before; I'm not a very competitive person, but something like this will be very useful for those who take the game of golf more serious than a stroll through the field. I'm sure that, if you've used these before, the layout and button configuration is a breeze. I'm new to this world (not golfing itself, of course), so the whole experience of using these is a tad overwhelming. I just keep telling myself that it’s like adding the map features from my golfing video games to the real world!

At first, I just wanted this book for the soup recipes. And there are plenty of those! The range of the recipes is pretty wide, but if you're not a foodie, not many of them are going to appeal to you. There are also some very difficult to find specialty ingredients in a lot of the soups. If you live near a large metro area, it likely won't be difficult for you to acquire them. If you live in more rural areas, you'll have a lot more trouble with a lot of the ingredients. (We're talking about things like Marmite, specialty cheeses, fresh chestnuts, celeriac bulbs, sunchokes, masa harina, kombu, nori, etc.) There are also several non-soup recipes. I was thrilled with the recipes included. And the recipes are huge, which is a plus for this large family momma.
But what really surprised me is how much I actually like the idea of a soup club. I usually shy away from dinner clubs, mostly because they just don't work for my family. But soup club is something I could really get used to. I look forward to finding a few friends to try soup club with me.
You'll need a few things to make this cookbook work for you. You'll need a huge stock pot. The soup recipes are intended to be split among 4 families. That means each recipe makes 8-9 quarts of soup. (And if you're a large family mom, like myself, that means their might even be leftovers!) You'll need an immersion blender for several of the soups. You may need a food processor for several soups. And if you're starting a soup club, you'll need quart sized jars, small jars for garnishes, and canvas tote bags for delivery.

There is just so much to say about this book... yet only so much that can be said without spoiling the read. Trust me; you DO NOT want to miss"The Unremembered" by Peter Orullian.

Orullian was a mainstay author in several anthologies I read. After enjoying short stories he has written, I was excited when his first novel was published this last April. I had browsed his website to find that there are even more anthologies I will be reading in the future. But I took pause to read his novel "The Unremembered" first. And I am truly glad that I did!!

Orullian is a gifted, passionate writer! I believe that while his strengths may be in Fantasy and Sci Fi, he could write in any genre... he has an amazing talent for the written word. And when that talent is coupled with his incredible imagination... the result is the great Fantasy read you will find in "The Unremembered".

One of the main reasons I found myself so engrossed in this book, is that Orullian obviously is an astute student of human behavior. It is clear that he notices how people around him act and react to their lives. Then he is able to articulate what he sees in a very descriptive and insightful way. Therefore the characters of his novel are multi-dimensional, complex but also familiar, and unique... as is the world he created for them. You are as much engaged by watching the growth of his characters, as they develop and face their fears... as you are by the story's rollercoaster ride of action, drama, and intrigue.

You will be impressed with Orullian's writing style... his chapters end with what could be considered a "cliff hanger". You may intend to read for a certain amount of time, but will end up reading much longer. Finding a chapter to end on for the night is difficult. This is a hard book to put down! My "honey do" list remained in tact and growing, as I put off other things to read this book.

It becomes clear early as you read that Orullian has a vision and you are now engulfed in his creation. This story, this journey... will become a part of your life during the read, lingering long after you finish... and you will be waiting, as I am, for the next book in this series to be released!

The world Orullian creates is ingenious; a true escape from our own reality. The world he creates is threatened, and under vicious attack! You will find "edge of your seat" encounters, as these characters struggle to survive and save their world. Then enters the magic and the power (unlike any seen before)... a chance to right the wrongs, to see victory, to overcome and become what is meant to be. Seriously GOOD stuff!

Professional C++ Second Edition is one of the few books I have found that adequately covers the recently adopted C++11 standard (to be fair, there are others, and more are hitting shelves all the time). Having been a C++ developer for years I looked at a few different books on C++ with the mindset of concentrating on the new standard and of the titles I found this one was the best of the bunch. It isn't a perfect book by any means, but it's a solid offering that teaches the C++ language quite well.

This is not just a C++11 book; it covers most of the C++ language and explains as it goes what is different in the new standard. But, there's more than just C++ coding in this book - it also covers application design and planning as well as stylistic considerations as well. These are just as important as knowing the syntax though these subjects apply to more than just a single language.

The book's material is broken down into four sections and 29 chapters. Each of the four sections progresses into more advanced material than the previous (which I hope is obvious). I did notice something interesting about the ordering and grouping, though - this book is almost organized like a textbook that could be used in a course setting. Mingled in with language features is software design and engineering concepts that are not language-specific. The only think lacking that would otherwise turn this book into a college textbook on Software Engineering with C++ is chapter exercises. This is not necessarily a bad thing, unless the idea is to use the book for teaching...

The final section of the book, "Part IV: C++ Software Engineering", is a collection of seven chapters outlining good software engineering concepts including design patterns. It is not an exhaustive study of such but is an excellent introduction to several important design patterns. There is also a chapter on good debugging techniques, another on testing and another on cross-platform development.

There are three chapters of this book that I think merit special attention. The first two are the chapters that deal with metaprogramming (generic coding with templates). This book provides excellent coverage and explanation of this material. I have struggled with template-based code in the past and I wish I had had this book when I was learning. The other chapter deals with multithreaded programming. While I have a reasonably good grasp on writing multithreaded applications this chapter really makes the concepts straightforward and easy to understand.

As I mentioned above, I purchased this book with the purpose of learning C++11 features. This book covers a lot of them and makes it a point to specifically point out features that are specific to the new standard. What this book does NOT do is provide a dedicated list or even a summary of the new features in the standard, which in my opinion is a shortcoming.

Professional C++ is a good book on C++ which includes coverage of the C++11 standard. It is not perfect and it gets deep into software engineering topics that are not necessarily specific to C++ but it does cover the language very well and very accessibly. When considering an up-to-date book on C++, this book is one that's very much worth consideration.

I would not say this book is complete. This is just basic, full color handwriting practice for a kid who needs some practice with handwriting. This is not the only book you’ll need for kindergarten through third grade. This is not even a full curriculum by itself. It is really just handwriting practice. I would say the writing is a bit small for a kindergartener. It looks more second grade size to me. It begins with shape practice on the lines. Working on the shapes needed to make letters. You have a full page of letter practice for each letter of the alphabet and then you have three pages of practice writing random phrases and sentences using those letters. Once you get through all the letters you have pages to write numbers, colors, days of the week, months of the year, etc. Basic stuff to practice. Then you have seasons, school words, family words, etc. to practice. Then you move to cursive with the same format, though different words, as the print section.
This is not a full handwriting curriculum. Yes, it does tell you which direction to form letters. It does not show you how to hold your pencil or how to position your paper. It does have plenty of practice opportunities for handwriting. The pages do show a lot of shadowing- you can see the next page through the current page. This is very hard in a handwriting book as kids may think they should trace the faint words they can see. As a practice book, I’d give it 4 stars. (As I would prefer to keep print and cursive in two separate books.) As a handwriting curriculum, which is what it is selling itself as, it just falls very short of what I would expect and doesn’t cover the mechanics of handwriting or even give enough detail about forming letters. I’m also not a fan of the writing random phrases and words. Seems like there are much better things to write than “Insects itch in the infield.”

THE DIABOLIST isn't your ordinary thriller--it's a primer on types of occult and Satanic religions (anti-establishment? devil worshiping? practicing magic?), and is filled with philosophical discussions about the origin of evil (created by God? created by an evil entity equal to God?) placed in a general context of Zoroastrianism. However, this serious content is presented in a way that isn't difficult for the reader to grasp, and it doesn't weigh the story down--certainly this book has plenty of exciting action scenes!

Dominic Grey (in his third series appearance) is a master of jujitsu; he partners with Viktor Radek, a Georgetown University professor of religious phenomenology (the study of religious and cult beliefs in angels, demons, ghosts, Satanic possession, alternate planes of existence, etc.). When Interpol calls Radek for help with an unusual murder--the leader of an infamous Satanic cult suddenly burst into flames before his congregation, in the presence of a black-robed figure that briefly appeared and disappeared--the partners commence an investigation that leads them to San Francisco, London, Paris and its catacombs, Cambridge, Whitby, York, and--ultimately--Sicily.

Dominic is a one-man army, but may have met his match in Dante, a universally feared master knife-fighter. Dante is the right-hand man of the Magus, a reclusive New Age prophet who is determined to merge all existing Satanic and occult religions into his own Order of New Enlightenment, and then to convert all mankind. The Order has its own terrible rituals--including Black Masses with human sacrifices--all performed in honor of the evil god-entity Ahriman.

THE DIABOLIST will appeal to readers having an interest in magic, Satanism, and the occult. Dominic's jujitsu moves, as described in the action scenes, are convincing and seem plausible (although I know little about the martial arts). The story is complex, with many unguessable plot twists, and all of the loose ends are tied up in a believable ending. The book itself works fine as a series standalone (this was my first Dominic Grey novel). However, at 468 pages, it seems longer than necessary. Overall, I rate it at 4 stars ("I like it" on the official Amazon scale).

I have looked at this title many times and talked myself out of buying it repeatedly until I finally caved in and treated myself to a copy. It's a respected title in the field of bread baking and I was eager to try out several of the recipes therein and to compare results with breads made from different authors' methods and formulas. While the results are usually outstanding, this particular cookbook suffers from some editing issues that make it feasible for experienced bakers but not so good for beginners.

I have made several of the loaves described in this book and each time the final product was well worth the effort. My favorite thus far has been the Oatmeal Potato Bread which is a good daily loaf and is suitable for gifting. Although the author does not subscribe to the mindset of slow-rise bread baking the resulting loaves are usually full of flavor and have good crumb.

There is a problem, though. Each recipe I have tried has been flawed in one way or another. For example, the very first recipe in the book (White Mountain Bread) requires quite a bit more flour than specified - more than can be explained away by changing measuring method - and bakes up better in 8"x4" bread pans than the specified 9"x5" plans. This is minor but will result in disappointment for the baker just starting to work with breads. A more glaring error occurs in the Oatmeal Potato Bread recipe, which calls for chopping and boiling a potato and THEN peeling it to remove the skin. It also calls for 9"x5" pans when 8"x4" pans result in a more attractive loaf after baking.

I have been baking breads for my family for close to 15 years and I have learned a lot about the process. I know how to adjust on the fly and I know how to deal with imperfect recipes and instructions. Someone just learning how to make bread for themselves, however, could run into some difficulties that may prove to be very discouraging. If I had started with this book, I likely would have decided that I lacked 'the touch' and would have given up (or just used a bread machine).

The Bread Bible isn't a bad cookbook. It's actually a good book with some really good bread recipes. Unfortunately it needs to be edited better before it can be a truly awesome book on bread.

I managed to find a copy of this cookbook after seeing it on a bookshelf. It appeared to be a lot more practical than something like Rachael Ray's cookbook offerings, so I decided to buy a copy and try it out. This book has exceeded my expectations.

One of the common problems with cookbooks like this is that they use uncommon ingredients that you typically do not have on hand or cannot find at a regular grocery store. This is not the case with this particular book; most recipes call for commonly available ingedients or are ingredients that you can easily find at almost any grocery store. This is a big plus, as it means that you don't have to write off a number of recipes like with other cookbooks.

One of the selling points of a cookbook like this is that the recipes can be prepared quickly and easily. This is indeed the case, at least with the recipes I have tried. "Spend 30 minutes or less in the kitchen" (as specified on the cover) isn't quite the case for me, though I definitely have successfully spent less than an hour preparing meals from this book. To be fair, I have found that most 30-minute recipes take me 45-60 minutes, but I attribute this to my being a little disorganized and probably too meticulous in my preparations.

So far, the meals I have prepared from this book have been flavorful and a big hit with the family.

I appreciate a cookbook that includes pictures with the recipes and this cookbook has a lot of pictures. There is probably a 3:1 or 4:1 ratio of recipes to pictures. And for me, so far, the end result of following the recipes looks just like the pictures.

This is likely going to be one of the cookbooks I use most, as it provides me a good collection of practical recipes that can be prepped in a relatively short amount of time with ingredients I have on hand. If you need a cookbook that has easy-to-prepare recipes that use common ingredients and have flavor, and you can find a copy of this this cookbook, grab it.

Writers of the Future, Vol 31

There are 13 stories in this anthology of new writers, not all the best I’ve read, and some end abruptly and are annoying. But the majority are interesting and definitely worth your time.

I won’t go through all the stories; just the ones I liked.

Switch by Steve Pantazis was great. A society that has perfected a drug that will make you super human, but also brings you crashing down. After a friend dies he makes a personal vendetta out of finding the guy who sold his friend these super drugs. He finds him but also finds the fight of his life as the criminal has a better super drug. All in all several fun fight scenes.

God Whisperer by Daniel J. Davis was odd; a society that sells little Gods and how to train them as pets. Creepy story and ends abruptly.

Stars that Make Dark Heaven Light by Sharon Joss, although the title is a bit long the story is not. Ettie is part of an experiment on this colony planet, where discoveries in genetics makes adaptation to other planets possible. But what if the changes to the human genome are such that you barely pass for human? And what if you run into a species that has not only perfected the science of this, but can become the species they meet? Fascinating premise; would make a cool novel.

I’ve read Hubbard’s articles and stories before. I always try to apply what he talks about in Art as a communication. When Shadows Fall is a fun sci-fi pulp story.

Larry Niven is no amateur and his story, Inconstant Moon, is great. I’ve read a lot of his early stories back in the day with his Kinzi and such. This story had a lot to do with humans not being able to fathom extinction. The story felt rushed, but was entertaining.

Poseidon’s Eyes by Kary English was fun too. It had me looking up all the Greek god and myth references throughout the story. Being part Greek myself, I could relate!

Bottom Line:

Overall a good start for many of these writers. I really hope they take advantage of this publicity and make a go of it. Kevin Anderson wrote a cool story in here about a guy who is a one hit wonder in the sci-fi world and never continued, but discovers an Alternate Earth where he did continue and the result. Philips GoGear Vibe 8 GB MP3 Player is a reasonably priced MP3 player from Philips Electronics. Small and with a good deal of memory, this MP3 player offers enough of the basic features to satisfy casual MP3 users' needs.

Let's talk about the good points first. This MP3 player is a good value and it has a long battery life. A full charge can last the better part of a day so it is ready when you need it. The compact size and durable construction are also plusses with this MP3 player. It takes up very little space and the metal construction is made to last. I like the menu navigation as well and found it very intuitive.

Most important to an MP3 player is sound quality and in this area, my feelings are mixed. My MP3 player experience is limited, so I have little to which I can compare. But based on other MP3 players, the sound quality with this Phillips device is a little below average. I was also very disappointed with the Full Sound option. This is supposed to improve the sound quality, but I could barely tell any difference. It has a little too much bass for my tastes, but others might find it acceptable.

Probably my greatest complaint with this Philips MP3 player is the included ear buds. They are the type that hugs the ear, but they do not contain a foam cushion and thus are not very comfortable or very good at blocking outside noise. The good thing, of course, is that an accessory like this can be replaced, which I recommend doing if you purchase this product.

MP3 players are nice and Philips GoGear Vibe 8 GB MP3 Player is a good MP3 player, especially for the price. There are certainly better MP3 players out there, but this is a good one for beginners or those with basic needs. I'm torn with my overall rating because of the division between the pros and cons. So, I will award this device with a middle rating of three stars and a modest recommendation.

An absolutely great read. This book managed to be complete while not being exhaustive or bogging down. It covered the gamut from anecdote to academic research. I have read a lot of the academic papers and reports he references and I can say from personal experience that he relays the findings very faithfully but in a far more engaging, enjoyable, and comprehensible manner.

The book itself can be separated into three parts, although book is intertwined throughout with the author's personal experience and a fictionalized life history of an individual bear.

Natural history - The first few chapters do a great job of setting up the environment of the polar bear as well as it's life cycle. The author does masterfully presents the Polar Bear's Arctic adaptations as well as it's relationship to its prey. It is eyeopening to see how well the bear is at home in such a harsh and unforgiving environment.

human history - The middle of the book sets up an overview of human interactions with Polar Bears. Especially fascinating was finding out that Egyptian and Romans had somehow kept captive polar bears despite having no first hand knowledge of their habitats. From there the book covers early run ins with Arctic explorers through commercial hunting trips to the conservation movement. The second chapter in this section covers Churchill Manitoba and the current bear tourism which had me googling "train fares to Churchill" before I was half way through.

Conservation - The last chapters look at the realities of Arctic warming and ice loss. I wish everyone, global warming proponents and opponents alike, truly understood the information covered in this section. Again it is not exhaustive, but thorough enough to encapsulate the issue, from multi-year ice, to possible changes in benthic to pelagic ecologies. The future doesn't look too bright, but it makes the species seem even more dear in the present. Excellent coverage.

All in all, the perfect book for anyone interested in Polar Bears, wildlife or the environment. I highly recommend it to anyone.

My wife and I love historical fiction. We both jumped at this book when we saw it because the premise of a 14 year old boy in World War I sounded perfect. Even, better it seemed to resonate with the idea of child warriors which have sadly become fairly common in our time. However we never seemed to be able to get into the character. The book seems choppy and disjunct. Maybe this is due to the translation, but the flow seems interruptive, unplanned.

The main reason I read historical fiction is an immersion into the events of the time. It is a way to bring text book history to life in a way that can touch students far more effectively than a chart of stats, a few dates, and a couple of dry facts. Here the book did fairly well, such as the description of Hells Gate and trench life. However a few facts seemed to sit a little awkwardly - like the concept of Lebensraum which seems almost vernacular to the characters in the book. I have always been under the impression that Lebensraum was held secret in World War I as a political goal to be brought out after a German victory. It was a social idea at the time, but not as widely spread as this book portrays. Definitely the idea was championed in World War II under Hitler. Little things like this seemed to block my trust in the portrayal. But I will look into some of the facts that troubled me.

The best thing I took away from this was a fact I had not known, that the author included in his notes. The inventor of many of the poison gases used by Germany later won a Nobel Peace Prize for his work with fertilizers. That is the kind of facts I hope to find in historical fiction.

This latter feature is one I wish was different. Often, you will want to watch and listen to the person at the door, but because you have to remember to keep pressing the video button, you could easily miss something important.

The book has some helpful tips, like:

1. Other than for famous people, a memoir is more literary than historical. Expression is more important than information. Beauty more than accuracy.

2. Memoir isn't always about the memories, but the bigger picture, like 'survival in Auschwitz.'

3. Discovery is the thing.

4. The things which good writers always have in common - a) writers write (most do every day) b) writers read (ditto).

5. Add variety, make it eclectic. Look at other books' first lines.

6. Use a map to trigger memories.

7. Scenes are vital. Showing more than telling. Sight, smell, touch, sound.- make a reader dream.

8. 'Automatic writing' - like start with 'on' and just write whatever comes to mind to generate ideas, new thoughts.

9. Write from the heart - warts and all.

10. Characters are the soul of creative nonfiction, even for memoirs. See yourself and people as characters and life between them as drama.

11. Read your draft out loud.

12. Metaphor is the source of all meaning. Adds layers of meaning. Make it new, like 'business is a dance.'

13. Adumbration -suggest what follows.

14. Develop a rhythm.

15. Do outlines last.

With both the Maxtor and SSD plugged in, I added an SD card. I could mount the card and read the files from it, or copy files from it to either of the hard disks or to my system disk!

I tried using both a CF card and an SD card at the same time. However, I was not able to successfully access both at the same time. When I removed the SD card, I could read the CF card.

The device came with a short manual which was written in broken English. It was marginally useful and largely discussed how to use the PC Clone EX program that came with the docking device.

The docking system includes a USB hub. To test it, I plugged a Seagate USB hard disk into the USB port on the front. I was able to copy files from my camera's CF card to the Seagate USB drive. This book is the result of designer Nico's experimentation with turning basic shapes--triangles, rectangles, circles, and squares--into lovely, wearable, knitted lace garments.

Knitters who are interested in designing their own lace garments will find the "design notes" that accompany each pattern to be especially worth reading. For example, the description of the Posies Wrap begins: "This simple wrap is the perfect social knitting project. It's a big rectangle, with armholes created by casting on and then binding off stitches, and its simplicity is the key to its form. The end result is a vest . . . with asymmetrical fronts . . . ." These design notes give real insight into Nico's personal creative process.

LOVELY KNITTED LACE isn't a technical reference book, but it does include a lot of solid discussion of lace knitting technique. Adventurous intermediate knitters should be able to knit the designs after reading the included explanations. Most of the patterns have both written out and charted instructions. The patterns call for a variety of yarn weights (light worsted to laceweight) and knitting needle sizes (US 8 to US 2). The more fitted garments have instructions for two or three sizes. The fact that many patterns use US 4 and larger needles makes this book a good choice for new lace knitters--the stitches are easier to track, and the projects don't take forever to finish.

My personal favorites are the Camellia Dolman, a large cashmere cape with "feathers" that begin at the neckline and end at the lower hemline (details of hem and front buttonband are well thought out); and the Starry Nights Bolero, a drapey bolero-shaped top that is knitted from luxury yarn and constructed from two rectangles. However, there is not a single design in this collection that I wouldn't be willing to knit and wear!

The patterns are:

Triangles: Triangle Tulip Shawl; Flutter Shawl; Poppy Shawl; Floral Tunic (pullover sweater)

Rectangles: Japanese Leaf Scarf; Cables and Lace Stole; Butterfly Stole; Posies Wrap; Starry Nights Bolero (bolero top)

Circles: Angel Shawl; Poinsettia Jacket (long-sleeved sweater with peplum at back); Traveling Vines Cape/Skirt (convertible garment); Orange Crush Beret (hat); Camellia Dolman (button-front cape, shown on book cover)

Squares: Dahlia Shawl; Aster Shirt (loose tabard-like pullover); Birch Jacket (long-sleeved shrug); Moondance Shrug (shrug with elbow-length sleeves)

I used to think that anything cooked outside, whether it was chicken, vegetables or pulled pork barbeque, was all just grilled and I had no concept of what it meant to barbeque or smoke food on a grill or a dedicated smoker. I learned the difference a couple of years ago and I have found a couple of books that delve into the topic of cooking with smoke. Smoke It Like A Pro is a new book on the topic and I was anxious to see how well it compares to other good books on the subject of cooking with smoke. In a nutshell, this is a great book on smoking and barbequing, very approachable and easy to read.

This book is specifically geared towards smoking and barbequing with a ceramic cooker, but it especially emphasizes the Big Green Egg. It is very possible to make some adjustments for using something other than a ceramic cooker, like using a Weber classic, but be aware that a ceramic cooker does retain its heat and a steady temperature more easily than a metal covered grill.

The book is broken up into 9 chapters as follows: “Fire in the Hole” (primer on using a ceramic cooker), “Low and Slow” (barbeque and smoke), “Roasting” (cooking with indirect heat), “The Big Sear” (traditional grilling), “One in the Oven” (baking), “Wet and Dry” (curing and smoking), “Deep Frying, Griddling and Wok-ing Around” (less traditional ways to cook with a ceramic cooker), “The Ins and Outs” (sauces, rubs, marinades and more), and finally “The Tail End” (maintenance and care).

There are many, many good recipes and ideas in this book and almost every one of them comes with a full-color photograph. I was especially surprised to find recipes for scones and oatmeal cookies, but there’s the traditional favorites in there too – burgers, beef steaks, pork tenderloin and classic pulled pork barbeque as well.

One thing I really appreciate about this book is the author’s writing style. He writes in a way that does not talk up or down to his readers; he shares a lot of knowledge but doesn’t come off as condescending or like he’s talking to a graduate class. The writing is on the level and very approachable, like having a conversation with someone who genuinely wants to share what they know and get everyone else excited about it too. Not all cookbook writers can pull that off.

I used to think that cooking on a grill or a ceramic cooker like this was for grilling burgers and little more. I learned otherwise and have a better appreciation for outdoor cooking. With this book my horizons have expanded even more – I never thought about using a ceramic cooker as an oven. I am still no expert but I’m learning. If you have a ceramic cooker or if you want to expand your knowledge of how to use an outdoor cooker in general, this is a great book to help you along.

I will start by saying that I am typically not a fan of ear buds. I will also say that the very best headphones I have is a set of Sony active noise canceling ear buds. I have always had good success with Sony audio products and I regard the brand as an upper mid-range line. These buds are disappointing in that, while they’re comfortable for ear buds, the sound profile is lacking, specifically in the midrange.

This is a basic set of ear buds that work as you might expect. They do not have ANC functionality, there is no battery or battery pack and there is no Bluetooth functionality. These are straight plug-in audio gear with no fancy features. These will work with just about any device that provides a 3.5mm audio jack.

Most ear buds are uncomfortable to me, but these are surprisingly comfortable and I can wear these for a good bit of time. They come with several inserts of varying sizes so you can find the size that fits your ear canal just right. The included inserts are soft and do not irritate my ears as much as others have done in the past. I still very much prefer over-the-ear headphones which is a personal preference more than anything.

So, where’s the problem? The problem lies in the sound profile which is unbalanced. Having used literally dozens of sets of ear buds and headphones over the past 3-5 years I have developed a good feel for what sounds right and what doesn’t. Most ear buds have one of two issues, either way too much bass or almost none at all. These are surprising in that they actually get the bass just about right, not too heavy and not too light. The highs are very bright and clear, perhaps a touch too piercing for my tastes but not to the point of being unacceptable. The midrange, though, is flat. The result is that music sounds somewhat sterile and lackluster. This is similar to the issue I have seen with my Bose headset. These still sound good, but they fall short of where they could and should be.

Normally I would rate ear buds with a glitch in the sound profile a little higher, as they’re still quite usable and they sound decent. But, these are much more expensive than the average and I have heard less expensive buds with more balanced sound. Sony makes a number of sets of ear buds and headphones, but these are not among their best offerings.

As a knitting history buff, I love DUTCH TRADITIONAL GANSEYS for its many, many early-20th-century photographs of Dutch fishermen wearing their traditional working garments (blue or grey gansey sweaters with textured patterns, tightly knit from fine yarn). I recognized some of the photographs from other books on knitted fishermen's ganseys (e.g., [[ASIN:0937274178 Knitting from the Netherlands]]) but most of the photos were completely new to me. Each of the 40 villages that produced the pictured ganseys is briefly described in terms of its historical importance, growth, and activity as a fishing village during the heyday of fishermen's ganseys.

As a modern-day gansey knitter, I love this book for the instructions that enable intermediate-to-advanced knitters to create wearable replicas of at least 47 of the ganseys found in the old photographs. (The 47 designs are shown in a gallery printed on the book's back end papers.) The book has a chapter with general instructions for knitting a generic gansey sweater. Then the "patterns" for the local village sweaters follow. The instructions for the individual ganseys include (1) an original source photo, (2) an ink sketch of the gansey and its stitch patterning, (3) knitting charts and swatches that illustrate the required stitch patterns, (4) information on yarn and sizing, and (5) a color photo of the modern sweater being worn by a young model.

Unfortunately, many of the sweater and swatch illustrations are printed in the gansey's traditional dark navy blue, and the printing is so dark that it's difficult to see the stitch detail. However, I found that the detail was nearly always there to be seen, if I viewed the illustrations under a good strong light with a magnifying glass. This same trick worked for viewing the stitch pattern detail in the smaller historical photos, which look blurry unless magnified.

This book makes a great addition to the history section of any knitting book collector's library. It is also a wonderful sourcebook for knitters who are interested in designing their own fishermen's ganseys. (Because of their simple shape, ganseys are easy to knit, and it's fun to put together your own combinations of traditional gansey stitch patterns.)

For several years, I have tried to master the art of rolling Japanese-style omelettes. I even brought home a gorgeous Japanese iron omelette pan from Japan with no luck, but thanks to the clear step-by-step photos, I finally feel like I'm one step closer to mastering the proper technique to make beautiful rolled omelettes. There are so many fascinating tidbits and tips that have helped me to better understand Japanese food (I took four cooking classes around Japan when I was working there previously in 2011), and I feel that I am a better / more confident home cook for it.

I highly recommend this for anyone new to Japanese cuisine; the step-by-step photos are truly helpful in understanding the basic preparation of common dishes such as chawanmushi, tamagoyaki, steamed dishes, wagashi, etc.

Book Description: Behind this study of Virginia Woolf's novels is an intense interest in the person revealed in the novelist. The criticism is warm as well as acute and the whole study is felt to be a tribute reasoned and justified.

2nd edition (July 25, 1975) Back Matter: More than most novelists, Virginia Woolf benefits by an introducer. She is never, either by intention or equipment, the expected novelist. She chose the novel to adapt it deliberately and progressively to be the vehicle of her own subtle perception. Behind this study of the novels is an intense interest in the person revealed in the novelist. The criticism is warm as well as acute and the whole study is felt to be a tribute reasoned and justified - to a woman sensitive, compassionate, passionately honest and eager only for truth; to an artist quite unsparing of her own labour, finely gifted, self-effacing, serious and humourous. Bennett added two chapters on A Writer's Diary and on Virginia Woolf's critical essays for the second edition. Both can help our understanding of Virginia Woolf the novelist; the Diary by the insight it gives into her creative process and the fuller understanding we can gain of technical problems, the essays because they are about novels and novelists.

Review of the hardback: 'A critical study which strikes me as a real service to us all and to the fame of the author it expounds. ... The closest discussion of Virginia Woolf's methods as a novelist I have read and some of the most penetrating appreciations of her mind and style that have been written.' Desmond McCarthy, The Sunday Times

KIRKUS REVIEW: The novels of Virginia Woolf, her treatment of character, of narrative sequence, of moral values and of form -- and within these categories, her development from uncertain, experimental beginnings to maturity and genius as a writer. This critical appraisal of her work is intelligent, extensive, sympathetic, but the copious quotations from the author herself suggest that what one should learn of Virginia Woolf is to be found by reading her own books. This may serve as a guide in that direction. The market? The selected literary minority already enthusiastic admirers. Pub Date: Sept. 27th, 1945 ISBN: 052109951X

Joan Bennett (1896-1986), also known as Joan Frankau and born Aline Frankau, born in London, England, was a Cambridge literary scholar and critic. She was the daughter of Arthur Frankau (1849-1904) and writer Julia Frankau (1859-1916). She married Cambridge literary historian Henry Stanley Bennett (1889-1972) in 1920. She was educated at Wycombe Abbey School and in Hamburg and Paris and came to Girton to read Modern Languages then English, 1916-19. She was a University Lecturer in English 1936-63, a Fellow of Girton, and College Lecturer in English 1953-63 (Life Fellow 1963-86), and wrote one of the first critical studies of Virginia Woolf. In 1959, she was one of the expert witnesses for the defense in the Lady Chatterley Trial, she confirmed D.H. Lawrence's reputation as a novelist,

Publications by Joan Bennett include—
Four Metaphysical Poets – Donne, Herbert, Vaughan, Crashaw, Cambridge University Press 1934
George Eliot – Her Mind and her Art, Cambridge University Press 1948
Sir Thomas Browne – "A Man of Achievement in Literature", Cambridge University Press 1962

Andrew Haswell Green (1820-1903) is the protagonist of this fascinating historical fiction novel. He was christened the father of New York City for a considerable array of accomplishments including early work to encourage and support the creation of the amazing space that became Central Park and later heading the Central Park Commission with many problem solving cost-cutting activities while fostering the creation of the Metropolitan and Natural History Museums. He is credited with successfully bringing about the five borough/single city structure of New York, the project that led to the name of this book as many people considered it a great mistake. He was involved in the creation of New York’s first state park, Niagra Falls, to protect the area. As executor of former Governor/dear friend Samuel Tilden’s estate, Haswell used funds from the estate and creatively merged existing private libraries to establish the world renowned New York Public Library. Who knew?! Of all the familiar names associated with NYC and its landmarks, I have never heard of Andrew Haswell Green. Lee imagines through a well-researched and reasonably imagined story the personal and historical context that led to Green’s successes. Green was murdered at age 83 by a man who accused him of interfering with the shooter’s relationship with a woman. I want to avoid spoilers, because this is a story that, much like a murder mystery, has twists, psychological drama, characters aplenty and regular shifts between the present (1903) and various, not chronological periods during Green’s formative years. Lee introduces us to well-developed characters, imagining their thoughts and feelings, each a real person found in the historic records: the police Inspector who has significant ambition but sticks to an honest, persistent approach to investigating the murder; an unusual madame and her celebrity cliental; Samuel Tilden, attorney and later New York governor, who befriends young Andrew when as a simple store clerk and ultimately inspires him to become a lawyer; his father who seems to find young Andrew too feminine in his approach to work on the farm, no matter how fast and effectively he works; Andrew’s boss on a sugar plantation in Trinidad; his housekeeper who witnessed the murder and knows Andrew as well as anyone can. While I personally like the leaps among years that help explain the very complex Andrew and develop the story beautifully, I imagine some will find it confusing. If you want your historical fiction accurate and engaging and to teach you something you did not know; if you love wonderful character development and thoughtful writing; if you like a good story and want to be entertained; read “The Great Mistake.”

I’m so happy to share my friend Rinku Battacharya’s new book “Instant Indian”; it features 100 authentic recipes from around India, including dals, idli, curries, chaat, biryani, pulao, and more! There are also recipes for paneer, no-knead naan, yogurt, and spice blends.

I previously reviewed Rinku’s excellent “Spices and Seasons”; in recent months, I’ve jumped on the Instant Pot bandwagon and have found myself purchasing several Indian and international cookbooks designed specifically for the Instant Pot. Previously, I would avoid cooking dishes with dry beans due to the long soaking and cooking time required, but the Instant Pot handles most types of dried beans in 25 minutes or less, making it perfect for adding more protein and fiber into my diet (dried beans are also a very economical option).

Instant Indian is divided into 11 chapters, including regions, spices and kitchen basics, make-ahead basics (homemade paneer, masala paste, spice blends, and no-knead naan), breakfast and snacks (idlis, upma, dosas), rice and noodles, legumes and soups, vegetables and paneer, fish and shrimp, chicken and eggs, lamb and pork, desserts and drinks, and chutneys and raitas. You’ll find many restaurant favorites like alu gobi, tikka masala, butter chicken, saag paneer, and yogurt lassi.

For my review, I tested several recipes from different chapters including the tamatar masala anda, rajma with azuki beans, anda rassa, benarasi alu dum, and misthi pulao. I tested all recipes in a 3-qt. Instant Pot. The flavor of the misthi pulao was absolutely amazing due to sauteeing the spices in ghee first.

One suggestion I’ve found helpful is it’s well worth purchasing several additional accessories for your Instant Pot: at a minimum, buy extra seals (I find the color-coded ones particularly helpful) as smells tend to linger, if you cook curries often it’s worth having a seal just for those. My other suggestion is purchasing the clear glass lid for making yogurt. The hardboiled egg stand / silicone roasting rack by OXO is great too. And if you plan on making idlis, you’ll need to purchase an idli mold that will fit inside your Instant Pot.

Each recipe includes serving size, total time breakdown (this is important with the instant pot, as in addition to prep time you also have to factor in time for the pot to come to pressure, cooking time, and natural or manual pressure release), and whether each recipe is gluten-free, vegan, or vegetarian (many of the vegetarian recipes can be made vegan by swapping coconut ghee or using firm tofu for paneer). As a huge fan of chutneys (which are difficult to find and expensive in Japan), I love making my own using Rinku’s recipes (at first I used her slow cooker version, now I love the sweet and tangy pineapple chutney from Instant Indian!).

The index is extremely user-friendly and thorough and not only includes recipes by ingredient, but also grouped by breakfast dishes, main dishes, etc.

There are numerous delicious ideas for sauteed and curried vegetable medleys using readily available vegetables and seasonings that will add color and nutrition to every meal, and enough variety to keep me happily cooking for months. Recipes are also labelled as vegan, vegetarian, and gluten-free, making it super-convenient for those who follow those diets.

Whether you are a longtime fan of Indian cuisine or simply looking for new recipes to incorporate using your Instant Pot, “Instant Indian” is a fantastic resource that deserves a place in your kitchen!

I'm a big fan of the micro-history and loved books like [[ASIN:0140275010 Cod: A Biography of the Fish That Changed the World]] and [[ASIN:0142001619 Salt: A World History]]. Often the most entertaining part of these books is how they myopically distort the importance of their subject, but in this case it's hard to understate the importance of Sugar in the world of the 16th through 19th centuries. As the basis of the triangular (or as this book and other sources say, circular) trade, it drove the economy and human movement of the era.

The facts in the book seem solid and it is well illustrated. Although, and I can't put my finger on it, I found the book a little less than satisfying. The facts were great and I appreciated the Haitian History and the post slavery use of almost indentured Asian labor. I definitely cannot knock the book for being informative, it was well worth the read and had lots of eye opening facts. It just seemed to miss a little focus on its thesis. Maybe it's that micro history myopia made some connections get stretched a little. I was a little less than clear on connection of sugar and equality, seems like enlightenment may have affected sugar industry more than sugar drove enlightenment. Also the connection of Ghandhi to sugar was a little tangential.

Where the book did really shine was the histories of the plantations and the rarely discussed post slavery plantation systems. It is good to see the coverage of the Asian laborers who replaced the slave system. This is a rarely covered subject which deserves discussion.

All in all, It was a very worthwhile read and a great reference text for the era and the circular trade. But like I said, it seem to miss something - some coherence, but this is more than made up for in historic information.

On the cover of this book is a picture of a melting orange popsicle, which seems to accurately resemble what my brain feels like as a Stay-At-Home-Mom some days. Frozen, melting, sticky. This is exactly the kind of cranial (and emotional!) atmosphere Scheibe is trying to capture in her debut novel What Do You Do All Day?

Touted as "an American answer to Alison Pearson's I Don't Know How She Does It" (from the book jacket...and I can't attest to it's veracity, since I haven't read the referenced book!), Scheibe simultaneously won me over with her wit and annoyed me with her characters and their "other half" lives. It took some time for me to care about people named Portia and Health and Thom and people who lived in NYC, sent their kids to private school, worked at Christie's. How's that for reverse snobbery? But I hung on, because the book is about a woman named - simply - Jennifer, and I could at least relate to her.

Jennifer is a SAHM, having left her career as an antiques specialist at Christie's in order to stay at home with Georgia (5) and Max (1). Although the particulars of her life are unlike mine - she's trying to write a book on Hannibal, she has a famous child-actor star for an ex - the emotional struggles she has as she examines every decision she's ever made as a wife and mother did resonate with me. From a passage in the book: "I fear I'm unconsciously making deliberate choices that run me off the friendship road. My love for Georgia and Max is frequently so all-consuming that I simply don't have anything left to give anyone else...My long days of laundry folding and bottle washing give me a kind of peace that is hard to explain, even to myself. And yet I fear the day when the children move away and I am left to mend all the fences I've let fall."

This book certainly qualifies as chick-lit. And it has WAY too much language in it for me to recommend to truly discriminating audiences. But it is well-written, funny in parts, and offers many poignant and truthful passages about the difficulties and delights of mothering.
