The book has lots of terrific tips in writing one's life story/memoir, like:

1. Don't lose stories. We are the stories we tell. We are the stories which family members tell about us and themselves.

2. A life story is a gift one generation bestows to another generation.

3. See which family patterns are revealed across generations.

4. Make a list of 10-20 of the most important events in one's life.

5. Look at your life in a sociological, historical and cultural context.

6. Create an extended list of relationships/events which shaped your life, then group them, to narrow down to a core list.

7. Think of people as characters in a story. Create a story with plot, action, and settings. Refer to senses - don't use abstract words.

8. Stories also need a point of view and tone. A tone could be pity, admiration, etc.

9. Start stories close to the climax, in order to create suspense.

10. Different choices for organization - chronological, thematic (like religion, careers, etc.), and biographical, or a combination.

11 Chronologies can be dull - add action and suspense, which imply consequences later on.

12. Besides just facts (the "what") go into the "why".

13. Underlying the writings should be a theme/message - the way you understand the story. The theme is "who am I", "why I became so", etc. It is OK to begin w/o a theme and discover it in the process. The theme affects every fact in the story. Having a theme can also help to avoid writer's block.

14. Personal myths - how we perceive the world/life can be part of the story. Archetypes - instincts, patterns of thought - like a martyr being always a giver, orphan who doesn't develop or maintain personal ties, prince-left-at-the-pauper's-door like always aspiring to more than is expected.

15. There is no correct sequence in writing one's story.

16. Don't preach - just tell your story.

17. Use transitions to link stories. Write in the active voice, not passive. Write in the first person. Always italicize foreign words.

18. Don't recap, it's an insult to readers. Always look to eliminate the last paragraph.

19. Verisimilitude - must seem true, real - not too many details. Avoid cliches, stereotypes. Be complete, concise, not redundant. Use the 10% rule look to eliminate 10%, to force conciseness.

20. Slow down. It's a process.

Kelly Kwok, founder of "Life Made Sweeter," has unlocked the secret to delicious restaurant-style stir fries, noodles, curries, and desserts just like those you get from your favorite Chinese, Thai, or Korean restaurants, but without the sinkful of dirty dishes and piles of pots and pans! You'll find all your Chinese favorites like Beef and Broccoli, General Tso's Chicken, Lemon Chicken, Kung Pao Chicken, Lo Mein along with Galbi (Korean-style short ribs), Thai curries, Bahn mi, tom yum, pho, fried rice, noodle dishes, sides and desserts.

Most of these qualify as one-pot dishes (despite the title, not all involve the slow cooker), making prep and cleanup easy. Ingredients are listed in both US and metric equivalents, and most ingredients should be readily available at your grocery store. Each recipe has a gorgeous full-color photo as well. The sauces in particular are standouts, even more so considering that relatively few ingredients are used (so no trips to the Chinese/Oriental supermarket trying to track down hard-to-find sauces and pastes).

As a vegetarian, I loved the Asian-inspired soups like the Thai pumpkin curry soup, miso soup with vegetables and soba noodles, and Chinese hot and sour soup. There is a whole chapter devoted to meatless mains, including a vegetarian mapodofu, Thai red curry vegetables, Chinese eggplant with garlic sauce, General Tso's Brussels sprouts and sweet potatoes, and Thai basil tofu and vegetable rice casserole.

THAI BUTTERNUT SQUASH CURRY SOUP

YIELD: 4–5 SERVINGS

5 cups (2250 g) butternut squash (or pumpkin), peeled and cubed
1 cup (200 g) sweet potatoes, peeled, roughly cubed
1 medium onion, peeled, diced
1 tbsp (8 g) fresh ginger, peeled
3 garlic cloves, sliced
3 cups (710 ml) chicken or vegetable broth
1 (13.5-oz [400-ml]) can coconut milk
½–1 tbsp (8–16 g) red curry paste, to taste
½ tsp turmeric
1 tbsp (15 ml) fresh lime juice
Salt and pepper, to taste
Drizzle of coconut milk, for garnish (optional)
Pumpkin seeds, for garnish (optional)
Chopped cilantro leaves, for garnish (optional)
Sliced red chili pepper, for garnish (optional)

Place the squash, sweet potatoes, onion, ginger, garlic and broth in a 4- to 5-quart (3.8- to 4.7-L) slow cooker. Cook on low for 6 to 8 hours or on high for 3 to 4 hours, until the squash and sweet potatoes are soft and cooked through.

Remove the lid and stir in the coconut milk, red curry paste, turmeric and lime juice. Allow the soup to cool slightly before puréeing. Using an immersion blender, purée directly in the slow cooker or pour contents into a blender and purée until smooth. Adjust seasonings as needed with salt and pepper.

Serve warm in bowls and garnish with a drizzle of coconut milk, pumpkin seeds, cilantro and sliced red chili pepper, if desired.

I love that so many of the ingredients are readily available; nothing is more frustrating than finding a dish that looks great, but not being able to locate specialty ingredients (especially true with some Chinese and Asian cookbooks).

The addition of desserts was a nice touch as I love to use my slow cooker for desserts (I also highly recommend Michele Scicolone's "The Mediterranean Slow Cooker" for its desserts chapter). Here you'll find a mandarin orange cheesecake, Asian pear pudding cake, black sesame brownies, Chinese steamed sponge cake, ginger tea poached pears, Lunar New Year sweet rice cake, mango coconut tapioca pudding, matcha green tea cake, sweet green bean soup, and Thai coconut sticky rice with mango.

Here is Kelly's recipe for Black Sesame Brownies: the ground black sesame seeds lend an almost peanut-butter-like depth.

BLACK SESAME BROWNIES
YIELD: 10 SERVINGS
1 cup (125 g) all-purpose flour
¼ cup (30 g) unsweetened cocoa powder
2 tsp (5 g) black sesame powder or finely ground black sesame seeds
¾ tsp baking powder
¼ tsp salt
½ cup (58 g) unsalted butter
½ cup (90 g) semi-sweet chocolate chips
1 cup (225 g) sugar
3 large eggs, lightly beaten
1 tsp pure vanilla extract
½ cup (90 g) semi-sweet mini chocolate chips, plus more for topping, if desired

Take a long piece of aluminum foil and fold it lengthwise into a long strip. Press it along the inside perimeter of your slow cooker, creating a ring. This will prevent the edges from burning. Next, line the bottom with a piece of parchment, leaving an overhang on the sides for easier removal.
In a small bowl, whisk together the flour, cocoa powder, sesame powder, baking powder and salt.

Place the butter and chocolate chips in a medium microwave-safe bowl. Heat on high power for 30-second increments, stirring well after each, until completely smooth and melted. Whisk in the sugar until smooth. Beat in the eggs, one by one, then add the vanilla.

Slowly stir in the flour mixture until just combined; do NOT overmix. Fold in the mini chocolate chips. Pour the batter into the lined slow cooker and smooth out using a rubber spatula. Top with additional chocolate chips if desired.

Cover the slow cooker with a double layer of paper towels then place the lid securely over the towels. This prevents any water from dripping into the cake batter.

Cook on low for 21⁄2 to 3 hours, then remove the cover and cook for an additional 10 to 15 minutes. Remove the insert from the slow cooker and allow to cool completely. Lift the parchment paper to remove the brownies and slice into squares.

Kelly has also provided a handy guide to browning, cuts of meat, layering, sizes and brands of slow cookers, and general tips. In addition, a section on the Asian pantry includes a brief overview of staples such as black bean sauce / paste, sambal oelek, coconut milk, doenjang, dried chilis, fish sauce, spices, and other seasonings that you'll need to create the dishes in "The Asian Slow Cooker."

Verdict: If you love Asian cuisine but think you don't have the time to create it at home, think again! "The Asian Slow Cooker" will have you throwing out your takeout menus in favor of easy homemade versions with far fewer additives, plus there is enough variety and range of Asian cuisines (Chinese, Thai, Vietnamese, Korean) to keep you happily cooking for months to come. Happy (slow) cooking!

I’ve recently suspected a very close friend of mine as having Parkinson's disease (PD) with both movement and cognitive issues. Since he refuses to seek medical counsel, I decided to learn all I could via Internet searches and by purchasing seven (7) books on PD. It was during my reading that I discovered there are many other diseases (including brain tumors) that exhibit Parkinsonian systems yet are not PD. The fact that my friend had one parent who died of a brain disease and another parent and brother of liver failure made me want to explore the possibility of Wilson’s disease because it’s a recessive (requires genes from both parents) genetic (inherited) disease of copper accumulation and toxicity that affects both the liver and brain.

Although this book is written for the patient or possible patient (those with a copper abnormality) of this treatable disease, I read this from the perspective of someone who does not have the disease but wants to learn about what the signs are, what a person's life will be like, what are their challenges, what are their options, and what is their life expectancy. I did not feel that the Internet had enough information and wanted to get an expert’s advice. Dr. George J. Brewer, the author, is an expert on this disease which he substantiates by his 15-page accreditation at the beginning of the text.

This book is written in a way any lay person can understand. I learned what the disease was about, what the signs are, and after reading this, am almost certain my friend does not have Wilson’s disease since he is over 50 with a speech abnormality that dates back about 51 years and no evidence of Kayser-Fleischer (KF) rings of the cornea. The symptoms that are present with this disease (many of which are typical of Parkinson's disease) are as important as those that are not present. For instance, with Wilson's disease defects in sensation or weakness are not part of the disease. Also, its peak presentation of symptoms is before age 50 and often in the teens and early twenties. In 99.5% of the cases, those with symptoms have Kayser-Fleischer (KF) rings, which are copper deposits around the cornea. Also, speech abnormalities typical of Wilson’s disease would not date back more than a few years.

In summary, if caught early enough this disease is highly and easily treatable throughout life. If caught too late, treatment becomes more difficult, symptoms may not be reversible, and death may result. Although this book is very thin (there are only 102 pages of actual information about the disease if the glossary is excluded), the information provided is invaluable, well-written, and easily understood. The only thing I did not understand was Table 5 (page 91) on the monitoring recommendations for anti-copper therapies as it appeared to me as if column headings are missing. Other than this, I found this to be invaluable as a Wilson’s disease resource even though it is written in 2001.

As a child one of my favorite things to do was to look at things under a microscope. I vividly remember gathering a water sample from a swamp near the house and looking at a sample and finding my first paramecium. It has been years since I have owned a microscope, but with this microscope I can see how things have advanced and changed. This one does not have the same magnification as that microscope I had as a child but it is a lot easier to use and I can still see things with it that I cannot see even with a good magnifying glass.

This unit looks more like a drill press than a microscope, in terms of the design. The scope itself fits on a metal shaft and two turning knobs make it easy to raise and lower the scope in relation to the base. The base has two clips for holding down your slides or paper or whatever else you want to look at through the scope. There is no eye-piece on the scope – the image is viewed on a computer screen instead and the connection is made via USB.

Included with the scope is a software CD and this must be installed to use the scope. Installation is quick and painless. I installed under Windows 10 64-bit and had no issues. After installation I launched the software immediately.

The software consists of a view/capture application and a supplemental application for saving your work. The main part of the view & capture app is a live window that shows what is visible through the scope. As the object or slide on the scope base is moved, the image updates in real time. I found it a little awkward to line things up just right at first but I finally did manage to get things in the viewer just as I wanted them.

I started with a gray piece of paper that I thought was solid gray, but I found that the gray is actually a micro dot pattern like magazine print. More interesting was the corner of a $5 bill showing not just the print pattern detail but the fine fibers in the paper. A penny, cat hair and a very close-up view of a microfiber cleaning cloth all proved to be interesting subjects. Attached to this review are some of those detailed images, my favorite being the penny. I have not yet gone to the culvert near the house to gather water samples.

The software allows for two different capture types – photo or video. I have only played with the photo capture so far but it it very straightforward – click the photo button, either on the application interface or on the USB cable where the light level can be adjusted and the image appears in a list on the right side of the application window. If you double click the image you can save the image to the hard drive, zoom in on it and do a few other operations.

Linked to a tablet instead of a computer, this is a great travel scope to take with you. It is well-suited for classroom use as well as for use in the office.

I like this microscope. It is very easy to use, it does a good job of magnification and images are nice and clear. It is very different than the microscope I used growing up, in ways that I like. It's so much easier viewing on a screen than looking through a viewer, making this more fun to use too.

You should read [[ASIN:0544947304 Bannerless]] before attempting this second “Bannerless” novel, THE WILD DEAD, because you need the backstory to understand what the brown-uniformed investigators (Enid & Teeg) are tasked with. Both novels are set in a near-future coastal California, some 100 years after a worldwide plague wiped out most of humanity. Without enough people to keep the infrastructure going, most human civilizations (and their cities) simply collapsed under their own weight (“the Fall”).

Survivors from the Fall saved what technology they could, and established new self-sustaining households along the Coast Road. But these households are governed by strict rules designed to preserve natural resources. All women receive contraceptive implants, and no household can have a child unless the household has been awarded a “banner”. Banners are in short supply. They are only awarded when a local governing committee determines that a household can support the additional person without straining existing resources.

After the Fall, there is little serious crime, except for households that break the Coast Road rules in attempts to illegally win banners. Whenever a rule breach is suspected or complained of, a two-person team of brown-uniformed investigators is dispatched (usually on foot, because only solar-powered vehicles still exist) to resolve the problem. The investigators are “the law”, and they are much feared for their authority to impose penalties and to even break up misbehaving households.

In both Bannerless novels, the main character is Enid, one of the investigators. In this novel, Enid is dispatched to the Estuary, several days’ hike up the Coast Road, to investigate a complaint about a local community’s refusal to help rebuild a structure belonging to one of its households. When Enid arrives, it is clear that the structure is in appalling condition, so deteriorated that it would be a waste of precious resources to rebuild it.

But before she can turn for home, a body shows up on a muddy beach. It’s a young woman with a grievous wound to her throat—clearly a murder victim. But the victim isn’t a local; she’s from “the wild”, the interior where groups of people are still living amidst the cities’ ruins. People from the wild don’t follow the Coast Road rules, so the crime is outside Enid’s jurisdiction—unless the murderer happens to be someone from the Estuary and the Coast Road.

Estuary people recognize the victim as someone they traded with, but won’t volunteer any information to Enid or Teeg, “the brown bullies”. Enid’s headstrong partner wants to hang the crime on the obvious suspect, without evidence. But Enid persists in seeking out the truth, even though it requires a dangerous solo trek into the wild.

I liked THE WILD DEAD, though not quite as much as I liked the earlier novel. Author Carrie Vaughn has done a terrific job in establishing a believable post-apocalypse society, and in developing the character of the thoughtful, likeable Enid. This is a police procedural carried out in a highly unusual setting.

In PERSONAL, Jack Reacher must take out a world-class sniper who's not only shooting at prominent world leaders, but also using Jack's photo for long-distance target practice. The sniper, a guy that Jack sent to prison for 15 years--some 16 years ago--spent all his prison time practicing yoga and focusing his hatred for Jack. That's why the army wants Jack to use for sniper bait. And what's worse, Jack's least-favorite army intelligence officer, General Tom O'Day, is running the joint U.S./British/French/Soviet operation aimed at neutralizing the sniper.

Thus Jack's motivation is both personal and patriotic. In tracking the sniper, Jack leaves a trail of bodies--all righteous killings, of very bad guys, in self defense or defense of others. For the reader's benefit, Jack explains the science of breaking down doors, of disabling/killing people in hand-to-hand fighting, and of taking out big-time politicians with 50-Cal bullets fired at outdoor podiums from sniper positions nearly a mile away.

As Jack knows from his army experience: "It's not the same with a sniper out there." Soldiers hate all snipers, because of their ability to deliver instant, unseen death without warning. In this book, the reader feels the sniper's target on his/her back, just as Jack does, as Jack pursues his personal sniper.

The book is a page-turner of the best kind--the kind that keeps you reading because you want to know what the main character will decide to do next. The pace of the plot is varied, with segments of heart-pounding action and bloodshed, but also with segments of quieter strategic planning that afford the reader some respite. There are many grisly, bloody scenes, but there is no torture or anything else included simply for shock value.

This was my first Jack Reacher novel, and it totally lived up to the "Jack Reacher" series hype! As someone who enjoys well-written spy thrillers, I've indeed been missing out on something very, very good. PERSONAL is a terrific standalone thriller, and it has made me into a Jack Reacher fan. Happily, this is the nineteenth book in the Jack Reacher series, and I have eighteen more to catch up on.

He kills a white man, and the fact it is in self-defense will not help him. Throughout this novel, that takes us from 1913 Port Barre, Louisiana to a remote improvised camp near a lake, to a farm near Jefferson, Texas, to many years in Shreveport Louisiana, David makes choices, learns skills and meets people who shape his future, but none of this changes his fundamental nature honed by his loving upbringing. I want so badly to tell this story from beginning to end, because Simonds' is one of those authors who captures character, dialogue and dialect, nature and cityscapes, periods in history and why people do things we do not understand so beautifully. But saying more would require so many spoilers, so I will just include some random quotes below and tell you that Stork Bite is a lovely, lovely book with more than one "can't put it down" story. Rose Reisman has authored several good books on low-fat cooking, including Enlightened Home Cooking. This particular volume's profits go to the National Breast Cancer Fund, and a foreward from the chairman of the National Breast Cancer Fund. It has been scientifically proven that a diet high in animal (saturated) fat and processed meats results in a higher risk of cancer, particularly breast cancer and colorectal cancers, so lowering your saturated (and trans) fat intake is a win-win proposition.

Rose begins by recommending tips on family nutrition, including assessing whether a low-fat diet is appropriate for young children, equipment to reduce fat (nonstick cookware, cooking spray, minimizing salt in favor of other spices and herbs), and low fat dairy. If you're taking your first steps towards a low-fat diet, this is a good place to begin. If you already eat a low-fat diet or are looking for something more drastic, check out Dean Ornish's very-low-fat vegetarian diet [[ASIN:B0002IM29W Eat More, Weigh Less: Dr. Dean Ornish's Life Choice Program for Losing Weight Safely While Eating Abundantly]] that's proven to reverse heart disease (the Ornish diet disallows all full-fat dairy and meats, oils, butter, nuts and anything with more than a few grams of fat).

The book is arranged in a fairly straightforward arrangement beginning with appetizers and finishing with desserts. There's even a chapter geared towards children's favorites. Each recipe includes an in-depth nutritional analysis, tips, and make-ahead suggestions perfect for hectic school nights.

Although I'm a vegetarian, there were plenty of veggie-friendly recipes that appealed to me, including mashed white and sweet potato casserole, sweet potato fries, pasta dishes, and egg dishes. Also included were several low-fat cheesecakes that I haven't had the chance to try, but which looked interesting.

"Food, Family, and Tradition" is part memoir, part cookbook, all love. It traces Lynn Kirsche Shapiro's family roots in Czechoslovakia and Hungary and the tragedy of the Holocaust, as well as family dishes that were preserved and handed down for future generations. The book began as Shapiro's way to complete two unfinished legacies: her mother's recipes and her father's autobiography, but along the way became so much more, chronicling the richness of Jewish life in Eastern Europe prior to the Holocaust and the role of faith and strong family traditions that allowed Holocaust survivors to rebuild their lives after the war. The preparations and meals carried an essential ingredient of remembrance that connected them to lost loved ones.

The first half of the book traces the author's family roots in Czechoslovakia (her father Sandor Kirsche) and Hungary (her mother Margit) through period photographs, biographies, a family tree of victims and survivors, and original vignettes about Jewish culture, kosher wine, holidays and traditions. Sandor opened Hungarian Kosher Foods (the largest kosher supermarket in the Midwest) in Chicago in 1973 and it still thrives today. More than just an all-kosher supermarket, it has also become a place for the Jewish community to gather and connect.

Part two features 150 family recipes from Czechoslovakia and Hungary divided into ten chapters ranging from appetizers and soups to entrees and desserts. All recipes are kosher and marked as parve, meat, or dairy, and Yiddish / Hungarian names are given when applicable. Each recipe is introduced by a family story or the dish's origins, and many contain helpful hints (identified by red dotted boxes). You'll find staples like matjes herring, borscht, and blintzes, but one thing that stood out from my many other Jewish and kosher cookbooks was the inclusion of Hungarian dishes like rakott krumpli, goulash, cabbage with noodles, and fruit soups. I found many new recipes like the sweet bread kugel and golden dumplings that I look forward to making on a regular basis.

I own many Jewish cookbooks and have read much on the Holocaust, but "Food, Family and Tradition" really resonated with me for several reasons. Many of the recipes evoked those of my Polish grandmother (stuffed cabbage, borscht, kasha, chrain), and my Polish great-grandparents were grocers in 1920s Chicago. This is a beautiful cookbook that captures the spirit of prewar Czechoslovakia and Hungary's once-vibrant Jewish communities; their legacy lives on through these recipes that have been lovingly preserved and updated for modern kitchens.

A pleasantly uplifting collection of 20 poems, sectioned into 3 parts: FAITH, FRIENDSHIPS, and FEELINGS. Each poem is concise, and all are presented in a simplistically straightforward style that would appeal to audiences of many ages, education levels, and backgrounds. While God and faith are mentioned heavily throughout, Edmond incorporates the theme from a non-denominational, Christian standpoint that is comfortingly approachable. These poems will touch you in the same way that Hallmark greeting cards share simple messages of love, hope, friendship and forgiveness.

I greatly enjoyed the poem that reflected upon the differences between solitude and loneliness, perhaps because it resonated with me so strongly as an introvert who has lived under the shade of both umbrellas. Solitude is the state of being alone – alone but alone by choice. Loneliness is also a state of being alone – alone but alone by circumstance. I also appreciated the line: “Some will have a life prolonged while some a life cut short.”

The majority of these poems are not meant to rhyme, not specifically meant to thrill or entertain. While some patterns emerge sporadically, there is no consistent structure discernable in length of verse or stanza, no evident pattern of punctuation utilized exclusively. They are poetic prose in its simplest form. Raw, meaningful, and honest.

A concise yet heartfelt compendium of Edmond’s lifelong reflections. His sincerity of tone is refreshing!

From the publisher's website - 1969 Twelve women meet during a women's liberation conference in Boston. At a workshop on "women and their bodies," they talk about their own experiences with doctors and share their knowledge about their bodies. The discussions at the conference are so provocative and fulfilling that the following summer, each woman researches a health topic close to her heart. They decide to put their knowledge into an accessible form that can be shared with others and that can serve as a model for women who want to learn about themselves, communicate their findings with doctors, and challenge the medical establishment to change and improve the care that women receive.

1970 A 193-page course booklet on stapled newsprint entitled Women and Their Bodies is published by New England Free Press.

1971 The authors change the name of the book to Our Bodies, Ourselves, to emphasize women taking full ownership of our bodies. Republished by New England Free Press, the book puts women's health in a radically new political and social context and quickly becomes an underground success. It sells 250,000 copies, mainly by word-of-mouth.

1973 Simon & Schuster publishes the first commercial edition of Our Bodies, Ourselves.

The writing on the back of the box serves as the instructions and there is no mention that one has to insert 4 AAA batteries to get started. Instead it says to remove packaging material, remove the USB connector from the back of the keyboard and connect to an empty USB on the computer and viola it works. Not true.

First I had to insert 2 AAA batteries into the keyboard and 2 AAA batteries into the mouse. Batteries are NOT included.  Then I removed the USB receiver from the back of the keyboard and inserted it into an empty USB on my computer. I then slid the mouse button into the on position and everything worked.

After using this for a while, I hate this set, particularly the mouse. First of all the keyboard and mouse are not ergonomically designed. They are so flat and low profile that my hands are not at a comfortable angle for typing. I like keyboards that have those lift feet in the back. This keyboard does not. The worst part is the mouse since the hand rests completely flat and not at an angle like most mice. I also find the left and right controls on the mouse very sticky in the sense that they do not respond quickly to my clicks. The roll wheel works wonderfully, however.

In addition to the above, if the mouse is not used continuously, it goes to sleep even though I leave it in the ON position. In order to wake it up, I originally thought I had to turn it on and off (because the instructions do not say what to do). However, if I press down on the wheel, it will wake up for use again.

In summary, this set is functional but not one that works for me due to the low profile of both the keyboard and mouse and the sticky mouse buttons. This review was written using this set.

I bought this book while trying to expand my collection of grilling recipes. I enjoy cooking on the grill and I wanted to move beyond the simple hamburgers, hot dogs, and barbequed chicken parts. I looked at a variety of books on the subject, and this one struck me as a good value. I have not been disappointed.
The first thing about this book that grabbed my attention is that is it organized and bound like Betty Crocker's Cookbook, in a 3-ring binder with divider tabs. Everything is well laid out and organized in such a manner that if you are looking for specific recipes that are in this book, you have no excuse if you cannot find them.
Sections include beef, pork, fish, and poultry as main dishes. There is also a section for appetizers. In a nutshell, the sections are clear, sensible, and well planned. Finding different forms of beef burgers will be in the beef section, not spread all over.
I have obviously not tried all of the recipes in this book, but the ones I have tried have been big hits with the family. The recipes balance flavors well and give the cook an excellent foundation should the cook want to experiment and tweak a little bit. The book does *not* help you in the flavor department if you have a tendency to burn stuff...
Each recipe has different cooking instructions corresponding to charcoal grills and gas grills. This is a nice feature that makes this book accessible to a wider audience.
Overall, this is a great book for someone wanting to do more grilling. It is well organized, has lots of pictures, well written...

I selected this cookbook based on the subtitle – 100 Fast and Easy Recipes for the Whole Family. Our family is often in a state of transit and many times we have found ourselves short on time for food preparation, and it was my hope that this book would give us some “quick and dirty” ideas for meals that come together quickly. The healthy aspect would be a bonus. This has turned out to be a decent book with some good recipes in it. My only real complaint is in the organization.

This book breaks down the recipes into several logical groupings. There are five chapters of recipes (plus some additional material: 15 Minute Prep, 30 minutes or Less, 5 Ingredients, One Pot or Skillet, and finally Slow Cooker. This is a double-edged sword. On one hand, it allows for finding recipes that come together in a time frame that fits your schedule, and that’s great. We live and die by the slow cooker so having this grouping is very useful for us. However, if instead you want to find recipes based on ingredients or cuisine, it becomes and exercise in hunting. Yes, there is the index at the back of the book and that does help, but having a couple of pages in the front with a different table of contents, organizing the recipes differently (though not rearranging the paging) would be really helpful.

What this book does not have a lot of is full-color pictures. There are some, but the majority of recipes do not have a pic with them. This is all right and it does cut down on the amount of paper and ink and therefore the production cost. It does mean that those of us that eat with our eyes first may find this presentation a little less exciting.

Surprisingly, this cookbook does not rely on weird or hard-to-find ingredients in the majority of recipes. Often, books that offer “healthy” recipes do so by eliminating common ingredients and bringing in more unusual ones (for example, chestnut flour). So far, the recipes I have tried have not required a trip to the health food store.

Every recipe is labeled with a brief health-conscious summary. These are labels such as “gluten free”, “vegan”, “nut free” and so on. This is great for people with dietary restrictions that need some ideas. If you look in the index, the recipes are listed not only by alphabetic order but also by these categories. So, finding a recipe that falls into one of the dietary categories (such as vegetarian) can be found in the index fairly easily.

I have not tried too many of the recipes yet. However, those I have tried have worked out well. Prep is usually easy and the results have been good. So far, I haven’t hit any duds.

This is not a perfect book, but it’s a good collection of healthy-minded recipes for busy families. It’s definitely worth a look if you want a collection of recipes that do not require a big investment in time and are on the healthier end of the scale.

THE ECHO KILLING: A MYSTERY is a competently, professionally written private investigator mystery, but it’s just plain boring. Also, the basic premise, that two murders committed 15 years apart must be linked because the crime scenes are almost identical, is weak and unconvincing from the get go.

In the novel, a journalist (Harper) investigates a career woman’s murder. The woman’s nude body was discovered on her kitchen floor by her 12-year-old daughter who had arrived home from school. Harper can relate to the girl, because the exact same thing happened to her when she was 12 (she discovered her mother’s nude body on the kitchen floor after school). The crime scenes are eerily similar—from the body’s unposed position on the floor to the fact that all of the evidence (clothing, fingerprints, blood, residue under fingernails) was removed.

Harper, hoping to finally identify her mother’s killer, is driven to investigate, and uses her special police reporter privileges to access evidence boxes, old and new police reports, etc. The investigation is a slog, as Harper manages to slowly recover various significant photos and documents. The only relief is provided by Harper’s illicit, white-hot relationship with an undercover police detective (Luke), who saves her life from time to time.

POSSIBLE SPOILER ALERT: The perp is guessable, though the perp’s motivation isn’t particularly believable—it’s wildly inconsistent with the perp’s character. There are a lot of reasonably well-drawn characters in the novel, but none of them stand out as memorable—not even Harper.

This book is beautifully designed, has a pleasing variety of interesting-to-knit sock patterns by leading designers, and loads of valuable instructional material. However, because the how-to information is organized around specific sock projects, this is more of a pattern book than a reach-for-it reference on sock-knitting techniques. For example, although many heel styles are explained (round, short-row, band, Dutch, etc.), the actual instructions are not all grouped together in a single chapter on "heels"--instead, you may have to go to one of the patterns that uses a particular heel type to find the actual step-by-step instructions.

The book includes ten top-down patterns, and seven toe-up patterns. Cast-on and bind-off techniques are illustrated with clear line drawings. Patterns are written out in standard sock pattern style (general information, leg, heel, foot, toe, finishing--or the reverse). Charts are included when appropriate (twisted-stitch and colorwork designs). There is a general chapter on designing, and there are notes and design tips scattered throughout.

A "Design Techniques" box accompanies each pattern. The feature breaks down the sock construction by the techniques used, and provides a "road map" to the page locations for additional how-to instructions on the techniques. For example, Veronik Avery's "Happy Go Lucky Boot Socks" pattern uses these techniques: (1) top down construction, (2) designing with slip stitches, (3) working with five double-pointed needles, (4) any elastic cast-on, (5) round heel, (6) wedge toe, and (7) Kitchener stitch.

All of the patterns are beautiful, as you would expect from these famous sock designers: Cookie A., Nancy Bush, Anne Hanson, Veronik Avery, Deborah Newton, Evelyn A. Clark, Meg Swansen, Ann Budd, Chrissy Gardiner, Kathryn Alexander, Priscilla Gibson-Roberts, Eunny Jang, Melissa Morgan-Oakes, Anna Zilboorg, and Cat Bordhi.

The book also includes a 95-minute DVD. Ann Budd discusses the individual projects (displaying the actual knitted samples and describing the techniques each uses), and demonstrates the knitting techniques. If you learn best by watching someone else knit, you will really like this "bonus" DVD. Because of the DVD, the book can dispense with step-by-step still photographs of the more complicated techniques, and include many more close-ups of the knitted socks themselves.

As a pattern book, I rate this at 5 stars; as a technical reference book, at 3.5 to 4 stars. My favorite Ann Budd sock knitting book is still [[ASIN:1596680296 Getting Started Knitting Socks]], for new knitters. Two really excellent sock-knitting reference books are [[ASIN:0823085538 The Sock Knitter's Workshop: Everything Knitters Need to Knit Socks Beautifully]], for somewhat experienced knitters; and [[ASIN:1564775704 Sensational Knitted Socks]], for all knitters, regardless of experience. Two personal favorite sock-knitting books are [[ASIN:0934026971 Folk Socks]], which has a lot of interesting patterns and good general instructions; and [[ASIN:0973394005 Lucy Neatby's Cool Socks Warm Feet]], a very popular book by my favorite designer, who is probably the most technically accomplished knitter on the planet.

"On What Grounds" is an entertaining mystery set in a novel location: New York City's Village Blend, a hundred-year-old coffeehouse run by Clare Cosi.

One of Clare's employees is discovered unconscious at the bottom of a service staircase. The police are quick to write it off as an accident, but Clare's gut feeling is that someone pushed Anabelle, in part because of the mysterious location of one of the shop's trash cans. She digs deeper into possible suspects: Anabelle's fellow dancers at Studio 10, her money-grasping stepmother, and her socialite boyfriend Richard (nicknamed "The Dick" by Esther, Anabelle's snide roommate).

For those of you who are addicted to Starbucks, Second Cup, Beaners, or another chain of choice, "On What Grounds" practically reads like coffee porn, with its sensuous descriptions of brewing ("That way the espresso oozes out of the portafilter like warm honey," "next came the steamed milk, splashing into the dark liquid like a white tsunami"), bean choice ("The sensual, sweet, full-bodied aroma of the [Jamaican Blue Mountain] coffee flowed over me"), and all things coffee (choice of brewing methods, roasting, storage tips). In addition, there are several intriguing recipes, coffee and otherwise, including Cappuccino Walnut Cheesecake (made with espresso), raspberry-mocha bocci, and the wickedly decadent coffee cocktail Screaming Orgasm (Kahlua, Amaretto, vodka and heavy cream).

The book does suffer from stilted writing and unrealistic dialogue at times, but the steamy tension between Clare and ex-hubbie Matteo (son of the Village Blend's French owner) and Detective Quinn, along with several memorable escapades to charity auctions, dance studios and New York's gay district Christopher Street, makes this a unique, decadent read that coffee lovers will drain to the very last drop.

In DARK TIDE RISING: A WILLIAM MONK NOVEL, Commander Monk returns to miserable Jacob’s Island, and it isn’t kind to him. I don’t like author Perry’s “Monk” series nearly as well as her “Pitts” series, and this “Monk” novel was extremely disappointing. I guessed the identity of the perpetrator within the first quarter of the book, and the plot winds up with a highly contrived, Perry-Mason-like courtroom scene.

In the novel, Monk is summoned by his friend, Sir Oliver Rathbone, to organize a ransom-payment and kidnap-victim-recovery operation at Jacob’s Island on behalf of Rathbone’s client, Harry Exeter. Exeter’s adored wife Kate has been snatched, and Exeter is willing to pay everything he has to get her back. When the Jacob’s Island recovery turns into a disaster, Monk has a new problem to solve--which one of his most trusted men was the one who betrayed his well-laid plans to the kidnappers?

The novel is well written, and nicely develops the character and backstory of Monk’s right-hand man, John Hooper. However, the plot isn’t believable--the perpetrator’s scheme was far too risky at the outset, because it depended completely on what certain other people might do and think after the initial kidnapping happened.

The novel works fine as a standalone, if you’re new to the “Monk” series. Author Perry really knows how to incorporate all the necessary details from earlier novels into later ones without giving away any prior plot endings or boring the reader with long passages of backstory.

I paired and typed with this keyboard on the following four devices:

1. iPad3
2. iPhone5
3. BLU Life One 4G LTE Smartphone - GSM Unlocked
4. Nexus 7 3rd generation

It paired easily with the first two iOS (Apple) devices. However, the first-time pairing with the Android devices (items 3 and 4) took a lot of trial and error. I spent about 20 minutes trying to get each Android device to recognize the keyboard. I wound up charging the keyboard thinking it lacked power but it had a sufficient charge. When charging the keyboard did not help the situation, I turned the keyboard on and off, turned Bluetooth on and off, kept trying the pairing button with each attempt, etc., etc. Eventually, it finally worked but not without a lot of frustration. Also, with one of my devices, it paired using the MAC address of the keyboard and not the name.

In order to pair a Bluetooth device, one has to:
- Turn on the keyboard. Note that keyboard light will flash blue but only for a few seconds and it’s hard to see it. (Sometimes it did not flash for me, instead it was a steady blue).
- Enable Bluetooth on the device you are pairing it with. The device must be no more than 32 feet from keyboard.
- Press and hold “pair device” button on keyboard for about 5 seconds--LED light starts flashing on keyboard.
- When the “Bluetooth Wireless Keyboard” is found on your device, select it to complete the pairing process.
- To maximize keyboard functionality, once paired press FN + S for an iOS device and FN + A for an Android device. It’s at this point that the keyboard is ready to use.

There are multi-function hot keys like Shift + ~ to return to the Home Page or Shift + ! to begin a Search using the default browser on the paired device. However, the best use of the keyboard is for straight typing, in my opinion.

PROS

- I like the feel of the keyboard. It’s pliable, folds easily, and does not slip out of my hands.

- A micro-USB charging cable is supplied for charging the keyboard.

- Supposedly, this is waterproof. However, I did not dare submerge it in water. I will take their word for it.

CONS

- This keyboard is not designed for a touch typist like me. For instance, the QWERTY keyboard layout is a bit off because the B key is located on the right-hand side of the fold. I use my left hand to hit the B key but with this keyboard, I either have to over stretch my index finger to reach the B key or use my right hand.

- There are no risers for the keyboard; instead it lies very flat. In order for me to effectively type on this, I have to prop the top end on a book so that the keyboard lays on a slant.

- The keys are not sensitive to the touch, so I have to press hard in order for the letters to type.

- It’s difficult to determine when the keyboard is powered on. Many times I had to press and hold the power button until the light flashed as a simple press of the button would not work. The instructions say the blue light flashes for three seconds when on but this did not always happen for me. Sometimes the blue light came on steady indicating the keyboard was on. It was not always consistent. I wound up either pressing the pairing button to see if the pairing light would flash or just tried typing when paired with a device. Depending on whether the keyboard worked or not, I knew whether it was on or not.

On another note, when I registered this keyboard on the VisionTek site, I got a confirmation email with my username and password in clear text. This is poor security as passwords should not be sent in clear text over the Internet.

In summary, had I tried out this keyboard in a store, I would have never selected it. Unless I am typing a lot with my Nexus 7, this is just too difficult to use due to the effort that has to be used to type, the flatness of the keyboard, and the slightly odd layout. I love the feel of the keyboard and its compactness but other than this, I’m disappointed.

I have had several pairs of Panasonic headphones and I regard them as a budget-grade phone that is better than generic but leaves room for improvement. I was hopeful that these phones would be better and would distinguish themselves as better than average. Unfortunately they do not and they suffer from the same issues I have had with other Panasonic phones in the past. They're certainly not bad, but there is some room for improvement.

First off, these look great, though I would stop short of calling them "retro" in appearance. They're styled to be retro-looking, but they betray their youth in the plastic details. That said, they have the cool factor that they are going for and the will stand out over most run-of-the-miss headphones than you'll find most people using.

One of the problems I have with these is strictly a personal preference. When I use over-the-ear phones like these, I want a phone that clamps down tight over my ear and applies some pressure. This does two things for me - it cuts down on the chances that they'll slip off when I look down, and it cuts sound leakage when I am listening to something. These are a more relaxed, loose fit, and this is not to my tastes. There's a good number of users that will be very happy with the way these fit, and as I said this is a preference, so I cannot say this is a fault. It's something to keep in mind, though. Aside from the tightness (or lack thereof), the pads and band are soft and these can be worn for a long while without issue.

These are Bluetooth phones, so I used them to connect to my Android tablet. They connected very quickly and without any real issues. I have no complaints there. They stay connected once paired and the range is good to at least 20-30 feet from the source which is good.

Where these headphones fail, though, is in the most important area - the sound profile. The highs are slightly muddy though not unacceptably so. The bass is present and not overdriven which to me is a very good thing. But, the midrange is not right at all, and as a result the music sounds like it is coming out of a tunnel when I am listening. Yes, I could fix this with an equalizer, but many people will not think to do that or do not have access to one. This is a familiar issue I have had with Panasonic phones, and unfortunately these do not correct the issue.

For speech, these sound just fine.

These are interesting phones and they look good. For those liking a loose fit, they're going to be very comfortable. However, there is an issue in the sound profile that anyone serious about their music will not be able to help but notice, and at the price point it's a more serious issue than if these were inexpensive (budget) headphones.

Sometimes you know that you have a great book in your hand. I felt this after reading just a few pages, it was reading classic literature, not just a kids book. In the end, I don't know that everything was brilliant, but at worst, it was all extremely well written. The characters are beautifully fleshed out. The relationship between Micah and his Grandfather was beautifully sincere and believable. The storyline was wonderfully braided and the back story of Aunt Gertrude was masterfully handled.

Stories about faith in magic are rather commonplace and could easily be cliché. I was afraid that this book might go the way of, well, every single Santa Claus story. And Micah's stalwart new friend Jenny does rather bluntly play the familiar role of pure logic against Micah's faith. But her character is also well crafted and it works fine.

But beyond the writing skills and crafting of the book, the most important thing is how readable this book is. It is fantastic and I plan on putting it in my Christmas/birthday book gift packages. This is easily the best juvenile lit I have read in a while, and I have read a lot as my kids progress to the tween years. I know that this book has been compared to Roald Dahl, who I love, but this story is so much better told than his plots are in general. Perhaps it could be compared to Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, but this book is so much more elegantly laid out than Dahl ever managed. Beasley's handling of Gertrude's back story where she is manipulated into testing her belief in magic is masterful. Also, the character or Victoria - not wanting to give spoilers - enters the story so smoothly. Her character is woven into the narrative so well that I want to read it again for the first time just to feel the way she mysteriously enters and so unmysteriously exits the story.

Also, I loved the handling of the Grandfather's miracle. It is kept under wraps well, and although I felt like I had a pretty good idea what the miracle was, there was tension about the details that kept me guessing till the last full reveal. This is truly a magical book. Bravo. Look forward to her next.

Karin Kallmaker's Acknowledgments
If you really enjoy something, I recommend doing it at least twice, especially if it involves partnering up with someone whose love of the results matches your own.
Working with Radclyffe is like finding the perfect partner for tennis--one challenging enough to get you out of your own zone, leading to the mutual goal of a fantastic volley based on complementary strengths. For this anthology, she lobbed balls over the net and waited patiently to see if I could return service. When I did, ooo, baby, did we have fun!
Having collaborated before on In Deep Waters 1, we spent less time making sure we were in sync and more time just plain playing. I hope readers are as amused and excited as I am by the results. Any resemblance of our characters to persons living are purely coincidental. Let's just say that I suspected Radclyffe of having a twisted and inspired sense of humor, and I wasn't wrong.
Speaking of characters, several of mine from previous works make an appearance in this volume. With a librarian's convention in town, "Twenty-One" of course makes Marian and Liddy from One Degree of Separation a natural choice. Brandy and Tess of "Lucky 7" first appeared in All the Wrong Places. "Lucky 7" continues the storyline from "Cruising Solo" in the first In Deep Waters. Author Carolyn and her agent Alison, from Paperback Romance, are attending the romance writer's convention, reaping the rewards of fifteen years' pride in "Payout."
Though I want to say that such stories, and the few other affectionate jokes in this volume, are all for the readers, honesty demands that I admit that I love revisiting my old friends. I truly hope that readers enjoy the results as much as I do.
Gambling is often compared to the risks of love and relationships. I'm not sure why, since inherently gambling means someone loses and someone wins, and the odds are always lopsided. So while we play with the metaphor, it is flawed. In practice, writing with Radclyffe about gambling, love, and sex defies the metaphor completely, because everyone comes out a winner.
-- Karin, January 2008

n 2006, at 14, Harry travels with his parents, Wayne and Chevrolet, to Tanzania. Already acutely aware that his parents are neglectful and not much his cup of tea, Harry calls them by their first names. Wayne is selfish, racist, boorish, politically a member of a third party, the "Purists," who just won the presidential election. They are obviously MAGAs but with their own party. Wayne is an untenured professor at an unnamed school in their fictitious town of Edward, Pennsylvania, located near the famous still-burning town of Centralia. Chevy is germaphobic, constantly critical, and runs an Ayurveda healing clinic. She's right in there with Wayne politically. In Tanzania, as Wayne and Chevy continually embarrass Harry with their xenophobic, racist and classist comments during tours and in the hearing of locals, Harry meets a "dark" man who pays attention to him and makes him a special gift. Harry never forgets that this man "saw" him and was kind to him like no one has ever been.

The family hits hard times financially and Harry essentially runs as fast as he can to college in New York by accepting a sell-your-soul opportunity that he recognizes as problematic. There, he meets Maryam, a Nigerian (although I'm not completely sure she's Nigerian from how she shares this with Harry) woman on a student visa. In New York, Harry also begins to actively work toward realizing his belief that he (is/should be/wants to b)e Black. Given this, one would think that his relationship with Maryam would be completely superficial, solely based on her being the right race and from a continent he associates with a happy experience. Instead, Okparanta creates a real friendship, a deeply loving relationship but one where Harry continually says and does things that shows his many assumptions about race that still reflect the common racism of white people in the USA. Maryam is fundamentally a decent person who is more mature than Harry, but enjoys him and sees his essential goodness. She subtly and not so subtly alerts Harry to his biases, but he does not realize how she has influenced him or how badly he has behaved until, he looks back at his life after their college years.

In the meantime Harry bobs along through life, trying to assimilate as a Black man, yet sounding suspiciously like a white guy who hasn't a clue. Okparanta constantly sneaks in just about believable incidents that test who Harry really is, often juxtaposed against Maryam, whose moral compass and sense of who she is is well formed. I think to like this book at the level I like it, you have to feel sympathy and compassion for the not always likable Harry. I see him as growing, but not as fast as he should because he isn't paying attention to Maryam's cues. And in other ways, his efforts to be Black are so inauthentic that Maryam is simply bewildered. Because, while he hints at this, he doesn't out and out tell her he is or wants to be Black.

I find Okparanta's satire priceless, she thoroughly schools us on how white "allies" who believe they have assimilated cannot and have not but in an amusing manner that even has heart for Harry.

I have always been interested in the links between the Old and New Testaments (OT and NT, respectively) in the Bible, and this book obviously grabbed my attention. It is a huge volume, filled with a lot of well-researched and thought-out information that draws connections between the Testaments when it comes to the Messiah in particular. I would stop short of calling it exhaustive, but it is a very good resource for anyone looking to connect OT prophesy with NT fulfillment of prophesy.

This is a big book – over 1,400 pages. It would weight a whole lot more and be a lot bigger in size if printed on normal paper but it is printed on the thin paper typically used in Bibles. Because of this it is roughly the size of a collegiate dictionary.

The table of contents contains a large number of chapter entries that are ordered by books of the Bible; that is, the first writings that are linked to actual OT chapters deal with topics in Genesis and the last end in Malachi. While this is not especially important in this volume (there’s no reason it had to be ordered this way in this case), being ordered in the same way as the books of the OT makes comparison and searching easier.

I will state up front that I have not read this whole book through yet. There’s a tremendous amount of material to cover and there just isn’t enough time to dedicate like I would like to do, but I have gone through some of the chapters. Those that I have read are very well researched and include a good number of references, very much like a research paper. Some of the annotations read like notes in a study Bible while others reference supporting material and papers by other authors who have conducted their own studies. Sticklers for identifiable references will be satisfied, though I suspect most readers will not bother digging so deep to follow all of those references.

Because the book is assembled from multiple sources written by multiple authors, there is some variance in the writing styles. While this is acceptable, there are occasions where one author makes a stronger case for a prophetic link than others. There is very definitely a difference in the conclusions at the end of each chapter as well – while some authors make their cases throughout the chapters they have written, others write a lot of historical information and contextual detail, and then use the conclusion (often a single paragraph) to tie the OT and NT together through less tangible statements. This is all well and good but it does mean that some topics are not as strongly argued.

I should mention that this is not an exhaustive volume that covers everything possible. On one hand, there are likely links that are not explored in this volume (or cases can be made to explore more OT passages and conclude that they foretell of the Messiah). Also, when trying to discern what OT scripture foretells about the Messiah and how it is fulfilled in the NT, theological frameworks should not be too relevant: this is a book on prophecy, not theology, and it sticks fairly close to making those connections without delving too deep into any particular theological framework (at least what I have read so far). That said, there are some who would disagree with me on that point and argue that theology is of utmost importance. That’s all right, but it is a distraction from the point of this book. On a more important note, though, is that some may disagree with conclusions drawn when it comes to the links between the OT and NT in some cases, and in those cases the references can provide some insight into how the link was made.

This is a very good resource for the student who is deeply interested in OT prophesy as it relates to the Messiah. The OT provides the prophesy, and the NT provides the fulfillment of said prophesy. This book highlights those connections. I would not call it exhaustive as I am sure more connections can be drawn, but it is a great starting point for the Bible scholar looking to “connect the dots” of scripture and gain a deeper understanding of how the OT and NT relate to one another.

I have kept a journal for many years, and though I have most of my writing and scraps kept on the computer in a software application I do have paper journals too. A physical journal has some opportunities for creativity that are difficult at best to achieve on a computer. With this book, I got more than I expected, and it is fair to say it goes beyond creative journaling, but does not address journaling techniques.

This book is absolutely stuffed with creative ideas, some of which are specific to journal-keeping and some that are less specific. For example, there are a number of creative projects for creating calendars, lists, maps, trackers and more. These are certainly in context in a journal but they stand on their own as special projects. Other things in this collection, such as unique paper treatment, book coverings and more which are very much in the realm of journaling.

This is not a book to tell you how to write in a journal, though. I have other books that are specific to actually writing out journal entries – techniques and strategies, if you will – and this book covers none of that. Rather, this book is more an idea book for creating more artistic entries and pages and papers.

This is a nice book on getting creative when building your journal. It is full of great ideas for making interesting entries and volumes. It does not address journaling techniques, so if you’re looking for a comprehensive book on journaling this isn’t it. However, if you want some great ideas for creativity and crafting when it comes to your journal, this is a great resource.

I like the English Standard Version (ESV) and it is my translation of choice (and has been for many years). Journaling in a Bible is something that I am not in the habit of doing but I see the value in it, so this seemed like a reasonable choice for me. It's a good idea but there is some room for improvement.

I'll start with the positives. I like the leatherette cover, which is a reddish color with an embossed pattern that makes this volume stand out and also has a nice, tactile feel to it. I prefer this type of cover to paperback and hard cover, especially since it seems to last longer than most. The inner pages are single column with a wide, ruled area for writing and journaling.

There are a couple of negatives that could be improved upon to make this volume better. The font size is small - 7.5pt - and that's uncomfortable for people with bad eyesight. It doesn't bother me, but it won't work well for those who need a larger font size to read comfortably. And, the ruled lines, which are supposed to be for journaling, do not leave enough room for actually journaling but are better used for a few sparse notes.

Overall, making this Bible larger would solve the two issues - more room to write and easier font to read.

I do like this Bible and I can see some use for it, but probably not as it was intended. It's fine for taking notes and I think it's fine for a reference Bible when traveling, but I would consider something larger if you truly want a journaling Bible.

The author, who was a professor at Stanford's Graduate School of Education and Business, suffered a stroke on Labor Day weekend in 2010. This is her narrative of the challenges she faced and still faces and how she had to re-frame her identity. Within the context of her story, she weaves the narratives of other stroke survivors from the age of 13 all the way up to 64 years.

What is very clear is that there is hope but there is also extreme disappointment when stroke survivors are not able to be the person they once were. Depending on the situation, the physical, speech, cognitive, medical, sexual, and support challenges differ as survivors navigate their life with a new identity.

It was clear that most of the people interviewed for this book have family and other support. There was not one person who was profiled that did not have at least some support at the beginning. In this case, this book is a view of "those who have." A stroke survivor who has absolutely no family or friend support and no money or insurance would most likely not even have the good to moderate recovery some the of the survivors profiled have.

In the end, the author lists the biographies of the survivors. Only one survivor was totally paralazed and mute and could only move her eyes. The rest did recover somewhat. What I love is that the author is forthright in saying she had help in writing this book due to her stroke. It makes one realize that accomplishments are possible if there is a support network available. Unfortunately for those who don't have that, the road to recovery, although possible, is bleak. I wish the author would have profiled those type people as well.

This is the 15th anniversary edition of Peter Reinhart’s now-classic work The Bread Baker’s Apprentice. Reinhart is a strong proponent of slow rise baking and using pre-ferments, and having started with this work I have turned out some of the most amazing breads in my kitchen, far and away better than when I first started baking bread. My older copy is well worn and the binding is starting to show its age. As soon as I discovered that this new edition was being released I ordered it, not only to find out what’s different in this edition but also to have a fresh, strongly bound copy with which to work. Much is the same as before, but there is some new material here too.

The author explains the ideas and concepts behind slow-rise baking in very good detail, through a series of steps with detailed explanations. Granted, some of these steps to not require a lot of thought or detail (organization, punching down the dough, etc.), while other steps benefit from a lot more detail and explanation. If you already use a slow-rise method, even if it is different than the author’s, it is good to read through this material and get a good feel for his approach as it is very possible that you can glean some good ideas from his methods.

Pre-ferments (or “starters” if you prefer) are another important topic, and Reinhart uses them heavily in his formulas. These really do have an important impact on the dough and the resulting bread, from the texture, the rise and of course the flavor. He explains the differences between the different pre-ferments, poolish (similar to a young sourdough starter) and biga (much like a small pre-made dough ball) in particular. Of the various formulas I have used from this collection, the ones that have been most memorable and have gotten the most compliments have been based on poolish pre-ferments.

Included is a very solid collection of formulas for making amazing loaves of bread. Most have full-color photos with them so you can see what you are making. Each formula includes an explanation of the hydration levels (liquid to dry ingredient ratios) which matters in handling the doughs.

There is a lot more to this book than just a collection of recipes on making bread though. Reinhart shares a lot of information on the history of breads, how gluten in the wheat works in the rise, materials and preparation and a lot more. While some of this might not be of much interest to the baker wanting to plunge in and get started, it is good material that is very much worth the read and provides a lot of insight on how to get better at making bread and how to do it right.

So, what is new in this edition that is not in the old? There are some obvious updates: the preface, the acknowledgments and the resources list have all been rewritten for this new edition. However, what is not obvious unless you look for it is the collection of notes that have been attached to each formula. The formula introductions have been changed in places too. These have been adjusted to reflect changes in the way the author understands ingredients or when he has found improved methods and supplies, and in some cases to communicate how a specific formula has been received and/or influential. There have been some formatting adjustments too, such as font colors and typefaces. What has not changed is the collection of formulas themselves (ok, there are some very minor adjustments but very few and very small, an example being the amount of flour used for Pain a l’Ancienne being more narrowed) or the photography, all of which stand on their own as-is, and the author’s passion for the subject which is undeniable.

So, if you have the first edition, is there compelling reason to buy the new one? To be honest, no not really. The formulas and methods are mostly unchanged and the tweaks made to all of the notes do not justify the cost of moving to a new edition. However, if you do not have the previous version or you need a new copy like I did, buy this one instead of the other, so you will benefit from the most current ideas and methods the author provides. The differences are in the fine-tuning, not the “big picture” ideas.

I am not an expert by any means, but this is the book I started with to learn about slow-rise breads and the first edition was a real eye-opener for me. The author is not the only one out there producing bread books espousing slow-rise and pre-ferments, but he is arguably the most well known and the most detailed and technical writer on the subject. Though this method takes a lot more time to produce excellent bread, the time investment is very much worth it and it is difficult to go back once you know the difference. This is the best starting point for learning how to make outstanding breads at home, and if you are willing to make a time investment you will be rewarded with some incredible breads. If you already have the first edition and it's in good condition, the need to move to this new edition is small, but this edition is a solid and excellent work in its own right. I am happy with copy of the new edition and will wear it down like I did the old one.

From the book jacket notes, you’d never guess that GALWAY GIRL: A JACK TAYLOR NOVEL is written in a quasi-Joycean style--with cryptic literary quotes separating chapters, frequently-changing stream-of-consciousness viewpoints, unexpected flashbacks that mix up the plot’s chronology, and many references to Irish culture and the Galway locale. There’s a mildly interesting story in there, but the reader must work to find it.

In the novel, a killer trio is out to get private investigator Jack Taylor--the three are Jericho, a psychotic “Galway girl”; Scott, the estranged son of a deceased Guard; and Stapleton (aka Stapes), a burglar. They have their reasons--Taylor killed Jericho’s lover, killed Stapes’ father, and witnessed Scott’s killing of a Guard. Jericho and Scott are evil, feeding off murder and destruction; Stapes mainly wants nice stuff and revenge. Taylor himself is his usual alcoholic-druggie mess, but is apparently worse than usual while recovering from witnessing the murder of his daughter four months earlier.

Much of the plot action involves Guards and civilians being unexpectedly shot in the face. Taylor is needed by his old Garda colleagues to solve the Guards murders, but they also want to bring him down. The climax consists of a particularly brutal and gruesome murder by falcon.

Most of the characters are returning from prior series novels, and from personal experience I can say that GALWAY GIRL does NOT work well as a standalone. (The series begins with [[ASIN:B003J48C1I The Guards]]). From reading reviews of some earlier series books, I gather that nothing good ever happens to, or around, PI Taylor, He just moves foggily along from experience to experience, generally hurting.

The dialogue relies heavily on the f-bomb (hardly noticeable after the first 10 or so uses); also on “Phew”, and the puzzling “Phew-oh”. The prose often morphs into quasi-poetic broken lines, into single words to a line, or into special “down, down, down” visual typesetting involving single words spaced across and down the page. This, I guess, is what constitutes the author’s “lyrical style” (as described by professional critics).

The novel’s genre is probably “literary detective fiction”. Had I known this, I wouldn’t have ordered the book. It isn’t all that hard to read, and the many short lines of type make it a short novel, but it’s neither decent literary fiction nor an exciting detective novel.

Cathy Glass (not her real name) is a foster mother living in the United Kingdom (UK) who has fostered over 100 children intermittenly over the past 25 years. I have never heard of this author or of her numerous books until now.

"Another Forgotten Child" is a detailed accounting of this author's day-to-day and week-to-week activities as a foster mom to help one severely abused 8-year old child named Aimee over a 1-year period. She highlights the difficulty she encounters as a result of agreeing to care for this child including risks that put her own family in danger. She also details how the child protection system has failed to actually protect this child, yet makes it clear that this is not an uncommon occurrence.

The run-around, constant switching of case workers, etc. etc. that the author descibes is very typical to what occurs in the United States (US). I know from personal experience as a former volunteer in the New Jersey (NJ) Supreme Court Family Division for the Division of Youth and Family Services (DYFS) that what the author describes is glaringly accurate here as well. At least in NJ, what I have experienced is that 98% of the child abuse cases are a result of drugs and alcohol that then lead to sexual abuse. Many abusers are never brought to justice and many times the child is afraid to name their abuser(s) as was in this case. It is also true that many children fall through the cracks and that the system is designed to sometimes comply with laws without relating to how that impacts the child. I've seen where paperwork had to be rushed just because there was a mandate to do a particular review by a particular date with the goal of the child's well-being coming as a secondary factor.

Cathy proves to me through this book why the mandate to first return the child to their parents or relatives is not always a good idea. In the NJ system (and I expect it's the same for all the US), it is the primary goal to rehabilitate the parents and return the child to them or their relatives even if the caregivers have repeatedly proven to be unsuitable.

I was grateful that Cathy mentions that all the child's possessions belong to the parent. Most people do not realize that the child does not legally own anything, not even the clothes on their back. I know that this was also true here and may still be. A child has no legal right to their belongings unless a judge orders otherwise.

Cathy also mentions "their lives aren't made any easier by the care system, which often seems to follow the 'letter of the law' while disregarding the realistic and compassionate." Her statement brought back memories of the one time I was being forced to sign paperwork to commit a child to a shelter as part of a permanancy plan. I refused to sign and the administration had someone else sign to accommodate the requirement that they have a signed permanency plan in place before xxx date. Cathy encountered a similar "farcical" scenario when she was required to attend a child-in-care (CIC) review for Aimee yet she was the only person in attendance who even knew the case.

There are both good and bad stories related to the child care system, whether it be in the UK or the US. There are also many caring and thorough caseworkers. This book is a superb representation of both the good and bad with unfortunately most of the bad glaringly obvious.

To me "Another Forgotten Child" was a positive representation of what a good foster parent can accomplish despite the obstacles presented. The details of Aimee's first 8 years of life prior to entering foster care are very sad and I'm afraid all too typical for many children in the foster care system. I suspect that some who are not use to reading about such subjects might find this book a disturbing read and cause some sleepless nights. I found it sad but was able to put that aside to see the positive elements that would now be Aimee's new life.
