I was drawn to "The Life of the World to Come" by the fact that the author, Dan Cluchey, was a speechwriter and advisor for President Barack Obama, whose speeches were, in my opinion, excellent. This is Cluchey's first novel, and it is an interesting if uneven read.

The narrator of this book, Leo Brice, is a 20-something young lawyer who has just gone through a near-universal rite of passage: he is madly, truly, deeply in love with someone he sees as his soul mate. Unfortunately, the woman he loves, Fiona, while she cares about him, does not feel the same way about him. When Fiona leaves him for another man and moves to Los Angeles to pursue her acting career, Leo is devastated. The first part of the book details the breakup, Leo's depression, and his philosophical musings about life, love, and death. I got tired of this after several pages, but it went on, and on, and on. . .

Fortunately for the reader, Leo is eventually asked to participate in a sort of Innocence Project investigation. He goes to Georgia to look into the case of Michael Tiegs, who is on death row for killing a man his wife may have been having an affair with. Michael has undergone a religious awakening in prison, but not the usual kind. He has been investigating all religions and philosophies, trying to figure out what life is all about, what if anything comes after death--all the usual but more or less impossible philosophical questions. His conversations with Leo are excellent, and in fact saved this book for me. The writing in this section is quite good, and the characters are much better developed (and more likable) than in the first section.

In the final chapters, there is a resolution and a coming together of these two strands. It is not a fairy tale ending, but it is very satisfying. I thought Cluchey really hit his stride as a writer in the final chapter. Earlier in the book I was annoyed by all the five-dollar words he used and wanted to tell him to take a page from Hemingway, who always used the simplest word possible. Cluchey seemed often to do the exact opposite. But the final chapter is beautifully written, and I actually thought of Fitzgerald's final chapter of 'The Great Gatsby' as I was reading it.

This book is not for everyone. If you are like me, you will be annoyed by Leo's inability to get over the loss of Fiona, especially since he has a really good support system of friends and colleagues. I wanted to ask, "Would you like some cheese with that whine, Leo?" on more than one occasion. And the pretentious diction is off-putting, to say the least. But the middle and end of this book are excellent, and in fact rescued this book from the dustbin. I recommend this book with reservations for those who have the patience to get through the first third and can be a little indulgent with a lovesick narrator.

Do you love Italian food, but are tired of greasy, unhealthy versions in restaurants? Looking to lighten up on fat and cholesterol? A vegan or vegetarian looking for authentic Italian without strange soy meat substitutes?

Enter Donna Klein's Vegan Italiano. Author of The[[ASIN:1557883599 The Mediterranean Vegan Kitchen]], [[ASIN:1557884382 The PDQ (Pretty Darn Quick) Vegetarian Cookbook: 240 Healthy and Easy No-Prep Recipes for Busy Cooks]], and the [[ASIN:1557885109 The Gluten-Free Vegetarian Kitchen: Delicious and Nutritious Wheat-Free, Gluten-Free Dishes]], Klein writes easy-to-follow, delicious vegan recipes that, best of all, are free of strange soy substitutes like TVP crumbles, soy sausage, tofu or tempeh. Only garden-fresh natural ingredients are used, with a touch of olive oil for flavor.

Naturally, Italian standards such as bruschetta, minestrone, gnocchi, and lasagna are included. Bruschettas include Asparagus, Apulian-Style with Cherry Tomatoes and Basil, and Cherry Tomato and Roasted Red Pepper. Lasagnas include Spinach and Eggplant and Zucchini. The main part of the book is dedicated, not surprisingly, to pasta, with numerous farfalle, linguine, and fusili offerings. There are also numerous ideas for fresh wild greens salads, vegetable side dishes, pizzas and breads, and desserts. Many of the dessert offerings would be perfect on a hot summer's day on the patio: fruits poached in red and white wine, macedonias, and granitas.

The great thing about vegan Italian recipes is that they're delicious as written, but if you want to add cheese, feel free. It's much easier to add animal products to a successful vegan recipe than it is to subtract them from a traditional one.

The majority of recipes are easy to prepare and contain detailed nutritional info. Fans of Donna Klein's other vegan and vegetarian cookbooks, as well as those looking for healthier updates on authentic Italian cuisine, will do well to check out Vegan Italiano. Although not as thorough as Klein's Mediterranean Vegan Kitchen (much of Vegan Italiano felt like carryovers from MVK), these are still healthy, delicious Italian favorites that are easy to prepare.

I am relatively inexperienced with tablets, having spent the majority of my time working with laptops. That said, I started looking for a tablet about a year ago with the intent of using one as an e-reader and I finally found a white Sony Xperia Z for a really good deal and snapped it up. I have had it for over a month now and so far I am pleased with it. There are a couple of little minor quirks that I would change but those are outweighed by the positives.

This particular tablet has a 10.1” screen with better resolution than the best 15” laptop I own. Images are very bright, crisp and clear. I don’t think I could ask for a better display in terms of image and color quality. The size is right for me, too – I had originally considered a smaller tablet which would have cost less but would have been a little harder on my eyes. Also, the screen is very responsive and has worked without any serious issue up to this point.

I have had one issue with the screen, though, and I have seen others mention this in the forums online. As I type, sometimes the screen will flicker. It does not do this every time and it is not a major problem but it is an annoyance. This is apparently an issue with this model and I read somewhere online that there is a firmware update that fixes this. I haven’t had the time to pursue this yet.

Battery life thus far has been very good. I usually have the tablet in standby when I am not using it (which to be honest is a majority of the time) and I have let it go for a couple of weeks without charging and still had enough power to work. I can’t really find any reason to complain about the battery life.

The sound quality is surprisingly good! When I have brought up anything that involved sound (such as an online video) I have been started by how well it sounds on this tablet even when I am not wearing headphones. I would expect the sound quality to be passable in a tablet but I have been pleasantly surprised.

Weight-wise, this tablet is a little heavier than I would expect but it’s not an unreasonable amount of weight. It is not uncomfortable to carry it around for extended periods or to use it as a reader for a while.

I am not really very savvy on the differences between Android versions but so far I have had no real complaints, both before and after upgrading. It has provided everything I want and need and has been very stable for me. I had a first-generation Droid phone for a long time and the Android version on that phone was nowhere near as advanced as what’s on this tablet, but it is similar enough to make using this tablet a very familiar experience.

I can’t find any real major complaints with the Xperia Z and I am happy with it. Other than the screen flicker issue when typing it’s about as perfect a device as I could want (and if there's a fix for it via firmware update then it's a problem only because I am lazy). The price is a little high – especially when not on sale – but so far it has been worth it.

I selected this cookbook with minimal knowledge of low-lectin eating, more out of curiosity than a desire to eat healthier. To be sure, I do have an interest in a healthier lifestyle so this book had some appeal there. The author does a nice job of explaining the problem with lectins and the health issues that arrive from consuming them. There aren't too many references to reputable sources, but the explanations make sense. It puts the whole situation in layman's terms.

There are twelve chapters in this book and there is a broad coverage of recipe types - breakfast, desserts, main dishes and so on. There's a little something for everyone here. And, the book has a lot of full-color photographs which make finding something that looks appealing much easier.

Where this book fails me is in the ingredients for the recipes. In almost every recipe there is at least one (usually more) ingredient that I would otherwise not buy or of which I had not heard prior. Many of these I have never even seen at my local market and I am not close to a health food store or gourmet shop to acquire these ingredients.

This appears to be a nice book and a good bit of effort went into creating the recipes and binding the book into an attractive volume. For me, though, it is not practical.

THE DEVIL'S TRIANGLE is my first Catherine Coulter thriller, and it doesn't inspire me to read more of her novels. Fourth in the "Brit in the FBI" series (the first is [[ASIN:B00C5R7H70 The Final Cut]]), it works fine as a standalone. However, it's a plodding, run-of-the-mill thriller in which a team of nearly immortal (you-can't-kill-'em-but-maybe-you-can-wing-'em-if-you're-really-lucky) covert FBI operatives save the U.S. Government and the world once again. Neither the exotic settings (Venice, Rome, the Bermuda Triangle), nor the fantasy elements (the evildoers' ability to control the weather, thanks to notes from Leonardo da Vinci; the evildoers' mad, obsessive quest for the Ark of the Covenant) are sufficient to lift the novel above the ordinary.

In the novel, a professional thief (Kitsune aka "the Fox") delivers to anonymous clients in Venice an artifact (Aaron's rod) that she stole from the military-guarded Topkapi Palace. Instead of paying
Kitsune, the clients send death squads after her. Kitsune enlists the aid of her FBI enemies from prior series novels (the "Covert Eyes" team of Michaela "Mike" Caine and British-raised Nicholas Drummond), by persuading them that a massive Gobi Desert sandstorm--currently burying Beijing and killing thousands--is not a natural weather phenomenon, but is a man-made event.

After Mike and Nicholas arrive in Venice, their meeting with Kitsune is thwarted by a shootout in the Piazza di San Marcos that leaves seven bad guys dead and one FBI team member (Lia) seriously wounded. Eventually Kitsune successfully contacts Mike and Nicholas. With her help and with help from the FBI team's incredibly skilled teenage computer expert (Adam), Mike and Nicholas identify Kitsune's clients as the evil, "identical" Korath twins (Ajax and Cassandra). They also figure out that the mad twins are seeking the Ark of the Covenant. Mike and Nicholas and Kitsune head off to beard the twins in the Koraths' castle stronghold near Rome, and kill a bunch more bad guys on their way. The novel goes on from there, with more killings and close escapes--it's a very long thriller at 512pp--and eventually the team winds up on an island in the Bermuda Triangle.

The well-written novel has lots of action scenes, even though it's not really a page-turner. It's a decent read, as thrillers go, but nothing to shout home about. I expected much more from an established, popular writer like Coulter.

This book is not original material. Rather, it is a collection of previously-written articles, compiled together by David Levy who is a well-respected authority on computer chess topics. He has divided the material into nine sections that make locating information easy: The Introduction, Famous Chess Programs, Position Evaluation, Tree Searching Techniques, Analysis, Writing a Chess Program, Special Purpose Hardware and Software, The Endgame, and Games Played by Chess Computers.

Most online sources mention different techniques (such as alpha-beta searching) but offer precious little in explaining what the techniques actually are or how to implement them. All too frequently, references are made to some open-source engine that implements one or more techniques but is so poorly documented (or is documented in another language) such that understanding is just out of reach. Where this book is different is that is not only explains the various techniques and ideas but more often than not it gets very detailed and offers diagrams and pseudocode to clearly present ideas in terms an interested individual can access.

There are several places within this book where games played by computers are analyzed and explained in detail, which at first may seem a little wasteful but in context with the rest of the material makes understanding a little more interesting. The games are from older programs and do not represent the quality of play seen in today's modern chess programs but they still provide a good reference point and demonstrate the ability of computers to search and evaluate.

This brings up a good point. Much of the material, while still applicable today, is regarded as older (1988 timeframe). Since the first printing of this book there has been appreciable progress in computer chess strength and playing ability. This may not be the most up-to-date material but it is still all very relevant and instructional and is still foundational for modern computer chess understanding.

Computer Chess Compendium is an exceptionally useful reference for anyone who wants to really understand how computers play chess. This is the reference for which I have been looking and I cannot say enough good things about it. If you want to really get a good understanding of how computers "think" when playing chess, or perhaps you are like me and want to write your own engine, this is a fabulous resource worth much more than the asking price.

I have two sons that have done a lot with voice recorders, each having their own and working with them extensively for recording all manner of things (frequently that means rude noises, but hey, they're allowed). When the Phillips DVT1500/00 Voice Recorder arrived I immediately passed it to them for testing - they would know exactly what to look for and how to put it through a rigorous test.

This is a smallish device but it happens to be slightly bigger than other voice recorders I have seen. It fits nicely in a pocket and is lightweight enough that it can be carried practically anywhere without causing any issue. It would have been nice to have included a wrist lanyard but this is a small thing.

We installed the batteries and turned it on, and within minutes we were able to record things without too much difficulty and without consulting any documentation. With the two microphones it records clearly and at decent volume so there is no issue with the sound quality - Phillips did a nice job with this recorder in this aspect.

Managing content is easy too. It's very simple to look through the list of recordings, play back and delete them. The screen is a little on the small side so people with less than ideal eyesight might struggle just a little with the display, even though the display is better (and larger) than on many competing devices I have seen.

This particular voice recorder comes with a special version of Dragon Naturally Speaking, which works ONLY with this voice recorder. Things that get recorded and are copied over to the PC are translated on the fly to written text which is a very nice feature.

It is the translation of the voice to text that is the primary issue, though. There is some training required to get the voice recorder transcribing the audio correctly. The training can take some time to get everything close to right, but it also means that others' voices may not transcribe properly. So, if the plan is to use this voice recorder to record lectures, such as in a classroom environment, there may be some real disappointment waiting.

This is actually a nice product and it works well. It records with decent quality and is transcribes to text easily after some training. If it is going to be used by a single person for a single voice source then it's a fine product. If the idea is to record and transcribe several voices, though, it may be more of a headache.

THE NEW NEIGHBORS is a rather slow-moving psychological thriller. In alternating chapters, two viewpoint characters (Jack and Sydney) recount the mysterious things that happen to them after they move into their new house. Some of the events are creepy (e.g., the discovery of something decomposing in the attic, a hand on the woman’s face at night). However, as Sydney says in an early chapter, it isn't a ghost story. It’s about hidden familial relationships, and about Jack’s and Sydney’s differing interpretations of shared events.

In the novel, Jack and Sydney (as yet unmarried) acquire and move into their hoped-for “forever home”. It’s a bargain-priced, 3-bedroom, detached home in London. It’s also packed with the previous owner’s furniture and junk. That owner left suddenly for Australia, leaving all his possessions behind.

Jack and Sydney have been in the house for a few weeks before they notice “the smell”. It’s emanating from the attic, and Jack climbs up to investigate. He’s shocked to find that the attic is empty--in stark contrast to the trash-filled rooms below--except for the disgusting source of “the smell” and a child's treasure box that has a name he recognizes scrawled inside. From then on, things can only get worse ….

The writing is pretty good, and the suspenseful story is told well enough to keep the reader reading if he/she has plenty of leisure time. The novel is pretty decent for summer or beach reading. However, the characters and the plot aren’t particularly memorable; and it’s unlikely that anyone could have pulled off the grand scheme that’s revealed at the end.

From the BBC - Intro Good evening, I'm Alistair Cooke. Tonight we begin a new series, called Poldark, based on the four novels of Winston Graham. It runs to sixteen episodes and I can only say that now is the time for the party to settle in to a spate of loving, dueling, poaching, smuggling, wenching, and marrying,--not to mention banking and copper mining. Copper mining plays a big part in this story because we are in the county of Cornwall in England at the end of the eighteenth century. I don't suppose today's tourists visit the copper mines, which are abandoned, but the Greeks and the Romans knew about them and at the end of the eighteenth century copper and tin were the main sources of wealth in a county that is otherwise practically treeless--barren but very beautiful. Those of you who have been there may have noticed those strange cones of pyramids on the horizon they are China Clay deposits. Maybe we should try to pin Cornwall down on the map. When I was a boy we were told that the map of Britain was that of a pig with a man on its back and it comes out very roughly like this [Cooke draws]. The trunk is England, with his very long head Scotland. The pig's face is Wales. And here what they call West Country which goes from Dorset, Somerset, Devon, and here is Cornwall the very end here is the tip of the island Lands' End. So we are in Cornwall, then, the end of the eighteenth century just at the close of the American Revolutionary War and the surrender of the British forces to George Washington and the Continental Army. The date, as any handy schoolboy will tell you, is 1783. And our hero, Captain Ross Poldark, who has been serving in George III's forces, has come home to Cornwall. He has just landed and is on his way home back to his estate, which has indifferent farming but two copper mines. It's called Nampara. During the War he has heard that his father is no longer alive, but his relatives don't know that he himself is alive. This is not surprising because during the war they didn't have any transatlantic mail service. In fact in this year of 1783, England saw its first domestic mail coach going between Bristol and London. So we open with Captain Poldark jogging home in a stagecoach to meet and amaze his friends.

SWITCHEROO, the 18th "skeleton detective" novel, is mostly a travelogue set in Jersey (in the Channel Islands). The mystery plot is thin, and the story is padded out with a lot of descriptions of archeological sites, present-day buildings, unusual geographical features (e.g., tar pits), and restaurant meals enjoyed by the characters. The mystery itself has an historical background, loosely tied to the German occupation of Jersey during World War II.

In the historical part of the novel, two Jersey families agree to swap their infant sons, so that the more sickly child can be evacuated to hoped-for safety in England until the coming German occupation is over. Only the families and their lawyer know about this arrangement. After the war, the evacuated parents return with the child to Jersey, and the parents who remained behind make good on their promise to deed over Jersey property in return for their child's safety. The children grow up, but both are murdered (the bones of one are recovered from a tar pit), and their murders remain unsolved.

In the present-day bulk of the novel, a bored Gideon Oliver is recruited by a high-ranking Jersey politician (Rafe Carlisle) to examine the tar pit bones (which are purported to include some of his father's bones). Rafe is a wealthy forensics enthusiast, and is curious to know what bone expert Oliver will have to say. From the outset, Oliver is suspicious of the official findings--which determined that the tar pit bones were the bones from two persons of specific ages--because specific ages cannot be determined from the examination of bones alone.

As always happens in mystery novels, it would have been best if Rafe had let sleeping dogs lie. Oliver's investigation naturally leads to another murder. In the course of his investigation, he sees a lot of interesting Jersey buildings, eats some excellent Jersey food, and learns a lot about the history and political structure of Jersey. Eventually Oliver solves the old, cold case, and the guilty present-day murderer is brought to justice.

I have read all, or nearly all, of the Gideon Oliver books, and found all of them, including this one, to be enjoyable. However, SWITCHEROO is definitely NOT one of the best of the series. Because it is slow-moving, has a thin mystery plot, and is somewhat lacking in Gideon Oliver's trademark skeleton analysis, I rate it at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

Fighter pilot Robin Olds was born with flying in his blood. His father Robert Olds was a captain in the Army Air Corps, and houseguests included the likes of Hap Arnold, Tooey Spaatz, Fiorello La Guardia, and other WWI pilots. When Robin's mother died when he was four, he asked his father if she was in heaven with all the other airplanes. He went on his first flight at age eight. Robin entered West Point in 1940, where he combined his love of flying with football. On June 1, 1943, Robin graduated West Point and entered pilot training in the P-38 Lightning, later transitioning to the P-51 Mustang. Stationed at RAF Wattisham, he became a major and squadron commander at age 22.

Post-war, after a brief stint as a football coach at West Point, Robin returned to flying as part of an aerobatic jet demonstration team. He missed out on the Korean War (in part due to the string-pulling by his wife, Hollywood actress Ella Raines) and was assigned to the Pentagon during the Cold War. He finally got his chance to plunge back into aerial combat in Vietnam, where he led the 8th Tactical Fighter Wing in Ubon, Thailand. And it's here that his leadership truly shone; he combined his WWII dogfighting experience with the lessons learned over two decades of active duty in the Air Force: know your mission. Know your people: what their job entails, and their role in the organization. Ask questions. Get your hands dirty (Robin learned aircraft maintenance from his crew chief Glen Wold at Wattisham). Recognize accomplishment. Accept ultimate responsibility. Foster unit spirit, but not at the expense of others.

Robin's command at 8th TAC marked a turnaround; unlike his predecessor, who'd only flown 12 missions in 10 months, Robin added himself to the flight schedule as a rookie, challenging his more combat-experienced pilots to train him in the F-4C Phantom. On January 2, 1967, Robin and his men launched Operation Bolo, an attempt to engage MiG-21's by masquerading as F-105s. They shot down seven MiGs that day (Olds himself claimed one). To keep himself from getting rotated out after his 100 missions in Vietnam, he'd secretly erase missions from the board, leaving his "official" tally just short of 100 (he actually flew 152 combat missions over Vietnam). Despite his wishes, Robin was eventually sent Stateside, where he briefed LBJ and encountered hippies and anti-war protesters for the first time. He was promoted to Brigadier General in 1968 and relocated to Colorado Springs as commandant of the Air Force Academy. His last post was director of aerospace safety at Norton AFB, and he retired on June 1, 1973 after 30 years of service.

Told in the first person, "Fighter Pilot" was completed after Robin's death in 2007 by his daughter Christina and author Ed Rasimus ([[ASIN:031294876X Palace Cobra: A Fighter Pilot in the Vietnam Air War]]). Far from ghost writing, Robin's gruff voice takes the lead, including plenty of colorful language and intense combat descriptions. But Robin has his share of all-too-human moments; his disintegrating marriage is a recurring theme that makes his homecomings uncomfortable (Ella refused to live on base or have her daughters attend base schools). True, there are some awkward transitions, such as when Robin loses close friends in combat or air accidents, only to be merrily moving along in the next paragraph, but overall, this reads like a conversation to a close friend (I can almost picture a group of fighter pilot aces sitting around in a bar swapping stories). It's worth the price alone for the fantastic descriptions of life in wartime England and Robin's first-hand account of D-Day.

There are some black-and-white photos of Robin's family, his early years during WWII, numerous photos from his time at Ubon, and a few from his later years. Included is a spectacular lithograph by Robert Taylor of Robin's F-4 low-level bombing of the Thai Nguyen steel mill (although it would have had greater impact in color). "Fighter Pilot" is a rollicking read that expounds on the beautiful combination of man and machine ("You are something more than earthbound man. Not just an ace pilot, he was a born leader and wasn't afraid to speak his mind in defense of his men. A must-have for military and aviation buffs and a must-read for anyone in the Air Force; I hope this becomes required reading and shows up on next year's CSAF Reading List.

LAST CALL AT THE NIGHTSHADE LOUNGE is a pleasant urban fantasy novel. It's based on the concept that bartenders (in Chicago) not only protect their customers from themselves (by limiting their drinks) but also from fearsome, night-prowling beasts (the Tremens) that just love to eat humans. It's a fun concept, but not terribly well executed, because the repeated idea gets tiresome over the course of the book.

In the novel, an aimless Ivy-League business grad (Bailey Chen) finds work as a "barback" (a bartenders' assistant) at her neighborhood bar (the Nightshade Lounge). At closing one night, she mixes herself a Perfect Screwdriver, which glows because it's made with oddball "CC" vodka. On her way home, Bailey encounters her very first Tremens, which she is able to dispatch (and live to tell the tale) because of a temporary superpower (extra weight) given her by the magical cocktail.

Bailey's encounter with the Tremens leads to her becoming a novice bartender for the Cupbearers Court (source of the CC vodka and other magical liquors). Initially apprenticed to an old high school pal (Zane), Bailey discovers she has a crush on Zane. The remainder of the novel proceeds as a light romance superimposed upon a series of exciting action encounters with various Tremens. The Tremens are defeated when CC bartenders imbibe the cocktails described in the CC bartenders' manual ("The Devil's Water Dictionary", which is reproduced in the novel). The cocktails grant the CC bartenders superpowers that range from invisibility (the Martini) to mind-reading (the Chimayo).

The included recipes will make very good cocktails, though the reader will have to locate CC liquors in order to make the magical, glowing ones! The novel is reasonably well-written, but the plot is very thin, and the main characters (Bailey, Mona, Zane, Bucket, Garrett, Vincent) aren't particularly interesting or likeable as individuals. For these reasons, I rate LAST CALL AT THE NIGHTSHADE LOUNGE at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

That is, you set a home location, and then when you travel away from home, the SmartThings app can show you on a street map where the device is currently located. There are many, many cookbooks available for people following the keto lifestyle. Picking one as a starting point isn’t easy. However, this one does make a good starting point and gives a strong hint to that end by the title “Keto Simple”. There are bigger collections out there that cover more ground, give more recipes, provide more information on the keto process and even give different preparation styles (such as pressure cooking and air frying), but this one keeps things relatively straightforward and easy.

The book is broken down into 8 chapters. Chapter 1 deals with introductory stuff – what is keto, how to shop for it, etc. The next seven chapters provide the recipes in logical groupings: Breakfasts, Snacks, Side Dishes, Soups & Salads, Lunch Items, Dinners, and finally Desserts. After all of this material, the book includes a little supplemental material, including a list of references, a short bio on the author, and acknowledgements.

The recipes themselves are straightforward and do not require unusual effort and usually do not require odd ingredients. They’re simple to prepare and the end results (at least the ones I have tried) work out well.

An interesting feature in this cookbook is a visual guide at the top of each recipe that is made up of symbols that indicate special features of each recipe. These include dairy-free, nut-free, egg-free, nightshade-free, vegetarian, and high in electrolytes. This is a handy guide for those that have dietary restrictions such as an aversion to dairy or allergies to nuts.

This isn’t the most complete keto book available and it doesn’t claim to be a complete dietary reference. It’s a great starting point, though, for those wanting to get into a keto lifestyle but don’t know where to jump in.

In quintessential Phyllis Reynolds Naylor style, this delightful story speaks straight to the heart of kids as they struggle to define themselves. From SCHOOL LIBRARY JOURNAL: Grade 2-4-Sarah Simpson's family thinks that she is extraordinary, but she feels ordinary and is anxious to find a special quality that sets her apart. This concept, by itself, is interesting and well fleshed out. At school, she tries to trick the substitute teacher by switching names with her best friend, but that doesn't solve her "problem." She tries other ideas to no avail. Her solution arrives with an opportunity to help the parents of a classmate whose restaurant isn't doing well. Much too quickly, Sarah comes up with a plan-a T-shirt advertising "Wongs' Wings," a house specialty. Appealing full-page and spot illustrations appear throughout. I have always liked the video footage taken by bikers as they barrel down a mountain trail or through a wooded area on their bikes (or the crazy base jumpers wanting to capture the drop). It gives a really good sense of what the rider was seeing when riding and you catch every bump in the road, every acceleration and deceleration. I have never used on of these little cameras before now so I was very excited to have a chance to evaluate one of these cameras. So far I am very happy with it and it works well, though I have learned that those with big hands and fingers will struggle a little bit with it.

This is not just a camera, it is a complete kit with the camera, a waterproof housing, cables, mounting brackets, double-sided adhesive pads - everything you need to use this little camera in just about any outdoor activity you might want to capture. I will write mostly about the camera but will touch on a couple of the accessories as well.

Except for cameras designed to be hidden and concealed this is the smallest and lightest camera I have ever seen or used. This is of course required for a device like this that is intended to be used on the go. It very easily can be slipped in a pocket or a bag or purse. It comes packaged in the hard plastic frame that is the waterproof case but even this case is small enough to fit in a purse or smaller bag.

I will say this - read the included manual! The manual is not perfect but it is better than what comes with most electronics and it gives a very good rundown on how to use this little camera. I had no clue at all what to do with this camera until I looked through the manual. I suspected it was touch-screen and I was right. Even though the screen is touch screen and easy to navigate the interface is only semi-intuitive. It is also complicated by the fact that there is an anti-scratch cover on the screen for shipping and if you do not peel this off the screen is a lot less responsive. This is where I had the most trouble - trying to work around the plastic sheet over the screen when I didn’t really even notice it before.

This camera has a lot of the same capabilities of a good phone camera. You can take still pictures, video and also play back that which you have recorded. The camera can snap stills up to 12MP resolution and the video recording can go all the way up to 1080P. These equate to very good image quality when used properly. There are a million little settings for these modes too, from white balance, ISO, anti-shake, motion detection and a lot more. Many of these will be familiar to anyone who uses their digital camera for anything more than just casual shots.

In testing my images and videos came out ok. I am still learning how to balance all of the settings on my big camera so I am no expert, but what I was able to produce was acceptable, particularly the video. I did manage to get the date set correctly and displayed in the corner of the video, I got the lighting right and color straight. I spent too much time playing with the zoom and I learned I am very adept at shooting videos of my hands.

This is a rechargeable device and a standard micro USB cable is provided for charging.

I ran into one issue with the camera and it related to the fact that I have huge hands and the camera is so small. I found that the only way I personally can work the touch screen is to use a stylus. Using my fingers I am unable to pinpoint the spot on the screen I want to touch and I got very frustrated trying to get certain things done on the screen. If you have really big hands, consider using a stylus on the screen.

There is no storage included in the package. The camera takes a microSD card so you will need one to save any pictures or recordings.

The waterproof case is a perfect fit for this camera and it seals wonderfully. It snaps closed without effort and it keeps the water out. It is supposedly good for submersion up to 30m (according to the description). I have not had an opportunity to test this.

There are a number of mounting solutions in the kit, including mounting screws for attaching to a selfie stick, bicycle frame/handlebars and helmets. In the case of the bike mount, it holds very tightly and a good series of bumps is not enough to rattle it loose.

Having never had a sport camera like this I have no basis of comparison but so far I am happy with this little camera. It is very compact and lightweight and it does a great job of taking pictures and video (though it is obviously not a full replacement for a dedicated point-and-shoot or a dedicated video camera). It’s inexpensive too (a LOT less expensive than GoPro) so I think it’s a great option for someone wanting to capture their adventures.

I enjoy eating most varieties of meats and I was interested in what this book could offer when I first saw it. At a glance (meaning, based on the title and cover art), it is easy to assume that it is a book specifically about grilling meats but that would be incorrect – this book covers a few different cooking methods and gives a fairly good overview of preparing and cooking a variety of meats. It’s not a perfect book, but it is a good starting point.

The book is broken down into some introductory material as well as four chapters of recipes – beef, pork, lamb & veal, and poultry. I was a little surprised to see that seafood (fish in particular) is not covered at all, which strikes me as an oversight of sorts. It’s not necessarily a bad thing, but many (myself included) do regard fish as a meat source.

Each chapter has fairly broad coverage of their chosen meat types and present a wide range of recipes to try. There is the occasional odd ingredient, but for the most part the recipes are made with typical ingredients that one is likely to have on hand and do not require a special trip to the store to find. Prep is also very straightforward and doesn’t require getting too “fiddly” in the kitchen.

One thing I like about the way the recipes are presented is the guide right under the titles that give some quick info about the recipe. This is a series of one or more tags including “one pot”, “make ahead”, “five ingredients or less” and more. This makes finding recipes that meet certain preparation requirements a little easier.

What this book really lacks is pictures. Most recipes have no picture attached at all, and as such most do not stand out beyond the title. It has been said in many places that you eat first with your eyes; this book doesn’t follow that.

This is a good book on preparing meat dishes with a good variety and easy preparations. It is not perfect and could use more pictures (and arguably a section on fish), but it’s a good starting place for many cooks looking to learn and expand their skills.

I've always enjoyed Jeffrey Deaver.  This is my first Colter Shaw novel.  Shaw general makes his money by securing offered rewards to find missing people.  In this case, he's asked to protect Allison, the brilliant ex-wife of a cop turned felon and her sixteen year old daughter, Hannah FROM her ex, Jon.  Jon has just been released prematurely from what was to be a three year sentence.  He brutally assaulted Allison in a drunken rage and now word is he is going to kill her.  Allison is already gone when Shaw comes on board, hired by her employer, a nuclear energy based company on the cutting edge.  Allison is their star scientist/inventor.  A very complicated story ensues involving police ambiguity (are they supporting their old colleague by their inaction?); crazy contract killers (why did Jon hire them?); Hannah's teenagerness and belief in her father until she doesn't (teen resistance to her mother's efforts to protect her or actually evil?) and ultimately, Shaw's relationship to the various tendrils of the investigation and his protection responsibilities.  He's that good.  But can he pull this off with all of these variables?  His childhood a a survivalist comes in handy throughout the story and hi ability to spot anomalies. Jake's Choice is an awesome sequel to the Britts' To Save A Life book. Seldom do authors improve on their first book, but the Britts have hit a home-run with this one!

Jake's Choice is a study in contrasts as the lives of Jake and Amy continue to unfold. Jake goes to Louisville, KY to live out his dream of playing college basketball for the much-heralded Cardinals while Amy is left behind in Oceanside, CA to pick up the pieces of her shattered dreams after giving up their daughter Emily for adoption to a wonderful church couple.

For Jake, who postponed going to Louisville for a semester to be with Amy during her pregnancy and the birth of their daughter, life starts to unravel the minute he gets there. The transition from former high school basketball star and popular man on campus and new Christian to another anonymous face arriving on a college campus jars his reality. There are no warm welcomes. Nothing. He finds himself with an interesting roommate (who hasn't been there?) who's also the basketball team, but worst of all his teammates dis him for not arriving sooner and being there for the team. Add to that the fact he isn't happy with the churches he visits and you have the recipe for the disaster that unfolds in the pages that follow.

Amy, on the other hand, is attending a community college in Southern California, and is living with regrets about giving up her daughter Emily. As her story unfolds, she begins to run with Andrea and eventually gets together with Cari, the youth pastor Chris' wife. Amy comes to faith in Jesus Christ and wants to share what's she's learning with Jake.

What unfolds is these two people who are living in opposite parts of the country are moving in two different directions: Amy closer to God and Jake further away. My wife drew a picture for me while we dating that amply illustrates a beautiful principle that applies here. On a piece of paper she drew a triangle. At the base of the triangle, on the left hand side, she wrote Me; on the right hand side, she wrote You. At the top of the triangle, she wrote God. Her point: as we each drew nearer to God we would be drawn closer together. Unfortunately, this wasn't the case with Amy and Jake. Amy drew nearer to God and Jake did not. Their relationship suffered as a result of this.

Without giving up too much of the story: Amy follows God's direction for her life and lives out her dream of going to Stanford University and is blessed beyond her wildest dreams. Jake, on the other hand, tries to win the approval of his teammates, makes bad choices, and goes through one trial after another. It isn't until an elderly man from the first church he visited in Louisville comes back into his life and challenges him to glow - to let his life shine before men so that they may see his good works and glorify his Father in heaven (Matthew 5:16)- that Jake starts to get his life back on track.

In my 23 years of walking with the Lord I have read a number of Christian books, both fiction and nonfiction, but I'll tell you in all honestly, apart from the Bible, I have never in my life read a book that truly puts into proper persective what it means to be a Christian than Jake's Choice. This is a must read book, as is it's a sequel To Save A Life. May God continue to use Jim and Rachel Britts in a mighty way to reach the lost and hurting for Christ. May the story continue!

This book is an in-depth analysis of personality types and how they relate to one another in terms of finding a mate. Much of this work has been done in other forms by other researchers, but some of the material is new.

The author lays out 4 base personality types, which she calls the Explorer, the Builder, the Negotiator, and the Director. She explains the strengths and weaknesses of each type, and she also explains what chemical influences in the body/brain contribute to the dominance of each type.

The idea of 4 base personality types is nothing new at all. My first exposure to this system was through a video series by Smalley and Trent, and they described the 4 types as Lions, Beavers, Otters and Golden Retrievers. Different names, but the personality types aligned almost perfectly with the author's definitions of the different personality types. That said, this is the first time I have heard the personality type system defined with associations to such bodily chemicals such as serotonin, testosterone and estrogen. These associations make understanding other people a little easier and a lot more interesting.

Where this work really diverges from other works is in the in-depth analysis of how these personality types interact, specifically in a romantic sense. Some of this has been touched in other projects, but not to the depth as is contained herein. I especially found interesting the anecdotes regarding conversation interactions with non-optimal matches, where things could get awkward.

The audio edition comes on 7(!) audio CDs. I have a long commute so I had opportunities to listen closely while driving in to work. The author reads this work herself and mercifully she is not monotone and expressionless but rather she reads with some expression and interest. Her voice is clear and understandable.

One negative - I thought she brought up her associations with Match.com and Chemistry.com a little more often that was necessary. On a couple of occasions it comes across as promotional.

This is an interesting book on an interesting topic, written in terms that most people can grasp easily. If you are interested in looking into personality type research and how the different types interact when finding romantic interests, consider this book as a plug-in point.

Rudy Simone's "Aspergirls: Empowering Females With Asperger Syndrome" is a wonderful starting point for all Aspergirls, whether you're an Aspergirl yourself or you have an Apergirl in your life. This thoughtfully-written guide examines the oft-overlooked Aspergirl, who's been clinically ignored in favor of male Aspies (traditional figures put the boy-girl ratio at 4:1, but that is rapidly changing as 1 in 100 children are believed to be on the autism spectrum). Because Aspergirls may be better at socializing in small doses and tend to be a little more expressive than their male counterparts, they may be able to "pass" as neurotypical (NT) and not receive a proper AS diagnosis other than being "shy" or "difficult."

Simone has interviewed numerous Aspergirls regarding their experiences in all walks of life, from surviving schoolyard bullies, PTSD, and selective mutism to college, dating, motherhood and employment. She also discusses the Asperger's "is it a gift or a disability?" debate. Each chapter ends with "Advice to Aspergirls" and "Advice to Parents," a thoughtful touch that includes the whole family in the discussion. The book wraps up with advice from Aspergirls to Aspergirls (inspirational bullet points such as the title of this review) and the cleverly-titled "Give Your Aspergirl some B.A.L.L.S.: Belief, Acceptance, Love, Like, and Support." Appendix A also features a handy chart of female Asperger traits and main female / male differences in Asperger's. There is a small list of references and resources, and I was surprised not to see any of Tony Attwood's books listed (although he's mentioned by name several times). Simone frequently promotes her own books [[ASIN:1849058032 22 Things a Woman Must Know: If She Loves a Man With Asperger's Syndrome]] and [[ASIN:1935274090 Asperger's on the Job: Must-have Advice for People with Asperger's or High Functioning Autism, and their Employers, Educators, and Advocates]] in nearly every chapter.

Simone and the various interviewees put Aspie sensations into words that NTs can understand; this is in itself a feat, since our first language isn't words, but images and sensations (see [[ASIN:0307739589 Thinking in Pictures (Expanded, Tie-in Edition): My Life with Autism (Vintage)]]). Simone discusses triggers (fluorescent lights, loud noises, scratchy fabrics) and meltdowns in detail, both internally and externally. In the chapter on stimming, she introduces the term "soothing," which has fewer negative connotations.

There are several chapters devoted to depression, medication, abuse and PTSD. I was particularly interested in Chapter 19, Stomach Issues and Autism. I've had digestive issues my whole life, and never previously connected AS with digestive disorders. At times, the book went into New Age-y territory, with suggestions on herbal supplements and discussions on psychic sensitivity, reiki, and chi, along with several popular AS diets, including gluten-free and casein-free (see: [[ASIN:184310055X A User Guide to the GF/CF Diet for Autism, Asperger Syndrome and AD/HD]] for more information).

When I was younger, Aspergers wasn't ever mentioned and hadn't gained the widespread recognition that it currently has. I sincerely wish that this book had been available throughout my rocky adolescence; hopefully, "Aspergirls" will smooth the path for today's young Aspergirls. If you're the parent of an Aspergirl, some of the stories in this book are on the lower-functioning end of the Aspergers scale; don't automatically assume that your daughter will exhibit *all* of these symptoms. Every Aspergirl is different. Just be proud of your smart, funny, and talented daughter. Or if you're an Aspergirl yourself...Aspergrrrrrl power!

SOLEFULL SOCKS is a must-have for the technical sock knitter's bookshelf. It describes a completely new architectural approach to sock knitting. Designer Betty Salpekar's imaginative sock structure makes it possible to reinforce the entire sole of a sock with carry-along yarn to solve the problem of wear (holes) on the ball of the foot or the bottom of the heel. An added bonus is the Foreword by Cat Bordhi. As Cat says, "Betty's work, which I think of as ceremonial clothing for the foot, . . . seems to be an entirely new class of footwear."

Betty's "solefull" sock begins in the middle of the sole with a provisional cast on, then proceeds outward in rounds, with the heel and toe formed by strategically-placed increases and short-row shaping. Once the sole is complete, the knitting continues upward in rounds, using decreases for shaping and a clever "zip line" that joins part of the round to form the lower portion of the sock top. From there, the sock top knitting goes on upward, using center front decreases to shape the instep. Finally, the knitting proceeds in ordinary rounds, with shaping optional, to form the ankle, leg, and cuff. To finish, the cuff is bound off with the method of your choice, and the stitches in the provisional cast on (on the sole) are grafted together.

All of this is explained with clear drawings, and with both charts and written-out instructions. Although I haven't yet tried to knit a pair of these socks, I can easily follow the concept, which is to knit a shaped cylinder to enclose the foot and leg. Although I'm usually a charts person, I think that the written-out instructions are the key to learning this new sock-knitting approach.

The book includes 18 amazing patterns for fancy "solefull" socks that use slip stitches, color stranding, traveling stitches, and lace stitches, in addition to ordinary knitting and purling to create stockinette fabric. My personal favorites are Irises (slip stitch color); Balanced Biases (bias bands wrapping around the leg); Fair-gyle (elaborate red and white argyle check design); Semi Aran (fancy traveling stitch cables); Meandering Mesh (the book cover design); and Twining Vines (lace vine patterning).

The included patterns, by technique, are:

Stockinette: Let the Yarn Shine; Shaded Golden Ratio; Canyon Walls

Purling and Slipping: Purl Trellis; Syncopation; Purl Parallelograms; Irises

Increasing and Decreasing: Balanced Biases; Flaming Arrows

Color Stranding: Fair Isle Trellis; Louvered Light; Fair-gyle

Traveling Stitch: Traveling Trellis; Semi Aran; Poinsetta

Lace: Lace Trellis; Meandering Mesh; Twining Vines

The pattern instructions are given in both charted and written-out form. Directions are given for sizes small (US shoe size 5-6, sole 8.75"), medium (US shoe size 7-8, sole 9.5"), and large (US shoe size 9-10, sole 10.25") for 15 of the 18 patterns. There are suggestions for yarns, and there is gauge information so that you can substitute yarn. The patterns call for US size 1 or 1-1/2 circular or double-point needles, and fine sock yarn. The patterns can probably be knit by adventurous intermediate knitters, as long as the knitters have some experience in knitting conventionally constructed socks.

POLTARNEES, BEHOLDER OF OCEAN

Toldees, Mondath, Arizim, these are the Inner Lands, the lands whose sentinels upon their borders do not behold the sea. Beyond them to the east there lies a desert, for ever untroubled by man: all yellow it is, and spotted with shadows of stones, and Death is in it, like a leopard lying in the sun. To the south they are bounded by magic, to the west by a mountain, and to the north by the voice and anger of the Polar wind. Like a great wall is the mountain to the west. It comes up out of the distance and goes down into the distance again, and it is named Poltarnees, Beholder of Ocean. To the northward red rocks, smooth and bare of soil, and without any speck of moss or herbage, slope up to the very lips of the Polar wind, and there is nothing else there by the noise of his anger. Very peaceful are the Inner Lands, and very fair are their cities, and there is no war among them, but quiet and ease. And they have no enemy but age, for thirst and fever lie sunning themselves out in the mid-desert, and never prowl into the Inner Lands. And the ghouls and ghosts, whose highway is the night, are kept in the south by the boundary of magic. And very small are all their pleasant cities, and all men are known to one another therein, and bless one another by name as they meet in the streets. And they have a broad, green way in every city that comes in out of some vale or wood or downland, and wanders in and out about the city between the houses and across the streets, and the people walk along it never at all, but every year at her appointed time Spring walks along it from the flowery lands, causing the anemone to bloom on the green way and all the early joys of hidden woods, or deep, secluded vales, or triumphant downlands, whose heads lift up so proudly, far up aloof from cities.

Anymore, an emergency radio has been largely replaced by smart phones for getting emergency updates and it is not a common item that people frequently buy or have around. That said, having a radio like this is useful when traveling and either cell service is bad or using a phone is impractical. In such cases a radio like this is a really good resource. For us, while not a necessity this radio sees daily use as a weather radio.

One of the things that has been around our house for many, many years is a weather radio. We are in range of two weather stations and we have a dedicated emergency weather radio that provides us emergency notifications as well as current conditions and forecasts around the region. The difficulty we have had with it is that reception is not the greatest and we often have static over the broadcast. We have a secondary weather radio that has even worse reception that our main one.

I did not have high expectations of this radio at all. We tuned it to the closest station with the expectation of hearing a lot of static and interference. Much to our surprise, the broadcast is clear and uncluttered. We tuned to the other station and got the same – a clear broadcast. What was a real surprise for us is that we could suddenly pick up a third station. We had no idea we were close enough to any other station to hear their broadcasts. It’s not as clear as the others, but it is clear enough to be understood.

As a weather radio, this unit is excellent. We have no complaints.

Most of the other features we have tried though do not use regularly. It has a flashlight built in that is bright enough to navigate through the house during a power outage and it has a couple of different modes such as SOS flash that make it useful in different emergency situations. It has different charging modes so it is ready to go when needed, the most frequent of which we use is the solar charging but it can be plugged in and it also can be hand-cranked to generate enough power for emergency use. A particularly helpful emergency feature is the ability to charge your phone, and the battery is sufficient to give one full charge to a smaller smartphone with power to spare.

If I could change one thing I would make it more ruggedized. It is good in that regard and should be able to handle getting dropped or jostled and bumped, but there is definitely opportunity to go farther. This is by no means a show-stopper or even a complaint, but a data point – if you need something that can handle a lot of abuse, this isn’t it, though in the price range it would be difficult to find better.

This is a nice emergency radio and my family really likes it. Though designed and marketed as an emergency radio, it actually sees daily use solely on the basis of how well it performs as a weather radio.

So I owned two of these cameras (argus eco). They work okay - miss a lot of events but that was not the biggest problem. I had both charging continuously with a solar panel. For some reason I had to take them in at some point because they were not charging. Reolink support recommended charging them indoors with the usb. Each of the two times I did that, the charging port sunk so far into the camera that I could not connect it. After dealing with this for a while with Reolink support, the bottom line was that since it was out of warranty, there was nothing they could do. By the way, one of these was a replacement camera they sent (for a different issued) that was only 6 months old but they do not count the warranty from that, they count it from the original purchase date. So this happened on a camera that was only 6 months old as well as one that was a little over two years old.

Since I could not charge the camera, it was not usable so I decided to take it apart to see what the issue was. The pictures show that the connection port is thinly attached to a computer board. The computer board is held in place (pushing the port up through the connection hole), simply with tape. So the tape dried out and now slides down (see pictures), taking the port with it when you try to plug in. This is a ridiculously simple problem to solve by the company. They should simply screw in the board to the part that holds it in place. So now I have two cameras that should work (well, one I destroyed by opening it up) but don't because there is no way to charge it. Also, the soldering that connects the port to the board is also very weak. It super easily broke off when trying to fish it out with tweezers.

So, I might be stupid in that I ordered two more reolink outdoor cameras (a different type this time). If the charging ports are built the same, I expect to have the same problem in the future. Then this will truly be the last outdoor reolink camera that I will ever purchase. The only reason I stuck with it is because it offers local storage. I have no interest in paying for a subscription or having my images on a cloud...although I will likely reconsider that if these two new cameras fail as well.

To those of you that have not yet run into this problem, maybe try to find a way to secure the porrt now, before you lose it to drying out tape.

The goal of this "project" is to get the reader to write "Thank You" notes to everyone who made a difference in their lives starting with the closest family member. The idea is to enumerate ways these people made an impact, helped you in the past, etc. Besides people, she even suggests you write to places and things and even yourself. Just writing the letters and not even mailing them is good enough is some cases.

I did feel the first 25 pages had a lot of filler text in it but after that the book is excellent. The author intersperses her story or message of thanks with some examples of what she wrote. She even writes letters to her grandparents who are dead so that she can experience the "depth of what she lost" but also thank them even though they will never get to read the letters.

In most cases the letters should be mailed and nothing should be expected in return. This is a way of telling those you love how they matter to you in a positive way. Including an apology in the letter is acceptable if there was something that you needed to apologize for.

In summary, the backstories and short snippets of the author's letters help the reader understand the message that should be conveyed. This is more a book of guidance than a "how to" text. More of us should follow this advice to help show appreciation to the people that matter most in our lives. It also serves as a legacy from you when you are gone.

Home Economics courses were once standard in high schools, though that seems to be a thing of the past now. I never had a home-ec class but I remember many of my classmates taking such classes. There was a lot to learn besides just cooking - balancing a checkbook, basic sewing, and more. This book is a good resource that distills down much of that knowledge into a handy volume.

For those of us that have been around a while, this book might seem full of the most obvious and trivial material. For someone who either showed no interest in the past or has not learned these things, though, the material presented might just be the ticket to basic productivity and survival. There are numerous categories in this book - Cooking, Sewing, Laundry & Clothing, Domestic Arts, and Life Skills. All of these things are important to successfully handling a household.

The largest section is on cooking, though this should not be confused with being a cookbook. It covers such topics as how to steam vegetables, how to measure flour, how to make mashed potatoes, and many more things. These all seem trivial, but for some they're not. In the cases where there's specific techniques related to cooking in particular, the book frequently includes a recipe to try which is a nice touch.

The sewing section is a good collection of useful tips including how to sew on a button, how to repair a tear in your jeans, and how to repair a zipper.

The laundry and clothing section is a collection of tips that relate to, well, clothing. How to use a washing machine, how to hand wash a sweater, etc.

Domestic arts roughly translates to house cleaning. It even includes a tip on how to make a bed.

Finally, life skills are miscellaneous tips that relate to life and interpersonal skills. It includes how to answer wedding invitations and how to pack a suitcase.

As I looked through the list of tips, my immediate thoughts was "I know how to do all these things already". That said, there are some people (my two adult sons among them) who need some help with such life skills. They'll be leaving us soon enough and when they do I will have a copy of this book in their hands.

The tips are all written in such a way as to not be condescending or demeaning, and they present the material in very matter-of-fact terms that are very accessible. Often there are illustrations as well to help explain better. This is a good approach and will not intimidate the reader who is a bit shy about lack of skills.

This is a fun, interesting and useful resource. It will serve well those that have not taken the time to learn or were not given the opportunity to learn the skills it presents. This is the perfect resource for people striking out on their own for the first time.

KNITTING ARCHITECTURE is a collection of patterns inspired by architecture, not (as I'd hoped) a technical book about the "architecture" (construction) of knitted garments. However, the designs are pretty and wearable, and a couple of them are technically innovative.

The Pompidou Wrap (by Grace Anna Farrow) is a black rectangle with colorful zigzag lines that wrap around the wearer. The lines are set far enough apart to create an elegant garment (not an op-art effect). The construction is intriguing--it begins with five separate triangles, and the triangles are added to and joined as you proceed through the 12 sections of written-out instructions.

The Hotel Tassel Wrap (by Asa Tricosa) is, for me, a "why didn't someone think of this before" design. It's a lace mesh rectangle with a border band of garter stitch and small cables. The band separates at both ends to outline mesh triangles that give the impression of sleeves when the wrap is worn.

Other designs that especially appeal to me are the Byzantine Pullover (by Tanis Lavallee), the Rococo Mittens (by Jane Dupuis), and the Tower of Pisa Shift (by Veera Valimaki). The pullover is a pretty top-down-knit sweater with a wide, colorful geometric-design band that runs around the shoulders; the band is set low, so it doesn't look like your usual Fair Isle yoke. The blue and white mittens (a charted design) have asymmetrically placed swirls on a background of knitted "lice" (single contrasting-color stitches that form v-shaped dots). The simple shift dress is knit mostly sideways, and achieves its shaping with strips joined as you go.

Each of the 20 included designs is accompanied by a photograph of the building or type of architecture that inspired it (e.g., Frank Lloyd Wright's Fallingwater, the beautiful Gothic King's College Chapel, the Sagrada Familia, Victor Horta's Hotel Tassel). The architectural photographs are displayed in sidebars with text explaining the featured architectural styles.

The book's patterns are not easy-to-knit designs, but an adventurous knitter with intermediate skills should be able to knit them. This is another beautiful book, filled with high-quality patterns, from knitting book publisher Interweave Press.

O. Henry was the pen name of William Sidney Porter, who was born on September 11, 1862 in Greensboro, North Carolina. Porter was a licensed pharmacist and worked on a sheep ranch in Texas. He was a draftsman for the General Land Office and a teller for the First National Bank of Texas. He was convicted of embezzlement and eventually served five years in prison. While in prison, he began writing short stories under his pseudonym and eventually wrote over 300. As O. Henry, Porter is one of America's best known writers, and his stories, such as "The Gift of the Magi" and "The Ransom of Red Chief", are still taught in schools. In 1918, the O. Henry Awards, an annual anthology of short stories, was established in his honor. Porter died on June 5, 1910.

The Gus Parker/Alex Mills series, which begins with [[ASIN:B01N22TFJ1 Desert Remains]], features Phoenix homicide detective Alex Mills, who unabashedly employs the services of psychic Gus Parker to help him solve tough cases. Like the first series novel, this second one, DIG YOUR GRAVE, has an elaborately constructed plot with all the loose ends tied up at the conclusion. However, the author seems to have attempted too much in DIG YOUR GRAVE, where the need to juggle two independent plotlines (the stalking of Gus; the finding of the killer who leaves murder victims in cemeteries) results in a book that's a slow, too-long read.

In the novel, Alex is called to a shallow grave in a cemetery that contains the body of a well-dressed John Doe. Alex summons Gus, who intuits that the solution to the crime lies in an investigation of long-ago events. The body is soon identified as the billionaire CEO of a company that promises “a better YOU”. A few days later, a second body is discovered in another cemetery; this time it’s a plastic surgeon who drives a Maserati. Alex sets his homicide team to work, and a lot of traditional, slogging inquiries begin to unravel possible connections between the men. The hard-won facts are supplemented by more visions from Gus.

Meanwhile, Gus is experiencing disturbing visions that don’t seem related to Alex’s investigation. He’s still involved in an idyllic relationship with popular singer Billie Welch, but the words “Stay Away From Her” keep popping up, in visions and in mysteriously-delivered notes. And he keeps hearing Spanish music. Will Gus succeed in sorting out his visions in time to stop a killer, and to save himself?

The book is reasonably well-written, though the prose takes more attention from the reader than is optimal for a mystery/thriller intended for a mass audience. The novel would benefit by slimming down from 410 to 330 or so pages; and from a rewritten conclusion that didn’t have to rely on a dry-as-dust FBI case summary to explain the killer’s motives. Also, the details about how the murders were carried out aren’t convincing; the added plot centering on Trevor is unnecessary; and the business about the victims’ wives paying for the killer’s legal defense is just plain silly.

Despite the flaws in DIG YOUR GRAVE, I found the novel to be entertaining, and I’m looking forward to the further adventures of Alex and Gus. Both are interesting characters in their own right.

THE FIFTH TO DIE (A 4MK THRILLER) is a continuation of [[ASIN:0544968840 The Fourth Monkey]]. It is NOT a sequel, and it will make no sense unless you’ve read the previous book, which contains the full text of the diary of the 4MK serial killer (Anson Bishop). THE FIFTH TO DIE chronicles Detective Sam Porter’s continuing search for 4MK, and centers on the “anomaly” among Bishop’s seven victims—the one blonde victim (Barbara McInley), murdered in revenge for a traffic accident, and the fifth to die.

In the novel, a federal team has taken over the 4MK case, so Porter’s team is focused on another serial killer. Someone is kidnapping teenage girls, drowning them in salt water, and dropping off their bodies in staged locations (e.g., under the ice at the frozen lake in Chicago’s Jackson Park).

At first Porter is convinced that Bishop isn’t involved. The 4MK signature is missing—there are no little white boxes containing the ear, the eyes, the tongue of the victims. But eventually a connection with Bishop emerges, and it becomes clear that he’s escalating. Now he’s targeting the drowned girls’ parents, too.

Even worse, Bishop clearly has help—the kidnapper, a former victim, New Orleans prison guards, who else? And he’s as elusive as ever, committing crimes in plain sight, entering locked homes and businesses silently without triggering alarms, escaping easily from federal agents and Chicago Metro officers alike.

The writing is excellent, effortlessly juggling multiple investigator and perpetrator viewpoints and locations. The characters aren’t exactly “developed”, because we learn little about their backstories; but they are well differentiated, so that the reader doesn’t lose track of where the characters are or what they’re working on in the investigation. The plot is twisty and astonishing, but NOT confusing.

READER BE WARNED: As previously stated, THE FIFTH TO DIE is a continuation of the Porter/Bishop story; and despite the novel’s length (over 500 pages), the story isn’t over yet. Thus the novel ends with another cliffhanger—Bishop gets away again, and his uncanny means of uncovering secrets and freely accessing victims’ homes/offices is still unexplained.

But despite the remaining loose threads, this is a satisfying thriller—a genuine page-turner. I can’t wait for the next novel in the 4MK series, though I do hope that the third one will finally wrap up the Bishop/Porter story.

I am a fan of cookbooks and when I was presented an opportunity to buy all 5 of the cookbooks in this series at a very reasonable price I jumped at the chance. So far I have been very pleased.

Casseroles is the first cookbook in the series that I purchased and was so pleased with it that I bought the other four the next day. I selected Casseroles first because I am always looking for ways to fill up my teenager, who has discovered that there is great joy in eating. With a good casserole, we stand a chance of having leftovers.

Favorite Recipes of Home Economics Teachers cookbooks are very similar to cookbooks you would expect to see put out by a church or other fundraising group, though they are larger and are hard-bound. They use the GBC-style binding which is great for laying them flat on the counter when following recipes. The table of contents is somewhat sparse, taking the reader to a general section instead of to specific recipes, but the index at the back is exhaustive and complete.

In addition to the recipes, each of the cookbooks in the series have sections for cooking tips and suggestions, conversion and temperate charts and definitions of common terms before progressing into the recipe collections.

Casseroles has a nice variety of recipes divided into the following sections, though some are not casseroles at all: Ground Beef, Poultry, Combination Meats, Variety Meats, Seafood, Meat & Vegetable, Vegetable, Skillet Dishes, Cereal/Pasta/Eggs/Cheese, Convenience dishes, Foreign Flavors, Breads, Quick Breads, Yeast Breads, and finally Foreign Breads.

I am a little uncertain as to why there are sections for breads, of any kind. Looking through, there are even recipes for the likes of doughnuts in this volume and that is certainly unrelated to casseroles, though the addition is welcome as far as I am concerned.

I looked through carefully for recipes that make large numbers of servings and I found a few that serve 10 or more. When I made these, the results were good and I was successful in having leftovers for dinner the following evening. Some of these have become family favorites now, in particular a dish with the non-descript name "One Dish Meal."

These are not gourmet recipes, by any stretch of the imagination, but they are instead family-style recipes that are suitable for company and for larger gatherings like pot-lucks as well.

It's difficult to find much wrong with any of the cookbooks in the Favorite Recipes of Home Economics Teachers series. Casseroles is probably my favorite of the bunch and it's the most useful as well. Considering the price, this cookbook is an absolute bargain and very much worth a look.

Sonchai Jitpleecheep, the only policeman in Bangkok who isn't on the take, is one of my favorite detectives. Forced to work for the utterly corrupt Colonel Vikorn, he performs the tasks that are assigned to him with long-suffering good humor; and he solves crimes, because he is one of those rare policemen who thinks outside the box.

Unfortunately, THE BANGKOK ASSET takes Jitpleecheep through a plot that is more science fiction than mystery/thriller. Jitpleecheep is assigned to investigate the brutal murder of a child whose head was wrenched off by a killer apparently possessed of superhuman strength--perhaps an alien. As it turns out, that is very, very close to the truth. As Jitpleecheep investigates, he quickly finds himself in the middle of high-level political intrigue that involves the auction of an advanced new military weapon--a "transhuman" possessed of such enhanced mental and physical capabilities that the once-merely-human individual relates to ordinary humans in the same way that ordinary humans relate to dumb animals.

THE BANGKOK ASSET is a well-written book that is entertaining to read. Jitpleecheep performs expertly, detects many things, finally learns the identity of his father, and handles himself extremely well (as always). The fictional explanation for the development of the new weapon (the race of transhumans) is fairly plausible and carefully plotted without leaving a lot of loose ends. But at the end, Jitpleecheep is still caught up in the science fiction situation. Apparently the author couldn't think of a way to end the book in a way that would be satisfying to a mystery/thriller fan like myself.

Because the extremely far-fetched plot is complex, full of twists, and entertaining, I rate THE BANGKOK ASSET at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale). But instead of looking forward to reading the next book in this series, I'll be headed back to read the older ones that I've missed so far.

Silman's Complete Endgame Course is arguably the most useful book on chess endgames available. Many titles have been written on the topic of endgames, and many of these titles are excellent and are filled with good instruction, but it seems that most of them are theoretical and abstract in nature, where Silman's book deals in more concrete terms. However, there are other things about this book that set it apart.

Author Jeremy Silman is a prolific chess author, and he is an International Master chess player with a good grasp on where fellow chess players struggle. He is an excellent instructor as can be evidenced in his other titles, especially in How to Reassess Your Chess and The Amateur's Mind. These titles, however, deal with more abstract material such as planning and relative value of pieces depending on the lay of the board. In this book, though, the material is more concrete and direct. This is more a function of the nature of the subject rather than writing or teaching style. That said, Silman does a superb job teaching concrete theory, and he does so in a clear and approachable manner. A big plus is that the condescending tone present in some of his earlier works is less prevalent.

The very best strength of this book is the organization of the material. Instead of breaking it up by material themes, Silman instead breaks up the subject material based on relative ratings of the readership. This is huge - it may make searching for a specific theme harder to find but it enables a rated player to add to his or her arsenal of endgame knowledge without stuffing their heads with material that is likely to be unneeded at their ranking.

Though I am a weak Class B player, the chapters for even the weakest rankings are still useful and I found them to be every bit as helpful. Some themes in those sections are good refresher courses, but there are a few things in those sections that were unfamiliar.

This is a great book on the subject of chess endgame studies. The examples are taken from real games, the material is concrete and the organization makes learning from this book easy and approachable.
