For years, I've been buying individual Noni bag patterns, just to get the directions for the gorgeous, realistic, decorative felted flowers. And now, at long last, Noni creative designer Nora Bellows has published this fabulous book, NONI FLOWERS, which includes instructions for 40 different Noni flowers. The flower patterns range from Sunflower and Dahlia through Pansy and Orange Blossom; the book also includes six lovely, well-worth-knitting, project patterns (May Violets Fingerless Gloves, Forget-Me-Not Pillow, Sunflower Infinity Wrap, Gossamer Fuchsia Wrap, Cherry Blossom Pauper's Purse, and Creeping Phlox Garden Clutch).

For the technically inclined knitter, NONI FLOWERS has a wonderful two-page illustration of how one flower pattern will look when knit with 12 different yarns and gauges. The tiniest flower, knit with silk yarn on six-0 (.7mm) needles, is 3/8" high; the largest flower, knit with merino top on US 50 needles, is 8-1/4" high. All of the flowers can be knit at any gauge, because the instructions are given in rounds and rows (no charts). The flowers can be felted, or not. Felting will make the knitted stitches more dense, but will not dramatically shrink the flower size.

Another beautiful two-page spread explains the anatomy of a knitted flower, and indicates the various small flower parts by their Latin names (the Latin names are used for the parts in the instructions). There are directions, illustrated with close-up photos, for special techniques, such as knitting with multiple colors in a single round, wiring stems and blossoms, or weaving in ends so that the flowers will not be marred by errant, poking-out ends.

All of the flower patterns give the difficulty level: starting out (easy, 13 patterns), on the way (some experience, 19 patterns), intrepid (experienced, 3 patterns), resolute (expert, 5 patterns). For example, the Creeping Phlox is easy; the Crocus requires some experience; the Gardenia requires experience; the Oriental Lily requires expertise. The Tulip on the book cover is an experienced pattern. The book also has two indexes: an unconventional one using lovely thumbnail photos of each flower pattern; and a very good standard one that lists the flowers, techniques, projects, etc.

This is a superb book that any knitter should welcome. Although there are many excellent knitted flower pattern books currently available, this is the one that I would select, if I could have only one in my knitting book collection.

This book is an enjoyable read. However, I still find it very difficult to explain the message within. To me love is common sense in business. I do not believe one can be truly successful unless they genuinely love their customer, company, employees, work, and themselves. 

I actually did not realize that the author was touting a LEAP Model until the end.  LEAP, in this business context, stands for love, energy, audacity, and proof. A business leader must cultivate a caring environment for their customer, company, employees, work, and themselves. Love also means the leader may need to make tough decisions. For instance, someone who loves their company may need to to fire someone who is not up to muster in order to maintain a healthy culture within their firm. A business leader must also generate an environment whereby their employees can get behind their vision, be shameless in achieving their goal with love, and provide evidence of success day after day by making what they do better and reaping the rewards.

If a leader is genuine and truly cares and then motivates their employees, the proof of customer satisfaction will be evident via the results achieved (monetary or otherwise).

The above is what I inferred from the examples in the book but was not specifically spelled out. It was a good read and there were many examples incorporated  throughout the text; however, I did not feel the information provided was concrete enough for me to sink my teeth into or describe to someone else. I feel love in business is just plain common sense in that one reaps what they sow and if the sow well, they and their customer and employees will be rewarded. It is also important to be genuine in achieving that goal.

I first heard about "How To Be A Canadian" on CBC's "Basic Black," in which Arthur Black interviewed the Ferguson brothers (Will and Ian) and they read some of the best parts of the book out loud. What can I say...I was hooked and rushed out to buy a copy at Chapters (Amazon.ca didn't exist then...sorry guys, I'm now a loyal Amazon.ca customer!). "HTBAC" reads fairly quickly, but it is an immensely enjoyable read, and explosively funny in spots (don't read this at work if you don't want coworkers giving you looks of sympathy after your random hyena laughter).
"How To Be A Canadian" conveniently packages our national heroes, cuisine, regional differences, literary endeavours, phobias, and odd social customs into a laugh-out-loud tome that is the literary equivalent of Timbits: tasty, bite-sized chapters on "Who To Hate and Why," "How To Waste Time Like A Canadian," "Mating Rituals," "Art and Stuff," "Progressive Conservatives, Responsible Government and Other Oxymorons," and "Twelve Ways To Say You're Sorry," along with how to insult Canadians, the official Canadian haircut and dress code (mullet, plaid shirt, skidoo boots with fake buckles), provincial "fact sheets" (Ontario: "Gaze Upon our Humble Magnificence and Bow Down Before Us!" Formal name: The Centre of the Universe. Provincial motto: "Celebrating over 100 years of narcissistic self-absorption") and more. To top it off the Ferguson brothers have written a clever little quiz at the end to test your Canadian knowledge (If you hear the name "Elvis" and immediately think of figure skating, give yourself one point. If you still don't know what the capital of New Brunswick is, give yourself 10 points. If you can't remember if you curled or not, because of how drunk you were: 50 points) You get the idea. Nothing is sacred for Will and Ian, which is what makes the book so funny.
So, if you're American and want to learn more about those mysterious neighbo(u)rs of yours to the north, this is the book for you. If you're a Canadian who needs a quick reply to "What makes a Canadian" (other than *not* being an American), this book is for you. I have bought "How to Be A Canadian" for a number of friends with different tastes and it's been a success all around. A funny, thoughtful book that hits the mark on all the issues and is certainly entertaining in the process (that's PROcess, not prahcess, eh?) Have fun, and good luck to any Future Canadians out there!

A SEASON TO LIE: A DETECTIVE GEMMA MONROE MYSTERY reads more like a romance than a mystery. The detective (Gemma) is a new mother--breastfeeding, of course--who must interrupt her active crime-scene investigations because her breasts are throbbing (it's time “to pump”).

Gemma is also a highly insecure female investigator who starts to experience a panic attack when, during a blizzard, she discovers a murdered man “skewered” to a tree with an antique knife through his belly. She finds relief when her male partner (Finn) joins up at the scene, wearing his “dark puffy parka and brimmed winter hat” that “were familiar, instantly grounding”. Gemma adds, “he made me brave”. Oh, please. Gemma seems to be in the wrong profession--how on earth did she ever make detective?

The whole story is told in first person, and it is generously padded with Gemma’s reflections on the surrounding scenery (the wind made tree “limbs dance and their few remaining leaves jump like marionettes”), and on the meaning of life and everything else (“I knew forces mightier than me were in charge, and those forces would dictate our next steps”).

And what about the flawed police procedure? To protect the evidence on the murder victim’s body (which is outdoors in a blizzard), Finn empties out a nearby trash receptacle to get the trash can liner and cover the body. Trash is now gone, and who knows what has transferred to the body?

Finally, the plot is a total snooze. It's about the inexplicable murder of a world-famous, best-selling writer, and the ending is expected and trite. (Novels and TV series about writers are rarely successful, probably because writers do the interesting stuff inside their heads.)

For escape reading, I prefer strongly-plotted mysteries that focus on the puzzle to be solved. Mysteries (like this one) that feature detectives who share their innermost thoughts, conflicts, and feelings in far too much detail leave me cold.

Laura Miller's The Magician's Book: A Skeptic's Adventures in Narnia is part literary history and critique, part biography, and part memoir. She combines all of these genres wonderfully in the pursuit of one goal: to convince readers that there is more to C.S. Lewis' Chronicles of Narnia than their reduction to Christian allegory.

Miller's intentions are not entirely benign; she takes the Christian themes of Narnia very personally, and is frankly put off by them. As a self-described "skeptic," she drifted away from the religion of her youth and settled on an idea of Christianity that leaves little to be desired. And yet, The Chronicles of Narnia remain the most important books of her lifetime. How can she settle the apparent discrepancy between her unbelief and her love of books so seemingly full of belief?

Miller constructs this book in three parts, which seem to mirror the progression of her own relationship with Narnia. In the first part, she articulates all the reasons to love Narnia. It's a magical place, full of talking animals, with the appeal of a secret, private garden. Children especially identify with the world of Narnia because there, children are tested and challenged, and what they do matters. There is a satisfying weight to their thoughts and actions, and in a real world typically condescending to kids, young people find Narnia liberating.

The second section of Miller's book details her discovery of the blatant Christian themes in Narnia. This was a betrayal to her, the idea of an agenda being injected into an otherwise pure reading experience. Now that C.S. Lewis the author is revealed in Narnia, she begins to realize there are other reasons not to blindly trust in the epic. Themes of racism, sexism, and elitism are apparent in the Chronicles, all stemming from Lewis' own flaws as a person. Miller is left feeling alienated and upset, until she gets some advice from author Philip Pullman, himself a detractor of Lewis and his creative worlds. Pullman tells Miller that if she is really interested in making peace with Narnia, she must find "another way in."

The third section of The Magician's Book is a scholarly examination of the influences on Lewis at the time he wrote Narnia. The English landscape surrounding his home and haunts, his interest in Norse mythology and medieval romance, and especially his close relationship with fellow author J.R.R. Tolkein - all of these experiences factored in to the creation of Narnia as much as Lewis' conversion to Christianity. In finding evidence of these other crucial contributions to Narnia's universe, Miller is in essence "reclaiming" (as she puts it) Narnia for the readers who gain little from a Christian examination of the books.

The Magician's Book is so well-written - I was consistently impressed with Miller's thorough research and amazing ability to transition from one idea to the next. Her interviews with other authors are seamlessly woven into the path of her journey here, and I felt the contemporary views really added to my understanding. Miller doesn't require her readers to be fellow experts in the Chronicles books - she does an excellent job summarizing parts of the books under examination. The only prerequisite to enjoying Miller's effort is a love of reading, and an appreciation for the many whys and worlds involved in the creation of any given text.

Finally, While it is clear that Miller is trying to come to a heightened idea of "full circle" (love-hate-love Narnia), I must confess that I got caught up in the centrifugal force of the final turn. The third section was very heavy in research, and I felt it lost some of the more intimate tone of the first two sections. Still, I came away feeling that this book is an important companion to anyone's understanding and appreciation of C.S. Lewis' Chronicles of Narnia. I will also be enthusiastically recommending this as a book club read, since there is much opportunity for discussion, and I'm eager to pick the brains of other book lovers and new fans of Laura Miller.

"Sadie" is the story of a nineteen year old young woman whose younger sister, Mattie, has been murdered and who is determined to find her sister's killer and bring him to justice. In that sense, it is a journey story--the "hero" leaves home on a quest, going out of his or her comfort zone, confronting challenges and obstacles along the way, helped by various people or creatures, until the quest is accomplished. In the classic story, the hero returns with something of value to his or her community, and has learned a lot about him or herself in the process. It is here that the analogy breaks down, but I do not want to go into too much detail. "Sadie" is a story of love, abuse, determination, accomplishment, and survival.

The book is structured in an interesting way. Every other chapter is from Sadie's point of view, and these chapters are more or less typical. The alternating chapters are in the form of a script for a podcast hosted by radio reporter West McCray, who has heard of Sadie's disappearance and is determined to find her. He is helped by May Beth Foster, a grandmother-figure who lives in the same trailer part as Sadie and Mattie and cares for them when their mother opts out of her parental responsibilities. It is through the podcasts that the reader gets necessary background into Sadie's life, her mother's experiences, and the social milieu of the time and place. I thought this was an interesting and effective device.

"Sadie" is not an easy book to read. You will love Sadie, admire her, be frustrated by some of her choices, and be exasperated at the same time. The book is heartbreaking on so many levels. If I were teaching high school, I would love to teach this book--it would provoke so much discussion of the issues kids are faced with today. Highly recommended.

CHASING PHIL: THE ADVENTURES OF TWO UNDERCOVER AGENTS WITH THE WORLD’S MOST CHARMING CON MAN is an extraordinary, highly readable account of a two-man FBI sting operation that lasted 8 months and ultimately snared financial con man Phillip Kitzer. Kitzer stole millions from unsuspecting individuals who paid him fees for phony letters of credit, certificates of deposit, and cashier’s checks, for them to use as collateral for needed loans.

Kitzer would issue the financial documents through banks that he controlled, and if anyone discovered that the documents were worthless because the banks had no funds, he would refuse to refund the fees. Kitzer operated across state and international lines, and in total confidence that the FBI wouldn’t bother opening cases against him because the details were so complicated that the cases would confuse juries.

Two young, ambitious FBI agents (Jack Brennan and Jim Wedick), with no training in undercover work, befriended Kitzer by posing as guys who wanted to enter Kitzer’s lucrative line of work. They partnered with Kitzer, spent hours with him, recorded conversations that would provide solid evidence of his cons, and eventually persuaded him to turn state’s witness against a ring of conspirators that included Mafia figures.

Without Brennan and Wedick’s operation, the huge Abscam operation (not discussed in this book) would never have happened. CHASING PHIL should interest true crime aficionados, persons interested in financial fraud, and anyone considering a career involving undercover law enforcement work.

But instead he discovers that his father has died, his home is overrun by livestock and drunken servants, and Elizabeth, having believed Ross dead, is now engaged to his cousin. Ross must start over, building a completely new path for his life, one that takes him in exciting and unexpected directions? Thus begins an intricately plotted story spanning loves, lives, and generations. The Poldark series is the masterwork of Winston Graham, who evoked the period and people like only he could, and created a world of rich and poor, loss and love, that readers will not soon forget.

Also from the Publisher: Tired from a grim war in America, Ross Poldark returns to his land and his family. But the joyful he has anticipated turns sour, for his father is dead, his estate is derelict and the girl he loves is engaged to his cousin. But his sympathy for the destitute miners and farmers of the district leads him to rescue a half-starved urchin girl; from a fairground brawl and take her home - an act which alters the whole course of his life...

From the BBC - Intro Good evening, I'm Alistair Cooke. Tonight we begin a new series, called Poldark, based on the four novels of Winston Graham. It runs to sixteen episodes and I can only say that now is the time for the party to settle in to a spate of loving, dueling, poaching, smuggling, wenching, and marrying,--not to mention banking and copper mining. Copper mining plays a big part in this story because we are in the county of Cornwall in England at the end of the eighteenth century. I don't suppose today's tourists visit the copper mines, which are abandoned, but the Greeks and the Romans knew about them and at the end of the eighteenth century copper and tin were the main sources of wealth in a county that is otherwise practically treeless--barren but very beautiful. Those of you who have been there may have noticed those strange cones of pyramids on the horizon they are China Clay deposits. Maybe we should try to pin Cornwall down on the map. When I was a boy we were told that the map of Britain was that of a pig with a man on its back and it comes out very roughly like this [Cooke draws]. The trunk is England, with his very long head Scotland. The pig's face is Wales. And here what they call West Country which goes from Dorset, Somerset, Devon, and here is Cornwall the very end here is the tip of the island Lands' End. So we are in Cornwall, then, the end of the eighteenth century just at the close of the American Revolutionary War and the surrender of the British forces to George Washington and the Continental Army. The date, as any handy schoolboy will tell you, is 1783. And our hero, Captain Ross Poldark, who has been serving in George III's forces, has come home to Cornwall. He has just landed and is on his way home back to his estate, which has indifferent farming but two copper mines. It's called Nampara. During the War he has heard that his father is no longer alive, but his relatives don't know that he himself is alive. This is not surprising because during the war they didn't have any transatlantic mail service. In fact in this year of 1783, England saw its first domestic mail coach going between Bristol and London. So we open with Captain Poldark jogging home in a stagecoach to meet and amaze his friends.

I am writing this review for the audio version of Palimpsest, so there are two elements to this novel for which I must comment. While the audio aspects are excellent and it is well-narrated, the actual story itself is very disjoint and difficult (at best) to follow.

Palimpsest is a magical place where people are transported and branded after a night of sex with others who have already visited. Every visitor receives a map of the city somewhere on their body, and there is no choice as to where it goes (one visitor gets her mark on her face). Traveling back once a visitor leaves requires another round of sex.

To be very honest, the concept itself is very interesting but the actual execution is unpleasant and hard to follow. The transitions back and forth are frequent and jarring, making following what's happening a struggle in its own right. Many reviewers have described this as an adult version of Alice in Wonderland and I partially agree - it is a hybrid mix of Alice in Wonderland, the X Files and a cheap romance novel with the romance removed and the sex left behind. I am not a fan of sex fiction (even very brief and lightweight depiction) so to have it frequently presented is a turn-off for me.

On the plus side, the narration is superb. The novel is narrated by Aasne Vigessa who does a fabulous job with employing accents and voice inflection at the right places. She reads clearly, at the right speed and with enough voice variation that she would have kept me interested in almost any other novel.

Unfortunately I did not like Palimpsest and cannot rate is too favorably. The narration of the novel is above average and drives up my opinion of the actual audio product but is insufficient to compensate for the story itself.

Siena, Tuscany, is famous for its Palio, a yearly event where ten of the city's seventeen Contrade compete in a brutal, blink-and-you-miss-it horse race. This tradition dates back to the 17th century in its present form. The Daughter of Siena is set in 1723, where Pia Tolomei, descendent of Queen Cleopatra, is told that she'll wed a man from a rival contrade on her nineteeth birthday. Hardly the news that Pia had hoped for. At the Palio the next day, a handsome stranger appears as the jockey for the Torre contrada. Pia is instantly drawn to him, unlike the cruel, calculating man her father has chosen for her. A shocking event puts a quick end to the normal Palio festivities, and the course of Pia's future is changed forever.

The remainder of Pia's story is one of political intrigue and thwarted romance. This is no lighthearted historical romp; there are quite a few graphic scenes. There are several dark undercurrents involving murder, torture, madness, and gluttony that were uncomfortable to read at times. The author includes a virtual menagerie of unlikable secondary characters, from a snaggletooth abusive maid to a gluttonous gay Medici who indulges all his corporeal appetites with impunity. Many of the figures are based on actual historical figures (Violante, Anna Maria Luisa de' Medici, Gian Gastone).

Marina Fiorato excels at her vivid descriptions of the Palio; they're informative and engaging without disrupting the flow of the story, and one portion of the Palio narrative appears word for word in a later chapter, bringing the story full circle. The elegant descriptions of period clothing were in stark contrast to the cutthroat world of court politics and damp cellars and ruins where secret midnight meetings were held. However, a good part of the plot feels recycled from Fiorato's earlier novel [[ASIN:0312606362 The Botticelli Secret (Reading Group Gold)]]. Still, fans of historical fiction (and Tuscany) will find much to recommend The Daughter of Siena.

I selected this book for review because I was interested in user stories of how people get through being a second victim. For instance, my best friend in the whole world committed suicide and at one point I felt guilty I could not prevent that. An acquaintance of mine was brutally murdered (stabbed over 41 times) and I wanted to understand all the emotions a parent goes through. Also, while on the way work one day, a middle-aged man ran in front of a truck (suicide) a few minutes before I passed him as a passenger in a bus. I always wondered how the truck driver coped.

Nevertheless, this book is not about any of that. It's a clinical look at what companies might do to help practitioner (doctors, pilots, nurses, cops, etc.) second victims cope with a tragedy they caused without blame or with minimal blame. There are some brief stories of these second victims which I found to be the highlight of this book because I could get into the mind of the second victim but that was to support the argument of why it second victims should be treated differently. Societies put blame on second victims and have drifted away from calling things accidents. As a result, corporations and facilities do not learn from their mistakes.

The book talks about the clinical implications of trauma, guilt, investigation, justice, retribution, etc. In summary, this 100-page text is a good read but it really was not for me. I'd believe people who are treating second victims would find the most benefit from reading this (5 stars). People who are the second victims themselves might find a benefit (3-4 stars). However, people like me who wanted a text that delved into the mind of the second victim would probably rate this (2-3 stars). At the current price of $31.93, I also feel this book is three-times what I would have paid had I purchased it. It is well-written, I liked it, but it did not achieve the goal I expected. What I learned from this book is that society, corporations, medical faculties, etc. do not want to learn from their mistakes. Instead they are more likely to blame the second victim and seek to punish them without providing them the support that is desperately needed.

My first introduction to Nava Atlas was when a friend gave me a copy of [[ASIN:0963024353 Vegetariana: A Rich Harvest of Wit, Lore, and Recipes]] several years ago. While I was browsing at a local bookstore recently, I ran across Vegan Holiday Kitchen and was drawn in by the gorgeous photos and recipes; I was particularly intrigued by the Jewish vegan updates of beloved classics like sweet noodle kugel, tzimmes, matzoh balls and challah.

Nava was kind enough to send a review copy, and I promptly singled out four test recipes: massaged kale salad, skinny figgy bars, citrus-roasted tofu, and the chocolate orange cake. The kale salad was delicious and easily modified; I've been making it with mustard greens and candied ginger since it lends itself to experimentation with other dried fruits, greens, and seeds / nuts. It takes only moments to throw together, and is a perfect last-minute side dish for a potluck or party.

The skinny figgy bars are a guilt-free update on Fig Newtons; a paste of figs and dates is perked up by a touch of lemon juice, cinnamon and ginger; the filling would make a great jam or spread on its own (I soaked the dates in hot water to soften them before adding them to the food processor). The quick-oat crust almost seemed too wet upon mixing, but baked up tender and moist. I also made the optional orange drizzle, which gave the bars an additional boost of citrus that complemented the lemon juice in the filling.

For the citrus-roasted tofu, I used Italian bitter orange marmalade, which is then mixed with dry mustard, soy sauce, and pepper. I left out the carrot and almond garnish, as well as the tarragon and curry powder, since I wanted the flavor focus to be on the citrus. One caveat: I didn't leave enough space between the slices of tofu while baking, so the edges didn't get as crispy as I would have liked. The final flavor was great, though, and I will definitely make this again using a larger roasting pan and would consider making 1.5 times the marinade, since much of it bakes off in the oven, and you're supposed to use the extra marinade to spoon over before serving.

Finally, the chocolate orange cake seemed to be a very thick batter (half whole wheat, half unbleached flour) that seemed to be a bit dense when it baked up, but the orange zest and juice made for a very moist, flavorful cake; it's difficult to believe that it's fat-free. There's even an unexpected touch of balsamic vinegar (I used some of my prized 18-year balsamic from Fustini's, which has an incredible depth). Rarely have I had a recipe turn out like the included photo, but the chocolate-orange cake looked runway-ready and was quickly devoured by an appreciative audience.

The ingredients and instructions are clearly laid out in an easy-to-read font, and there are plenty of gorgeous full-color photos throughout. I loved that the recipe titles were color-coded to correspond with the section they were in (Passover titles were in blue, Easter recipes in purple, etc.). I loved that the dishes arranged by season, so you can easily make use of the freshest seasonal produce. All of the recipes I tried turned out as described without requiring any tweaking, and I would definitely make them again. There's a huge wealth of influences; you'll find Middle Eastern-inspired dips and spreads, Mexican and Asian flavors, Eastern European and Jewish comfort food, and Native American influences for Thanksgiving.

Two small things that could have improved the book for me would have been nutritional info and an easier-to-use index; the index font is about half the size of the recipes, and it's difficult to quickly locate a given ingredient or recipe since they're lumped together in paragraph form, but overall "Vegan Holiday Kitchen" is a wonderful addition to anyone's cookbook library.

(Review copy courtesy of Nava Atlas/ Sterling)

"Your Inner Fish" looks at how humans evolved. I was hoping the book would have been more insightful like, 'OK, we evolved from earlier life, but what does that mean, besides where we came from?' Anyway, the book covers evolution well, mentioning things like this:

1. 99% of species which ever lived are extinct.

2. Fossils are one of the major lines of evidence we use to understand ourselves.

3. About 375 million years ago appeared the first intermediate form of life in fish which led to the appearance of a land animal. Specifically, this is when fish fins began having bones like in our upper arm, forearm and parts of the wrist.

4. There are exceptional similarities among creatures as different as frogs and humans.

5. Genes are switches to make fingers, arms, toes, etc.

6. Teeth are important to study - likely evolved when animals began eating other animals - feathers, scales, etc became necessary because of teeth.

7. The head is made up of plates, blocks and rods. No developing living thing begins with a head. Stages of development for every creature are similar. There is an 'organizer cell'.

8. Collagen is important for body development - it comprises 90% of a body's protein, by weight.

9 Probably, when oxygen first appeared in the air, did land animal bodies develop.

10. Since soft tissues in bodies don't fossilize, that is why DNA is so important to study the history of bodies.

11. The sense of smell developed as a tool for survival. DNA is present in every cell, but certain genes are only turned on in certain cells, like only in nasal cells, here. Sense of smell genes make up 3% of the human genome, but most are inactive/useless unlike other animals which needed better senses of smell to survive. Likely, most of such human genes are inactive because they weren't needed as the eye was developed so well in humans. Likely, the eye developed the ability to see in color when so many different colors of plants/food emerged.

12. The bottom line is that every living thing has parents, the operative term being 'descent with modification.'

THE NIGHT MARKET is memorable for its portrait of a grim, dystopian, near-future San Francisco, where it rains all the time due to climate change, and decaying buildings everywhere are being dismantled by desperate kids seeking copper and bricks to sell.

As in the other two novels in Jonathan Moore’s loosely connected San Francisco trilogy (see [[ASIN:0544811828 The Poison Artist]] , and [[ASIN:1328745562 The Dark Room]]) the story in THE NIGHT MARKET shows great promise, but kind of fizzles out at the end, as if the author didn’t quite know how to finish it off. For me, there are too many coincidences and oddball connections/clues in the plot for the ending to be completely satisfying.

In the novel, SFPD homicide inspector Ross Carver is called to investigate a dead body located at one of the few remaining elegant mansions on Filbert Street near Telegraph Hill. VERY MINOR SPOILER ALERT: The rapidly decomposing body is covered in a gray moss that seems to be alive.

Before Carver can even mentally process what he’s seeing, several people clothed in hazmat suits burst in, and whisk him and his partner off to a decontamination truck. When Carver awakens a few days later, he’s back in his apartment at Grant and Bush. A beautiful woman (Mia Westcott) is reading to him.

Carver’s memory of visiting the house on Filbert has been erased, but incompletely. Vague memories of seeing the Fairmont Hotel wrapped in silk, with thousands of people lined up outside to witness the launch of a costly perfume (Black Aria), are enough to put him squarely on the path to reconstructing the homicide scene, and learning the dangerous, frightening truth about what really happened there.

It turns out that climate change—due to the collapse of the Pacific Ocean, whatever that means (the event isn’t explained)—is the least of San Francisco’s problems. The world has changed in an insidious way that actually accounts for the entire populace’s obsession with purchasing luxury goods from mailed “glow card” ads. The question is, can Carver do anything to help set the world right again?

Author Moore lived in San Francisco in the late nineties and early two thousands, so he gets the local details right. I liked the descriptions of the actual Old St. Mary’s Church, the imagined deterioration of the western neighborhoods, and the real “mermaid” who used to “swim” in a fish tank behind one of the North Beach bars. However, although the technologically advanced plot details are chillingly believable, the plot itself—as previously stated—isn’t fully satisfying.

Also, I would have liked this novel more without the “Black Dahlia” copycat murder details. That crime was horrific, and its details serve as a shortcut for painting the murderer as psychotic, but its inclusion is kind of a distraction.

After reading THE VALLEY, I feel like I've been living in the mountains of Afghanistan for a week, stationed at the worst imaginable, impossible-to-defend, remote combat outpost ever (cop Vega). The descriptions of the terrain, the local village, the politics, and the firestorm attacks all ring very true to me. This novel made me appreciate more than ever the sacrifices made by our U.S. troops stationed in Afghanistan.

Lt. Black is in the Army, hates the Army, and is handing in his request for release from the Army. But he is assigned one last task--go "up the Valley" to conduct a thorough "15-6" investigation of the shooting death of a goat (although the goat's owner has already been paid for his loss), and of a warning shot fired into a villager's mud wall. It's a ridiculous assignment, especially because Black must travel by an overland supply convoy to get to the Valley--cop Vega is too dangerous for helicopters to fly there except in the most extreme circumstances.

As Black arrives at cop Vega, the commanding officer, Lt. Pistone, jumps into a departing convoy truck to take leave "on some sort of R&R". Predictably, as Black pursues his 15-6 investigation, none of the outpost's personnel will talk openly or honestly about the reported shooting incidents. Forging on, because he cannot leave cop Vega without filing a complete report, Black uncovers layer upon layer of secrets. The lies told him ultimately jeopardize the very existence of cop Vega and of everyone assigned there. At the heart of the problems enveloping the outpost is the extreme disconnect between "the boots on the ground" and the decisions made by high-ranking army officers and nations' politicians.

The intricate plot is confusing in places, but only because Black is being fed misinformation as he investigates. At the end, the strands come together, and the explanations are fairly complete--as complete as you can expect from something that involves immersion in the lives of combat soldiers.

There are many memorable characters: the alpha male, Sergeant Merrick; the regular army guy, Sergeant Caine; the disaffected Lt. Black; the undercover operative, the Monk; the interpreter, Danny; and the ordinary soldiers, Hill, Corelli, Oswalt, and Bryson, who get caught up in an impossible situation simply because they were assigned to the absolute worst, most dangerous combat outpost in Afghanistan.

For me (having little knowledge of what it's actually like to serve in the military), the portrayal of army life was fascinating. The battle scenes are vivid and exciting, and the ever-present danger surrounding cop Vega is palpable--making THE VALLEY into a genuine page-turner of a thriller.

This cookbook has a nice variety of recipes. However, the subtitle and the back jacket which states they are 5 ingredient, 15 minute recipes is misleading. It really means each recipe either has 5 ingredients or has more ingredients but takes 15 minutes to prepare.

However, this isn't even true because some recipes take more than 15 minutes to prepare and the ingredients border on the absurd. For instance, a recipe can call for pre-packaged chopped onions. My supermarket doesn't sell this, does yours.

Although there's variety in every category (soups, sandwiches, salads, vegetarian, fish, meats,and poultry), I don't think every cook looking for a fast meal would be satisfied with this cookbook, since preparation might take longer than expected or the prepackaged ingredients difficult to find.

If you don't mind spending a little more time than 15 minutes cooking and don't mind chopping your own ingredients or adding Campbell's canned soup to a recipe (although I wouldn't call that "fresh"), then this book might be for you. It certainly has enough variety and interesting tidbits for the average cook. My two most favorite characteristics of the book are the gorgeous pictures of each recipe and the calorie, fat and protein breakdown of each menu. These two charactistics are five stars and the two recipes I tried were also tasty. However, due to the misleading subtitle (as well as the word Fresh in the title--canned is not Fresh) and some of the absurd ingredient suggestions, I have to give this cookbook three stars overall.

THE LAST DAYS OF NIGHT is a fascinating, superbly readable, fictionalized account of lawyer Paul Cravath's dealings with George Westinghouse, Thomas Edison, and Nikola Tesla, during the famous alternating current/direct current wars that preceded the electrification of America. As author Graham Moore explains in his concluding "Note From the Author", the events in most of the major scenes did actually occur--though the chronology may be fudged "to help the reader's tracking of the many story lines and to give narrative shape to the messily discrete events of history".

This is historical fiction at its very, very best. Although the author adds imagined details to make the dramatization of real events read like a novel, the underlying historical facts are NOT distorted so that the reader takes away a false view of what really happened. The novel is based in part on a nonfiction work by Jill Jonnes, EMPIRES OF LIGHT: EDISON, TESLA, WESTINGHOUSE, AND THE RACE TO ELECTRIFY THE WORLD, which I'm now planning to read. Lawyers will recognize Paul Cravath as the founder of a prestigious law firm (Cravath, Swaine & Moore) that survives today.

In the novel, a young, exceedingly green attorney (Paul Cravath) lands the job of representing George Westinghouse in his legal fight against Thomas Edison over whose system for delivering electricity (alternating current or direct current, respectively) will be adopted. The inventor that wins will ultimately reap the immense financial rewards to be had from holding the monopoly over electricity. Edison has filed more than 300 lawsuits alleging that Westinghouse's electric lamp infringes on Edison's very broad electric lamp patent. If the courts uphold Edison's patent, Westinghouse will be put out of business.

As a countermeasure (in case they lose the court battle), Westinghouse and Cravath hire Nikola Tesla to develop a new, non-infringing Westinghouse lamp. But the crazy inventor Tesla turns out to be unmanageable, and then he suffers a mental breakdown, so that the Westinghouse lamp development is delayed indefinitely. Edison's winning lawsuits and dirty tricks (such as providing financial backing to the developer of an electric chair that uses "unsafe" alternating current) nearly drive Westinghouse into bankruptcy. For a time, Paul's situation appears hopeless. However, with help from an opera singer (Agnes Huntington), from another inventor (Alexander Graham Bell in a rare wholly imaginary scene), and from a legendary financier (J.P. Morgan), Paul eventually ensures that Westinghouse's superior alternating current system becomes the ultimate winner.

Graham Moore is an extraordinarily talented writer, to be able to weave together all of the disparate threads of this story and present it a way that brings the characters to life and keeps the reader engaged. THE LAST DAYS OF NIGHT is entertaining from beginning to end, and I loved reading it.

I do a lot of work with shell scripts in a Linux environment so I do need to use regular expressions on a fairly frequent basis. I have O'Reilly's Mastering Regular Expressions book and while it is helpful it is not a reference that really works for me most of the time. I had much higher hopes for the Regular Expressions Cookbook, and what I have found is that it's usually a good starting point.

O'Reilly's Cookbook titles follow a similar format to one another - they start by presenting a problem, offer a solution and go into discussion about the solution. This title is no different and it's a format that works fairly well. Frequently, there is at least one problem/solution that is in the ballpark of the real-life problem and from there the reader can usually figure out what needs to happen to get to the final solution.

There are nine chapters in this books, breaking the material up into logical groupings: Introduction to Regular Expressions, Basic Regular Expression Skills, Programming with Regular Expressions, Validation and Formatting, Words/Lines/Special Characters, Numbers, Source Code and Log Files, URLs/Paths/Internet Addresses, and finally Markup and Data Formats. With the exception of the introductory chapter, each of these has 15-25 subsections dealing with the overall topic.

My sole issue with this book is that it is so language-centric that is does not account for the formats needed on a Unix or Linux command line when working directly with the shell. The book covers C#, Java, JavaScript, Perl, PHP, Python, Ruby and VB.NET which in itself is an impressive coverage list, but the formatting is different when working with bash or C shell and a utility like grep or awk, which is where I spend a large amount of time. The solutions all get me close to where I need to go but still require some trial an error to get the syntax just right. Keep this in mind if you are coming from a perspective other than that of a coder. I wish the authors had taken into consideration this usage scenario.

Overall, this is a good book on regular expressions and will serve the reader will. It's not a straight textbook on regular expressions so it does not present everything in one nifty chapter from which everything else flows, but it does present enough in the introduction to allow a reader to skip around and find what's needed at the time. Though it does not cover Unix/Linux command line usage it is enough to help most people get the solutions they need.

Case Logic 16-Inch Full Size Security Friendly Laptop Case is a storage and organizational device that is very useful for storage of both laptops and related accessories. I use this case when going on vacation and making other short trips. My laptop almost always accompanies me, and having a safe place to keep my computer is important.

This laptop computer bag looks much like other computer bags from the outside. Its black color and Case Logic metal badge with logo make it look like a briefcase when viewed from a distance. This gives the bag a more professional, serious look that makes it a good choice for businessmen and businesswomen. At the same time, the bag looks casual enough that others can use it as well. It could even double as a storage bag for other items and many students could use this case for hauling around a few books, folders, notebooks, and papers.

Opening up the Case Logic 16-Inch Full Size Security Friendly Laptop Case reveals an obvious fact: This is no ordinary briefcase/laptop carrying bag. There are separate sections and zippers galore. There are four main sections and these are subdivided into other storage sections with variations in each section that help users find the perfect place to store their notebooks, cell phones, calculators, pens, etc. One of the end sections is designed exclusively for your laptop and includes pillow- like walls to keep your laptop computer safe from damage. The other sections have a combination of pockets without zippers, pockets with zippers, deep pockets, shallow pockets, and even a nylon mesh pocket. With so many pockets and storage areas, one can quickly find the perfect place to store everything from cell phones, to calculators, to CD's, and more.

Carrying the Case Logic 16-Inch Full Size Security Friendly Laptop Case is made easy through the two available options: The briefcase- like handles and the optional shoulder strap. I usually use the handles, but if my bag is overloaded, I have found that the shoulder strap is the best way to go. Not only can this strap be used to carry the bag hands- free, it can also be used to strap the bag to a piece of rolling luggage, for even more freedom of movement. The strap is long enough to fit around most any piece of luggage, making a quick run through the airport fast and simple.

One other nice feature of the Case Logic 16-Inch Full Size Security Friendly Laptop Case is that it is designed with airport security in mind. This is one of the main appeals of this laptop bag because more often than not, when I am packing my laptop into a bag, it is for taking it on a trip and more than half of my trips involve flights. Case Logic designed this laptop case in compliance with TSA government guidelines so that you don't have to remove the laptop from the case in order to pass it through airport security. This is great for those who don't have time to waste and need to get to their gate as quickly as possible.

Case Logic 16-Inch Full Size Security Friendly Laptop Case has many great things to offer, so are there any cons? I can think of only a few. One is the lack of padding in the majority of the compartments. The laptop compartment is protected by padding, but the rest of the case is not. Thus, you have to be careful not to place anything delicate in one of these non- padded sections- particularly the one on the outside. These more delicate items will have to be placed toward the center of the bag instead of at the ends. Another possible con is that this bag is not expandable. Granted, it has enough storage space and is large enough that most anyone can find a place to store what they have. But the lack of expansion means you cannot place a large object inside this storage bag and it also means that some of the larger laptop computers may not fit.

Still, in spite of these minor inconveniences, the Case Logic 16-Inch Full Size Security Friendly Laptop Case is a very nice computer case with many great things to offer. It can be used to store your laptop computer and related accessories in many different ways, with a design that is both practical and imaginative.

A LONGER FALL is the second “Gunnie Rose” novel; it works as a standalone, but just barely. Readers new to the series, like myself, are surely better off starting with the first novel, [[ASIN:1481494937 An Easy Death]], which sets out the fantasy background. In Gunnie Rose’s world, the United States is a failed country that is now broken into independently governed regions where the “Holy Russian Empire” is seeking to gain traction.

The second novel is rather slow-moving, but is interesting enough to make me want to purchase and read the earlier book. That one probably explains why the HRE is headed by Tsar Alexei (the hemophiliac son of Tsar Nicholas), when in our timeline Alexei and his entire family died during the Russian Revolution (in July 1918). Also, the first book probably tells us more about the grigori, the powerful wizards who inhabit the current world, and more about the backgrounds of the hero (Eli) and heroine (Lizbeth) of the novel.

In the novel, Gunnie Rose is traveling by train from Texoma to Dixie. As a “gunnie” (a crack shot and professional gun-for-hire), she belongs to a crew that was supposed to guard a crate until it reached its destination in the Dixie town of Sally. But right outside of Sally, the train blows up. There is considerable loss of life, and in the resulting confusion, the crate is stolen.

Relatively uninjured, and with most of her crew out of commision (murdered, dead from the train wreck, or seriously injured from the train wreck), Lizbeth is left with the task of finding the crate. She runs into an old friend, Russian grigori Eli Savarov, who desperately needs to find the person who was receiving the crate. He persuades Lizbeth to team up and guard him while they pursue their overlapping missions.

Lizbeth must shed her guns, jeans, and boots, and don traditionally feminine clothing, in order to “pass” in Dixie. The Dixie of this fantasy world is a throwback to the 20th century South, where the inhabitants have strict ideas about “proper” styles and behavior for white people, and about the “place” of their black servants. Deviating from the norm can get you killed, so Lisbeth and Eli are in constant danger.

Novels by Charlaine Harris are always worth reading, although some of the author’s series are much stronger than others. The Gunnie Rose series is probably the weakest of those that I’ve read (True Blood, Midnight Crossroad, Shakespeare). However, Lizbeth and Eli are likeable characters, the novels are professionally written, and the plots are overall entertaining.

It is 2019. Kat is the successful daughter. Flora is the one that married and has a four year old son who's a bit of a terror. And Laurie is the damaged one whose mother, Dixie, recently died. Charles Finch, their father, was a renowned artist and renowned philanderer. The women each have a different mother. Flora's mother was married to Charles when she was born. Kat was born five months later to Charlie's lover. Lauren was born thirteen months after Kat. During the summer, Kat and Flora joined Charlie and his parents at Rock Point, their Victorian summer home by the sea in Wales.. Lauren did not meet her Granny and Grandpa or her sisters until she was nine, when Dixie let her join them at Rock Point. Charlie has issued something of a command that the three of them come to Rock Point. Bertha, the African Gray parrot, formerly their grandparent's bird is back.

It has been twenty years since the daughters visited Rock Point. In 1999, the summer of a complete solar eclipse, something bad happened at Rock Point. 1999 was the summer the sisters sat for a portrait, now recognized as Charles' Finches' masterpiece, "Girls and Birdcage. Rock Point is atmospheric, the young teen aged girls' relationships with one another complicated. Kat and Flora have known each other from birth and are very close. They can be kind or terrible to Laurie. Laurie assists her father with his studio and hangs out with local girl, Gemma whose mother cleans for them.

Through the point of view of each daughter the stories of the return to Rock Point and the events of 1999 spool out in a dual timeline, Tension, some competitiveness and love play through the present. Everyone is worried about Lauren who was already fragile and now mourns Dixie. Flora is exasperated with her son's antics and loves him fiercely. Her husband wants a second child. It's obvious she is uncertain. Kat is on the phone constantly for business and seems lost in that world. Charlie explains why he has called them all there and it's unsettling. Throughout, each is thinking about 1999. How can they not, when they haven't returned since then? And someone is leaving them vaguely threatening notes. But why?

All in all I found The Birdcage an enjoyable read, particularly the characters, their interrelationship, their locale and the persistent air of mystery. Obviously that part of the book is not action packed. We are in the minds of each daughter. I like that. There is more action in the telling of the past and in the wrap up, but there are many ways to spoil the story, which I do not do in writing about my reads. I strongly recommend this if this description grabs you.

For years my understanding of sushi was “raw fish on rice”. Of course there’s more to it than that, but I was blissfully unaware. Sushi seems like a relatively simple item to prepare, but it’s easy to create rolls that look spectacular but are mediocre at best. Even if you’ve made sushi in the past, this is a good ground-up book to get you on the path to making good sushi.

The most important ingredient in sushi isn’t actually the fish or vegetables – it’s the rice. The author includes a detailed explanation of how to make sushi rice in a pan so that it turns out right every time and is easy to work with. This is followed up with information on how to prepare other ingredients such as the fish you might use, vegetables and more. All together, this lays out a good foundation.

Following is a good collection of actual sushi dishes you can prepare – nigiri, rolls, and a lot more. Some of these include pictures, but most do not. What surprised me is that there are still more things after all of the sushi recipes that you can make – miso soup, pickled vegetables, sauces, teas and more.

There’s more here than I expected. And, it all seems to work. The author does a great job of explaining the process of making each dish, doesn’t talk down to the reader and very clearly knows the subject very well.

This book might be for beginners, but it is suitable for anyone wanting to learn about sushi, wanting to make it themselves, and learn a little bit more about Japanese cuisine as well.

I discovered An Ellis Island Christmas while trying to research my own family's journey from Poland in 1917. Growing up, I remember my babcia (grandmother) storing her sewing supplies in a small wicker hamper with a cloth lining. This was the same container that brought my grandmother and great-grandmother's possessions from Zamosc, Poland. When I flipped through An Ellis Island Christmas and saw that beautiful watercolor of a Polish willow hamper that matched my own heirloom, it was an emotional moment.

The picture book tells the story of Krysia, a six-year-old Polish girl whose father has already left for America (as was frequently the case). Now, Krysia and her mother and brothers are boarding a steamship that will take them to Ellis Island. Their journey is a tiring one, first having to walk on foot to reach their point of departure, then facing seasickness and storms at sea before arriving at their destination. Because this is a book aimed at ages 5 and up, there are brief hints of immigrants deported for illnesses and the threat of WWI, but the story does not dwell or linger on these darker moments, instead focusing on Krysia's wonder at the journey, her friend and shipmate Zanya, and her dolls.

Christmas Eve at Ellis Island is a wondrous experience for Krysia, who discovers that Father Christmas has made the journey all the way from Poland. She also discovers bananas and electric lights for the first time.

The beautiful watercolor / colored pencil graphics truly bring Krysia's experience to vibrant life; the haunting image of the Statue of Liberty must have been exactly as my grandmother saw it when she was a little girl. The sepia-toned illustrations of a rustic Polish cottage and the imposing Ellis Island hallways are softened by the melancholy Krysia, until she smiles at last when being reunited with her papa.

This is a beautiful book to introduce younger readers to the Ellis Island immigrant experience, and it's even more meaningful for those of us who had a grandparent who immigrated in recent memory . I was lucky enough to finally track down the original ship manifests and Ellis Island documents for my Polish grandparents (who immigrated at roughly the same time as Krysia), and my personal experiences as a second-generation Polish-American made An Ellis Island Christmas even more meaningful.

In the French legal system, an investigating magistrate (a judge designated "juge d'instruction") performs the fact-gathering job carried out by a police detective in the United States or Great Britain. Thus THE HONEST FOLK OF GUADELOUPE is actually a police procedural novel, set on a Caribbean island that is geographically located in the West Indies but politically a part of France.

In this book, "madame le juge d'instruction" Anne Marie Laveaud looks into two suspicious deaths. First, there is the "suicide" of a popular television personality who threw himself off a 14-story building when police visited his office to inquire about his alleged misappropriation of some public funds. Second, there is the mysterious death of a young tourist woman whose body is found, without any obvious cause of death, decomposing on a little-used, remote beach.

Despite political pressure to close the TV personality's case without further investigation, madame le juge conducts her usual formal investigation. She reasons that jumping off a roof is a rather extreme response to the TV personality's potentially being ordered to pay a fine that he could easily afford to pay; besides, the personality's wife is claiming that "the police hounded him to death", and there are rumors that the police may have caused the death. Still, madame le juge puts the case temporarily aside, and concentrates for most of the novel on determining the cause of the tourist's death. The tourist's death must be explained, because of its potential for negatively impacting Guadeloupe's tourist-based economy. Eventually madame le juge gets to the bottom of both cases, though I found the outcomes mildly unsatisfying.

The novel is constructed in a puzzling fashion. The story is told almost entirely through Anne Marie's conversations as they are conducted in the course of her investigations, with the result that it jumps around a lot and can be hard to follow. The reader has to work a bit to remember (or figure out) why madame le juge is interviewing certain individuals at particular times. Also, background characters (e.g., madame le juge's long-suffering, self-deprecating law clerk, Monsieur Trousseau) are frequently introduced for the first time in conversations, and then the explanations of who they are will follow a page or two later. Also, madame le juge's own character is puzzling, because she's suddenly thinking about returning permanently to France, even though she's established herself on Guadeloupe for ten or twelve years, and she and her children have developed strong emotional attachments to Guadeloupe.

The novel has excellent descriptions of the physical island of Guadeloupe. It also contains a lot of analysis of local attitudes toward skin color and ethnicity that seem to drive residents' daily interactions. The analysis rings true, but is somewhat surprising--as politically incorrect--to this U.S. reader. Because I've never visited Guadeloupe, I can't say whether the locals really do take skin color and ethnicity so heavily into account in the island's political and social structure. Because of its exotic setting, well-described French legal procedures, and reasonably well-done plot, I rate THE HONEST FOLK OF GUADELOUPE at 4 stars ("I like it" on the official Amazon scale).

I confess to having difficulty working my way through this little book. It is not a hard book to read in terms of the language or grammar, nor is it so deep and difficult to understand that it is over the average reader's head. The difficulty in reading this book comes from it being very raw, exposed and quite personal. It reads very much like a personal journal, but it has elements of a devotional reader and at times it read like the transcript of a personal interview with the author.

From the beginning we learn about the author and how far he has come. He does not sugarcoat his past and makes it vey clear that he was a broken and very flawed individual with turbulent moments in his past. This puts him on the same level with most who would read this book.

In spite of his flaws he writes about God - and God's desire for us - in a deep, understanding and passionate way. He breaks up the discussion in bite-sized chunks, one of the chapters being exactly two pages, and follows up most sections with a "Consider This" section with questions requiring some serious searching within or instruction.

The insights are brilliant, and the points the author makes are clear. However, the book is as much about the author as it is about God and His relationship to us. Maybe the author's point was to use himself as an example in this book, but it takes away somewhat from the main subject as expressed in the title - God and His love for us.

This is not a bad book. It is actually quite good and I can recommend it. That said, it is a little hard to read, especially if you can find a few parallels in your life with that of the author.

I knew right away that these would be my office headphones. I have a mechanical keyboard that I use at work, and the office I work in is semi-open. There's a *lot* of noise coming every-which-way. These are a much-needed accessory to my work productivity, as I'm easily distracted by things in my periphery, whether visually or auditory.

The presentation is great. The box is very high quality, reminiscent of the recent Samsung Galaxy device boxes. A smooth matte feel with gloss--weirdly pristine. The box slides out of the slipcover and you get the headphones already in the case. What I like is that they're folded, and there's even a little sheet underneath the phones that always reminds you how to put them back in. Also included is a 3.5mm cable in case you don't want to use Bluetooth, a charging cable, and an adapter. The case is nice, but as I keep mine at work I can't testify to its durability. There's a thin mesh net on the backside in case anyone needs to store one or two thin headphone accessory/-ies along. The accent colors are a nice light copper/rose gold color. I love that color; I'm glad it's getting more attention in recent years.

It didn't take long to charge the headphones, so they come with a little bit of juice. As soon as you turn them on, you get a soft beep along with a voice indicating they're turned on. Nice responsive feedback. Once I put them on I could hear the headphones working to drown out the sound; there was a thick veil of soundproofing that was draped over my ears as soon as the earpads touched them.

The first thing I did was listen to podcasts through the Pocket Casts app and .flac music through Poweramp v3. With podcasts, the difference was phenomenal. Listening to "Wait, wait... Don't tell me!" made me feel as though I were in the audience. The music was fantastic...until I tried on my other headphones which I use for music only.
I thought the bass might've been too strong with the Sony headphones, and I was right. After using even "cheaper" headphones like the Audio-Technica M50x, I could tell the Sony had too much bass. I'm not sure if that's partly because of the noise-canceling technology or what, but the bass can be toned down a bit, methinks.

I then proceeded to download the supplementary app to get the fullest suite of attributes the headphones can get. The app works well, and I didn't experience any hiccups while actually using the app. The only hiccup was when I was trying to download the update. It took *forever*. Almost an hour and it was just halfway through. I decided to bring them to work the next day and let the app sit there while updating. Thankfully, it remembers the progress, even though the app kept crashing during the update process.

There are some optimization tweaks in the app, some sound profiles to let you configure the noise cancelation level (yes, level; the noise cancelation is pure software; you can set it to drown out the most noise as possible or have no noise cancellation at all), and even a little snippet of what is currently playing through the headphones. A simple UI with all the features you need.

The first few days I used it I was active, and I kept noticing that my ears sometimes would pop depending on whether I sat down or arose quickly. Another weird thing is that when I take the headphones off, my ears sometimes need a minute or two to adjust. There's so much noise in the world! After taking the headphones off I can hear HVAC activity and my loud work neighbor who's otherwise not that loud.

I had some headphones with some touch controls before and always found them tacky. I used them once when I first got them and never again. But with these headphones, I'm always using the tap gesture to play/pause and the swipe gesture to raise or lower the volume. There are also swipe gestures to skip or go back a track, but since I never do that anyway I never use those gestures. You have to be careful with the tap; when it works, it works. But the whole surface isn't the active portion and you have to hit it right in the center. Sometimes I'm hitting my finger against my ears trying to find the spot and hurting myself in the process. I tested the gesture where you put your entire palm on the cup to turn off the noise canceling feature and let the mic allow incoming conversation, but not after the third try. I could hear the other people just fine, but I found the right hand over my ear felt awkward, and one person didn't realize I could even hear them. Putting your hand over your headphones isn't a gesture people immediately see as you paying attention to them.

The headphones are extremely lightweight and comfortable to use; I left them on for about two hours once before having to take them off. I actually was surprised with how light they were; when I got the Amazon box I didn't believe it was my headphones. It was much lighter than expected.

For my first noise-canceling headphones I'm pleased. The sound balance can be better (less bass), but they make for fantastic headphones to use at work. I wasn't sure what I was expecting with noise-canceling technology. I thought it would drown out all noises, but you still can hear the occasional mutter; it just won't be distinct.

Oh, forgot to mention the battery life. I charged it only once and have been using it for a week, at about an hour or two each day. Still going well. If you press the power button once it will tell you the battery level. AFter the initial update the voice indicator might give the wrong battery level (it did for me), but give it about ten or fifteen minutes to adjust and it will go back to normal.

1.She writes about her bedwetting as a youth and how it affected her, depressing her quite a bit. Her father and his father were also bedwetters. The depression peaked with her taking as many as 16 Xanax pills a day

2. She talks about a key bad experience with a boyfriend, early on.

3. She became a vegetarian out of her concern for animals.

4. At 13, when visiting her sister at Berkeley, she got exposed to drugs by a neighbor of hers and he also gave her a gift of Playgirl and Penthouse magazines, and she claims that is what really began her focusing on sexual stuff for her comedy. Since the 3rd grade, she always knew she wanted to be a comedian.

5. Her parents never hit her and they encouraged her and gave her lots of love. Beginning at age 15 her parents let her take shuttle trips from New Hampshire to New York City and she knew early on she wanted to eventually get out of New Hampshire and live in NYC. She said she felt like a goat among sheep in NH, but a goat among goats in NYC. She enrolled at NYU, majoring in drama, in Greenwich Village after HS. She would hand out flyers at a comedy club after classes eventually getting chances to do stand-up. She then quit NYU before starting her sophomore year and her dad offered to pay for her to live in NYC since it would be cheaper than going to NYU and he knew what she really wanted to do anyway - comedy, so she did that, living in Greenwich Village.

6. Never had stage fright - she thinks because after she stopped bedwetting, nothing could be as embarrassing as that.

7. Her approach to everything gross in life like drugs, sex, etc is to "make it a treat," that is everything in moderation.

8. At 22 she got interviewed by Saturday Night Live and got hired as a writer/performer, however none of her skits made it past dress rehearsal and coincidentally or not was fired after one year after hitting Al Franken in the temple with a sharp pencil - a joke gone bad. She claims Chris Farley positively influenced her with an incident where Farley had been with SNL 3 years, but was still in awe of what had gone on before he came there. So, it gave her the strength to face future challenges.

9. Always felt she didn't know how to dress and her disastrous Emmy Awards dress was a result.

10. Being creative, she puts in a midword in her book, to take a break and say what she was doing when not writing. Likewise, she wrote her own foreword in the book - she claims groundbreaking.

11. She writes about disputes with the publisher/editor about things like the title and other stuff.

12. She writes about the racism she sees in the media - more nuanced than in the past - really uses her comedy to fight racism.

13. She writes about her incidents as host at MTV award shows - and her loss of tact with her comments about Paris Hilton and Britney Spears.

14. Writes about her film, "Jesus is Magic" and the "Sarah Silverman Program" on Comedy Central and how the network was tolerant of her edgy stuff also showing some of the hate mail she received about how God was presented in her program. Also writes about her pro-union position even when facing cost control issues from the network.

15. She talks about love and that she only really needs a man around a lot is for watching TV while cuddling in bed.

17. Near the end of the book she has a chapter writing about being a Jew and what she thinks about Judaism - although she is secular she thinks Judaism is an OK religion, with many criticisms about Catholicism like the ostentacious Vatican and the child-abusing priests. Overall, since Sarah Silverman is controversial, I recommend the book for those who like her, but probably not for those who don't.

I was stationed in Japan for six months, and while there, I took four Japanese cooking classes. I purchased Kansha from Amazon Japan in December 2010, and enjoyed leafing through the many intriguing vegan recipes inspired by traditional Japanese Buddhism (because of my living arrangements in Japan, I didn't have a kitchen in which to try out these recipes). Being vegetarian in Japan is more difficult than it sounds; nearly every Japanese dish (with the exception of shojin ryori, vegan Buddhist temple cuisine) contains fish in some form, whether in the dashi (stock) or shavings of katsuobushi (dried bonito flakes). The traditional Japanese diet, which was heavy on fish and fresh and pickled vegetables, is being replaced by deep-fried cutlets and American-style fast food joints like Mos Burger.

I was lucky enough to attend one of Elizabeth's Kansha workshops in Osaka shortly after the March 11 earthquake, and it was a much-needed chance to focus on appreciation (the English translation of "kansha") that my Japanese coworkers' and students' friends and families were safe. We made several of the recipes from Kansha around a hanami (cherry blossom viewing) theme, including Thick Fried Tofu & Broiled Tofu Braised with Root Vegetables, Simmered & Blanched Mountain Vegetables Tossed in Nutty Tofu Sauce. Rice with Salted Cherry Blossoms, Burdock and Wheat Strips in Dark Miso Broth, and Home-Made Nuka-Zuke. After the class, we went on a supermarket tour, where Elizabeth pointed out various types of sansai (wild mountain vegetables) and gave us a primer on soy sauces and basic pantry staples.

Despite the fact that the book is marketed as "Vegetarian and vegan traditions," Kansha is totally vegan (if you're looking for egg-based dishes like Japanese omelettes and chawanmushi, those can be found in Elizabeth's previous book Washoku). You'll find mock-mackerel sushi made from eggplant, light and springy cherry blossom rice, and a variety of pickles. There are some lovely regional recipes like goya (bitter melon), a popular vegetable from Okinawa, where it is commonly served in a stir-fry known as chanpuru. Yes, tofu gets its own chapter, but it's served in a variety of preparations that are commonly found in Japan, including a soymilk version of chawanmushi (steamed custard with savory bits of veggies), fried tofu (atsu age), yuba (rather substantial soymilk "skin"), and instructions on how to make your own tofu from soymilk. Varietal tofus (especially fried tofu skins used for inarizushi and in miso soup) may be near-impossible to find in your local grocery, but you can always fall back on that most Japanese staple of summer, hiyayakko: buy the highest-grade tofu you can find, cut into cubes, garnish with grated daikon, wasabi, or fresh grated ginger, drizzle with soy sauce and serve!

The book is gorgeously illustrated, and the recipes are very clearly laid out and explained step-by-step. The ingredient and kitchen tool section is excellent as well, but again, you will most likely have to mail-order many of the specialty items like rice molds, miso strainers, etc. I've ordered from Korin.com; they have a wide selection of imported Japanese tableware and kitchen tools.

The biggest challenge that home cooks will face is finding authentic fresh Japanese ingredients like mitsuba and shiso (herbs), burdock root, and takenoko (baby bamboo shoots) and prepared ingredients like dried seaweed (most US stores only carry nori sheets for sushi, but there are many common varieties in Japan, like hijiki, kombu, and wakame), umeboshi (pickled plums), and seasonings (unfortunately, our Japanese market did stock konnyaku, my most loathed Japanese ingredient; imagine a squiggly, translucent, chewy block of tasteless speckled jello).

I'm lucky in that my city has not one, but several Japanese markets and a large network of Japanese, but it's still difficult (and extremely expensive) to buy these ingredients in the US (I miss my local Heiwado grocery store in Japan!). Unfortunately, these recipes call for very specific ingredients without American substitutions, so for some Kansha may end up as a beautiful coffee table book. It's a beautiful volume and fine companion to [[ASIN:1580085199 Washoku: Recipes from the Japanese Home Kitchen]], which includes Japanese fish, meat and egg dishes, and vegetarians, vegans, and Japanophiles should certainly add this to their collection. If you're looking specifically for Japanese Buddhist temple cuisine (which is vegan), [[ASIN:4770024932 The Enlightened Kitchen: Fresh Vegetable Dishes from the Temples of Japan]] covers that niche in greater detail.

I have been picking up Ghori’s Linux RHCSA/RHCE training book for every edition since RHEL 5 (when the RHCSA cert was the RHCT instead), so this edition makes this the fourth book I have picked up in the series. Typically his books are well-suited for reference in addition to being good for certification preparation which is the primary reason I prefer his to Jang’s certification books. This is another good book in the series, though there has been a significant – and unpleasant – change this time around.

I will get right to the main complaint I have with this book. Instead of covering the RHCSA and RHCE exams, this one only covers RHCSA prep and does not cover RHCE at all. This is not the only title that avoids RHCE coverage and I am not sure why this is the case. I am hopeful that the RHCE exam will be covered by a later work, though it isn’t guaranteed. With no RHCE coverage, the cost of the volume has not appreciably changed which is a bit concerning.

This book is very typical of Ghori’s previous editions and takes a deep dive into RHEL 8 and the exam requirements for the RHCSA exam. It walks you through installation, basic command execution, SELinux basics, file systems, services, the firewall, user management, package management and so much more. Though the emphasis is on exam preparation, it is perfectly adequate for use as a handy reference and it is a great book to have on hand if you are a system administrator who is trying to fine tune a system and get it ready for basic production use.

As in previous editions, the author includes a short quiz at the end of every chapter to test knowledge learned. Some of the questions asked are somewhat remedial and seem less important than some of what you’d expect to find on the exam while other questions are much more geared towards knowing bits of information that are very relevant and will help when taking the test. Also included are “challenge labs” that are designed to give the reader things to accomplish with the goal of being well-prepared for the exam. Finally, there are practice exams that are similar in form to the actual exam. The practice exams in previous editions were a bit more verbose and wordy, which was inconsistent with the actual test, whereas the exam tasks seem much more in line with the exam format now.

When preparing for the exam, do the labs – all of them, even the simple ones. You’ll be well-prepared when you take the test.

A lot has changed since RHEL7, and this book is a good resource for gearing up for the RHCSA exam. It bothers me that RHCE prep has been removed without a significant impact on the cost of the book, but otherwise this is an excellent resource if you’re wanting to gear up for the RHCSA exam for RHEL 8.
