Here is an excerpt from the publisher's page which isn't up yet here:

Chapter One

LIZZIE

Every window on the train had been painted black, blocking any possible view of the passing scenery. Lizzie knew the paint was necessary to hide the train’s lights from German planes, but she wished she could see outside where there might be farmland, mountains, or rivers to watch. Instead, as the train sped along the tracks, all Lizzie saw was her own frizzy-haired reflection in the blank black rectangle of glass.

Children from Lizzie’s school were crammed into the train carriage. Some sat on suitcases in the aisle while others bickered and jostled for room on the crowded seats. Some sat blank-faced with their gas masks slung over their shoulders and their possessions in their laps. A few of the older children played a card game using a suitcase for a table. A tiny girl cried, “Mummy, I want my mummy,” over and over again. Lizzie couldn’t reach the girl to comfort her ?— ?there were too many other children in the way.

In the strange cocoon of the carriage, Lizzie had lost all sense of time. It had been early morning when she’d taken Peter’s hand, said goodbye to their mother, and climbed onto the double-decker bus outside their school in Hull. It had still been morning when the bus had stopped at the railway station and she’d guided Peter to a seat on the packed train. They’d long ago eaten their potted meat sandwiches, but Lizzie’s watch had stopped at eleven o’clock, and she had no idea how many hours had passed since then on the rattling, clattering train.

“Look after Peter, love,” her mother had said after giving Lizzie a final kiss. “Don’t let them send you to different homes. Seven’s too young for him to be on his own.”

Lizzie had turned in a sudden panic on the bus step and said, “Do we have to go?”

Her mother’s eyes had glistened. “Yes, love, you do. We’re at war now. It won’t be safe in Hull ?— ?the Germans will bomb the city.”

“Why can’t you come with us?”

“I have to stay behind, Lizzie. Parents aren’t allowed to go.” Her mother had painted a false smile on her face and said, “You’ll have such an adventure in the country. You’ll be safe there, and I’m sure someone kind will take you in.”

Lizzie had heard this so many times from her parents and her teacher, Mrs. Scruton, that she could recite the speech herself. She knew that city children had to be evacuated to keep them safe from the bombs. She knew that most of their fathers would join the army to fight the Germans. She knew that most of their mothers would take the place of the men in the factories and offices. But knowing the reasons why she had to leave didn’t help ?— ?Lizzie would rather face the bombs than live in a strange place with people she didn’t know. After all, they had a bomb shelter now.

Before he’d left to join the army, her father had removed the roses from their back garden and dug a big hole in the lawn. He’d made walls using half-buried sheets of corrugated metal and a roof from more of the metal sheets before mounding a huge pile of soil over the top. When the bomb shelter was finished, he’d put two camp beds inside for her mother and grandmother to sleep on and a little Primus stove for them to make tea.

“That’ll do nicely,” he’d said. “You’ll be safe in there.”

The shelter was cramped and damp and probably full of spiders. Still, if it would keep Mummy and Nana safe in a bombing raid, wouldn’t it keep Lizzie and Peter safe too?

But Lizzie hadn't been given a choice to stay.

She shifted on her seat and pushed Peter’s lolling head into a more comfortable position on her shoulder. He made little whimpering noises in her ear as he slept and his head was heavy, but she was grateful for the relief from his endless questions.

“Where are we going?” he’d asked as the train pulled out of Hull Station. “Why didn’t Mummy come with us? Who will look after us?”

Lizzie’s stomach flipped a somersault. Who would look after them?

She reached into her school satchel and felt for Nana’s gift. Her fingers gripped the smooth hard box for comfort. Inside the box, nestled on a bed of white satin, was a beautiful new fountain pen.

“That’s not fair,” Peter had complained when Nana gave it to her. “Her birthday’s not for ages.”

But Nana had patted his head and said, “Hush, now. We don’t know if you’ll be home in time for Lizzie’s birthday, so she’d better have it now. Be-sides, she’ll need it to write me lots of lovely letters.”

Nana had given Lizzie a whole sheet of stamps ?— ?so many stamps. Would they really be gone long enough for Lizzie to write that many letters?

She rested her feet on their suitcase, leaned her head against the back of the leather seat, and closed her eyes, but she couldn’t stop the thoughts. What if the people in the country weren’t kind? What if they didn’t like her? What if she couldn’t look after Peter?

What if you stop worrying? Nana would say.

How would Lizzie manage without Nana to reassure her?

We’re two peas in a pod, you and me. Nana said that all the time, which was funny, because Nana was short and stout like a barrel on legs, and Lizzie was as thin as a rake.

Who would make Lizzie laugh now? She twisted a loop of hair back and forth between her fingers as the train swayed and rattled on its relentless way.

She woke to a sudden jerk and the harsh squeal of brakes.

Mrs. Scruton stepped into their carriage. She took the hand of the little girl who’d been crying for her mother and said, “This is our stop, children.”

Lizzie picked up their suitcase and poked Peter when he almost left his gas mask on the seat. Together they clambered down onto the platform. A long line of train carriages stretched through the small station, and Lizzie wondered if there were any children left in Hull.

Billows of steam wafted from the hissing engine. A man wearing a dark uniform and cap waved a green flag and blew his whistle. The train, their last connection with home, pulled out of the station and disappeared into the misty distance.

There are a lot of Bibles on the market, and they vary between target audience, extra content, physical volume, and of course (and probably most importantly) translation. Selecting a Bible for reading and study is a very personal choice and requires some thought. This particular Bible is a devotional Bible with notes from Matthew Henry, using the New King James (NKJV) translation.

Chances are, if you are looking at this Bible you already know who Matthew Henry is and likely do not need information on him. That said, for those that do not know, Matthew Henry lived in the 1600's and 1700's and wrote one of the more comprehensive commentaries on the Bible that is still a solid reference today. Those writings are that on which the daily devotional writings are based.

The translation, as mentioned, is the NKJV, a well-respected and accurate translation. It is one of the more literal translations and follows a word-for-word translation process. In spite of the name, it is not a derivative of the original King James Version (KJV) and is a completely separate translation, though it does have some similarities. If you're looking for a translation that is reliable, trustworthy and very readable, this is a good choice. I personally prefer the English Standard Version (ESV), though that is strictly a personal preference.

There are 366 devotions in this Bible, all based on Matthew Henry's writings in his commentary. They tend to be short, half-page writings that engage the reader on the scripture quoted. They're different than most modern devotional writings in emphasis, in a way that is hard to put into words but is difficult to miss. The language is not flowery or emotional but is very direct and still very eloquent. I like these writings and will enjoy going through them all.

There is a lot to like about this Bible, but there are some areas where there is room for improvement. One thing comes to mind is that there are no chapter introductions or historical notes at all. Another is that the devotional readings are not in chronological order and they require flipping through the volume to work through the sequence, though there is an index of devotions by date at the front of the volume so they're easy enough to look up. I think this might have worked out better as two volumes, one a reference Bible and the other a stand-alone devotional.

The physical volume itself is very nice. I have the leathersoft version and it is a two-tone blue with a nice tree logo embossed on the front and again on the spine. Perfect for first timers!! Raised by an OB/GYN, I was always taught… The best pregnancy book is one you only look at pictures in.. Let’s go over this book!
•Ok, I broke the cardinal rule- This book does not have photos.. but, ‘what to expect when expecting‘ has got that covered as well as, the google button! Just to be clear- in case, summer expecting a photo glossary.

•This is formatted like a pregnancy Bible. Being you can read the book cover to cover if you wish- or, you can look a specific question/topic up in a beginning section.. and just flip to an answer on specific page- nice!

I love this for 1st time parents.. it encourages things you can do along the way which I feel, helps pass the time (never does time moved so slow, except maybe in covid lockdown?!) and it helps get couple excited and ready- a win/win... win!!

•So, why do I say great for first-time parents? Truly, the info given will become common knowledge after a first pregnancy. But, as I mentioned- I am from a family where my daddio had largest single OB practice in the US- Yep, in Provo utah..!! SCHOOL FOR PSYCHICS: BOOK ONE is an easy-reading, entertaining thriller, if (like me) you have a taste for supernatural/paranormal stuff. I really want to believe in the existence of people with actual psychic powers, so I enjoyed reading about how the novel’s colorful characters employ their differing skills (starting fires, communicating with animals, receiving death warnings, telepathy, telekinesis, etc.) at their government-sanctioned school for psychics. A plus factor for this S.F. Bay Area resident is that the school is supposedly located on lovely Angel Island (in the middle of San Francisco Bay).

Unfortunately, the novel reads like it’s intended for a young adult audience. That’s okay with me, but I got awfully tired of main character Teddy’s plotting with her “team” to break into locked school offices and break any and all school rules. She’s a 20-something (really too old for that kind of thing), and her crazy schemes shouldn’t succeed as well as they do. Also, she keeps getting caught doing things that should get her expelled, but she’s allowed to remain at the school anyway.

The plot is pretty thin. Secrets are being kept from adopted Teddy (about her birth parents and the real purposes of the school); and the competing intra-school squads of Alphas and Misfits hate each other, even as individual members struggle to develop and master their personal psychic skills. All of the “recruits” are being groomed for jobs with the FBI or Homeland Security.

The 20-something kids remind me of the Scooby Gang in “Buffy the Vampire Slayer” (which I loved), but the novel isn’t as well done as the TV series. Nor does it have the charm of the Harry Potter books. SCHOOL FOR PSYCHICS Book One ends with a cliffhanger of sorts, although most of the threads are tied up enough to create a reasonably satisfying, if unsurprising, ending.

Although I enjoyed the novel as extremely light reading, neither the characters nor the cliffhanger is interesting enough to make me want to read Book Two.

THE GUILTY DEAD (Monkeewrench #9) is a fast, enjoyable, relaxing read. I’d call it a “cozy police procedural”, because it chronicles a complex murder/anti-terrorist investigation by Minnesota police and the Monkeewrench software team, but focuses on the characters’ comfortable, familiar, joking personal relationships.

In the novel, an FBI agent (Dahl) approaches the Monkeewrench outfit (Harley, Grace, Annie, Roadrunner), seeking software to automate the interpretation of metadata (online chatter) intercepted from terrorist suspects. Monkeewrench has just the ticket—a beta program in development, no current buyer—and the program immediately detects an imminent bomb threat against Minneapolis City Hall.

The federal anti-terrorist operation turns out to be interwoven with a local police investigation by detectives Leo Magozzi and Gino Rolseth into the double murder of a wealthy local philanthropist (Norwood) and a freelance photographer (Stenson). The murders are staged as a suicide and a hiking accident, but the police aren’t fooled for long. A single bit of information supplied by Norwood’s daughter—the first name of Norwood’s personal private investigator—is the key that unlocks the whole case. The killer’s motive is tied up with the long-ago murder of a pregnant 14-year-old girl.

The plot is twisty and interesting, though it’s totally predictable that Monkeewrench’s very pregnant Grace will be delivering the baby (Magozzi is the father) in the middle of a major terrorist bombing attack. The writing is good, the characters are well-developed, and the novel works fine as a standalone.

I like spicy foods (to a point) and I look for cookbooks that give me an opportunity to make foods with a little more flavor than the ordinary. I looked to this title to get me there and it does not disappoint in that regard. There is a caveat I would like to point out, though.

Based on the title, one would suspect this is a book about making chilis in particular and possibly specialty spice mixes as well. That's only part of the story here. There is more to this collection than just chilis. There are seven chapters - "Appetizers & Snacks", "Light Meals & Fast Fare", "Hot Sauces & Rubs", "Vegetable Mains & Sides", "Meat & Poultry Mains", "Fish & Seafood Mains", and finally "Baking, Desserts & Drinks". Obviously, there is more to this book than just simmering pots of spicy hot beans.

The recipes I have tried and looked more closely at are generally not too hard to assemble and don't require a lot of extra work. The exception is when making your own sauces or rubs or spice mixes instead of using pre-made, and that adds some time and effort.

Not all of the recipes are all that spicy, to be honest. A good example of this is "Spicy Hamburgers with Guacamole & Potato Wedges". The meat is seasoned, yes, and one of the seasonings is chili powder. However, these do not pack any kind of kick and the seasoning is subtle. And this brings up an important point - what is your definition of spicy? I think most people regard something as spicy if it has at least a little heat to it rather than just seasoned to give flavor. In that regard, this book has some recipes that may come as a disappointment.

There's a little bit of everything in this book, from chili to burgers to roasted vegetables to desserts. Everything is seasoned a little differently than would be typical (red papper flakes in brownies?) so this is not a go-to when you want to entertain someone who likes the average and expected.

Almost every recipe comes with a nice, full-color photo. This is a big plus for those who eat first with their eyes.

This is a nice book on making well-seasoned foods. It has a fairly wide collection of dishes you can make, some of which are spicy-hot while others are seasoned for a deeper flavor profile. Keep this in mind - your definition of what is considered spicy can influence your view of this book.

THE DEHYDRATOR BIBLE is exactly what I hoped it would be when I ordered it: An excellent dehydrating reference and recipe book that supplements the brief "getting started" guide that came in the box with my [[ASIN:B000FFVJ3C Nesco FD-75PR 700-Watt Food Dehydrator]].

The book begins with a clear, easy-to-understand chapter that explains how drying works, how to tell when food is dry enough, how to store dried food properly, and when to rehydrate food. It also includes general troubleshooting tips.

Next, the book has useful charts that tell you how to handle dehydration for specific herbs (e.g., cilantro, mint, parsley), fruits (e.g., cherries, citrus fruits, peaches, pineapple), and vegetables (e.g., asparagus, radishes, sweet potatoes, tomatoes). For each type of produce, the authors discuss preparation (peel, cut into quarters, etc.), drying (how to arrange on trays, what temperature to use), time (hours required for drying), doneness test (e.g., plums should feel dry and leathery), and tips (e.g., blue or Italian plums give the nicest texture). The book has similar charts for beans, tofu, grains, and dairy products. It also includes a chapter on methods for dehydrating meat, poultry, and fish.

The bulk of the book has recipes for cooking "at home" and "on the trail" with dehydrated foods. These recipes are interesting to me, even though I intend to use my dehydrator mostly for fixing fruit snacks, beef jerky, and dried herbs. Should I end up with too many dried peach slices, for example, I can use them to make "Warm Peaches With Ginger". Also, there are a couple of sections of full-color photographs of selected prepared recipes--these, of course, are more or less obligatory in any food book that calls itself a "bible".

The last part of the book briefly discusses other uses for a dehydrator, including making cat and dog treats, crafts items (e.g., Christmas ornaments), and gifts (e.g., soup mix, herb teas). I like this book a lot--it's a useful, encyclopedic kitchen reference to be kept right next to my dehydrator.

I felt like a voyeur reading this book. Since the text is sprinkled with cuss words and EXPLICIT sexual escapades and drug episodes in all its virtual detail, you will feel as if you are a "fly on the wall" watching his life play out. I have to commend the author for his forthrightness (whether some of it was embellished or not) as some would have been highly embarrassed to describe all the intimate details in the way he did.

At first I found the text hard to follow because it reads like a chat session vacillating from one subject or thought to the next. However, the details got clearer as the author's life unfolds from college on into a professional legal career and marriage. This is one person's story told as a participant in his own life as well as an observer to his friends' lives. You will find some interesting details about what some women think is the typical male mind as well as what some attorneys are all about. The "lawyer side" of things is what I found most interesting.

To me this book is controversial because reading it will offend some and enthrall others. People who read non-fiction, dislike crude language, or dislike reading about someone's immaturity will probably begrudgingly accept this book but be disappointed by the language and explicit sexual detail. These types of people like to learn something from books and this text will not provide much learning experience. People who are young, crazy, and live life with immature wild abandon or who once lived life like that will probably love this story. Also, people (especially males) who like to read about other people's lives no matter how sordid will also enjoy it.

It definitely was not my kind of book, but was still sufficiently interesting enough to finish reading.

I bought a ZuneHD 32GB as a replacement for my iPod Video. I still have the iPod but I don't particularly care for it (never really did) so I decided to search for a better MP3 player. After digging online for a while I decided on the ZuneHD which has proven to be far and away better. It is not a perfect device but it's excellent for my needs.

Looking a lot like a small smart phone, the ZuneHD is a sleek and attractive device with a nice touch screen and a brushed metal back. Having never before used one of these I was a little confused at first on how it worked but the learning curve is easy and it took little time to get used to it. It works a lot like a tablet, actually. The screen is very responsive and navigation is simple.

I confess that I never used the ear buds. Instead, I use a set of really nice noise-canceling head phones and the sound coming out of the Zune is excellent. My music of choice is usually techno-trance stuff so there is a lot of base and a lot of synthesizer, and by default the sound is well-balanced and clear.

So, my main use for an MP3 player is to connect it to my car. My car has voice-controlled everything and I wanted to be able to listen to my music collection in the car without fiddling with the player directly. When I used the iPod I found that the system frequently got confused and the player would often select the wrong song. If it got confused enough, it would hang the voice activation for controlling the MP3 player for weeks at a time, so I gave up and put my Zune in the car instead. So far, the Zune and the car work together nearly flawlessly. As a bonus, the car keeps the Zune charged up.

The only drawback I have found with the Zune is that there is no way to expand the storage capacity. It would be nice to have the ability to add a MicroSD card in to expand the capacity.

I am exceptionally satisfied with my Zune. I likely will never buy another iPod again, now that I know how much better an MP3 player can be.

The ARDUINO PROJECT HANDBOOK: 25 PRACTICAL PROJECTS TO GET YOU STARTED is different from most other Arduino books in at least four ways:

(1) The finished projects are useful (e.g., intruder sensor, plant monitor, weather station, fortune teller (!), wireless card entry system). The focus of the book is on “plug-and-play electronics”.

(2) Each project starts with a clear, usually short, explanation of “How It Works” (e.g., the strobe light works by turning a potentiometer up or down to change the speed of flashing lights already installed on a breadboard).

(3) Each project is illustrated with full-color photographs of the required component parts and the finished build with all its connections. A full-color circuit diagram accompanies each project.

(4) The sketches (project code) are printed in colors to make them easier to read, understand, and type. The included sketches are also available for download from the No Starch Press web site.

This book also includes a good introductory discussion of the equipment needed for Arduino builds (e.g., wire cutters, glue gun, soldering iron), as well as a helpful “Quick Soldering Guide”. Various Arduino projects require special components (e.g., potentiometer, HL-69 soil sensor, servomotor, joystick) that are described (and pictured) in “Appendix A: Components”. Sources for the components are eBay, Amazon, or the US and UK retailers listed in the Appendix.

As a beginner, I like this book because it gets me started with “instant gratification” projects that are fun to build, even as they’re teaching basic circuitry concepts and “the way things work”. The book isn’t only for beginners, though, because the final project explains how to “Build Your Own Arduino!” from simple components.

Another book that I like is [[ASIN:1118446372 Arduino For Dummies]], which has a very detailed discussion of soldering, which I’m new to. That book explains how to choose soldering equipment, and gives step-by-step instructions (with black and white photos) on soldering techniques. Yet another book that I like is [[ASIN:1593274483 Arduino Workshop: A Hands-On Introduction with 65 Projects]], which aims at technical mastery of Arduino circuitry and coding—for example, in Chapter 4, topics include learning to read schematic diagrams of electrical circuits, learning about the capacitor, working with input pins, using arithmetic and test values, measuring analog voltage sources at different levels of precision, and more).

The primary lens I have on my camera is a good 18mm-55mm lens and it does great for capturing images that are a foot or more away. When I get much closer than that my camera is unable to focus properly and I end up with a crummy shot and I either have to give up or back up so that it can focus – not what I want most of the time. These magnifying lenses are a good solution, but there are somethings you have to keep in mind when using them.

I will start with a statement that should be obvious: make sure you have the correct lens size when you are purchasing add-on lenses like this set. This particular set can be used only with a lens where the thread size is 55mm. If you have a lens that has a different sized thread, you should consider looking for this kit in a different thread size. You can use a ring adapter, but getting the right size at the start is better.

There are four lenses in this kit, a 1x, 2x, 4x and 10x lens, each increasing in power as the numbers suggest. You can somewhat view these as magnifying glasses for your camera, but that metaphor is not completely accurate. They do magnify the image for you, but they allow a closer shot as well and you can get very close to your subject when you have one of these attached to your lens. Perhaps a better way to describe them is to realize that they make your camera very nearsighted and your camera can see close-up well and distance not at all when using these lenses.

The main thing to remember about them is that as they go up the scale in strength they introduce a lot more edge distortion. This is most obvious with the 10x lens. If you take this lens and hold it so that you can see things through it clearly in the center, you cannot help but notice a large area around the edge of the lens that is distorted. The effect is less then you get it close to something on which you wish to focus but it is something to keep in mind. If there is too much distortion, use a less powerful magnification lens.

These particular lenses have a little bit of heft to them but they are not what I would consider heavy. Because they are glass they are a bit more substantial than resin or plastic lenses.

Overall, these are nice lenses. I have been able to use them for taking very close shots that I otherwise would not be able to take with my camera, such as ridge detail on a penny or dot patterns on magazine print. These are not real-world examples but they definitely show off the capabilities of such lenses. If you are looking for good magnification lenses for your camera, this is a good set that works well. Just make sure you have the right thread size before you buy.

THE NEW YORK TIMES DISUNION: A HISTORY OF THE CIVIL WAR is a curated collection of a series of essays published in the New York Times between 2011 and 2015, in commemoration of various anniversaries of Civil War events. The essays make for fascinating reading, even if you’re NOT a serious Civil War buff and possess only a casual interest in American history.

The essays are short--each is only a few pages long--but many present new takes on Civil War “facts” that we learned in school and thought we knew. For example, Sherman’s burning of Columbia, South Carolina was an accident of war, not an intentional act by either the Union army or the residents of the city (as Sherman always claimed). Or, as another example, General Lee’s home on Arlington Hill--still standing on the site of Arlington National Cemetery--was never owned by the general, but was the property of his wife, Mary Anna Custis Lee, whose great-grandmother was Martha Washington.

The book has black-and-white illustrations, and is well-indexed.

I spend a good deal of time with headphones on or earbuds in my ears and I have formulated some very strong ideas of what makes a pair of headphones or earbuds worth consideration. I was anxious to try the Sound Intone i66 earbuds and they have far exceeded my expectations, especially considering the cost (as I write this, they are going for about $11, but price may change). For such low-cost earbuds these are among some of the best I have used.

Ok, right out of the package - I received a pink pair of earbuds. Bright, bubblegum pink! That does not bother me in the least as color is irrelevant but being pink these are just perfect for a teenage girl. These also come in brown so there is a choice if pink is not desired.

In the package are the earbuds and three sets of ear inserts so that getting the right fit is easy. The inserts are a little more stiff than some of the others I have used but they are not uncomfortable. The slight stiffness might be slightly less comfortable than more supple inserts but they’re much less likely to tear. To me that is a very worthwhile tradeoff. When inserted these buds create a very good seal and they do a fine job of sound isolation.

Like most headphones available today these have a talk feature that allows them to be used with a cell phone for two-way conversation. I admit that I have not tried these for conversation but will try these and come back to update this review when I have done so. I do like the fact that the microphone hangs about 6" from the ear piece which positions it almost perfectly by the mouth.

The most important aspect of any set of earphones or earbuds is the sound profile. For a very inexpensive set of earbuds, these get the sound awfully close to perfect. The highs are right on target and they are clear and crisp without being oversharp. The midrange is solid and full. The bass is strong - very slightly overdriven but not to the point of extreme. I compared these to headphones costing over $100 and these compete very well.

I am very hard-pressed to find much to fault with these earbuds. These fit well and they seem to be well-made, but their strength is their sound quality which is tough to beat in the under-$20 price range. And, if you really want a pair of pink earbuds, these will definitely fill the need. Regardless of the color, these are surprisingly good earbuds, better than most, but definitely one of the best values available.

Yarn manufacturers like Classic Elite publish knitting pattern books to sell yarn, but this usually means that the knitting patterns are highly "commercial"--meaning that the designs are above-average in attractiveness, and that the patterns are clearly written with relatively few errors. With this book, Classic Elite adds a new level of technical or educational interest, by taking 20 ideas (e.g., a lace pattern, a short row technique, a Fair Isle star design, a "fun and funky" theme, an eyelet stripe, a jewel tones color scheme, a cable pattern, a textured stitch pattern) and then developing each idea into three variations.

Sometimes the variations will be for three different scarves; sometimes for a wrap, a scarf, and a cowl; sometimes for three different wraps. The variations use different weights or types of yarn (e.g., lace weight, mohair, worsted weight, chunky). For the technical knitter or the emerging knitwear designer, it's particularly interesting to look at and compare the photos of the variations, to see exactly how a single idea can be developed into quite different looks, depending on the choice of yarn fiber, weight, and color.

CLASSIC ELITE SHAWLS, WRAPS & SCARVES is a book for the intermediate (or more experienced) knitter, because so many of the designs incorporate charted lace patterns or complicated multi-row stitch patterns. Other than that, the patterns do not appear difficult to knit. Although the patterns specify various Classic Elite yarns, the book includes complete gauge information, so that a moderately experienced knitter can easily substitute other similar yarns in making the designs.

With 60 total variations to choose from, it's hard to imagine not finding something worth knitting in this book! However, because the patterns strike me as "traditional", without any one pattern standing out as particularly new or exciting, I rate this pattern book at 4 stars ("I like it" on the official Amazon scale).

I was unaware that this book was part of a series when I selected it, though that would not have inhibited me from selecting it anyway. I have an interest in drawing and I am technical by nature so I thought this book would be an interesting introduction to drawing more geometrical things, specifically buildings and man-made structures. It’s an interesting resource and I like it but it is not quite what I expected.

If you’re looking for a book to teach you drafting techniques, this is the wrong book though its approach will help with drafting later. It does not delve into drawing precision or to-scale structures that are measured but is more of a semi-freehand approach with a straight-edge as a guide.

The approach is different than other books on drawing I have seen (and I assume it is very similar to other books in the series but that’s speculation). In the first couple of pages, the author explains the steps to drawing out a structure - framing, adding contextual details, adding textures and shading, and finally cleaning up and adding the finishing details. That’s very straightforward. What’s then surprising is how each structure is presented: the drawings are presented in progressing steps, with no text. I do not have a problem with this but it was startling at first. If you’re looking for a hand-holding approach, this certainly isn’t it.

This book covers more than just buildings (and it presents buildings of many different kinds). It presents drawing examples of monuments, bridges, stadiums and more.

This is a different kind of drawing book and it works. The presentation style is very different than most others I have seen and it covers a lot of ground. Some may find it to be very sparse in instruction and in some ways that’s true, but if you need just a breakdown of the approach to drawing something you have pictured in your mind this approach might be the key to getting it on paper.

Curry is trending in cuisine these days and it is not uncommon to walk into the kitchen in the office and smell someone’s freshly warmed curry. Also trending is the electric pressure cooker, which greatly speeds up cooking in a lot of dishes. This book combines both of those into one volume, and it does so very well.

I will start with a confession – I am no fan of curry. The smell alone is often enough to turn me off, so I was apprehensive when I selected this book. The spice mix in curry powder is often sub-par and results in a poor curry that is unbalanced and in the worst case just flat-out inedible. There’s also no guarantee that the powder you buy in the store is fresh. This book was an eye-opener for me: very few recipes actually call for curry powder directly but instead make use of the individual spices like coriander, cumin, turmeric and more. There’s an opportunity here to make fine adjustments if you favor one spice over another or if you just dislike one particular spice you can reduce it or eliminate it (that does mean you may not be making curry, though).

The book is broken into chapters based on geographical region, which is very sensible since curry from one region is very different from another. The chapter breakdown is “The Indian Subcontinent” (the largest chapter in the book, “Thailand & Other Asian Countries”, “Middle East & Africa” and finally “The Caribbean & Latin America”. Each of these have their own signature dishes when it comes to curries, and the author does a good job of sectioning these out.

There is also a chapter on making spice mixes, pastes, rice, and couscous. This chapter has a formula for making your own curry powder which is superior to buying a premade blend. This alone is enough to make it worthwhile to try curry again.

The other aspect of this book is that it is written to accommodate the electric pressure cooker. Each recipe is preceded by a quick summary explaining the prep time, cooking method (sauté, high/low pressure, NPR vs. quick release, etc.), and total time for meal prep. Whereas the stovetop versions may take more time, the pressure cooker turns the process into a faster, less messy undertaking.

So, if I were to offer a single criticism of this book, this is it – there are very few pictures of finished dishes. More pictures would make this book even better.

Like curry? Like using your electric pressure cooker, or prefer shorter cook times? This is the book for you.

Decades ago I got my first Lonely Planet Guide to Southern Africa. I remember tips like going to a certain bar and asking for an individual who could take you into Zambia for a fee. The book had the feel of a fanzine, written by a vagabond elite of backpack travelers for their own. Since then I have gotten their Alaskan guide which seems to have moved more towards guides like Frommers. This book seems to have taken the rest of the leap to The Eyewitness guide format. Which is beautiful at the expense of depth.

Not that this change is bad. For one, I am no longer looking for dirt cheap solutions to travel while walking the seedier streets. So it fits my life better. The images are alluring and just flipping through the book makes me want to get on the plane. However, where the series once gave amazingly detailed secrets, this book does not delve so deep. The suggestions are rock solid and if you followed their itineraries, or their top 25 destinations you will have an amazing trip. I was just taken aback how mainstream the book seemed.

There is some great information in this book and the page by page design is impeccable. All in all a great and beautiful guide. The maps are crisp and again beautiful. The writing is clean and readable (I read it cover to cover). I would have given it 5 stars except that it seemed to lack a depth I was expecting. However, there are plenty of insights that will help you prevent scheduling mistakes or to make sure you don't miss a specific highlight, it's just seems a little weighted toward design over written content.

If you do know someone who is thinking about going to Japan, get this book, it will seal the deal. It is a great starting point toward planning a trip.

This isn't a good first telescope, if the intent is to introduce and encourage someone to pursue the hobby of astronomy further. The images were fuzzy and distorted and varied in focus across the field of view. Any reflector telescope, even this small one, requires the mirrors to be precisely aligned (collimated) to get sharp images. Out of the box, the two mirrors were not aligned well. I did take it apart. I unscrewed the primary mirror holder from the bottom and drilled out larger diameter holes so that I could adjust the positioning of primary mirror I reseated the secondary mirror (below the eyepiece) which was not level. The 3 existing screws in the secondary mirror can be adjusted to adjust the alignment of the secondary mirror. After some manual collimation, the image is now much better. Stars no longer look like fuzzy balls. But this process isn't easily done in this telescope, nor is it described in the included instructions. Reflector telescopes can be quite persnickety because of their need to be precisely adjusted. My advice is to either spend more money on an reflector which has better optics which can be collimated, or choose a refractor telescope which I think is easier to use for a beginner and doesn't require such adjustments such as this one for not much higher cost:
Celestron 21035 70mm Travel Scope https://www.amazon.com/dp/B001TI9Y2M/ref=cm_sw_r_other_taa_QTn5zbPV2FBNX

THE PERPETUAL SUMMER (A CHUCK RESTIC MYSTERY) isn’t as consistently funny as the first series novel ([[ASIN:1945551046 The Silent Second]]), but it still has a lot of weird characters, and many more hilarious jabs at corporate culture and silly “MBA-speak”. Amateur detective Chuck’s account of his strategic interviewing tactics (near the book’s end) in seeking a promotion to a job he never wanted is priceless!

In the novel, Chuck is summoned to a private meeting with by a powerful, dangerous, unfriendly real estate developer (Valenti) that Chuck previously crossed swords with. Valenti’s granddaughter (Jeanette) has disappeared, and Valenti offers Chuck $100,000 to find her. The catch—other than that failure is not an option—is that Chuck must do his investigation while being driven by Valenti’s thuggy, silent chauffeur (Hector). Chuck’s recent divorce has left him short of cash, and he’s bored with his job (as usual), so he accepts the offer.

The granddaughter’s trail is a convoluted one, and Chuck follows it only by unraveling the tangled relationships within Valenti’s dysfunctional family. There’s a despised former son-in-law, still director of a Valenti-owned art museum, that Valenti torments by installing abominable art in the director’s public office. There’s Valenti’s disinherited daughter (Jeanette's mother) who’s running through her inheritance while chasing eternal youth. Other weird characters include Valenti’s first wife, now confined to a dismal nursing home, and an employee-background-checker (Badger) who’s almost as scary as Hector. Chuck’s former wife (Claire), who happens to be Valenti’s lawyer, also plays a role.

Read this well-written mystery primarily for the characters, and for the astute jabs at corporate culture. The plot is convoluted, and isn’t particularly memorable, though it’s entertaining, and all the loose ends are properly tied up at the end. I’m looking forward to Chuck’s next investigative adventure.

It took joining a local chess club and repeatedly getting clobbered right out of the opening to realize that in order to stand much of a chance I needed to invest more time in the study of opening theory. I already have a copy of MCO but it is heavy on spewing out moves, light on explanation and has more than a few typos that sometimes make following the variations difficult. I researched books on opening theory and finally settled on Watson's Mastering the Chess Openings series. This is a somewhat more costly resource than many of the others available (four volumes instead of a single book) but it's a worthwhile investment.

Volume 4 of the series covers a lot of odd openings that did not fit into the other three volumes, some of which are not often seen in higher levels of play but are very useful for the surprise factor. Of the four volumes, this one is the one I use and appreciate most. It covers the following openings and systems:

- Reti: Open and Closed Variations
- Reti: Slav Variations
- Modern Kingside Fianchetto
- Modern Queenside Fianchetto
- Gambits
- f-Pawns and Reversed Openings (this includes the Dutch and Bird Openings)
- Symmetry and its Descendants (Petroff, Four Knights and two variations on the English Opening)

It also includes a couple of chapters that suggest how to select openings for study and also try to predict the trends in opening theory.

I was especially interested in the Dutch Defense and this volume really helped me to understand the themes behind it. I have been successful with it though I still have more to learn.

Watson does a great job of explaining all of these opening systems (or opening defenses as appropriate). That is, rather than give a summary blurb about the opening and then just prattling on with move after move, he walks the reader through the opening, explaining the purpose behind each move. Then, once finished with the main sequence of moves, he includes one or more instructive games with relevant analysis and variations. This is so much more helpful than a cold and clinical presentation of silent moves.

Watson's writing style is very clear and approachable. He neither talks down to his readership nor does he assume that everyone has a doctorate in chess.

This is a superb series on chess openings which will leave the reader with a much clearer understanding of not just the moves involved in the openings but also an understanding of the purpose and goals of any given opening and variation covered. Although the cost of the series is more than that of a single volume it is well worth it.

Each location is documented with a series of beautiful pictures, a map showing the route or location, descriptions of highlights to look for, discussion of cuisine, and when possible alternative routes or travel paths. I have loved Elizabeth Strout's writing ever since I read--and reread--"Olive Kitteridge," so I leapt at the chance to review her new book, "My Name is Lucy Barton." This latest of her books is shorter than the previous two, and I think it is more personal as well, though I have no way of knowing how much of the action, if any, comes from real life.

As the book opens, Lucy Barton, a successful writer, is in the hospital with a mysterious complication of surgery that is never fully explained. She remains in the hospital for nine weeks, largely isolated from the outside world--her husband hates hospitals and rarely visits, and her two daughters are too young to come on their own. Suddenly, Lucy's mother, whom she has not seen in several years, shows up and stays with her in the hospital for five days. During this time, the action alternates between the present and Lucy's past, her childhood and young adulthood, and the reader gradually comes to an understanding of both Lucy and her mother. The two reminisce about various events and persons from the past, and in particular, they discuss the marriages of various friends and relatives. As the book develops, the reader sees that all this talk of other people's marriages is a way for both Lucy and her mother to avoid the elephant in the room, their own marriages and relationships.

Lucy's mother's visit is not all sunshine and roses. In chapters alternating between past and present, we see the truly terrifying past that Lucy has overcome, and her mother's limited awareness of the damage she has done to her daughters and son. Lucy's brother and sister are mentioned in small but important glimpses into the past, and the reader sees the childhood of poverty and abuse that is her heritage. Despite all this, however, Lucy loves her mother and desperately wants her approval. She slowly comes to a realization of who she is--the time in the hospital could be compared to an extended retreat, without the religious element--and we see the results of her epiphany in the last part of the book.

I loved the way this book was written. There is very little action; most of what happens is conversation and memory and conversation about memory. The point of the book is the development of a self, an identity, an awareness of who you really are--thus the title: "My Name is Lucy Barton." The book reads very quickly--it has fewer than 200 pages--but it will stay with you long after you have read it. I recommend this book for anyone who enjoys contemporary literary women's fiction.

"Whatever happened to J. Bruce Ismay?" was a seldom-asked question in the last 25 years of the White Star Line owner's life. Immediately after the 1912 Titanic disaster, Ismay was vilified as a coward, because he left the sinking ship by stepping into a lifeboat partly filled with women and children that was among the very last to depart. But once the American and British inquiries into the shipwreck were complete, and the accompanying news frenzy subsided, Ismay was able to retire to a quiet, rather ordinary, routine life. Until his death from a stroke in 1937, Ismay enjoyed annual golfing holidays in Scotland, spent summers in Ireland, and during the rest of the year attended business meetings in London that oversaw his interests in railways, steamships, banking, and seamen's and steamship insurance companies.

For those of us who never tire of watching or reading new TV documentaries or books about the sinking of the Titanic, this book provides a fresh perspective by focusing on the Titanic's most infamous survivor, J. Bruce Ismay. It recounts in some detail the responses that Ismay gave when he was cross-examined by members of the U.S. Senate and the British Board of Trade. Throughout his two ordeals, Ismay insisted that he was blameless: he maintained that he was a "mere passenger" on the Titanic; that as the ship's owner he had no authority over the Captain's decisions regarding the Titanic's route or speed; and that he had merely taken an available space in a lifeboat when there were no more women and children to load.

The book includes new material regarding Ismay's apparent infatuation and doomed romance with fellow shipwreck survivor Marian Thayer, whose husband was among the Titanic's drowned passengers. This account is based on a post-shipwreck exchange of letters between the two, who were physically situated on opposite sides of the Atlantic. Also, the book describes in considerable detail Ismay's odd behavior and seemingly catatonic mental state while on board the Carpathia, completing his ill-fated crossing. The author has an intriguing theory as to why Ismay actually stepped into the lifeboat, a theory that serves to partly exonerate Ismay from personal responsibility for his apparent decision to save himself.

I would have enjoyed this book far more, if the author had simply omitted the lengthy, forced comparisons between Ismay and Joseph Conrad's famous character, Lord Jim. Conrad finished writing Lord Jim in 1900, the Titanic did not sink until 1912, and the author concedes that Ismay probably never read Conrad's novel. Thus the many parallels that the author finds between the characters of the fictional Jim and the real-life Ismay are nothing more than speculative academic exercises. The same is true of the parallels the author finds between Ismay and certain Titanic survivors, and Conrad's other famous work, "The Secret Sharer". The literary analysis substantially detracts from the author's otherwise excellent portrayal of Ismay's life before, during, and immediately after the Titanic disaster.

Brix, a small tabby cat at a local animal shelter, dreams of being adopted by a new family, but she is too shy and hesitant to confidently approach any of the strangers who often come to visit. She watches as her friend Compton gets adopted, and she desperately wishes for a similar outcome. When one visiting couple proceeds to comfort her with gentle hugs, she can’t help but give into several purrs of contentment. When that same couple then gives her a fresh start in a new home, she soon receives a new name and a new lease on life.

Trixie quickly becomes quite a pampered pet, and as she begins to roam curiously about the house, she starts to explore her new world with an awe-inspiring sense of wonder. She sleeps on the dining room table, slides comically across the floor, and spends most of her days happily perched on a breezy, sunlit windowsill. One day, she meets a squishy little gecko named Pete, and she soon learns the meaning of everlasting friendship.

I enjoyed seeing many comedic and light-hearted moments described throughout this book. The heartwarming dialogue was complemented by several colorful illustrations that showed Trixie’s initial trip home from the shelter, and they provided visual depictions of her new home and all of its creature comforts.

The story was 45 pages long and was separated into chapters. The chapters loosely divided Trixie’s life into four separate chunks of time. Young readers would likely be able to pick up on all of the feelings of nervous anxiety, anticipation, excitement, and relief, and they’d enjoy seeing Trixie’s eventful exposures to new people, new trucks, new smells, and new friends.

Since this tale was based on a true story about a tabby cat the author and his wife adopted many years ago, it held a meaningful sentimentality. The plot would likely resonate with anyone who has suffered the loss of a beloved pet, and I would recommend this children’s book to young readers who like illustrated short stories full of memorable animal adventures and lasting connections!

A tagine is a form of a Dutch oven (of sorts), and I only relatively recently became aware that such even exists. I have been looking for cookbooks that are specific to using the tagine as a cooking method. This is the first I have seen, and so far I am pleased with it even though I have not used it much yet.

I should state that tagine can refer to the stoneware pot and lid, and it can also refer to a stew made in said pot. In the context of this review I am referring mainly to the pot and lid.

One flavor I truly dislike is coriander. I was concerned that this book would be loaded with recipes that have coriander as an ingredient (or as a component to a spice mix, such as most curry powders). There are a few recipes that call for it, but these are not in the majority. I was very pleased off the bat to discover this.

There are 6 chapters in this book. The first chapter deals with the tagine itself and covers the basics: what is it, how to use it, how to clean and maintain it and so on. The remaining five chapters are recipe collections and are categorized mainly by the protein (or lack thereof): “Lamb and Beef”, “Poultry”, “Seafood”, “Vegetables”, and finally “Staples”. The Staples chapter presents a number of formulas for spice mixes that are used throughout the rest of the book and will be a section to which most will have to refer often.

The recipes are well written and are easy to understand and follow. The format is consistent, ingredient lists in green and instructions in black. Following these recipes exactly results in predictable and fine results (at least the couple of ones I have tried). Many times, books that are advertised as for beginners, well, aren’t, but this one definitely is beginner-friendly though still appropriate for the more experienced cook.

The one thing that would improve this book would be more pictures. There are precious few. More pictures would drive up the cost but would also make the book more visually appealing. This is a trade-off.

This is a very nice book on Moroccan cooking in general and using a tagine in particular. It’s well-written, easy to understand and follow, and good for those just getting started.

To me this book is full of common sense because it has been the way I conduct my life since youth. I found this more of a reminder of how passion can be either fulfilling or destructive. EXAMPLES of REMINDERS:

- "The best route to making your passion a bigger part of your life is to do so gradually."

- "Someone who embodies the mastery mind-set judges herself not on whether she accomplishes her goal but rather on how well she executes on her process."

MY UNDERSTANDING:

The sentences below sums up what this book is to me and not necessarily what was exactly said or meant in the text:

- Pursuing an interest and becoming a successful master (or mistress) requires being intrinsically motivated to achieve results rather than being externally motivated on reaching the goal. In other words, satisfaction and passion must come from within otherwise it can become toxic.

- One must be self-aware and re-evaluate their passion.

- Pursuing a passion means life is unbalanced by default but if we look at our entire life as a whole, we are usually balanced.

- We must be patient and keep striving toward our passion to achieve success.

- Some of us may have many passions and choose to re-evaluate where we are at different times in our lives so as to re-direct our passions.

- What helps us to achieve the life we want is to think about death, This helps us realize there is only so much time that we have so we should be doing what moves us.

- There is a fine line between passion and obsession.

In summary, this felt like a pep-talk and a reminder of how I already live. I was not personally enlightened although I did appreciate the inspiring notes in the margin.

Eating a diet that is lower in cholesterol is not a passing fad but is a diet plan that many people have followed for years in the interest in cardiovascular health. There have been some questions regarding some of the things you can do to reduce your cholesterol but there have been some solid, consistent steps to follow, such as reducing certain types of fats, cutting back on certain meats and more. And, there have been a bunch of books on the topic. This cookbook adds to the growing resources available. It’s a good one but there is some room for improvement.

This cookbook covers a good bit of ground. It starts with a discussion of what cholesterol is and why it’s important. It discusses dietary changes that are easy to make (as well as some that are not quite so easy), how to stock your kitchen and other tips.

It then launches into the recipe collection, broken up into nine logical sections: Smoothies/Beverages/Breakfasts, Fish & Seafood, Poultry, Beef & Pork, Plant-Based Dishes, Potatoes/Pasta/Grains, Soups & Stews, Desserts, and finally Sauces & Dressings. There is a little bit of bleed-over between the chapters of course but this is true of just about every cookbook. There are a couple of supplemental chapters as well that cover foods most frequently tainted with pesticide residues, a measurement conversion chart and a list of resources for more information.

The recipes themselves are straightforward and easy to follow, and most require easy-to-find ingredients that you can get at a normal grocery store. I noticed something subtle about each recipe though that might escape notice – each recipe is tagged, right under the title, with a type label such as “vegetarian”, “vegan”, “pescaterian”, “gluten free” and “nut free”. This is a useful resource for people who are following more stringent diet plans or have nut allergies. Below each recipe is a nutrition statement.

The book layout is mostly good, with easy-on-the-eyes text colors and themes. What is sorely lacking are photos with the recipes, which are few and far between. The photos that are in this book are printed on normal, non-glossy paper and on inspection look grainy. This is unfortunate. While including more pictures and putting them on glossy pages with higher resolution would increase the cost of production, it would make this cookbook more appealing.

This is a good low-cholesterol cookbook with good recipes and some helpful information. The lack of photos makes this book a little less appealing that many, but that does not take away the fact that this is a good resource for someone looking into eating healthier for cardiovascular health.

In recent years, I've been growing more and more disheartened at the inevitability of escaping "Made In China" labels. I've launched my own sort of Chinese boycott in recent years, and gladly pay more for American- and European-made goods if it means avoiding China's far-reaching economic grasp. When I heard about "A Year Without Made In China" and saw Sara Bongiorni interviewed on CNN, I ran out to pick up a copy to see if her observations on buying Chinese-free meshed with my own.

Sara Bongiorni's family spent one year in a boycott of Chinese-made goods, and "A Year Without Made In China" chronicles the author's eye-opening journey into the Chinese incursions on American manufacturing and investment. She already expects that certain items such as shoes, electronics, and small appliances come from China, but so do birthday candles, printer cartridges, humane mouse traps, plastic bags at the grocery store, lamp switches, hardware, craft supplies, and holiday decorations. The book includes a nifty index if you want to see the extent of China's influence looming over our daily lives.

It is especially salient in light of the recent numbers of toxic Chinese products that have been recalled: children's toys full of lead paint and dangerous magnets (80% of toys in the US are made in China), flammable and poisonous clothing (a recent report in New Zealand found formaldehyde present at 900 times the "safe" level), toxic toothpaste and counterfeit medicines, and poisoned pet food responsible for the death of thousands of cats and dogs. Bongiorni's book does not address the issue of Chinese recalls; this would make an excellent follow-up investigative report, along with a topic she briefly touches on: Chinese food in our grocery stores (Sara was horrified at her weekly purchases of Mandarin oranges when she realized where they came from). Because most foods do not tell where individual ingredients come from, Chinese-made ingredients are virtually impossible to identify (take the recent Veggie Booty recall using salmonella-tainted seasoning powder from China).

Bongiorni makes it clear from the start that she's not out to "get" China; in fact, she has a distant Chinese ancestor, Mr. Chang, who immigrated to Germany. Nor does her boycott have anything to do with "Free Tibet" politics, or as a commentary on how the Chinese government treats workers in its sweatshop factories. It is not pointing a finger at the environmental rape, industrial pollution, and global warming that China is contributing to. Instead, Sara and her family (husband Kevin and two young children) want to see if it is even possible to live without bringing China into their home as a simple economic experiment.

The boycott hits hardest for Sara's two young children, toddlers Wes and Sophie. She finds it impossible to explain the boycott to four-year-old Wes, who is constantly asking for green plastic light swords, robots, and "mote katrol" (remote control) trucks. She also has a gargantuan task in finding non-Chinese toys for Wes to take to birthday parties, and Christmas shopping is similarly fraught with Chinese toy peril. Sara spends hundreds of dollars on a German dollhouse family that seems woefully inadequate to modern kid sensibilities.

At the end of the experiment, Sara finds that her husband Kevin, the one she's dubbed The Weakest Link for smuggling Chinese contraband into their China-free house, is in favor of continuing the boycott. They eventually discard this as impractical, since it would leave them with no way to repair broken appliances, but it did make the Bongiorni family much more thoughtful as to where their merchandise came from.

Yes, it's still possible to find non-Chinese goods, but it requires diligent label reading, spending more money (Sara's husband Kevin is surprised to discover that France's tourist trade is becoming as Chinese as the US), and many annoyed salespeople (her conversations with catalog customer service are priceless). In light of the dozens of hazardous recalls of Chinese products, maybe everyone should read (and try!) "A Year Without Made In China."

Book #1 [[ASIN:B00BH0VOCU A Killing at Cotton Hill: A Samuel Craddock Mystery]] The chief of police of Jarrett Creek, Texas, doubles as the town drunk. So when Dora Lee Parjeter is murdered, her old friend and former police chief Samuel Craddock steps in. He discovers that a lot of people had it in for Dora Lee. The conniving rascals on the farm next door want her land for nefarious purposes; her estranged daughter could be seeking vengeance; her grandson wants money for art school; and then there's that stranger Dora Lee claimed was spying on her. Does Craddock still have what it takes to find the killer? In this debut novel, the strong, compelling voice of Samuel Craddock illuminates the grandeur and loneliness of the central Texas landscape and reveals the human foibles of the residents in a small Texas town-their pettiness and generosity, their secret vices and true virtues.

Book #2 [[ASIN:1616148713 The Last Death of Jack Harbin: A Samuel Craddock Mystery]] Right before the outbreak of the Gulf War, two eighteen-year-old football stars and best friends from Jarrett Creek, Texas, signed up for the army. But Woody Patterson was rejected and stayed home to marry the girl they both loved, while Jack Harbin came back from the war badly damaged. The men haven't spoken since. Just as they are about to reconcile, Jack is brutally murdered. With the chief of police out of commission, it's up to trusted ex-chief Samuel Craddock to investigate. Against the backdrop of small-town loyalties and betrayals, Craddock discovers dark secrets of the past and present to solve the mystery of Jack's death.

Book #3 [[ASIN:1616149965 Dead Broke in Jarrett Creek: A Samuel Craddock Mystery (Samuel Craddock Mysteries)]] Jarrett Creek is bankrupt. Gary Dellmore, heir apparent to the main bank, is dead, apparently murdered. Samuel Craddock thought he was retired but now he's been asked to return as police chief. Dellmore supposedly had a roving eye, although his wife says he was never serious about dallying. Still, Craddock wonders: Did the husbands and fathers of women he flirted with think he was harmless? What about his current lover, who insists that Dellmore was going to leave his wife for her? Craddock discovers that Dellmore had a record of bad business investments. Even worse, he took a kickback from a loan he procured, which ultimately drove the town into bankruptcy. Many people had motive to want Dellmore dead. Then the investigation turns up another crime. As Craddock digs down to the root of this mess, many in Jarrett Creek are left wondering what happened to the innocence of their close-knit community.

Book #4 [[ASIN:B00N6PCQQC A Deadly Affair at Bobtail Ridge: A Samuel Craddock Mystery]] In the course of their developing friendship, Samuel Craddock has learned to accept that his neighbor Jenny Sandstone’s personal life is strictly secret. But when her dying mother tells Craddock that Jenny is in danger, he is confronted with a dilemma. He wants to respect Jenny's privacy, but he is haunted by the urgency in the dying woman's voice. When Jenny is the victim of a suspicious car accident, Craddock has no choice but to get involved. He demands that she tell him what he needs to know to protect her and to solve the mysteries surrounding the strange events that began taking place as soon as Jenny’s mother passed away. Forced to confront the past, Jenny plunges into a downward spiral of rage and despair. She is drinking heavily and seems bent on self-destruction. Craddock must tread lightly as he tries to find out who is behind the threats to her. But only by getting to the bottom of the secrets buried in Jenny’s past can he hope to save her both from herself and from whoever is out to harm her.

Book #5 [[ASIN:B00SED1L3K The Necessary Murder of Nonie Blake: A Samuel Craddock Mystery]] "She was a dangerous girl and people think she'll be a dangerous woman." Nonie Blake is back home from a mental institution where she has spent the last twenty years, and people in Jarrett Creek are worried. Maybe too worried, for within a week of her return, Nonie is murdered. Chief Samuel Craddock thinks the only possible suspects are members of her tight-lipped family. Ever since Nonie tried to kill her sister when she was fourteen and was sent away to the institution, the family has kept to itself. Clues are scarce and Craddock is stumped. So he checks with therapists at the mental hospital to see whether they can add anything useful to his investigation. But he discovers that she has not been there for ten years. Now Craddock has to find out where Nonie has been all this time. Soon Craddock finds himself dealing not only with murder, but layers of deception and secrets, and in the midst of it all—a new deputy, one Maria Trevino, sent by the sheriff to beef up security in the small Texas town.

I used this book to research potential attractions for an upcoming trip to Italy (Stresa, Milan, Venice, Cinque Terre), although not as a primary guide (for that, I split duties between [[ASIN:1598806580 Rick Steves' Florence and Tuscany 2011]] and [[ASIN:0756669537 Florence and Tuscany (EYEWITNESS TRAVEL GUIDE)]] since most of my trip is in Tuscany). I have several other Fodor's guides, and Fodor's Venice and the Best of Northern Italy doesn't disappoint. It's full of useful sightseeing tips taken from Fodor's message boards, gorgeous photos, and really handy maps, particularly the bird's-eye view on cruising the Grand Canal, which points out notable buildings and attractions with concise footnotes. There's a hefty emphasis on regional foods and even handy primers on language differences between regions.
There is also much space devoted to art and architecture, particularly the multi-page spread on Andrea Palladio's distinctive architecture.

Predictably, Venice alone takes up over forty percent of the book. There is a handy removable laminated map in back that includes sightseeing information and also includes the vaporetto routes. A good portion of those two hundred pages is restaurant reviews and shopping advice; you'll find recommendations on where to find handmade crafts like gilded picture frames, handmade lace (much of what is currently sold in Venice is machine-made in China or Taiwan), coda di pavone, and yes, Murano glass and masks. If you're looking for Italian designers, you'll find several pages devoted to high fashion, including the addresses of trendy Dolce & Gabbana, Armani, Prada, Gucci, Bulgari, Versace and more shops in "The Fashionista's Milan."

I will be visiting several of the towns in Cinque Terre, and would have liked to see more space devoted to each town, rather than the brief one-paragraph overview that each is given. I realize that these are small towns with loads of tourists, but surely each of the five contains some notable churches, museums, shops, etc.? Some of the cities felt like tacked-on afterthoughts, and I could have done with less food coverage and more in-depth info, but overall, this is a good starting point for planning a trip to Northern Italy.

Gina DePalma's Dolce Italiano: Desserts from the Babbo Kitchen collects a treasure trove of desserts and savories from Mario Batali's Babbo restaurant ([[ASIN:0609607758 The Babbo Cookbook]]) in NYC. There are several forewords, including one by Mario Batali himself and Colum Sheehan, wine director of Babbo. Gina's thorough introduction includes her own earliest memories of her Nonni's kitchen and growing up in a Italian-American family that still revolved around the Italian style of shopping and cooking. She includes a section called Learning Italian that covers various regions, DOP and IGP origins, a recommended reading list, ten Italian ingredients you should know (some will surprise you!), and a brief, effective section on equipment.

The first section is devoted to Italian cookies and includes several almond-based cookies (almond fingers, chocolate kisses, mostaccioli), semolina cookies (lemony semolina cookies), polenta cookies, chestnut brownies, and several biscottis (almond, orange and anise, mosaic, polenta and sesame). Many are light and refreshing rather than the heavy, dense, cloyingly sweet desserts that Americans prefer, and the presence of polenta gives baked goods a rather toothsome crunch that will be unfamiliar to American palates.

Cakes include several gems, including grappa-soaked mini sponge cakes, citrus-glazed polenta cake, chestnut spice cake with mascarpone cream, almond and raisin cake, chocolate and walnut torte from Capri, zucchini-olive oil cake with lemon crunch glaze, yogurt cheesecake with pine nut brittle, obsessive ricotta cheesecake filled with candied orange and lemon rind, and Venetian apple cake rich with honey, spices, and polenta. The Venetian apple cake had just the right touch of sweetness from the shredded apple and honey, and the almond cake from Abruzzo was a delightful blend of toasted almonds, semolina flour, chocolate, and Amaretto.

Spoon Desserts consist of bonets, custards, bavarians, panna cotta, and zabaione, many of them savory additions such as pumpkin, fresh bay leaf custards, yogurt with caramel, aged balsamic, and pine nut brittle, and a lovely cool rhubarb soup with orange and mint fior di latte that is a refreshing start to a spring or summer dinner.

My favorite section was the Tarts, a personal favorite of mine. Unusual choices included a fresh cranberry tart perfect for fall, a sour cherry custard tart very similar to a French clafoutis, a blueberry and coconut tart, the divine honey and pine nut tart (you can't convince me that this isn't what angels eat!), chocolate and polenta tart (obscenely good with a scoop of gelato), and fruit tarts (fig, lemon, apple crumb, hazelnut and grape).

The next section sounded good, but lacking an ice cream maker, I was unable to try out any of the ice creams or sorbets. However, if/when I do purchase one, the fig and ricotta gelato, ginger honey gelato, and espresso cinnamon gelato are tops on my list.

I don't eat fried foods, so I haven't had the chance to sample any of these firsthand. Fried treats include fritters (pumpkin, herbed goat cheese, lemon ricotta, apple), Florentine doughnuts with vanilla custard, Neapolitan doughnuts with warm chocolate sauce, and cream puffs.

Ways with Fruit includes traditional fruit-and-alcohol combinations such as strawberries in Chianti, Balaton cherries with grappa and mascarpone, white peach and prosecco gelatina, honey-baked figs stuffed with walnuts, sweet apple omelet, and marmelades (Meyer lemon and spiced blood orange).

Celebrations includes holiday dishes such as St. Joseph's Day cream puffs (served on the feast day of St. Joseph, March 19), Easter egg bread, sweet grape focaccia (served at the annual grape harvest), chocolate "salami" (relax, vegetarians, it's made out of chocolate and nuts and rolled in powdered sugar to look like casing!), panforte (a traditional fruit-and-nut-stuffed bread from Siena) and pandoro (sweet Christmas breads).

The final chapter, Savory Bites, includes breadsticks, taralli (similar to pretzels), semolina and sesame crackers, calcioni, and cheese puffs (Gina includes notes on her favorite Italian cheeses).

Dolce Italiano is an absolutely gorgeous cookbook that is unparalleled in terms of culinary technique, the quality of Gina's experiences in and out of various kitchens, and the delicious end results, whether sweet or savory. The only potential downside is difficulty in locating specific Italian ingredients such as millifiori honey, decent grappa, Piedmontese hazelnuts, fresh chestnuts and chestnut flour, fresh (not commercial) ricotta and mascarpone cheeses, "OO" flour, aged balsamic (although I've had luck at Zingerman's Deli in Ann Arbor, [...]) and Sicilian pistachios, although Gina includes a "Sources" section at the back of the book (that is, if you don't mind the expense of having your cheese overnighted from NYC!!).

If you're a fan of Italian / Mediterranean cuisine, you owe it to yourself to add this to your collection, presto. This is a beautiful cookbook that will bring you hours of enjoyment as you discover traditional Italian desserts that combine sometimes unlikely pairings that result in taste bud-tickling creations that taste like something your Italian grandmother would have baked.

Yiddish, the Germanic language of Eastern European Jews that was imported to the US during waves of Jewish immigration, was once a thriving language that fueled vaudeville, newspapers such as the Forverts, Yiddish comedians, radio dramas, and a rich literary tradition. Sadly, few speakers or vestiges of Yiddish's cultural beacon survive in the US. Numerous Yiddish words such as bagel, chutzpah, glitch, klutz, maven, and schlep have made their way into American vocabularies (for an excellent discussion on Yiddish and its influence, read [[ASIN:0061132179 Born to Kvetch: Yiddish Language and Culture in All of Its Moods (P.S.)]] by Michael Wex).

Originally broadcast on NPR, the Yiddish Radio Project was the brainchild of musician/historian Henry Sapoznik. He discovered few dozen acetate-coated aluminum discs at a rummage sale, then spent the next 17 years rescuing surviving discs. Some had been melted down for WWII scrap metal drives, others tossed or disintegrated, but the rare surviving copies opened the door to a long-lost glimpse of Jewish immigrant culture in the mid-twentieth century. We hear bilingual advertisements for Barbasol, Manischewitz, and Hebrew National Meats among others, Yiddish swing, and fascinating Yiddish radio dramas (the soundtrack is available as a standalone CD, [[ASIN:B000060P7J Music from the Yiddish Radio Project]], featuring highlights of commercials and swing melodies).

Narration is by Scott Simon, and translations are provided by Carl Reiner and Eli Wallach. The two-CD tribute includes segments on Yiddish commercials, radio dramas, and rabbinical radio courts, filled out by snippets of tantalizing products long gone, such as Brillo Kosher Soap: "the Star of David is worked right through the soap, it never disappears"! This is a treasure of those of you who grew up in a Yiddish-speaking household, or who might want to reconnect with the culture of our immigrant grandparents.

BABY’S FIRST FELONY (A CECIL YOUNGER INVESTIGATION) is a delightful blend of the private investigator and cozy mystery genres. It’s really an extended shaggy dog story (along the lines of “How I Met Your Mother”), presented as an allocution by criminal defense investigator Cecil Younger to a 3-person panel of sentencing judges. (Yes, Cecil is in deep, deep trouble.) This is the 7th novel in the Cecil Younger series, but the first for me; it works fine as a standalone.

In the novel, Cecil discovers a box containing $50,000 in cash when investigating the facts behind the disappearance and murder of a teenage mother he’d helped. Ignoring the advice of his public defender boss (David Ryder), he doesn’t turn the money in right away. He hides it in his attic, which violates one of the “rules” included in David’s handout for first-time felons (“Baby’s First Felony: A Guide to Avoiding a Life in Crime”). Specifically, in the chapter on physical evidence, BFF suggests hiding incriminating evidence in public areas where they’re not easily traced to you.

Soon, Cecil’s investigation gets him involved with a Mexican drug dealer, who is murdered with a shotgun blast to the head--with Cecil standing near him in a hotel room. After that, it’s all downhill for Cecil, as events conspire to entangle him more and more in felonious criminal activities.

In a concluding “Author’s Note”, author John Straley states that the novel ”is a hallucinatory dream of everything that could have gone wrong for me while working thirty years as a criminal defense investigator in Alaska.” No doubt his real-life experience spawned quite a bit of the pithy, amusing-to-the-reader advice in David’s handout (for example, “When talking on the jail phone, Pig Latin is not an unbreakable code”).

Although I fear that this novel may be the last in the Cecil Younger series, I am looking forward, at the very least, to reading the previous six novels (starting with [[ASIN:B004HW7DWU The Woman Who Married a Bear]]). BABY’S FIRST FELONY is well-written, has great characters, and is highly entertaining.
