I recently got my first air fryer and I have been looking for good cookbooks to give me ideas of what I can do with it. I have had some limited success with it, but without a couple of good recipes to get me started I am a little limited. In looking for cookbooks I found this title, and based on the mostly positive reviews I decided to order it (I have ordered others as well). It might be a good book but it has to be one of the most poorly edited books I have ever seen (not just among cookbooks - any books). I never enjoy writing critical reviews, particularly about books because a lot of time and effort goes into writing them, but this is one of those occasion where I need to do so.

Let me cover the good parts first, before I get into my complaints.

This book has a nice collection of recipes, logically broken up into sections: Breakfast, Meat, Poultry, Seafood, Sides, Snacks/Appetizers and Desserts. While that’s a reasonable breakdown, I probably would have sectioned it a bit differently. That’s a personal preference, though - the sections make sense, and each contains a good collection of recipes.

The book starts with a discussion about air fryers and how to choose one, even offering up a selection of summary write-ups about several different brands. That’s a great start and while not meant to be exhaustive it will get you going in the right direction.

A lot of these recipes require a larger model air fryer that can handle baking trays and the like. I have not seen any collection that gives you any kind of indicator of what size fryer you need with the recipes, this book included. It would be a nice addition to include such, which would be a great time saver and would elevate the collection over the competition.

This is a self-published book, which is not a problem if you either take the time to polish your work or if you have a decent editor that takes the time to go through and make corrections. It appears that the only editing that this book received was getting fed through an automatic spell checker. There are so many typographical errors, but not misspellings - this is a case of the wrong word being used. For example, in the recipe for Pesto Sirloin Steak, the instructions say “Preheat flyer to 350 degrees F.” The recipe for Orange Pecan Crusted Lamb says “Season the lamb into the fryer...” (more subtle). Some recipes have all the ingredient names capitalized, most do not. Page 1 of the introduction starts a sentence with “The unfortunate truth us that...”. There’s even an error on the back cover - an extra blank line in the middle of a paragraph. I could go on for a while here, naming many more errors, but that’s not productive. None of these render the book useless or unreadable but they make the book seem more like an uncorrected proof than a completed book.

In light of the numerous errors I am having trouble recommending this book. It’s not bad, and it’s clear a lot of effort went into the writing, but it is so riddled with errors that it’s difficult to rate it any higher. There are better edited, more polished books on air frying available. I can only hope the Kindle version is better than the paperback.

Fishing is one of the activities I have loved ever since I was very young and able to hold a fishing rod. Though I have used several types of fishing reels my personal preference is spinning reels. There are a number of reputable brands available and I have tried several - Lew’s, Quantum, Daiwa, Mitchell’s, Shakespeare and more. Until recently I was unfamiliar with KastKing as a brand and had no experience with their fishing tackle, and in a short time I have come to realize I have been missing something important. I received a Triton 3000 spinning reel for test and evaluation and have been thoroughly pleased with it.

This reel has some heft to it, very solid and tight. It’s more substantial than many reels I have used but it’s also not the largest or heaviest either. In terms of size and weight, it falls in the middle of the pack of reels I have used for freshwater fishing and it’s a bit on the small size compared to many saltwater reels I have used. I have larger hands and the size it about right, but someone with smaller hands might find a smaller size (like the Triton 2000 or 2500) a better match. In terms of assembly, there is nothing loose or flimsy on this reel at all and there is nothing that required tightening or adjustment right out of the box (which has been a problem with some others I have used in the past). Overall, this is a solid and well-assembled reel.

Appearance-wise, this reel is absolutely gorgeous. It is a deep shade of purple, almost black, with chrome and nickel colors on the spool, bail and handle. Appearance is not really all that important but it certainly does add to the package, and this is a reel that you won’t be embarrassed to break out in front of others. It relies on simple elegance, not bright flashy colors to make its statement.

This reel has a good-sized spindle on it and it can hold a good amount of line. I put at least 150 yards of 8-lb test on this reel and there’s a lot of room for more. The spindle is tall, not deep.

Ok, on to the really important stuff - how does this reel perform?

This reel has 10 ball-bearings for forward reeling and the reel is about as smooth and quiet when retrieving as could be. Cheaper reels (cheaper meaning lower quality) tend to grind a little bit when retrieving or they make substantial amounts of noise, and some reels even have a clicker in them to mask the sound when retrieving. Some also feel hollow when retrieving, but the Triton feels solid and smooth without a hint of inferior build quality. As nice as the reeling forward is, one of the most important features in a good reel to me is a zero-reverse clutch and this reel has it down. When engaged, the reel will not reverse even a little and to me this is worth its weight in gold.

One very real issue I have seen with some spinning reels is a poorly shaped bail that interferes with the distance when casting. If the bail is too shallow and does not allow enough clearance to allow the line to fly freely off the spindle, it can seriously impact casting distance. Fortunately, this reel has a very wide bail that has plenty of clearance around the spindle and it does not impact the cast at all. I get very good distance when casting as a result. Instead of concentrating on distance, the angler can instead concentrate on accuracy (and after years of practice I am still working on improving my accuracy).

I tested the drag and am pleased with it as well. When tightening the drag the dial does not get more difficult to turn like on some other reels and the drag gradually makes the spindle harder and harder to turn. It is not a graduated turn, meaning it does not increase in steps so there is essentially a limitless variance in how tight the drag can be adjusted. The dial remains easy to turn all the way through the turning range until it is tightened completely, at which point it just stops.

When reeling, either forward or backward, this reel remains balanced and does not wobble much at all. It is hard to notice wobble when the reel is attached to a rod so I tried something when I had not yet attached the reel to a rod. Holding the reel in one hand by the assembly and giving the handle a good spin, I was able to feel the reel gyrating very slightly but not appreciably. I tried the same with another high-quality reel and it was similar. This is not the case with cheaper reels which may or may not balance.

I love the fact that the reel is mounted on an arm long enough to prevent the bail from whacking me on the knuckles when I retrieve. A reel mounted too close to the rod due to a short arm can have this unpleasant effect and I look for this problem specifically so I can avoid it. I also appreciate that the handle is far enough from the reel body to avoid hitting my hand.

In the box with the reel is a velvety microfiber cloth bag for storage and transport when the reel is not in use. This is the only reel I have ever had that has come with such and it’s a nice touch. The bag is useful for keeping the reel clean and also for keeping supplies with it, like a small container of lubricating oil, an extra spool of line or even an extra lure or two (though this is no substitute for a tackle box).

I am very hard-pressed to find anything to criticize about this reel. It is a solid and well-made, looks great and works like a dream. I believe I have found my new primary reel.

I have worked with several tripods and I have concluded that there are really two distinct classes of camera tripods: there are heavy durable tripods that are designed to be stationary most of the time and take some abuse, and there are those that are much more lightweight and are designed with mobility in mind. There is some that are somewhere in between but to be honest I have seen few of these types. This particular tripod falls under the more lightweight category and is a decent one, though there is one feature about it that gives me some pause.

This is a very lightweight tripod and it comes in a nice nylon case, making the whole thing well suited for travel. The whole weighs under 5 lbs. which is great when you have to pack it for moving or need to toss it in the car. No complaints there.

It’s easy to work too. The legs work via locking latches and extend in three segments, and I am able to so this with one hand (though it is much easier when using two hands). When the legs are fully extended and the head is raised to the maximum height, the whole stands about 5’ tall which is good for a majority of uses. If you need a taller tripod, please keep this in mind.

The head is very smooth and it gives full motion to the camera. It is comparable to most tripod heads I have used in that it allows motion in three directions so that the camera can be oriented in just about any desired direction (though not inverted of course). Motion is smooth and does not require a lot effort, though it is tight enough to prevent the camera from moving when it should not. The head can be “locked” in place via tightening knobs to keep it firmly in place.

My one complaint with this tripod is the feet. These are hard plastic feet that can be adjusted to balance the tripod slightly, but each has a hole in the bottom which exposes the end of a leg – a sharp point that is all metal. This is a double-edges sword. On one hand, the feet can allow the tripod to easily move and slide on hard floors if adjusted properly which might be the goal. On some hardwood flooring, though, they gauge the floor and leave permanent marks. I have hardwood flooring in my house and I am extremely careful with this tripod, but this is the only one I have used that poses this problem.

I like this tripod, especially for travel and mobility. It is very lightweight and easy to adjust, and of course it is quite affordable. If you have hardwood floors, watch the feet; otherwise, this is a decent tripod that is worth consideration if you need one that travels well.

There seems to be a never-ending stream of devotional Bibles hitting book shelves, targeting all different manner of people with different needs. The difficulty becomes choosing one that meets the need of the person for whom the Bible is intended. There are devotional Bibles for new Christians, seasoned Christians looking for a deeper walk, the seekers, sportsmen, outdoorsmen and so many more. The Great Rescue is a Bible that seems to be well-suited for younger Christians. Though not perfect, it's a good resource that will reach its audience.

First, this is an NIV Bible, which is a widely accepted English language translation that does a fine job of bringing scripture to a broad number of people based on its easy reading level, without sacrificing accuracy. The choice of using the NIV for the basis of this Bible is a good one as it will be accessible by a large percentage of people. I am not particularly a fan of the NIV translation myself but this is a personal preference, not a theological issue.

The primary criticism I have with this Bible is the small typeface. Though the font is pleasant and the color scheme used for the text in this volume is pleasant, the size of the font itself is a bit small and will make reading a little difficult for those who struggle with smaller typefaces. There is some give and take with this, though, as a larger font means a larger overall volume for a Bible that already has some heft to it.

The devotional sections consist of a one-page devotional insert every few pages with four distinct sections: Read, Think, Live and Next Level. Some of these read like a typical devotional like you might find in a small group study. Some of them read like short stories. Regardless, these materials are presented in bite-sized chunks, with easy-to-understand language and word choices that make them accessible to all. I have noticed that these devotionals do not necessarily reference the section of scripture in which they appear, though, so there is some leafing though pages that must occur to follow everything through.

There is a total of 365 devotional sections, and each one is placed a few pages apart from the next, which has the subtle benefit of leading someone through the Bible in a year.

There are some great study helps in the back of this Bible that are helpful to anyone really wanting to dig in. There is a "Tour of the Bible", a 90-day reading plan for someone really wanting to get a quick overview of what the Bible is all about. There is a "30 Days for New Christians" section that provides an essential quick-start. "30 Days with Jesus" is a fine track for those seeking a solid overview of Jesus' life, ministry and purpose. "30 Days in the Psalms" is not an exhaustive run through all of the Psalms but a highlights tour. "30 Stories You've Probably Never Heard" is a great walk through some important sections of Scripture that tend to be overshadowed by more "popular" stories. Finally, "30 Stories of Love and Friendship" provides some inspirational encouragement. There is also a mini-concordance/topical index.

Overall, this is a good devotional Bible that will encourage and challenge people that are looking for a better understanding of the Bible. More seasoned Christians may find this particular Bible a little "basic" for them but younger Christians have a lot to gain from it.

At 5:36 p.m. on Good Friday March 27, 1964 a 9.2 magnitude earthquake devastated Anchorage Alaska and created landslides and tsunamis throughout the state and around the world.  Genie Chance, a radio broadcaster for KENI in Anchorage was on her way with her son to buy a book and wound up in the middle of the quake. She immediately goes on to broadcast the news from Alaska and was the only one to do so in the initial stages.

This narrative is an archival review of what happened that awful day and the chaos and stories that unfolded.  Genie was the voice of reassurance during this tragedy and her voice was eventually heard by the lower 48 and beyond. A woman as a broadcaster was uncommon in those days and a woman who held it all together the way she did was almost unreal.

Based on Page 243 of this book only 115 people died in Alaska (9 of which were in Anchorage). However, if one does an Internet search, numbers such as 131 people were killed during the earthquake with 119 of those dying in tsunamis are reported. These numbers also include deaths from tsunamis caused by the earthquake that were outside the state of Alaska.  The fact that there were not more killed was miraculous.

In summary, the author weaves a superb archival narrative. He held dozens of interviews, reviewed Genie's personal papers, and even listened to captured radio broadcasts that Frank Brink, founding father of Anchorage's theatre with an interest in producing oral history records, and Genie's family both recorded. This text is not so much a timeline of events as it is a variable story of tales from Genie's past interpersed with the earthquake's present and her past again.

I never heard of Genie Chance and did not even know about the earthquake, so this was educational for me as well. As the author mentioned, there were many stories from the earthquake but he chose to highlight this one individual as through her we can get a picture of what it was like. The author Jon Mooallem is definitely a gifted researcher and writer. He made the earthquake come alive for me as if I were experiencing it myself.

THE FEED: A NOVEL is a slow-moving, confusing, post-apocalypse survival novel. The apocalypse is the collapse of “the Feed”--a continuously streaming, Internet-like connection that communicates directly to people’s brains. It can be switched off, but almost no one does it, because it substitutes for speech in modern society. Everything, even ordering a meal in a restaurant, is done by thought, via the Feed.

Then the President is assassinated, live on the Feed, the Feed goes down, and society collapses. Why this happens isn’t immediately explained. Instead, after the assassination is announced, the reader is dropped into the world as it exists “six years later”. In this world, the main characters are nearly starving, and they’re struggling to eke out an agrarian existence along with a small group of friendly survivors. Their difficulties are increased when their electrician expert is “taken”--apparently by some mysterious remnant of the Feed that grabs people’s minds.

You have to read and read and read to find out what’s happening in the “six years later” world. There are pages of conversations about what the survivors should do next, and about what they can and can’t remember from their pre-Feed-collapse base of knowledge. (Everyone’s knowledge was ripped away by the collapse.) The main characters leave the farm; encounter the usual crazed competitor-survivors in other locations; form a new camp that is attacked; discover that their daughter has disappeared; and so on.

Information about what happened to the social structure, and about what is controlling the remnants of that structure, is parsimoniously dribbled out. The main characters are very ordinary people, not particularly interesting--they just do what they must to survive (including strangling anyone who is “taken”). Following the convoluted story is made even harder by the long, long chapters that are told from different characters’ viewpoints (“Tom”, “Kate”) and that include the characters’ individualized flashbacks to the intervening years after the assassination. It takes a dedicated reader (which I am not) to slog through this mess of a novel.

A collection of attractive Fair Isle designs that remind me of the best contemporary knitting designs from Norway, as seen in [[ASIN:1893063011 Norsk Strikkedesign: A Collection from Norway's Foremost Knitting Designers]] and [[ASIN:1893063046 Poetry in Stitches: Clothes You Can Knit]] (both available now only from third-party sellers). The talented Kathleen Taylor's approach to Fair Isle knitting is to use patterned bands with geometric or nature-inspired motifs, stacked harmoniously, to create the fabric for a variety of largely unisex Fair Isle garments.

The "Fair Isle Basics" chapter has a wonderful discussion of steek finishing techniques that is illustrated with photographs showing crocheted, hand-sewn, and machine-sewn steeks both before and after cutting. The chapter also discusses a couple of intriguing technical innovations: (1) knitting Fair Isle sleeves two-at-a-time and sewing them in (instead of picking up the sleeve stitches around the armholes in the traditional fashion); and (2) shaping curved necklines after the knitting is off the needles by folding back a facing.

Unfortunately, the "Fair Isle Basics" chapter seems inadequate for novice Fair Isle knitters. For example, the discussion of placement of yarn balls--one color on the chair arm and one color on the lap--doesn't really communicate the need to knit the yarn colors (and floats) with one color always above the other color. The advice for beginners to knit one color at a time, as the easiest Fair Isle method, fails to mention that the knitter must skip the stitches to be knit in the other color when knitting the first color, and says nothing about spreading the unknit stitches or otherwise controlling the tension along the "twice-knit" row. Also, the chapter doesn't really explain how steeks relate to the rest of the knitting (the fact that extra stitches are cast on at an opening, which will be cut open later).

There are a couple of chapters that I really liked for their technical presentation. "Geometric Dazzle" includes three designs that use the same chart with different colorways, and clearly illustrates how dramatically color choices can change the total look. "Stripes, Checks, and Curliques" explains how to use self-striping and gradual-color-changing yarns to knit from charts and get a Fair Isle look from only two yarns, so that most weaving in of ends is eliminated. The book cover design is a two-yarn design.

Be sure to check the "Look Inside This Book" feature, to see whether there is a pattern included that you would like to knit. My personal favorite, the "Nordic Snowflake Dress" with a Fair Isle yoke, is not shown, but its close relative, the man's "Nordic Snowflake Pullover", is included. Another favorite of mine, also not included in the preview, is the Christmas stocking with reindeer, tree, star, and Santa-hat motifs.

I rate this book at 4.5 stars, rounded up to 5 stars, because of the author's excellent ideas for "fearless" (somewhat simplified) Fair Isle knitting. Although brand-new Fair Isle knitters probably will not be able to knit the designs in the book by relying solely on the "Fair Isle Basics" chapter, they can get the additional information they need from online videos, or from either of the classic Fair Isle reference books, [[ASIN:0486472183 Alice Starmore's Book of Fair Isle Knitting]] or Ann Feitelson's [[ASIN:1596681381 The Art of Fair Isle Knitting: History, Technique, Color & Patterns]].

The AipTek PenCam Trio HD is a multi-purpose gadget that includes an HD video camera, a 5MP digital still camera and an MP3 player. After experimenting with this device, I came to the conclusion that it is a mediocre device for imagery but acceptable for audio. I will explain each feature separately, then I will discuss some other things about this device.

First and foremost, this is billed as a pen-sized video camera. It does indeed record video, at a reasonable resolution and frame rate, up to 100 minutes worth. It's easy to work with, just set the mode, turn on the power and start recording. The audio on the recorded video is loud and clear, but the video itself is very grainy and not of the best quality. Worse, zooming in and out is not smooth AT ALL, being very jumpy and erratic. There is a light that can be turned on to enhance the light balance when recording but it is not enough to rescue the otherwise poor quality. The 5MP camera is very limited in capability. You can turn the flash on and off, zoom in and out, and snap pictures. *** UPDATE 11-29-2009: I was told that a mini CD with the manual should come with the gadget. Mine did not. I hope I am an isolated exception...

The screen is actually the biggest complaint I have about this device. It is small in the interest of keeping the overall device small, but it is so small as to be hard to see for some people. I struggle with seeing the image on the screen, and that's a deterrent for using it.

I am a complete and utter beginner when it comes to drawing and art. I have for years struggled with drawing the most basic things, and I recently decided to step out of my comfort zone and learn to draw. I selected this book as my self-directed study guide and so far I am very pleased with it.

This book is set up exactly for the purpose I am using it - as a course book for learning to draw. It starts off quite slow by introducing a few small exercises designed to get one comfortable with holding a pencil and marking paper with it. Though a mundane and seemingly simple exercise, it did work to get me more in tune with how to use a pencil for something other than handwriting.

The first major exercise in the book is to simply draw some basic pictures - a cat's face, a boat, and a house are among some of the sample pictures the author offers up. This is followed up with drawing very basic shapes like squares and circles, then turning them into 3-dimensional shaped like cubes and spheres. This then proceeds into how the basic shapes and pictures tie in to the shapes with volume, such as a small clock turned to the side to show the frame in 3 dimensions.

After this introductory material, the book moves into the meat of the whole subject of drawing - how to draw real objects that look like something instead of labored doodles. The method presented here is so simple and straightforward: visually break objects down into basic shapes and sketch the basic shapes first, then fill in the details slowly. I never once thought about approaching drawing this way before. Now I find myself looking at everything and mentally decomposing those things into basic shapes.

There is more to it than simply drawing a circle and having the shape morph into an apple. The author presents a number of shading methods, light sources, shadows, horizons & vanishing points, one- and two-point perspectives and so much more. This really is a good, solid introductory course in drawing.

I am not far into this book and I have still only just barely gotten started but I am seeing results already. While I "get it" and am farther along than I was before I started, I have a long way to go - knowing the method does not translate into proficiency. Practice, practice, practice... But the pleasure in drawing is already coming, and this is the book that has helped me get there. If this book can help me learn to draw, it can likely help anyone.

Lovers of historical police procedurals should enjoy THE SOLITARY HOUSE. Author Lynn Shepherd does a wonderful job of immersing the reader in the Dickensian world of impoverished Londoners that existed in the early 1850's. The open prostitution, the impossibly overcrowded housing, the gambling and shooting establishments, the unsanitary cemeteries, the tanners' district stench--it's all there, in vivid detail.

The mystery itself is interesting, although fairly predictable as the reader nears the end. The subject matter--the abduction of young women and girls for the use of wealthy men of noble birth--is not particularly pleasant. However, the private investigator Charles, and many of the other characters, are likeable and well-drawn. At the end, the plot elements are neatly drawn together, although I must confess that I had to go back through the pages fairly often to pick up on various threads that I missed the importance of at first.

As the author states in the concluding Acknowledgments, THE SOLITARY HOUSE draws on Dickens' [[ASIN:1843548534 Bleak House]] and Collins' [[ASIN:1613821395 The Woman in White]], and tells a new story that fills "a 'space between' these two great novels". This, I think, is the chief weakness of the book--that it draws on classical authors' works for its characters and settings, and tells a story as it might have been told by an earlier author, rather than being totally original with the present-day author. Probably I would have enjoyed THE SOLITARY HOUSE much more, if I were familiar with the two classic mysteries--both of which I have started, but have never had the persistence to finish.

Author Shepherd writes extremely well, and demonstrates a mastery of Dickens' all-knowing author viewpoint and style. Overall, I enjoyed reading THE SOLITARY HOUSE, and now I'm interested in reading Shepherd's previous novel, [[ASIN:B006QS36PQ Murder at Mansfield Park]], because I'm much more familiar with Austen than with Dickens.

Risotto is one of those comfort foods that most people will never, ever try to make for themselves. A basic risotto can be nothing more than a creamy, cheesy rice dish whereas a more complex risotto may have seafood, vegetables, truffles and more. This book is a good introduction to making risotto, but there is a catch or two.

One of the first orders of business in this book is a quick how-to on risotto-making basics. The process is the same, regardless of what recipe or embellishments are used, so an introductory course is a welcome starting point. The author presents step-by-step instructions, complete with full-color photographs, of what to do, what to look for and how to know when to move on.

The recipes in this book are broken down into three main sections: Comforting Recipes, Sexy Summery Recipes and finally Dinner Party Recipes. Each of these sections is further broken down into three subsections: Cheese/Herbs/Spices, Vegetables and Mushrooms, and finally Fish and Meat. While this is ok, it does mean that finding a specific recipe probably results from digging through the index at the back of the book. To me, it would have made better sense to group the recipes together by ingredients, not by anticipated applicability.

This is a gorgeous cookbook with plenty of full-color recipes. Roughly one third of the recipes contained within have fill-page photographs.

There is one thing that caught my attention that merits mention. The author's recipes usually call for ingredients measured by mass, not by volume. While technically more accurate and more consistent, most American cooks tend to cook by volume. Without a kitchen scale, many of the recipes will not be too easy for such cooks.

This is by no means a bad book on risotto and is a good addition to the collection if one wants to make fine risotto dishes. The organization of material is a little unusual though, and the measure of ingredients by mass vs. volume might make preparing these recipes a little more difficult for some, but overlooking these this is a good cookbook on the subject that's worth a look.

This debut novel is told in first-person narrative, largely in flashbacks, in alternating “now” and “then” chapters. (Sadly, this seems to be the current fashion in debut-novel-writing.) There is enough interior angst to fill a dozen novels. The angst is mostly in the form of the artist’s vicarious imaginings of how her abandoned husband and daughters are reacting and feeling after her disappearance and apparent murder.

To the extent that this novel purports to examine the conflicts faced by an ambitious “career woman” who finds herself trapped in the role of “stay-at-home mother”, it’s stale and trite. It really has nothing new to offer on the subject, and the unlikeable “unreliable narrator” isn’t to be excused for escaping from suburbia in the extreme, selfish, and delusional manner that she chooses. One night, leaving a gambling club where he has run up a considerable tab, the young painter Francis Bacon, accompanied by his lover, sees a man gunned down in the street. They do what they can to stanch the flow of blood, but the Frenchman dies in the hospital. Soon afterward, Bacon receives a strange offer from the club owner: He will erase Bacon’s debts if the painter delivers a package to the dead man’s widow, Madame Renard, on the Riviera. What gambler could resist a trip to Monte Carlo? After handing over the parcel, Bacon learns that Madame Renard is dead—and the striking young woman who accepted the delivery is an impostor. The Riviera may be lovely, but in 1945, its sun-drenched beaches can be just as dark as the back alleys of London

MOON OVER TANGIER (2014) In colonial Morocco, a painter navigates a conspiracy of forgery, corruption, and murder. For Francis, life with David grows more dangerous by the day. When sober, he is charming, but when he drinks, he is violent, slashing Francis’s paintings and threatening to gut the painter, too. When David leaves London for Morocco, Francis cannot help but follow this man whom he loves but can no longer trust. In Tangier, they find a thriving community of expats who guzzle champagne while revolutionaries gather in the desert. But in Morocco’s International Zone, death does not wait for rebellion. After Francis identifies a friend’s Picasso as a fake, the police call him in to investigate the forger’s demise. If he refuses, they will throw David in jail, where inmates and the DTs will kill him within the week. Between the bustle of the city and the emptiness of the desert, Francis finds that in Morocco, even the fakes can be worth killing for.

The book cover gives us the story's setting: it's a wild, stormy night. The house perched precariously on the valley's edge shelters three young children and their 20-something cousin. The children's parents have left under somewhat mysterious circumstances, the entire area has evacuated, the power is out, there is no food. How to pass the time, calm the nerves, weather the storm? The cousin begins a story. HIS story, apparently, and the story of What-the-Dickens.

Turns out What-the-Dickens is a tooth fairy - orphaned and born in a tuna can, he doesn't know what he really is until he stumbles upon another fairy at work (Pepper). He is then introduced to the fairy world, its rules and customs and beliefs. He tries to figure out how and where he fits in, while growing closer and more loyal to Pepper. The story is told in fits and starts as we also learn about the condition of the children and the status of the storm.

I think What-the Dickens can be read two ways: as a straight-across fairy tale aimed at mainly 5th-8th graders. Or it can be read with more adult undertones of religious and political themes. There is some discussion of faith, purpose, and sacrifice. And war, aggression, and territory. I wouldn't say there is enough fodder for philosophical debates or personal paradigm shifts, but there is a little meat to gnaw off the bone.

Maguire's talent with words does not disappoint, and the character of What-the-Dickens is a wonderfully complicated little skibbereen (the technical term for "tooth fairy"). He is at times simple, and yet honest and full of heart. If I'm being honest, I'll have to say that I cared more about the fate of the little sprite than I did about those stuck in the storm.

At just 250-ish pages, Freed manages to infuse a significant amount of longing into this brief novel. The book is about young Cressida, her scandalous mother, her vacant father, and the benevolent neighbor who seems inextricably bound to all their fates. I truly enjoyed the intimate circle created in this book - the back and forth in tiny orbits, almost like the rest of the world didn't exist outside of a handful of main characters. This did make it a greater challenge, however, to remember when and where this story was taking place. We are supposed to be in post-WWII South Africa, but the setting fades to gray in the face of so much personal and domestic drama. I was generally alright with that, though I wondered if that would be true for all readers.

I mentioned the theme of "longing" in this book. It's the one emotion I felt just emanated from every page - a longing to be loved, to be cared for, to belong. There are a few of what I consider "throw away" characters meant to forward the story of Cressida and ultimately her neighbor and benefactor, George Harding. But really, it's only Cressida and George I ever really cared about. I've seen their story compared to that of Pygmalion - the older, more experienced gentleman crafting a lower-class girl into polished womanhood. I understand - and mostly agree with - the comparison, so take from that what you will about the course of the story.

I truly enjoyed Lynn Freed's The Servant's Quarters, and was satisfied by the conclusion.

below is a very brief history of Hugo for first time readers:

The Bookseller: October 9, 2012; Max—an elderly Paris bookstall owner—is abducted at gunpoint. His friend, Hugo Marston, head of security at the US embassy, looks on helplessly, powerless to do anything to stop the kidnapper. Marston launches a search, enlisting the help of semiretired CIA agent Tom Green. Their investigation reveals that Max was a Holocaust survivor and later became a Nazi hunter. Is his disappearance somehow tied to his grim history, or even to the mysterious old books he sold? On the streets of Paris, tensions are rising as rival drug gangs engage in violent turf wars. Before long, other booksellers start to disappear, their bodies found floating in the Seine. Though the police are not interested in his opinion, Marston is convinced the hostilities have something to do with the murders of these bouquinistes. Then he himself becomes a target of the unknown assassins. With Tom by his side, Marston finally puts the pieces of the puzzle together, connecting the past with the present and leading the two men, quite literally, to the enemy's lair. Just as the killer intended.

The Crypt Thief: May 7, 2013 It’s summer in Paris and two tourists have been murdered in Père Lachaise cemetery in front of Jim Morrison’s grave. The cemetery is locked down and put under surveillance, but the killer returns, flitting in and out like a ghost, and breaks into the crypt of a long-dead Moulin Rouge dancer. In a bizarre twist, he disappears under the cover of night with part of her skeleton.One of the dead tourists is an American and the other is a woman linked to a suspected terrorist; so the US ambassador sends his best man and the embassy’s head of security—Hugo Marston—to help the French police with their investigation.When the thief breaks into another crypt at a different cemetery, stealing bones from a second famed dancer, Hugo is stumped. How does this killer operate unseen? And why is he stealing the bones of once-famous can-can girls? Hugo cracks the secrets of the graveyards but soon realizes that old bones aren’t all this killer wants. . . .

The Blood Promise: January 14, 2014 Hugo Marston must figure out what lies hidden inside an old sailor's chest before a 200-year-old blood promise is revealed and claims another life. In post-Revolution Paris, an old man signs a letter in blood, then hides it in a secret compartment in a sailor's chest. A messenger arrives to transport the chest and its hidden contents, but then the plague strikes and an untimely death changes history. Two hundred years later, Hugo Marston is safeguarding an unpredictable but popular senator who is in Paris negotiating a France/U.S. dispute. The talks, held at a country chateau, collapse when the senator accuses someone of breaking into his room. Theft becomes the least of Hugo's concerns when someone discovers a sailor's chest and the secrets hidden within, and decides that the power and money they promise are worth killing for. But when the darkness of history is unleashed, even the most ruthless and cunning are powerless to control it.

The Button Man: September 2, 2014 In this prequel to The Bookseller, former FBI profiler Hugo Marston has just become head of security at the US Embassy in London. He’s asked to protect a famous movie-star couple, Dayton Harper and Ginny Ferro, who, while filming a movie in rural England, killed a local man in a hit and run. The task turns from routine to disastrous almost immediately. Before Hugo even meets them, he finds out that Ferro has disappeared, and her body has been found hanging from an oak tree in a London cemetery. Hours later a distraught Harper gives Hugo the slip, and Hugo has no idea where he’s run off to. Taking cues from a secretive young lady named Merlyn, and with a Member of Parliament along for the chase, Hugo’s search leads to a quaint English village. There, instead of finding Harper, more bodies turn up. Teaming with local detectives and then venturing dangerously out on his own, Hugo struggles to find connections between the victims. Is this the work of a serial killer—or something else entirely? Knowing he’s being tailed, the killer prepares for the final, public act of his murderous plan, and Hugo arrives just in time to play his part. . . .

The Reluctant Matador June 2, 2015 A nineteen-year-old aspiring model has disappeared in Paris. Her father, Bart Denum, turns to his old friend Hugo Marston for help. Marston, the security chief at the American Embassy, makes some inquiries and quickly realizes something is amiss: Bart’s daughter was not a model, but rather a dancer at a seedy strip club. And she headed to Barcelona with some guy she met at the club.With his friend and former CIA agent, Tom Green, Marston heads for Barcelona. The two sleuths identify the man last seen with the girl, break into his house, and encounter a shocking scene: Bart Denum, standing over the dead and battered body of their mysterious stranger. Though Bart protests his innocence, under the damning circumstances, Spanish authorities arrest him for murder.The two American investigators are faced with their biggest challenge ever: find the real killer, prove Bart’s innocence, and locate his missing daughter—without getting killed along the way.

Unfortunately when this book was listed for 14 to 17 year olds I started to read it through the eyes of the middle school kids my wife teaches history to. My wife and I are avid readers of historic fiction and the idea of a child living in the canal zone during construction sounded like it would have great insights. However I was put off by what turned out to be kind of a smutty tale of a 17 year old girl hiding an affair with an older man. I'm not a book banning type, but the story line does not seem appropriate for 14 year olds, maybe it's target juvenile audience should be moved up a few years.

Otherwise the book did deliver on painting a picture of the construction conditions in the canal zone. There is a good sense of the complexity, difficulties, and grandeur of the project. The plight of the common workers is well handled and much of the historical background is credible and illustrative of the time. However, there were a few too many historical coincidences. The main character goes from living next door to the Wright brothers in Ohio, to the jungles of Panama where she meets the childhood friend of a Spanish prince. It borders on too much, and hurts the credibility a bit.

Otherwise the only thing that kind of stuck out was a shallowness in the main character. She rails against girls who care only for boys, then gets involved in a steamy relationship with an older man who pretty much tells her what her political views should be. Sadly this is probably pretty authentic, but it would have been nice to have a story where the main character forms her own convictions from her own observations and thoughts.

It is an OK book, but will not be added to our library. I do have to warn parents who are looking for a historic fiction books for kids on the lower end of its age range, it does have mature sexual themes.

365 THINGS TO DO WITH LEGO BRICKS is my absolute favorite DK LEGO-building book to date, because it includes generalized instructions for a huge variety of projects, puzzles, and games, as well as tons of master builders' tips. One of the authors is Alice Finch, who is famous for her enormous LEGO model of the Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry. The book also has contributions from master builders Barney Main, Rod Gillies, Joshua Berry, Kevin Hall, Jason Briscoe, Drew Maughan, and Naomi Farr and Stuart Crawshaw. (Unfortunately the book doesn't identify the specific projects with the designers' names.)

The book doesn't include any LEGO bricks, but it does come with a battery-powered project-selector and game timer. You push the ? button to randomly select one of the 365 projects; you push the Clock button to set the countdown time for games and timed builds. The timer is glued into the book's cover, and you'll probably want to leave it there so it doesn't get lost. You can access the battery compartment through an opening in the book cover. The timer arrives with a 2032 coin battery installed and ready to activate by pulling a tab.

Many of the projects require specialized bricks (e.g., the bedside lamp calls for a LEGO "light brick" containing a LED light; the pantograph drawing machine needs Technic gears and beams), but these are available from the online LEGO Store or from independent LEGO brick sellers' websites.

My personal favorite projects include the Magic Show (with the stage box that makes the magician's assistant disappear); the Box of Dominoes; the Build Your Own Home project; and the Bedside Lamp--but it's really hard to pick favorites from this assortment. The book has something to represent just about every kind of thing that you can build from LEGO bricks, and, as LEGO enthusiasts know, there aren't many things that can't be built or simulated with LEGO bricks.

The Table of Contents is especially nicely done. Instead of appearing in a list, the projects are organized into categories (e.g., "For the Sports Lover", "Build in Micro-Scale", "Get Arty", "Give a Gift") that help you quickly find the projects that you're most interested in.

I have only recently started using UGREEN cables and so far every one of their cables I have used has been a top-notch product. I was interested to see how well their lightning cable would work out for me and, based on my experiences with their other cables I expected this cable to be excellent. I have not been disappointed.

First things first – this is an Apple-certified cable which is not insignificant. Because it is certified it will work right with your Apple device and the device will not complain about it being an unrecognized cable. If you have used cheaper cables that do not come with a certification you have seen the warning messages that appear when you connect it. This one will not cause that problem which is good right out of the box.

This cable seems to be well made and so far I have found no issues with build quality or assembly. The insulation is nice and thick and it securely attached on both ends so it will not pull away from the plugs. Each plug is shielded in an aluminum sheath which protects the plug and makes it a little easier to grip. I have the 5’ version of this cable which is nice; I like that I have a little more leeway with the extra length of the cable.

There’s something I want to emphasize about this cable which many might not consider or may think is insignificant. UGREEN has put their name right on the plug ends, where it is easy to see and read. This says that they believe in this product enough to brand it, which is actually uncommon. Most of the cables on my desk are not branded so it is very nice being able to identify a cable by manufacturer. When one goes bad, if it is not branded it is difficult to know where that cable came from. The very best micro USB cable I own is by UGREEN and because it is branded it is very easy for me to identify in the tangle on my desk. Now I can tell which lightning cable is theirs too.

I have not had this cable long enough to see how well it will hold up over time but in the time I have had it, it has been reliable and compatible. I like the extra length too which gives me some flexibility when figuring out where to put it and the device I connect to it.

It's an arson fire that he barely escapes from alive; it totally destroys the home that originally belonged to his grandparents, and he loses everything inside.

As you would expect from a novel written by the author of the [[ASIN:1400031575 Kurt Wallander series]], the surgeon is a man given to personal and philosophical contemplation, and the story includes a mystery. The mystery of the arsonist’s identity is a thread that runs through the plot, although it doesn't really drive the plot.

A continuation of [[ASIN:0307472248 Italian Shoes]], this is an interesting novel, but hardly a remarkable one. I bought this book after carefully researching it, trying to decide if it would be a book I would use or a book that would sit on my shelf and collect dust. The recipes in this book look more time-consuming than those found in my other bread books, and I finally decided that, based on other reviews of this book, it was worth a shot.

Almost all of the recipes in this book require more than one day to make; the author bases a great many of his recipes on some form of starter, whether it's a stiff dough or a liquid sourdough starter. He asserts that this style of baking brings out the most flavor in the flour. He's right. The recipes I have tried [so far] in this book do indeed have a better and stronger flavor, in spite if the fact that the base ingredients are the same as that of other recipes in other books.

The author does more than provide a bunch of good recipes (he refers to them as "formulas"). He describes the chemistry behind the ingredients and how they react to one another when mixed. He also shows, with photographs, many different shaping methods and intermediate steps that are required in making bread dough.

The author writes the techniques and recipes in this book like a man who has a deep interest in the subject, not just a desire to crank out another cookbook. He demonstrates, through his discussion in the book, his deep understanding of the art of breadmaking. For this man, bread making is a joy and a pleasure, not just a profession. When reading this book, the reader gets pulled along into the excitement the author has for his topic, which makes the process of breadmaking even more pleasurable.

This book is not for the lazy baker. If you want to make breads that are fast and easy, look for other titles. But if you want outstanding breads, and you're willing to work for it and be patient, then this book is a superb choice.

Hurricane Sandy made landfall in New Jersey in the fall of 2012 and Money Island and Bay Point located in the Bayshore area of Cumberland County, New Jersey were never rebuilt. Instead they are like ghost towns with only a resident or two remaining as of 2019.

I never heard of these shore towns on the New Jersey side of the Delaware Bay. I also thought it was mostly the ocean-side communities that were hardest hit. This author grew up in the Bayshore area and then left and came back to write this story. These towns were forgotten during Sandy's rebuild mostly due to the fact that it did not make economic sense to put money where tourism dollars were unlikely to be spent. Instead many homeowners sold out to the Blue Acres program that bought up the properties to turn it back into nature.

What I found very disconcerting was that the Health Department in Cumberland County started issuing violations to Sandy victims for septic failures that were either the result of years of decay or Sandy's storm damage. How can these poor victims pay for daily fines and fix issues when they do not even have the money to rebuild? We can always depend on the government to destroy a person further when victims are homeless due to no fault of their own. Although, I can understand that the cost benefit analysis of investing in infrastructure for "ghost towns" does not make economic sense, it also does not make sense that these towns were not even known by the bureaucrats when allocating funds. One has to be aware of a problem before it can be fixed.

In summary, I found this story to be very interesting and also sad. I am amazed at the fortitude of the couple of homeowners who remain behind and did not sell out (particularly Mike and Kate).

"This is indeed India...the cradle of the human race, the birthplace of human speech, the mother of history, the grandmother of legend, and the great grandmother of tradition...Our most valuable and most instructive materials in the history of man are treasured up in India only." Mark Twain

"Spices and Seasons: Simple, Sustainable Indian Flavors" by Rinku Bhattacharya ([[ASIN:0781813050 The Bengali Five Spice Chronicles]]) introduces readers to the cooking of today's India - a cuisine that is innovative, inspired, and full of possibilities. Many of us are only familiar with the heavy, cream-laced dishes in Indian restaurants, but Rinku's goal is to show that Indian cooking is more about flavors, freshness and love. Her emphasis on fresh, local ingredients (preferably from your own backyard, farmer's market, or CSA) and sustainability pair beautifully with Indian spices and simple, nourishing preparations that will delight family and friends.

Beautifully photographed and printed in the USA, the book begins with several short primers to sustainability in the Indian kitchen and learning the essentials (spices, oils, tools). Unlike some Indian cookbooks, "Spices and Seasons" does not require a long list of exotic imported cookware, and many of the ingredients should be readily available at larger grocery stores. Each recipe has a vibrant, full-color photo illustrating it.

Beginning with appetizers, you will find many great ideas that come together quickly. Some standouts include the mango and goat cheese mini crisps, shortcut vegetable samosas, chicken tikka and almond and saffron salmon kabobs. The remainder of the recipes are grouped by season; not surprisingly, there is a whole chapter of lentil and bean-based recipes, several of which are prepared in the slow cooker. I loved the comforting slow-cooked chickpeas with tomatoes and ginger (I used chipotles in adobo since that was what I had on hand) and the egg curries as I am always looking for new ideas to incorporate hard-boiled eggs.

Each recipe is prefaced with a brief introduction to its region, family history, and handy tips that will ensure a great result every time. Simple, flavorful preparations make the most of seasonal ingredients. I loved the tandoori spice roasted baby potatoes with mint, broccoli with toasted cashew nuts, the autumn dishes for shrimp in a mango basil sauce and salmon with a blood orange and tamarind glaze, and rich coconut curries. Other meats are featured, but the seafood section really shines. One of my favorite discoveries was the Japanese-inspired wasabi ginger fish with fresh blackberries; the sweetness of the maple syrup and blackberries offsets the umami of the soy sauce and the pungency of the ginger.

Chapter nine features pilafs and grains, which oftentimes are a main meal for me. There is also a chapter featuring traditional breads and crepes like naan, puri, dosas, and oothapams that take the mystery out of homemade breads to accompany your Indian feasts. Desserts are on the lighter side, and many feature fruit or fruit ices.

Several basic wet and dry spice blends are also included (chaat masala, tandoori masala, garam masala, curry powder) that give a much different, more vibrant flavor to your finished dish than using bland premixed blends from a grocery store and it is well worth investing the extra time to make up these mixes in advance.

In addition to being very suitable for vegetarians and pescetarians (there are many meat-free options and appealing seafood recipes), there is a gluten-free and vegan/vegetarian index and all recipes are also marked as vegan, vegetarian, or gluten-free.

This is one of those rare cookbooks that I am compelled to cook my way through cover to cover; I have not had the pleasure of reading / cooking from Rinku's first book "The Bengali Five Spice Chronicles," but based on my experience with "Spices and Seasons," it will be next on my list!

Verdict: "Spices and Seasons" is an absolute must-own for anyone who enjoys Indian food or is simply looking for simple, healthful ways to make the most of an abundance of garden vegetables or a CSA box.

Thank you to Rinku for the review copy!

SAMSUNG GEAR S2 FOR DUMMIES does an excellent job of explaining how to set up and use the Gear S2 smartwatch. The book describes in detail every preinstalled app and setting. It gets you quickly up to speed on handling telephone calls, text messages, and emails. It has good chapters on troubleshooting, and on finding online help and support. Surprisingly, it even has a chapter on designing, developing, and selling your own Gear S2 apps.

However, I question whether any new owner of a Gear S2 really needs this book. The Gear S2 is a rather simple device, and the interface is quite intuitive to use. I figured out the watch features fairly quickly (all by myself, without benefit of any detailed manual) just by rotating the bezel and tapping on the icons to see what they did.

It did take me a while to realize that the Gear S2 does NOT run wholly independently of an Android smartphone (e.g., an interactive NBA watch face on my Gear S2 stopped updating game scores whenever my phone went to standby mode). This book would have saved me some troubleshooting time in that area--it tells you on page 2 that you need a smartphone running to make full use of the watch.

Switching the watchbands is very tricky, and this book has photos and step-by-step instructions that show you how. However, there is a Samsung video available online that demonstrates the method. There is also a complete Gear 2 User's Manual available online from Samsung that explains all the apps, settings, and capabilities of the device, just as this book does.

Without a doubt, author Eric Butow does a fine job of covering the S2 Gear in this "Dummies" book. It's not his fault that the Gear S2 is limited in things it can do, so that there isn't a whole lot for him to write about. However, at its current Amazon selling price (about $23 in paperback format), I don't think that this book is enough of an improvement over the Samsung User's Manual to be worth the money. I rate it at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

FIELD OF GRAVES is J.T. Ellison’s lightly-revised, previously-unpublished, first novel (and my very first J.T. Ellison novel). FIELD OF GRAVES also happens to be the first “Taylor Jackson” novel; although, strictly speaking, the first published novel, [[ASIN:B00UFIH4X8 All the Pretty Girls]], is the real beginning of the series. Some of the writing is awkward (especially at the beginning), but the plot drew me in, and I ended up enjoying the book.

In the novel, the gorgeous Lieutenant Taylor Jackson leads an investigation into a series of baffling Nashville murders. The body of a young woman is found posed on the steps of the Nashville Parthenon; the body of another young woman is pulled from the river near Riverfront Park; a priest and his student are burned to death in a confessional; a pregnant Vanderbilt student disappears and may be another victim. Early in the investigation, medical examiner Samantha Owens (who has her own J.T. Ellison series) finds signs that the dead victims were all poisoned, and that they may have been sacrificed by a ritual killer.

Taylor is recovering from having shot a fellow police officer to death. She’s suffering from recurring nightmares that feature a field of graves. Luckily, she joins forces with Dr. John Baldwin, an FBI profiler who has been severely damaged by losing three Behavioral Science teammates in a recent BSIS operation. The two damaged detectives turn out to be just what the doctor ordered--for solving the case, and for each other.

The amateurish parts of the book include the heavy use of Taylor’s nightmare dreams for characterization and filler, and the insertion of a poem authored by one of the perpetrator’s targets. These passages exist mostly to show off the author’s creative writing skills, and aren’t really needed to advance the plot. Also, Taylor works the investigation over several days without getting any meaningful sleep, and that sort of “superwoman” stuff strains my willing suspension of disbelief as a reader.

However, despite the novice writer elements, the plot is highly intriguing and has lots of unexpected twists and turns. Also, the characterization is pretty good. I rate FIELD OF GRAVES at 4 stars ("I like it on the official Amazon scale).

This is an excellent manual for new iPad owners or for those who are considering the purchase of an iPad. I don't own an iPad but am very interested in learning about it and I absolutely enjoyed this book from cover to cover (skipping over the "how to" steps, of course). The author reviews the iPad functionality in a very basic manner that is actually enjoyable to read. He also transitions well from one subject to the next. Although, there are many "how to" steps throughout the book, there is enough information included to enlighten non-owners about the iPad's functionality.

Brian Proffitt does a comprehensive job of covering how to operate your iPad that takes up the first 95 pages. For instance, if you plan to connect with 3G, the author includes current cost tables for the US, Canada and UK wireless plans as of fall 2010. He tells you how you can take a screen print of your iPad by holding down the Home key and then pressing the Sleep/wake button at the same time.

From Chapter 7 on, he takes you through the various applications that you can use for business purposes (and personal) such as using iWork (Numbers for spreadsheets, Keynote for presentations, etc.). You will learn how to print from the iPad, access information in the cloud, connect with Facebook using Friendly, use task management software, customer relationship management, book flights and track them (sort of creating an itinerary for your trip), writing blogs from the iPad, etc., etc., etc.

By no means does he provide you with a guide on every possible application or tool you can use on the iPad, however, he gives you sufficient enough information to get you stated so that you can discover the rest on your own. The intention of this book is to educate the iPad user on how they can use this device for business.

Those who are proficient with the iPad might find this book too basic. However, for the new iPad user or the person who is just interested in learning more about what an iPad can do for you, this book is an exceptionally well-written and easy to read manual that's worth the purchase.

All too often, prequels are thinly-plotted novels that appear in long-running mystery/thriller series after the author has run out of new ideas. Happily this is NOT true of THE VANISHING MAN: A PREQUEL TO THE CHARLES LENOX SERIES, which is not only a worthy addition to the series, but even works as a standalone. Basically, it traces some of Lenox’s earliest days as a private investigator, when he is still ignorant of surveillance techniques, and needs to hire and learn from the consummate “vanishing man”, Thaddeus Bonden.

In the novel, a duke engages Lenox to investigate the theft of a painting from his study wall. The duke badly wants to know WHO stole the painting-- the painting itself is of little value. He suspects that the thief was after the priceless painting that was hanging nearby--a William Shakespeare portrait painted from life. The nature of the painting, a national treasure, is a jealously guarded family secret, and the duke insists on Lenox’s utmost discretion.

Suspecting an inside job, Lenox eventually hires Bonden to watch the duke’s home and to find out certain essential facts. The intricate plot really thickens after the duke, suspecting the thief’s return to his study, shoots and kills his faithful manservant, Craig.

The novel contains interesting background on Lenox’s romance with his still-married friend, Lady Jane Grey, as well as background on his early relationship with his manservant and associate Graham. Like other novels in the series, this one convincingly evokes the atmosphere of Victorian-era London.

"Raw, Quick & Delicious!" is a beautifully compiled recipe book of various dishes made with raw food. Raw food is a diet that contains whole nuts, seeds, legumes, and grains that are considered unprocessed and generally not heated past 105 degrees F.

I selected this book with the misguided thought that assembling (it's not really cooking to me) and eating a raw food recipe would not be much different from my steaming and eating an entire plate of various vegetables for dinner which is something I regularly do. Well, I could not be more wrong.

First, most of the recipes are eaten cold and uncooked.

Second the ingredients are high glycemic because the ingredients are processed by chopping, slicing, grating, pureeing, juicing, or liquefying.

Third, the ingredients are not always low cholesterol because some recipes call for coconut oil or coconut butter.

Fourth, several recipes called for ingredients that are not stocked in my kitchen such as coconut oil and coconut butter, hemp seed, wheat-free tamari, raw agave nectar, and sheet raw nori.

Fifth, about 40 pages are dedicated to smoothies, drinks and juices and 13 pages to dressings. Also, about 13 pages are allocated for "in the pantry" recipes that consists mostly of sauces and dressings (8 sauces/dressings to 7 other recipes).

I decided to make the "shred-me-up-slaw." I found this recipe easy to make and it tasted pretty good. However, since I'm not use to a raw food diet, I should have eaten it as a side salad and not a main meal because I started to feel nauseous during the last couple bites. There are only about three other recipes that I would make in this book such as the chunky tomato marinara sauce, the avocado cucumber hand rolls and perhaps the lime, tomato and avocado chile.

Having read through the entire introduction and scanned the recipes, I know this type of eating is not for me. However, I do feel this is an excellent recipe book for those who are into raw food and I cannot discount this book just because my personal tastes do not prefer this type of diet.

I took off one star only because the title of the book is misleading. The book title claims 5 ingredients in 15 minutes or less but this is not always technically true. The author does not count the salt or water ingredients mentioned in the recipe since everyone has these in their house. Also, if a recipe relies on one of his "in the pantry" recipes, then he counts the "in the pantry" item as one ingredient. This means if the "in the pantry" item was not previously prepared, there would be two recipes required taking 15 minutes each in order to complete the meal.

Although this is definitely not a book for me, that is no reflection on the quality of this guide. Personally, I feel this book is excellent for raw food lovers. The introduction provides details on what tools are used in a raw food kitchen such as a cutting board, mandoline, high-powered blender, etc. The recipes are explained well, the few pictures provided in the book are gorgeous to the point that I wanted to eat the recipe or ingredient shown right off the page. I particularly loved the look of the lime, tomato and avocado chile and the avocado cucumber hand rolls.

A TIME OF SCANDAL: CHARLES R. FORBES, WARREN G. HARDING, AND THE MAKING OF THE VETERANS BUREAU is a scholarly (but reasonably readable) biography of Charles R. Forbes, the thoroughly disgraced bureaucrat who established the U.S. Veterans Bureau, but later served time in Leavenworth prison for rigging government hospital-construction contracts. In this account of Forbes' life, author Rosemary Stevens questions whether he was in fact guilty of defrauding the U.S government of more than 200 million dollars.

Because the papers of President Harding and Forbes himself are missing (and presumably destroyed), Professor Stevens bases her revisionist biography on new material found in "the papers of significant figures, military and civilian personnel records, records of the Veterans Bureau and Department of Justice (including the FBI), congressional and court records, prison records, and more".

Like so many histories written by academics, this one has long, long paragraphs that are filled with every factual detail that the author uncovered during her research. It's a standard biography with Forbes' story told in more or less chronological order.

While I'm sure that Stevens' revisionist take on "the Harding scandals" (Veterans Bureau and Teapot Dome) is of great interest to scholars of the Harding/Coolidge era of U.S. politics, it's a real slog for someone like myself who has only a casual interest in learning more about the scandals themselves. I rate A TIME OF SCANDAL at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

FRACTURED is a very good novel, but the plot is the type that I always lose patience with. At the beginning, a life-altering, tragic event is hinted at. Then the actual details are dribbled out in the remainder of the novel, through one or more viewpoint characters' flashbacks that recount the events that produced the tragic one. This type of plot must be extremely difficult to write well--and this skillfully written novel is an example of how to pull it off--but as a reader I prefer a more straightforward plot, without flashbacks.

In the novel, the author of a best-selling first novel (Julie) relocates her family from Tacoma to Cincinnati, because she needs to escape the attentions of a particularly troublesome, threatening stalker (Heather). Julie and her unemployed, married neighbor (John) are attracted to each other, and the attraction sets in motion the events that result in tragedy for all.

John, Julie, Julie's attack dog (Sandy), and Julie's twin children all run afoul of the ever-changing "neighborhood rules" written (and emailed) by an officious neighbor (Cindy). Cindy, the self-appointed neighborhood leader and organizer of compulsory monthly block parties, is both amusing and frightening. John's teenage son (Chris) and Cindy's teenage daughter (Ashley) also figure in the complex plot. Ultimately, neighbors end up confronting neighbors both in civil court and in grand jury proceedings.

The Cincinnati setting, in Mount Adams and Eden Park, is incidental to the plot. (This was a disappointment to me, because I was interested in reading about the Cincinnati locale.) The characters are well-drawn--Cindy is particularly memorable, as the type of well-meaning but overbearing person who always seems to turn up in neighborhood groups. Because FRACTURED is well-done, but the kind of novel that I find tedious, I rate it at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

In GRAND DELUSION, Jacob Burns is back--still making the questionable daily-life decisions of the sort that landed him in so much trouble in his delightful debut mystery, [[ASIN:B00AFLQK1M Breakfast at Madeline's]]. When a crooked cop, Jake's hated nemesis and very-public-enemy, is shot at 1 a.m. outside his home, Jake investigates. But his timing is way off. He arrives at a deserted crime scene, and is standing in his bathrobe over the body, when his cop friend and neighbor Dave arrives. What else can Dave do, but arrest Jake as a cop killer?

Of course the innocent Jake talks freely to the cops at the station, and his wise-cracking results in a "confession" that mires him even deeper. Naturally Jake decides to investigate the crime himself--against the advice of lawyer, wife, friends, and cops--and ends up escaping from police car chases, hiding in bushes, hanging off tree limbs, and breaking into buildings. In this adventure, Jake is aided by a neglected and streetwise child, Tony, who sleeps in the local cemetery to get away from his substance-abusing mother.

Although GRAND DELUSION is an enjoyable cozy mystery--especially if you're already familiar with Jake--it's not as much fun as BREAKFAST. It's well-written and well-plotted. However, I don't particularly care for mystery/thrillers that build suspense by putting the main character "in the frame", or by making him/her the target of a serial killer or the actual killer being hunted. Since I would have enjoyed this novel a lot more if Jake had been investigating on someone else's behalf, I rate it at 4 stars ("I like it" on the official Amazon scale). That said, I'm still looking forward to reading the next book in the series, [[ASIN:B00DDT55W8 Strange Bedfellows]].

On a Night of a Thousand Stars takes place in 1976 and 1998. In 1976, Santiago Lerea is a law student from a prosperous family in Argentina. In 1998, he and his wife Lila live very well in the United States with a house in the Hamptons and an apartment in Manhattan. Thye have one daughter, Paloma, who lives in Brooklyn and is in college. What drew me to read this book, was that these years were my law school and young adult years, including when I was raising my child and reading about the Argentine disappeared. It was an in your face painful period to read about and emotionally has never left me.

By way of background, in the late 1970s through the early 1980s, a military junta in Argentina fought a war of kidnapping, torturing, raping and disappearing as many as 30,0000 of its its own citizens: some were vocal activists or revolutionaries, some the families and friends of these more active people, and some that could not be categorized by more than their art or their volunteer work or being in the wrong place at the wrong time. Many were students but certainly not all. Whole families were taken. Priests shot. No parent or grandparent or spouse or partner could discover their loved one's fate during that time and much remains unknown. Some of this was in the news in my own post-high school years in college and law school. Now it is in the news again as DNA is being used forensically to identify the bodies that have been found over the years. And always, my heart ached over these stories.

Clark writes a story that both captures this period and its aftermath. It is both engaging and compelling and tells the story, but is mostly not hard to read. This is quite a feat! In 1998, Santiago, Lila and Paloma go to Argentina for a visit and for his investiture as the ambassador to the United Nations for Argentina.Paloma is casually dating an Argentine polo player so she plans to spend part of her time in Buenos Aires while her parents are at the family ranch/farm with her grandfather. She has only casual knowledge of this travesty but an old friend of her father's shows up at a huge gathering in the Hamptons and she hints to Paloma that her father somehow saved or spared some lives during the 1970s period of the junta's activities. Her father shows extreme displeasure with Grace, who leaves the party. As Paloma runs to say goodbye to Grace, Grace recommends an author to her.

On a Night of a Thousand Stars becomes a detective story and a coming of age story as Paloma seeks to learn more about her father and the period he is so quiet about. I found the writing spare but compelling and while I can't claim an emotional connection to Paloma what I found was a deep interest in her story, her parents' stories, their friends' stories and the stories of the children and grandchildren of the desaparecidos, still seeking answers and today in 2022 they are till seeking answers. As she learns about her father, his friends, one of his girlfriends and more, she joins up with Franco, whose mother disappeared and whose father was killed on the spot. He has experience and connections with finding some answers as part of an activist group calling attention the the fact that over ten years after the overthrow of the junta, relatives of the disappeared still knew almost nothing. And one document at a time, one witness at a time, one photo at a time, Paloma learns a complicated story that makes this a wonderful and compelling read.

Yet, recently he wants to end world poverty. So, I want to hear what Nina Munk, a recognized critic of Sachs, has to say about his goal to end poverty.

Munk focuses her study on eastern Africa, mostly the northeastern region of Kenya, especially Dertu, a disputed area of Kenya by Somalia, including Al Shabab. Nomads populate this area, where a man's worth is judged by how many camels he has. So, this and the general area is where Sachs has concentrated his efforts with the Millennium Villages Project.

Anyway, my takeaway from the book is that he had only marginal success, while such marginal success was also achieved in most parts of sub-Saharan Africa. So, an extremely complex task, especially because cultural natures of these mostly tribal people are so difficult to change.

But, seems to me, the most important thing a person does has nothing to do with the result, but what the person tries to achieve. So, I see some people and their welfare being changed for the good. And, never give up, by all. So, I see Munk's criticisms valid, but short sighted. But, I have learned much from the book.

MELISSA LEAPMAN’S INDISPENSABLE STITCH COLLECTION FOR CROCHETERS is a basic crochet stitch dictionary containing about 200 patterns grouped into six sections: (1) Simple Solid Patterns, (2) Shell and Fan Stitch Patterns, (3) Openwork and Lace Patterns, (4) Textured Patterns, (5) Colorwork Patterns, and (6) Edgings. For each pattern, there are written-out instructions, charted instructions, and a color photo showing a crocheted sample of the pattern.

Because I’m a big Melissa Leapman fan, I was looking forward to this collection of her personal favorite crochet patterns. However, Melissa does NOT include any personal commentary on the individual patterns (e.g., why she likes the pattern, how or where she has used the pattern, etc.). In a brief introduction, Leapman states: “This collection includes 200 of my favorite crochet stitch patterns gathered from nearly thirty years designing for the yarn and fashion industry. Some patterns are long-standing favorites, such as Solid Shell Stitch on page 18; others, like the Saxon Braid Panel on page 99 are original to this collection.” As far as I can tell, Leapman does not otherwise indicate which patterns are old, and which are new.

The book provides a good selection of stitches for new crocheters, and is a good standby reference for experienced crocheters, but it doesn’t go very far beyond the stitch collections generally found in how-to books on crocheting (e.g., [[ASIN:156477998X A to Z of Crochet: The Ultimate Guide for the Beginner to Advanced Crocheter]]). If you’re looking for a more complete crochet stitch dictionary, you might consider [[ASIN:1454701374 The Complete Book of Crochet Stitch Designs: 500 Classic & Original Patterns]]), and the other two titles in the Linda Schapper series.

Because the book has only 200 patterns, and lacks commentary by the author regarding their selection for inclusion, I rate MELISSA LEAPMAN’S INDISPENSABLE STITCH COLLECTION FOR CROCHETERS at 4 stars ("I like it" on the official Amazon scale).
