I decided to purchase a new laptop after my old laptop was taken over by the family for a variety of tasks. I was mostly happy with the system I had, a nice HP Pavilion system with a decent feature set, but considering that it is 2-3 years old and does not run everything I want to run anymore I wanted to make my upgrade to a new system worthwhile. In researching I found this particular system and I pounced on it, as I found it at a steal of a price. It is not perfect, but there is an awful lot in this notebook.

My very first notebook was a Sony Vaio, so I imagined that this would be familiar territory. I was greatly mistaken, as things have changed dramatically since then, mostly for the better.

First off, this is a fast system with lots of expansion room. This is very important to me because I do a little bit of everything - I do some gaming, I write software, I write short stories, I hang out online. I am not considered a power user in that regard so an AlienWare ultra-high-powered expensive gaming rig is not really what I need, but I don't need an entry-level system that is good for little more than checking email either. My needs are for a well-rounded machine that can do most things well. This notebook fits that need.

I am especially impressed with the bright, large screen. I do occasionally toss a movie DVD into the system and treat myself to a private showing of whatever movie I have chosen, and all of that screen real estate makes for an enjoyable experience.

As for DVDs... With Blu-ray built into this system, watching new media movies is not a concern. That's a very nice plus.

I like the fact that this system has two individual hard drives instead of one large one, as I want to create a dual-boot system and not wipe out the whole thing. I was unaware of this when I purchased the system, thinking I had a unified drive, though that was an oversight - the labeling and documentation are clear.

The system comes with 3 GB RAM, expandable to 4. Up to this point things seem to be comfortable in that amount of room.

My first task was to strip off the trial software I don't want or need, which includes MS Office 2007, Webroot SpySweeper and Norton 360. Some people will appreciate these applications but for me they are in the way and clutter the hard drive with unneeded stuff. If these applications were full-release apps with more than 30-90 days of use, I likely would keep them all but in my case I already have licensed software to use that meet the same needs.

The documentation states that there is a firewire port, a VGA port and an S-Video port, and it took searching the web for a manual with technical diagrams to reveal that these are hidden on the right side, under a cover. Nothing that came with the system says where to find those ports, and the cover that conceals these ports blends in well enough to truly hide them - I did not find them without help.

Even more concerning to me is the number and placement of the USB ports. There is one on the back, and two on the right side close to the front edge. I work with an external mouse but I use the built-in keyboard, and I am right-handed. So, if I plug anything at all into those two front edge USB ports, the cords interfere with my mouse use. The solution, then, is to plug a 4-port hub in the back and then plug everything in there.

The built-in speakers are all right, though nothing special. If you want better speakers plug them in and all is well. That said, the built-ins are quite acceptable for most use. You would not want to use them for listening to symphony music, of course, but they're just fine for gaming and general music.

I am very pleased with the graphics. My litmus test for gaming is Neverwinter Nights 1 & 2, and both of these play quite smoothly. I have not loaded up Unreal Tournament 3 yet - that's next - but it should have no difficulty at all with that game.

I did run into one problem that required a call to Sony technical support. Because Sony does not include recovery media with their systems, it is up to the owner to create them and Sony makes it easy with included utilities. There are two options for creating the media - 1 dual-layer DVD or 2 single-layer DVDs. I chose the single dual-layer and after an hour of writing and grinding, the DVD ejected and the system said the creation failed. Assuming it was the target medium, I tried again with the same result. I called Sony thinking I needed to request the recovery DVDs and the technician told me that the single-layer DVD creation would work but that a glitch with this specific model prevents the dual-layer media creation from working. When I used two single-layer DVDs, everything created without a hitch.

THE MISSING HOURS is a slow-moving, confusing novel about kidnap-and-ransom consultants (experts who are hired to negotiate for the safe return of kidnap victims). It’s a hide-the-ball mystery, told in chapters that shift viewpoint characters (mostly alternating between sister-and-brother detectives Leah and Finn), and timelines (ongoing investigations and “disappearance” flashbacks). Interspersed among the mystery/thriller plot chapters are (1) fictional “case histories” of kidnapping cases supposedly handled by the main-character consultants, and (2) fictional “published professional articles” about the same.

I guess that the author knows a lot about real-life kidnap-and-ransom negotiations, and decided to educate readers about the field by incorporating her knowledge into a novel. However, the case histories and articles don’t add to the plot; and the rather unbelievable plot is thin, boring, and in its own way predictable.

Why anyone would choose to present a mystery/thriller intended for a mass market audience in such a complicated format is beyond me. As for the kidnap-and-ransom-negotiator content, I prefer nonfiction when I need to be introduced to, or educated about, such a specialized topic.

I recently received a copy of this book when it appeared on my desk at work while I was away at lunch. I have been trying to make good pizza and this book appeared to hold a lot of promise. So, I dug in! I discovered that some of what I discovered in this book has been improved upon in the time between now and when it was written.

I cannot say this is a bad book, because it's not. It's actually quite a good book and a VERY good introduction to pizza. At the time, this probably was quite authoritative and complete, and while some of the material can be set aside as having been improved upon, it still holds value for allowing someone starting out to make pizza that is worth serving to company.

The book has a number of sections, including sauces and crusts as well as some complete pizzas that you can make in your own kitchen. There is good variety in it and there are a number of angles with which to experiment.

My primary interest in pizza is in the crust, so I attacked the recipes in this book for crust first. My family complained that I had changed the way I made pizza when I did so. The difference is that the crusts in this book are all "fast rise", bowl to peel in a short period of time, and several other books on the subject have migrated to a slower rise and more gentle handling of the crust. The result with the former is a firmer crust but with less flavor, while patient handling and letting the dough age longer results in a stronger flavor.

I experimented with the sauces and this worked out better than my attempts with the crusts. There are a few sauce recipes in the book and the ones that I have tried have definitely improved my offerings from the oven. That said, each is a matter of personal preference I and found myself tweaking and adjusting. This is not a shortcoming; I suspect the author had this in mind.

I have not tried to make the specific pizzas. That is a matter of pairing the crusts and sauces together with specific toppings.

There are other recipes for things such as focaccia, and I have found these to be ok at best and dull at worst. Again, this comes down to method and patience, and neither of these seem to be considered. That said, for a quickly-produced product the end result is usually pretty good!

It depends on what is important to you - speed or quality. I personally prefer quality, whereas this book favors speed. That said, the results that come from following the recipes in this book are certainly better than take-out pizza and are likely better than what you will find in other basic pizza books. There are better books on the subject now, but this one is a fine starting point.

Canada's need for more people, but white resistance, even from existing minorities.

I have worked with a lot of active noise canceling (ANC) headphones, from a large variety of manufacturers. Every set I have owned, from the top-of-the-line to the weakest and cheapest, has had its strengths and weaknesses. Until recently, Bose was the one to beat when it specifically came to the ANC function, though many others have a better sound profile. My favorite ANC phones are a set of Sony in-ear buds that rival Bose in ANC and trounce them in sound quality. When I found out that Microsoft had made an ANC headphone as well I did not have the highest of expectations – I expected mediocrity with the ANC and a reasonably good sound profile. I was dead wrong in both presuppositions – these are incredible headphones and are worth every penny of the asking price. They’re not absolutely perfect, but they’re better than one could reasonably expect.

I’ll start by saying that I am sorry in advance for the lengthy review. I have a lot to say on these, and I would much rather give far too much information than not enough. The present asking price as I write this is $349 and that’s a lot of money to drop, so more information is better.

Right out of the box these are relatively nondescript and don’t jump out as either flashy or gaudy. The controls that are visible and obvious are limited – a power button and a mute button, as well as the USB Type C power jack and a 3.5mm audio input jack. There are more controls, though, and it takes a quick glance at the documentation to get a feel for what’s there. There are two dials, one on each can, for controlling the level of ANC and for controlling the volume, L and R respectively. The flat portion of the cans facing outward are multi-function touch controls that allow you to play/pause, skip forward and backward, handle calls and also interact with your digital assistant. I will come back to that last point a little farther down.

I powered these on and they immediately announced that they were ready to pair. I paired them to my iPhone and they connected and were usable quickly, faster than most Bluetooth devices I have used. I put them on, tapped once on the right ear and Pandora immediately started up. That was easy!

The sound quality is very good though I will stop short of calling it audiophile level. The bass is good and not overdriven. I don’t care for deep, pounding bass and that is a problem with a lot of ANC phones I have used (Dre Beats being among the most aggressive in that regard). It softens as the volume level is dropped and that is very normal. The midrange is actually quite good with the proper amount of depth, so music sounds full and warm and not like it’s being piped through a tunnel. The highs are bright and clear though not piercing. Overall, these are among the most balanced ANC headphones when it comes to the sound profile. I cranked the volume and they don’t distort.

The ability to adjust the ANC is not new; however, the way these headphones do it is very innovative and unlike anything else I have seen. The dial that controls it gradually lessens the amount of ANC that is applied when listening, in small but perceivable steps, until the ANC is turned off. With the central air on in the house, I gradually went from no ANC to maximum and it very gradually wiped out all of that sound. When at the maximum level the ANC is almost as aggressive as Bose, with a lot less of the the weird pressure sensation on the ears.

A unique feature of these phones is integration with Cortana. When paired to a device running Cortana, simply saying “Hey, Cortana” gets its attention and you can interact with the same types of commands you use on the command line or the search window. It does require that Cortana be properly configured. I have Cortana installed on my iPhone (yes, you can do that and it works well), and the integration with the headphones when connected is good. I had a Windows Phone when they were still available and I would have liked to try this with that phone.

There’s some debate on whether these are on-ear or over-the-ear phones. These are very definitely over-the-ear phones unless your ears are huge. The cups are buttery soft as is the head band, and these are very comfortable. I am able to wear them for long periods of time without fatigue. They do get warm after a while, so keep this in mind.

One area a lot of headphones skimp on is the carrying case. The case with these phones is better than average. It is crush resistant and provides good protection for the phones. Included within is an audio cable for input as well as a USB charging cable.

These headphones bring a lot to the table and were quite a shock for me. I had much lower expectations, for the ANC function in particular but also for the sound profile. Both exceeded my expectations and the comfort factor is the cherry on top. These are excellent phones and I am very pleased with them.

KNITTING: FASHION, INDUSTRY, CRAFT, is a knitting history book that rivals Richard's Rutt's classic, [[ASIN:1931499373 A History of Hand Knitting]]. Sadly, the currently available, reprinted editions of Rutt's wonderful book leave out the full-color plates that illustrate the best examples of historical knitting (e.g., the knitted "carpets"--tablecloths or hangings--that were required for a journeyman to qualify as a master knitter in a knitter's guild).

But Sandy Black's book does not stint for one second on full-color photographs. It is positively crammed with full-color photographs (along with many black-and-white photographs) of museum-quality knitting that dates from the third century to the present. Of course, there are few photographs of the very earliest knitting, because so few examples of early textiles have survived to be cared for by today's museum conservators.

However, there are gorgeous color photographs of (1) a 14th-15th century Egyptian fragment done in brown and black stranded and intarsia knitting; (2) a 1781 Alsatian guild carpet depicting the Dream of Jacob; (3) knitted Tudor caps from the 16th century; (4) German knitted seamless cotton stockings from the 1800s; (5) an extraordinary all-white knitted petticoat from the 1740s that is covered with animals, birds, foliage, insects, and flowers; and (6) a 19th century beaded miser's purse from Britain. These are only a few examples. There are photographs of many, many more beautiful knitted items, both ancient and modern.

The book is divided into four parts: (1) History, Tradition, and Mythology (from the Third Century to the Late Nineteenth Century); (2) Livelihood and Industry (Hand- and Machine-Knitting from the Seventeenth to the Twenty-First Centuries); (3) Knitting in the Home (from the Eighteenth Century to the Present Day); and (4) Classics to Couture (Fashion Knitwear from 1900 to Now). The photographs in each part are accompanied by a coherent, easy-to-read text that explains exactly what was happening to knitting and knitted garments during the particular time period: the invention of new tools and machinery, changes in popular demand for knitted items, and dramatic fashion statements made by each era's foremost designers. There are photographs of knitting machines, women in full-body "sanitary" woolies, fishermen wearing ganseys, modern pattern booklets, famous designer pieces (e.g., a Kaffe Fasset coat), and pretty much anything else you can think of that relates to knitting!

The book also has an extensive bibliography, as you would expect from an author who is Professor of Fashion and Textile Design at the London College of Fashion. If you're fascinated by knitting history, you will definitely will want to own this book. I also highly recommend Black's previous book on knitting and fashion, [[ASIN:0500284016 Knitwear in Fashion]].

The U.S. Government's "Philippine Reservation" was one of the most popular exhibits at the 1904 St. Louis Exposition. It displayed some 1300 native Filipinos, taken from a dozen different tribes, with the intention of building popular support for the continuing U.S. occupation of the Philippines after the Spanish-American War. The human exhibits of daily tribal living served to illustrate to the U.S. citizenry that Filipinos were innocents who were unready for self-government. When the Exposition closed, the Filipinos were returned to their native land.

A few years later, two impresarios (Truman Hunt and Richard Schneidewind) independently brought small groups of Filipinos from the Igorrote tribe to the U.S. to continue as human exhibits. In Hunt's case, some of the Igorrotes were returnees from the St. Louis Exposition. All of the Igorrotes came willingly, having been promised pay for their performances. Schneidewind treated his Igorrotes well, setting them up in an authentic village that was clean and pleasant. Schneidewind's exhibit also included informative lectures, so that it had a strong educational ethos.

In contrast, Hunt set his Igorrotes up in Luna Park (on Coney Island) and forced them to build fake structures (e.g., a "medicine man's hut" on stilts), to prepare daily "dog meat" feasts (even though the Igorrotes held such feasts only on special occasions such as weddings), and to stage a pro forma "native wedding" to draw in curious crowds. Hunt made up many stories about the Igorrotes' customs for publicity purposes (although it was true that the Igorrotes were head-hunters, and normally wore little clothing). After Hunt landed in considerable legal trouble (beginning with an accusation of a bigamous marriage), he went on the run with some of his Igorrotes and produced a traveling show. Eventually the Igorrotes sued Hunt for taking their money, and a lengthy trial ensued.

THE LOST TRIBE OF CONEY ISLAND tells the full story of Hunt's exhibition and involvement with the Igorottes--from Hunt's selection of Igorottes in the Philippines, to his initial wild success at Luna Park, to the impact of his legal problems on the exhibit, to his final total loss of the Igorrotes' trust, to the messy conclusion of the Igorrotes' lawsuit against Hunt.

The narrative itself is immensely bloated, filled with the author's speculations about the participants' thoughts and feelings at every stage of their disastrous experience. For example, the opening of Chapter 3, "The Journey from the Tropics", about the group's trip from the Philippines to the U.S. on the steamship RMS Empress of China: "The tribespeople bent their heads back as far as they could, but still they couldn't see the tops of her funnels. Tainan felt a fluttering sensation in his stomach. With wide eyes, he jumped up, as if hoping the few extra inches would help him take in the ship's full splendor. . . . Daipan wished her father were there to witness the incredible sight before them. The RMS Empress of China was a huge, hulking beauty . . . ."

To my mind, Hunt's exploitation story is a story that isn't worth retelling--certainly not in a 338-page narrative (exclusive of footnotes). I rate this book at 2 stars ("I don't like it" on the official Amazon scale).

After Zara's beloved stepfather dies in front of her and she falls into a months-long depression, she's sent to stay with her grandmother in rural Maine. Moving from sunny Charleston, Zara resents being sent to the icy backwater, until she meets the sexy bad boy Nick. The gorgeous jock also happens to drive some shiny wheels ("stupid shiny Volvo owner," anyone?), in this case a Mini Cooper.

Turns out that Nick is hiding a supernatural secret of his own. And Zara, Nick, and her new friends Issie and Devyn must band together to fight an ominous supernatural threat to their town, one that's been preying on teenage boys. Without giving too much away, there are some serious parallels to Twilight's ending.

So is Need simply a Twilight clone? Although there are several glaring similarities, Zara comes across as more likable than Bella; she's always signing petitions and writing letters on behalf of Amnesty International, she's strong-willed, and independent. To overcome her fears, she chants the names of various phobias, which also cleverly double as chapter headings. She's fiercely faithful to the hyper Issie and nerdy Devyn, who's been confined to a wheelchair after a hunting accident.

The various supernatural mythologies (yes, there are at least two major varieties of supernaturals here) are fleshed out just enough. There are no sparkly vampires. I read this through in a marathon session. I have to admit that I am not one for poetry, but the use of iambic pentameter was refreshing and engaging. Occasionally the verses get a little rough, but that is totally forgiven for the many brilliant turns of words that filled the pages. I thought that the form would be a hard read, perhaps thinking back to high school Shakespeare. But the verse just carried me along.

And perhaps that comparison to Shakespeare may not be to far off. Both he and Rakof have devastating wits and were able to finely craft verse. And maybe not so tightly constructed as Shakespeare, but Rakof spins moral tales with plenty of debauchery to keep the audience's attention. Well, perhaps Rakof does not so much spin moral tales, although he does have a great scene where a cuckold gives his oral come uppence to his former wife and best friend which is worthy of the bard. But mostly he gives frank coverage to life stories which in turn capture the spirit of their times, from the rough floor of a turn of the century slaughter house to the 70's and 80's San Francisco gay scene, to the emptiness of 80's materialism. He covers Aids, abortion, alzheimers and more, creating a time capsule of social ills of times not so long ago.

I'm amazed at how well the story spun from the verse. But at times the words and the rhymes took front stage and seemed to overpower the narrative. I think I have to read it again from beginning to end to get the whole story straight. But I delighted in the words as I worked through the rhymes and wit. And maybe I might also have to read it aloud to truly appreciate the poetics.

I truly enjoyed this book and appreciated the satisfying loop back at the end. It's David Sedaris meets Shakespeare.

If you already own the previous four volumes in the STITCHIONARY series, you may want to purchase VOGUE KNITTING STITCHIONARY VOLUME FIVE: LACE KNITTING to complete your set. However, VOLUME FIVE is nothing more than a rather unwieldy coffee-table-book collection of "more than 150" lace stitch patterns "taken from the pages of Vogue Knitting magazine."

The patterns are organized into general categories: easy/mesh, edgings, chevrons, allover, panels, combos, and motifs. However, the "lace knitting" title is misleading, because there is no instructional material on (1) combining lace stitch patterns into garments, shawls, or stoles; (2) selecting patterns that are appropriate for different kinds of projects; (3) attaching edgings; or (4) understanding or using the charts and written-out instructions.

There is one page of instructions for yarnovers (illustrated with line drawings). This page appears to be taken from the publisher's very good general reference book, VOGUE KNITTING. There is also a short glossary of knitting terms used in the book. For each stitch pattern, there is a beautiful, enlarged, color photo of a swatch knitted in the pattern. The selection of patterns is somewhat random, because VK magazine is the pattern source, but many basic lace patterns are included. There are also quite a few complicated "designer" patterns (evidently created for specific patterns published in the magazine) that may be of limited practical value to knitters seeking ideas for lace items of their own design.

Many other stitch dictionaries are currently available that provide more patterns, and therefore offer better value (e.g., the Mon Tricot stitch dictionaries, the Barbara Walker stitch treasuries, the Lesley Stanfield stitch treasuries). One very good lace stitch treasury is HARMONY GUIDES: LACE & EYELETS: 250 STITCHES TO KNIT. One general stitch treasury that includes a good sampling of lace patterns and edgings is the Reader's Digest ULTIMATE SOURCEBOOK OF KNITTING AND CROCHET STITCHES. Two excellent books that provide copious instruction on lace knitting and designing, as well as some lace stitch patterns, are Sharon Miller's HEIRLOOM KNITS and Jane Sowerby's VICTORIAN LACE TODAY.

I wanted a wired connection in a far room out of reach of my router. This works perfectly for that by allowing me to use any power outlet in my condo as a way to extend my wired network.

I tested my upload and download speeds with a network cable plugged from my laptop directly into my router and compared it to a wired connection with the Netgear Powerline Outlet. There was no discernible difference either positive or negative. I even ran video under both scenarios and I detected no difference in performance.

When my laptop was plugged directly into the router, my ping was 12 ms, download was 17.08 Mbps, upload was 5.17 Mbps.

When my laptop was plugged directly into the Powerline using my electrical house wiring, my ping was 12 ms, download was 16.63 Mbps, upload was 5.20 Mbps.

Although these speeds are not great, that is the performance I usually get with the router and service provider I have. Based on my results, this works as designed. Below is a list of what comes in the package and the PROS and CONS.

The package includes two Netgear Powerline 1200 Outlets each with an extra outlet and one Gigabit Ethernet port, two 6.5 foot Ethernet cables, and a quick start guide. For the initial installation of these units, both outlets have to be used because one Powerline must be plugged into an outlet near the router so that the Ethernet cable from the Powerline can plug into the router. The other Powerline can be plugged into an outlet anywhere else in the home. The other Ethernet cable is then plugged into this unit on one end and an Ethernet-enabled device such as a laptop, SmartTV, etc. on the other. If additional Powerlines are purchased then both units can be used for two additional wired connections.

PROS
- The LEDs on the Powerline enable the user to diagnose if there's power, Ethernet connectivity, or the ability to "Pick A Plug" (a.k.a. electrical outlet) with the strongest performance.

- There's an extra outlet on each Powerline. This unit covers the second outlet if it's plugged into the top outlet of a two-outlet receptacle. However, I do not see that as a problem for two reasons. First, there's an extra outlet on the unit. Therefore, I am still getting the ability to plug in two items like I would have had I not been using the Powerline. (In this case the Powerline is one item and a light is another.) If I want to turn my outlet into a three outlet receptacle, then all I have to do is plug it into the lower outlet. This would allow me, for instance, to plug in a lamp in the top receptacle, the Powerline in the bottom receptacle, and another item into the extra outlet on the Powerline.

- According to the manual, the network can be secured by pressing the security button for two seconds and then pressing the security button on one of the other adapters in the existing network. If additional adapters are added throughout the house when security is already enabled, then ALL the adapters should be factory reset. To re-enable security, all that has to be done is press the security button for two seconds on one adapter and then select any ONE other adapter (it's not necessary to do all adapters) and press that security button for two seconds. Both security buttons have to be pressed within two minutes time.

- There's a 1 year warranty plus 90 days basic customer support.

CONS

- I see none at this time.

I will write Netgear to find out what is meant by security with these security buttons. Up to 16 adapters can be installed in a home. I know if I were to install another set of these, I would actually be able to use both Powerlines for extra wired connections, thereby increasing my wired connections to three from one. It's only for the first installation that the extra Powerline is lost because that is used to connect to the router.

In summary, I feel this Netgear works as designed with no discernible difference in speed over a wired connection whether I was plugged directly into the router or the Powerline. Installation was simple and turning any one of my electrical outlets into a wired connection was practically instantaneous.

UPDATE April 27, 2015 - I contacted Netgear for an explanation of why there's a security feature on these adapters and exactly what that means to me. Below is Oleg Fishel's (of customer support) response which I slightly paraphrased.

The security refers to encryption between each of the Powerline adapters on my network. A random key is generated and shared among the adapters when the security setup button is used. All traffic is then encrypted using the highly secure 128 bit AES encryption protocol that prevents any unauthorized person from accessing the communication on my network. The reason enabling this security is recommended is to prevent someone from coming into my home with another Powerline adapter and connecting directly into my network to get information or for free Internet access. Although this scenario might be rare, this may be a concern with apartment buildings and offices where electrical circuits might be shared and in the case of homes that have outdoor electrical sockets. In summary, it is best to enable security. It is especially important when the Powerline is on a shared electrical circuit where someone can come along and plug one of these adapters in and piggyback off the network.

In regard to another question I had regarding the use and installation of 16 adapters all at once, he said "The HomePlug standard (HPAV2) used by the PL1200 supports up to 16 adapters on the network working together simultaneously. So if you purchased 7 kits (14 units) in addition to the original kit, you could have a 16 node network."

I have worked with a lot of Bluetooth headphones, all of which have their strengths and weaknesses. These headphones by Panasonic are on the less expensive end. The question is whether they are worth the asking price. In my opinion, they could be better and are still priced a little high.

Comfort-wise, I do not care for these but this is a personal preference. I like a headphone that fits tightly and presses down on my head, and these are very light-fitting. They adjust well enough and there should not be too much trouble getting these to fit almost any head, but keep in mind that they’re not the type that clamps down tightly.

The build quality is sub-par. These are very lightweight and feel quite flimsy and fragile.

I found an issue in the sound profile. The bass is good and not too heavy, and that’s good news for me. I dislike strong bass which is good for giving me headaches. The midrange is on target too and the music has some depth. Where the problem lies is in the highs. When listening to music I noticed some distortion in the highs. It’s not in-your-face and it doesn’t ruin the listening experience unless you are really fussy about your music. These will be fine for listening to speech, though.

I had no trouble connecting these to my laptop via Bluetooth. These come up quickly and connect without any issue and are ready to go in seconds. These aren’t the absolute fastest connecting phones I have worked with but they are among the faster ones I have used.

There’s no protective case for these phones in the box, not even a sleeve. These do fold up nice and compactly but I am not sure what is the point without a case in which to store them.

As I write this, the asking price for these phones is $60 which is a bit high in my eyes. If the sound profile was perfect, or if the build quality was higher, I would be more amenable to that price but the truth is that less expensive phones can be found that have a better sound profile and are constructed more solidly - and they have a case.

These are not bad phones, but I think they leave much to be desired. The build quality is mediocre, the sound profile is imperfect and the cost is a little high for what is in the box.

I have a TomTom Start and I have disliked the EasyPort mount from the day I got it. I had been telling my wife for months that I was going to get a “proper” mount for my TomTom and that day finally came when I accidentally broke the EasyPort mount. After a little research I decided on this particular mount, and so far I have been very pleased with it.

I wanted a more “normal” windshield mount - a suction cup with a lever instead of a twist ring, and that led me to this particular mount. The design is simple - press the suction cup against the windshield and flip the lever to make the cup stick to the window. In operation this is an easy-to-use mount and it seems to hold the navigator in place without too much trouble. As expected it does not hold well when it the windshield is cold, which is an issue with every suction-based mount I have ever used - including the EasyPort.

The ring in which the TomTom attaches to the mount holds the TomTom in place well enough but I have observed that it does not hold the navigator tightly. That is, the TomTom has a tendency to turn a little in the ring. So far this has not been an issue and the TomTom has not fallen out of the ring so this really does not bother me.

The mount is adjustable and provides for a couple of places where the position can be tweaked for maximum visibility. There should be no issue with getting the position of the GPS just right so it can be seen but not in the way.

So far I am pleased with this mount and am happy to recommend it. It’s a lot easier to use than the EasyPort mount that comes with the TomTom and it’s adjustable enough to make visibility a non-issue, even while in motion. If you have a TomTom and you don’t like the EasyPort mount, this mounting system is a big improvement.

LOCKDOWN: A NOVEL OF SUSPENSE is by Laurie R. King, and she's such a good writer, you can't ever go too far wrong with one of her novels. However, the problem with LOCKDOWN is that it isn't particularly suspenseful. It's the story of a disadvantaged middle school’s “Career Day” event that ends in a shootout and a school lockdown.

The story is told through shifting viewpoints: certain students (Chaco, Brendan, Mina, Nick, etc.), the principal (Linda), the principal’s adventurer husband (Gordon), a cop (Olivia), a janitor (Tio), a parent (Thomas), the school itself, and others. The school is struggling, and the mood of students and teachers alike is negatively affected by the recent disappearance of a female student (Bee).

The point of the story is to show the threads of different ethnicities, races, sexes, family backgrounds, and whatever that weave together to create the tapestry that is a school’s identity. The ending is exciting, and the shooter’s identity is a surprise. However, the plot is slow-moving, the characters aren't particularly memorable, and the novel is much more of a literary effort than a suspense novel.

This is the fifth edition of this book. The story starts in 1973 and ends with the current status on whale capture and where whales stand now. In 1973 the author started out as a soundman whose job it was to record whales for a documentary film about killer whales during a sailing expedition along Canada's Pacific Coast. That one job evolved into him becoming a whale researcher and learning that killer whales are really not killers of humans at all unless in captivity.

This text is a delicate balance between his and his colleagues scientific research and his whale watching excursions. I often felt that I was in the zodiac, canoe, or boat watching along with him.

There are many traits he learned from the whales and many facts he discovered as well. For instance, one whale pod trait that resonated with me was his observation that "the spirit of the killer whale pod is cooperation, rather than competition." Another trait we could learn from killer whales is "how to get along with each other. The importance of family." One fact is that whales can live as long as humans do. Another fact is that various whale pods have different dialects.

Over the last century, too many whales were captured and died as a result of the public's need to see them in aquariums. Although sentiment has changed about keeping whales captive, dangers still exist with captures by China, Japan, etc.

In summary, this book is a gem to me. I loved the author's preservation and naturalist spirit. Reading this reminded me of a whale farewell I experienced at the end of my 2005 trip to Antarctica. As our tour left the Penola Strait and went through the gorgeous and breathtaking Lemaire Channel, we passed Cape Bernard (two peaks that looked like bookends) as we sailed from a beatifully sunny afternoon into early evening. There were some interesting clouds that were just suspended in mid air between the water and the middle of the mountains. The sun lit up the snow and ice and also brought out the blue in the icebergs. Nature was all around us.  As if to say a final farewell, we saw two humpback whales (a mom and calf). The calf slapped the water with its extended flippers two times as if to wave goodbye. It was certainly a wonderful end to our last day in Antarctica. Even though these were not killer whales we saw, this author's story transported me back to the tranquilty of that trip and experiencing whales quietly in their own playground where I and the author believe they should remain.

I have built systems with SSDs for the last several years and I have come to see where they have their strengths and weaknesses. Not all SSDs are the same, and some have distinct advantages over others though the gap is definitely narrowing. This is my first experience with Samsung’s SSDs, and so far it has been a very positive experience. It has given me no issues at all and has performed well.

I installed the drive in a Dell Inspiron laptop which was running Windows 8. On the SSD, I installed Linux instead. Installation was very smooth, it was quick and I had a working system up and running in no time. I have now been running the system constantly for over a week (no powering off or hibernating) and the drive has shown no signs of trouble.

I loaded up a virtual machine and ran it on top of the main installation. The VM and the host install both have performed admirably and have not suffered from any noticeable I/O lag. Running smartctl against the drive after the past week of testing, it has reported no errors and a very healthy drive across the board.

Aside from the speed advantages of an SSD over a platter-based drive, this drive is absolutely silent (no surprise there) and so far I have not had any heat issues. It has given me no indications of any trouble in operation and my system is running as smoothly as should be expected.

The one issue I have with this drive, and it’s not a performance or quality issue, is the pricing. It is a little more expensive than most, and so far I have not seen any real justification for it over the likes of Crucial, Kingston or other branded drives. There may be justifiable reasons that reveal themselves later (I do not know how long this drive will continue to work but it should literally last for several years, even under very heavy use), but for now it seems a tad expensive compared to competitors.

Operationally I cannot find fault with this drive. It works well, it’s fast and quiet (as should be expected) and so far I’ve not had heat issues with it. Utilities I have run against it have shown that the drive is very healthy and has reported no problems out of the box. This is a good drive that will serve well. Time will tell, though, if it is worth the slightly higher asking price.

I first heard about "The Fearless Baker" through Sur La Table's "Fearless Baker" cooking classes, and was intrigued. I'd expected the recipes to stick to simple (read: bland) beginner's recipes like sugar cookies, but far from it: you'll find exotic touches like cardamom shortbread (cardamom is a popular seasoning in Scandinavian baking as well as a staple of Middle Eastern dishes), pine nut fig cookies, and orange date ricotta tartlets. Emily gives new bakers the tools to learn and master baking techniques (toasting nuts, cutting butter into dough for pie crusts, etc.) through a series of clever sidebars consisting of dialogues between Emily and her Fearful Bakers (FB).

When I first started out on my own as a baker in 2006, I had precious little baking experience other than licking the spoon or dropping cookie dough onto waiting cookie sheets as a kid. After several years living overseas or in dorms without a kitchen, I finally took the plunge and began baking, first with simple quick breads, then Bundt cakes, then on to yeast breads and laminated dough. There were several messy (and occasionally expensive) mishaps and missteps along the way, and I only wish that Emily Luchetti's "The Fearless Baker" had been around at the time!

There are nearly 200 recipes to choose from. I'm more of a breakfast baker myself (I love a good coffee cake, babka, or muffin), and curiously enough, the breakfast section is the very last one in the book. You'll find a tempting array of scones, muffins, breakfast breads, sticky buns, and more to get your day off to a sweet start. This might be the best place to start if you're brand new to baking; there are very few steps (or dirty dishes involved) to whip up quick bread or muffins.

The first recipe I tried from Fearless Baker was the mocha cream cheese brownies. I used Scharffen Berger Mocha bars from a previous Amazon Vine newsletter (the original recipe called for semisweet), and the mocha chocolate added an additional dimension of coffee flavor (there is instant coffee in the mocha cream cheese layer; I used espresso powder). The cream cheese layer was about twice the thickness of the brownie layer, and despite my best attempts to marble the cream cheese and brownie layers, it was so thick that it didn't cut through the brownie layer (they still tasted wonderful). I also had to add an additional ten minutes onto the baking time.

The next recipe up was the chocolate orange crinkle cookies. These unassuming little cookies pack a citrusy punch from grated orange peel and orange liqueur, bound together with ground toasted hazelnuts and a lot of melted bittersweet chocolate. The dough is really wet due to the liqueur and melted chocolate, so it needs to firm up in the fridge for an hour or so before baking. You roll the balls in granulated then powdered sugar before baking, so they have a pronounced crinkle effect. I may not have let the dough chill enough, though, since the powdered sugar became soft and gummy as the cookies came out of the oven, and I had to add extra powdered sugar after the cookies had cooled. But the end result was fabulous; the citrus added a burst of unexpected sunshine to the delicate, airy dough.

The book's typeface is clear and easy to read, with required equipment printed in orange and ingredients in black. The whimsical vintage art brings to mind 1950s cookbooks. Instead of food stylist-tweaked food photos, you'll see photos of actual Fearful-to-Fearless Bakers in their home kitchens as they work their way through the recipes. It's yet another way that The Fearless Baker serves to ease new bakers into the kitchen in a friendly, down-to-earth manner. However, if you're someone who likes to see color photos for each recipe, you might be a tad disappointed.

Even if you already know your Bundt pan from a batter bowl, there are plenty of creative, tasty recipes that pair uncommon partners to delicious effect (golden raisin-lime scones, lemon prosecco sabayon, pineapple-raspberry upside-down cake). There's something to appeal to everyone's sweet tooth, and even experienced bakers may learn a new trick or two; I know I did!

I selected this book more out of curiosity than anything else. I have heard about some of the exotic cocktails and mixed drinks described in this book but I knew little about them. This book is packed full of formulas for some pretty exotic drinks, some of which I have heard before and some I have not. But, this is not just a simple list of recipes. Rather, a majority of them comes with a short history - its origin, who thought it up, the occasion on which the drink was formulated, and many more little factoids. If you like to know a little bit of info regarding one of your faviroite drinks, this book just might have somehting to offer.

And, there's pictures...lots and lots of pictures. Many are historical monochrome shots, while others are modern, full-color prints.

The recipes are divided up in an interesting fashion. There are two sections for prohibition-era drinks, one for non-alcoholic drinks and one for drinks that were illegal at the time. The largest chapter includes a number of drinks of historical interest that were highly sought after, or were modernized, or were unique in some way. Some of the recipes are for classic drinks like a Zombie (of which most people have heard at some point in their lives) as well as many that are from ages ago and have been all but forgotten.

This is a great book for the cocktail enthusiast as well as for the historian that wants to know a little bit more than just how to make these drinks. It is full of great stories, wonderful pictures, memories from ages past, and of course memorable cocktails.

I have been making homemade breads for my family for 25 years and I have learned a lot over the years as to what makes bread good versus what makes it great. Sometimes, simple and straightforward is better than complex, and this book is a case in point. The recipes in this book are mostly quick-rise formulas (excepting the chapter on sourdough), and the results are good enough for daily baking.

This book is marketed as aimed toward beginners and that's a fair assessment. Many people are intimidated by the bread making process and think it's a hard and complex process. To be honest, it's actually simple (and in my experience it's simpler and easier than making a layer cake). The majority of the recipes in this book are formulated to bake in the same day, very often within 3-4 hours of starting the process.

The initial chapter deals with bread basics - flour types and kneading, to be specific. After this, the rest of the book is dedicated to different bread types by chapter: Classic Breads, No-Knead Breads, Sourdough Breads, Buns & Rolls, Quick Breads, Flatbreads & Crackers, Muffins & Scones, Biscuits & Cornbread, Boiled Breads (Bagels, Pretzels, Dumplings), Doughnuts & Fried Breads, and finally Gluten Free Breads.

Bread bakers who have been at it for a while expect formulas to have the ingredients measured by mass (weight) instead of by just volume. This book sticks to the volume measures which is not a problem for the beginner. It is easy enough to convert to mass measures if you're feeling so motivated. However, chances are that if you need the ingredients measured by mass then you're likely not a beginner and you're not in the intended audience.

The formulas are straightforward and are easy to read and follow. The results are good and will encourage anyone just starting out. I wish I had had a resource like this when I started.

This is a very good collection of bread formulas, intended for beginning bakers who want to make homemade breads and need a starting point. The formulas are easy to understand and follow and the results are satisfactory. Though I am an experienced baker I still find use in this book when I need to make bread on a shorter time scale.

I really liked designer Lucinda Guy's earlier book of Scandinavian knitting patterns, [[ASIN:1596681713 NORTHERN KNITS]]. This sequel, NORTHERN KNITS GIFTS, isn't nearly as interesting. Because the book is published by Interweave Press, it has beautiful photographs, lovely charts, and clear pattern instructions. But there are only a few designs that I would actually want to knit--and nearly all of the complex designs require much more knitting time and effort than I would be willing to invest in "gift" knitting. Many are charted Fair Isle designs, and most are knit at 5-7 stitches per inch, so they're NOT quick knits.

The designs I liked best are the Tovio Mittens and Hat (Fair Isle knitting, shown on the book's cover), the red-and-white Freja Twined Scarf (two-ended knitting), the delicate white Dimitie Scarf (Shetland lace, shown in "Look Inside"), the Birta Twined Hat with simple flower-design border (Sweden-inspired), the stylized hen-shaped Oluffa Doorstop (Faroe Islands, shown in "Look Inside"), the colorful lice-patterned Onni Child's Sweater and Hat (Finland, shown in the "Look Inside" photo montage), and the felted brown Noomi Slippers with classic Norwegian star on the instep (Norway).

Not so successful (to my eye) are the Liisi Open Cardigan (Estonian knitting, with nupps and flowers on the shoulders and lace body, shown in "Look Inside"), the shaped, drab ecru/white Marna Woman's Cape (Faroe Islands), the plain gray man's Fridmar Hat (Iceland, shown in "Look Inside"), the oddly colored Mootie Fair Isle Socks (Shetland, shown in "Look Inside"), the bird-motif Ida Icelandic Lace and Patterned Mitts (lace and Fair Isle knitting), the French-knot-embroidered Asa Mittens (Sweden, shown in "Look Inside"), the white and gray Nanna Twined Mitts (Norway), the brown-and-white Oda Baby Blanket with rows of stylized Fair Isle hearts and stars (Norway, knit at 4 stitches to the inch but still a large project, shown in the "Look Inside" photo montage), the little girl's stuffed Annelli Doll (Estonia, shown in "Look Inside"), the damask-patterned Adda Socks (Denmark, shown in the "Look Inside" photo montage), and the strangely-shaped Rya Flower Cushion (Denmark, shown in "Look Inside").

If you want a book of patterns for 2012 holiday gifts, you should probably select something else (for example, Ann Budd's excellent [[ASIN:1596680911 Interweave Presents Knitted Gifts: Irresistible Projects to Make and Give]], or Debbie Bliss's [[ASIN:1570764611 The Knitter's Year: 52 Make-in-a-Week Projects-Quick Gifts and Seasonal Knits]]). Because none of the designs in NORTHERN KNITS GIFTS particularly inspire me to grab my knitting needles, I rate this book at 3 stars ("It's OK" on the official Amazon scale).

"The Musician's Daughter" is a magical blend of the grandeur of 18th-century Vienna and the Esterhazy court, Haydn's lush string quartets, and the plight of the Romany (Gypsies). Fifteen-year-old Theresa Maria adores her father, a court violinist, and treasures his music lessons teaching her to play the viola. But her world is turned upside-down one Christmas Eve as her father is murdered, his beloved violin is missing, and he's wearing a strange golden medallion.

Theresa Maria, called Rezia by her friend Zoltan, is a strong female protagonist and struggles to hold her family together; her very pregnant mother is confined to bed, household finances are dangerously low, and her younger brother Toby is utterly bereft, crying himself to sleep every night. She draws upon hidden reserves of courage as she struggles to piece together the truth behind her father's murder and discovers that he was leading a secret life under their noses. This necessitates her placing herself in great physical danger in order to uncover political schemes involving a treacherous relative.

Meanwhile, her love for the violin and music is nurtured by her godfather Franz Joseph Haydn, the court composer who is slowly losing his vision to cataracts. After her father's death, Haydn hires Rezia to copy his music as he composes it, and even allows her to play at a ball. At fifteen, she also experiences her first crush on Zoltan.

The gradually complicated web of lies, buried truths, and blackmail was well-paced, but I found the political elements overpowering to the musical ones; for a novel called The Musician's daughter, I was hoping for more passages devoted to the power of music in Theresa Maria's life, although there are several passages involving Gypsy musicians that are very evocative. Several of the plot elements, particularly the climax, seemed to come together a little too neatly after all of the danger and heartbreak involved, and the rushed final paragraph is either a mini time capsule of the narrator's future, or a lead-in to a potential sequel. Either way, the final paragraph felt far too rushed and might have been better dealt with as an epilogue.

The novel is aimed at readers age 12 and up, and the author Susanne Dunlap holds a PhD in music history, which lends this delightful period tale an air of authenticity. 18th-century Vienna is brought to vivid life through her shimmering descriptions of high fashion and the opulent palaces contrasting sharply with the poverty of the Romany camp. There is a strong message of social justice, racial tolerance and female empowerment unusual for the novel's time period. A reading guide or a "who's who" of 18th-century Vienna (or a brief history as to which characters were fictitious and which were based on actual historical figures) would have been helpful. Overall, this is an engaging read, particularly for young readers who love period dramas, music, or political intrigue.

I bought this book with the impression that it would be a good book for system administration of a generalized UNIX system. I knew that it would not cover every scenario for every flavor of UNIX, but it should at least be a great foundation.
The title is quite misleading. "Bible" implies that this is an authoritative and complete tome on UNIX issues. It is definitely neither of these. The cover even says it is 100% accurate and "what you need". Perhaps if one was looking for general guidelines, this would be true, but then the book's title would still be misleading.
This book is by no means an exhaustive work on even the generalized issues. One case in point is the section on system security. It goes into great depth on describing one scenario where a hacker broke into a system and mucked around. It gives log listings, printouts, and descriptions of what was going on - in this specific scenario. This is all well and good, but it only goes far enough to show one single possibility.
The authors are adept at making sweeping generalizations without too much elaboration. They pull in one or two very specific examples on certain topics, and then move on. This is just enough to make the reader hungry for more, but never delivering.
The CDs that come with this book have an old, light copy of Slackware. Sure, it's a system that will work, but an update would be of much more use.
What the book tends to avoid, and this is in my opinion the biggest problem I've encountered, is elaboration as to the differences between the different flavors of UNIX -- Solaris, AIX, HP-UX, Linux, BDS, IRIX, etc. It's all generalizations. Perhaps this makes the book more helpful to some people, by giving the bare necessities. But, that does not make it "what you need" as the cover says.
Granted, this book is not a complete waste. There are some interesting sections that give nice discussion, such as organization of file systems and so forth. But these pockets of usefulness do not make up for the rest of the problems.
There are better UNIX tomes out there, even available for download. Check those out before you seriously consider buying this book.

I am a fan of good Bibles and I am always looking for better ways to reach people that need help. I had hoped this Bible might be a good tool for ministering to those who are struggling with difficult issues. While the highlighting of specific Scripture verses is a good idea toward that goal, this Bible falls short.

There is no introduction that explains why this particular Bible is available save for what's on the dust jacket. If the dust jacket is gone, one might not realize why there are some verses highlighted and what might set this Bible apart. Most people do not read the introduction included in Bibles, but one here is really needed.

There is a small index near the end of the pages that lists certain aspects of God's character and where to find verses that describe Him. This is helpful but something more complete and more accessible would be an improvement.

My biggest complaint with this Bible is that is it billed as a Bible designed to help hurting people find hope, yet the extent of that help is in highlighting verses here and there. There really needs to be more than that - short studies on God's character, His love, His mercy, etc. would add so much more to that end goal.

All is not lost on this Bible, though. The NIV is a popular translation and is quite readable, and Zondervan has chosen a very easy-to-read typeface that makes this particular Bible a little easier on the eyes. This is not to say it's a large print, of course, but it is a little larger than average and makes for a nice "reading Bible".

The Find:Hope Bible is a good idea with the feel of being poorly thought out. There are better resources that accomplish the same intended goal.

One thing that is mentioned in this book’s description but is not emphasized on the cover is the heavy influence of international flavors, in particular Latin American and Asian styles. This is not simply a collection of recipes with the occasional international dish; quite the opposite, dishes that would be classified as American cuisine seem to be in the minority. This is does not serve this book very well – if you’re looking for a good collection of international cuisines it is easy to blow past this book in the search. On the other hand, if you happen to be looking for a book that is geared more towards American cuisine this book could come as a shock. This isn’t a fault of the collection, but rather it is a marketing issue.

There is something else I noticed that makes this book different from almost every other cookbook I have used. This one lists the directions for preparation, and then it lists the ingredient list at the end. This is the reverse from most books which list the ingredients up front and then spell out the directions. While it is not a problem, per se, it is a bit unsettling when not used to this presentation.

Formatting and marketing aside, this is a very interesting collection. It covers a lot of ground, including breakfast (it has a recipe for egg in a basket, of all things), vegetarian dishes, main courses with various meats and even desserts. My family has already informed me that the Chocolate Chip Pan Cookie Sundae needs to be in the regular rotation in the house.

This is a book that is geared towards the cook who likes to leave their comfort zone and try new flavors. It is likely that there are more cuisine types in this book than most people have tried to prepare already. If you really like international flavors and you want to enjoy them by using your air fryer, this is a good collection that is full of interesting ideas.

I love my air fryer and I use it almost weekly, though admittedly the majority of its use involves reheating and crisping foods that are already made and finished. I have a couple of air fryer books and the recipes therein typically make good alternatives to more traditional fried foods. However, reduced fat does not always mean low fat and low calorie. I looked to this book with the thought of getting a better selection of lower fat/calorie foods, and to some extent that is what I got. But, to say that this is a diet and weight loss book is not accurate.

The advantages of using an air fryer are well advertised – use less oil, cook faster, crispy results, and so on. Using an air fryer *can* make preparing foods a lot better for you. A case in point is breaded onion rings – almost no oil is needed to get crunchy and juicy onions rings which is a big drop in calories and fat. Sausage patties, though, are barely better off (if at all) when done in an air fryer than when using a non-stick or cast-iron skillet.

This book is full of great recipes that work, and it definitely has some fantastic replacements for their more fat-laden counterparts done in more traditional ways. However, many recipes aren’t that much better. For example, the recipe for Baked Potato Breakfast Boats is basically a loaded baked potato skin with traditional breakfast foods like eggs, bacon and cheese. According to the recipe these have over 330 calories per serving, never mind the fact that practically every healthy diet plan out there anymore lists potatoes in particular as forbidden food (high starch and full of carbs as a result). Another questionable inclusion is Eggroll Pizza Sticks. This is another higher-calorie recipe with questionable ingredients, just air fried instead of deep fat fried.

There are a lot of good recipes in this book that actually are healthy, such as Sweet and Spicy Broccoli and other vegetable-based dishes where the air fryer has the opportunity to reveal it’s prowess in cooking healthy foods for you.

A reduced-fat diet is not a weight loss diet when sugars and carbs and starches are used in place of the fat you’d otherwise use. The problem with this book is a marketing issue – it is not a weight loss book at all. I would rate it higher if instead it billed itself as containing lower-fat alternatives to more traditional foods the recipes attempt to replace.

My kids are older now and are past the age where a resource like this would be useful to them but I was interested in this book anyway and decided to take a look. It’s very much geared toward younger children and it is well suited for leading its target audience in an exploration of the Bible. It’s not a comprehensive plan to read everything the Bible says (most adults have trouble getting through in a year so such would be a wasted effort on most children), but it does hit the highlights and it does so in bite-sized chunks that are easy to handle.

This is set up as a 1-year study plan, with something to do every day. Each week covers a specific topic, usually defined by a chapter in a given book, and it is broken up into daily readings. These are short chunks to read, 3-8 verses in length in the majority of cases, which makes it ideal for those with a short attention span (where was this when I was growing up?). The plan includes a place to record prayer points, it asks the reader to choose the highlight verse that defines the passage for the week, and it includes space for notes.

There’s not a tremendous amount of theology presented which in my opinion is good. The author stays close to factual presentation without digging too deep into topics that divide the church (things like pre- and post-tribulation trials and the like). For this age group, focusing on the clear black and white is best and the author does a good job.

This is a resource that would have been handy when my children were young. They would have enjoyed this plan, and we would have enjoyed working through it with them and the discussions it would have sparked. If your children are young (elementary and middle-school aged), this is a good resource for them that will give them a decent tour of the Bible in easy-to-handle bites.

I wish I could say I understood and enjoyed this book but I did not. Based on the title and the one 5-star review that existed, I decided to read this. I thought this would be a non-fiction work written by a father who coddled his son so much that the son became unable to cope with the world or was too shy to be effective in society.

This book is not that at all. Instead, it is a jumble of non-fiction stories the author experienced (or was writing about) with people who appear to have a death wish. The only chapter I found interesting and understandable was the one about Tim the snake man who likes to get bitten by poisonous snakes and live to tell about it. All the other chapters were a jumble of events with some appearing to have been written by someone who was drunk. For instance, the author disjointedly writes about his attendance at the Gathering which is apparently a music festival of Juggalos where people behaved very badly. It reminded me of the stories of Woodstock.

From what I can gather, the author's father is apparently a crass alcoholic and brash with his son (the author) who appears to be following in his father's footsteps. Various snippets or what seem like flashbacks of his experiences with his family and in life are peppered throughout the text as he goes almost chronologically from one subject to the next about men who appear to have a death wish. These men such as Brophy the ice hockey player, Ryan his friend who is a military fighter, the snake man, etc., temp fate with their lives.

On the positive side, I learned some new words I never heard before like Juggalos. I had to look that up. As per Wikipedia Juggalos is a name given to the fans of a group called Insane Clown Posse or similar Psychopathic Records hip hop groups.

Nevertheless, the text is disjointed and full of babble, vulgar with expletives throughout, and it sometimes felt like I was reading the work of someone who was stoned while writing it. Except for the one chapter on Tim, the snake man, I kept asking myself these three questions:

1. What is he talking about?
2. What is the message here?
3. What in the world am I reading?

Toward the final chapters (even in the Amish chapter which was better written than most) I was just reading words as one sentence faded nonsensically into the next. I painstakingly finished reading this only because I had to do a review. This non-fiction work left me scratching my head confused. I doubt "Lawrence Welk" would understand this and neither do I. I kept wondering "what's the point of this book," especially one with such an intriguing title.

When I ordered MERCURY: A NOVEL, I was under two misconceptions. First, that it was a mystery; and second, that it was a novel about a horse. It is neither. What it is, is a very good literary novel about a wife's obsession with a horse that doesn't belong to her (a horse that she believes can fulfill her lifelong dream of winning championships in jumping competitions). Her obsession, unobserved at first by her husband, subtly breaks up their marriage, destroys their friendships with other couples, and physically damages some people within their circle of friends.

Much of the story is told through the husband's eyes, as he looks back at events in a sort of "had I but known" fashion. This is an extremely well-written, easy-to-read novel that insightfully probes the subtle layers of human relationships, and the shifting nature of friendships. It's not my kind of novel, but I recognize its excellence as a work of literary fiction.

I have a copy of Eat to Beat Disease and until I saw this companion cookbook I didn't even know that such existed. I like the original book so I thought this cookbook would be a natural extension and a useful resource. I was right, and it's a good cookbook if you're looking for a way to eat healthier without settling into a rigid diet plan (like a dedicated low-carb diet).

The book starts with some introductory material that explain how the body regenerates and heals itself and how certain foods play into that equation. Especially interesting are the charts that explain what specific roles different foods play in body health and maintenance. Some of the foods and ingredients listed are well-known and obvious while others caught me by surprise.

The recipes provided in this book are broken down into several chapters: "Breakfast", "Salads and Soups", "Seafood", "Chicken", "Vegetarian Mains ands Sides", and finally "Desserts and Baking". For the most part the recipes use easy-to-find ingredients and typically are easy to prepare. I am a huge fan of Israeli cuisine and have read numerous cookbooks in the last several years focusing on this diverse cuisine, so I was excited to be offered "Modern Israeli Cooking" by Danielle Oron, the creative force behind Moo Milk Bar and the blog "I Will Not East Oysters." Danielle's family moved from Tel Aviv to New Jersey when she was a toddler, and her family was known as "those crazy Israelis." In her words, these recipes combine her culinary background in French technique with classic Israeli flavors to create new and modern dishes.

Modern Israel is a melting pot; you'll find cuisine from Morocco, Eastern Europe, Yemen, Egypt, Iraq and Turkey. Dishes are served family-style with a lot of side plates consisting of salads and dips; this is my personal culinary heaven. The recipes are divided into weekdays (chicken shawarma rice bowl, kofta kebab freekeh salad, za'atar chicken, pashtida), Fridays (challah, ricotta and za'atar ravioli, lemon chicken with olives, harissa lamb meatballs), beach (peel and eat harissa shrimp - if you haven't guessed already, this is NOT a kosher cookbook), salmon ceviche, chermoula fish tacos, seared sesame tuna), slow cooking (braised pomegranate short ribs, roasted garli and apricot chicken, hawaij oxtail ragu, pastrami), brunch (shakshuka, bourekas, babka French toast, za'atar sesame mini bagels), midnight (za'atar fried eggs, feta grilld cheese, cinnamon challah), salads and sides (tabbouleh, carrots several ways, pickled beets), sweets (saled tahini chocolate chip cookies, tahini-swirled brownies, halva morning buns, honey and apple cake), and stapes (tahini, ancho chili harissa, labne, schug, preserved lemons, dukkah). Ingredients are given in US (volume) and metric.

Danielle's commentary is on the hip side; recipe subtitles frequently involve food puns and cultural insights, like the mild red pepper harissa: "If you like the flavor, but you have a death wish / enjoy S&M, add more of the Thai chilis and a bit more hot paprika.") or tahini: "We put this sh*t on everything."

True to the book's goal, you will find classic flavors with modern twists; the beloved sabich has been turned into a breakfast bowl with shredded potato hash, falafel gets some help from spinach and is served with green tahini and sauerkraut, you'll find Sephardic pastries like bourekas supersized and dressed up with mushrooms and caramelized onions, Milky has been reinvented as a decadent, boozy pot de creme. I loved the peppered watermelon and feta, as watermelon + mint + Bulgarian feta is a staple breakfast in my house; here, Korean red pepper flakes and black pepper kick this up a notch.

Overall this is a fun, young take on modern Israeli cooking - you'll find many familiar flavor profiles (za'atar, tahini, sumac, schug, dukkah) and plenty of colorful veggie salads and sides to dress up your table. From a comfort food perspective, it contains the most amazing grilled cheese recipe (feta grilled with Kalamata olives - heaven!), eggs and sumac soldiers, and many warming dishes that would be great for cooler nights (braised pomegranate short ribs, sweet shredded honey lamb, beer-braised holiday brisket, homemade pastrami).
*For those who keep kosher, please note that this is NOT a kosher cookbook - it contains shellfish recipes as well as meat mixed with dairy. However, most of the recipes are (or can be made) kosher with a little tweaking.

[[VIDEOID:a61b4b7382e94a85b3a11da33ebf4c55]] INCREASE DECREASE is the comprehensive knitting reference on this subject that I've been waiting for! Judith Durant gets everything right: spiral binding (so that the instructions stay open and lay flat); large, clear step-by-step photos; step-by-step written instructions printed in easy-to-read type; photographs of swatches that show exactly what to expect from a particular increase or decrease; and compact size (small enough to carry in a knitting bag).

The short "Special Circumstances" section, on shaping cable, lace, and color patterns to best effect, is by itself worth the price of the book. The only increase/decrease that I could think of that is NOT shown, is the "nupp" used in Estonian lace knitting (lily of the valley pattern), which requires two rows. (Every time I pick up my lily-of-the-valley shawl project, I wonder whether any motif is pretty enough to be worth all the grief of picking up multiple yarnover loops in a single decrease.)

The photographs illustrate the techniques with the yarn held to the left in "continental" (pick) knitting style. This should not detract from the book's value for knitters who hold the yarn to the right in "English" (throw) knitting style. In either style, the yarn must be positioned on the needles in exactly the same way to get specific desired effects.

Another book that deals with increases and decreases as they are used in shaping garments (and includes how-to instructions with small photos) is [[ASIN:161769021X The Shape of Knitting: A Master Class in Increases, Decreases, and Other Forms of Shaping]]. However, THE SHAPE OF KNITTING is project-oriented. INCREASE DECREASE is the book that belongs on the knitter's reference shelf or in his/her knitting bag.

Another terrific, comprehensive spiral-bound reference book, very similar in look and feel to INCREASE DECREASE, is [[ASIN:1603427244 Cast On, Bind Off: 54 Step-by-Step Methods]], which deals with techniques for casting on and binding off.

Every year we make a car trip to the Midwest and there is a store along the way where we stop to buy some fudge. This is a traditional stop for us but the fudge is not the best and it's expensive. I decided to investigate making our own fudge for the trip and the search for books on the topic led me to this book. While by no means perfect it is an excellent introduction to making fudge and it enables the beginner to hit the ground running.

The book starts off with a short story about how the idea for it was conceived after which it launches into an interesting account of the history behind fudge. This kind of writing does not really make a cookbook more useful but it adds nonetheless. I enjoyed the historical time line of fudge-making and likely will read that section again.

The author's basic method for making a batch of fudge revolves around a ten-step process. These ten steps are the basis for most of the fudge recipes in the book and though some recipes skip one or more of the steps, most follow the pattern fairly closely. Another reviewer wrote that some of these steps are not applicable or are unnecessary for the making of fudge but I haven't found any reason to purposely omit anything - so far, the fudges that I have made from the recipes in this book, following the ten steps, have turned out well.

The most valuable tidbit of information regarding fudge in this book involves using a slow cool-down method. The temptation is to find a rapid-cool method to get the fudge to candy faster, but doing so leads to grainy, crystallized sugar in the fudge. The taste is fine, of course, but the texture is not. By letting the fudge cool more slowly the fudge will be less grainy and more smooth - highly desirable.

There is a great collection of recipes in this book. In addition to basic fudge recipes, there are recipes for more fancy fudges, caramels, fondants, nougats, divinities and even marshmallows. So far I have stuck to the basic fudge recipes but all have turned out nicely. By far the easiest recipe I have tried is the basic bread and butter fudge recipe, which is always a hit with my family when I make a batch.

My one real complaint with this book is not with the content or the recipes, but rather with the author's writing style. When she writes, her words come across with what seems like forced sensationalism instead of natural enthusiasm and I find it mildly irritating and distracting. This is a matter of personal preference.

Overall, this is a fine book on the subject of making fudge and other candies. So far the recipes I have tried have turned out well. The recipes - and the basic steps presented for making fudge in general - are easy to follow and for me have yielded excellent results.

One Extra Corpse is the second entry in Hambly's Silver Screen mystery series. Emma's husband died in WWI and, after losing her parents and brother as well, she eventually ends up in Los Angeles with her sister in law Kitty, a gorgeous and untalented star of silent film. This is a light and a well-researched, well-written and well-plotted mystery. Without risking spoilers, Hambly examines the early days of the studio system where stars were made because of how they looked.  We learn about the common practice of ensuring notoriously gay actors appear in public with "romantic" people of the opposite sex.  Extras were were so expendable that they risked life and limb to appear in crowd scened involving guns or explosives.  The casting couch entry to the profession was definitely in place. Hollywood was a small, small town when it came to knowing everyone's business. Hambly weaves in famous actors and directors whose backstories are known to  us. Emma has a cameraman boyfriend, Zal.  It's been four years since she left England and this budding relationship has potential,  but she sometimes longs to be back in England continuing her studies at Oxford. In addition to serving as Kitty's assistant, Emma has work as a screenwriter. This could be problematic as her knowledge of ancient history is frequently set aside when, for example she's instructed to make a character Christian in a period falling eighty years before the birth of Jesus. I enjoyed this enough to buy the first book in the series so I can fill in the back story. Fun characters, fun geographical background, fun locale, interesting resolution to the murder. Definitely recommend.
