If you haven't read any others in the series here is the basic info to save you some time looking:

2005 Simply Sarah (Book 1): ANYONE CAN EAT SQUID!: Sarah Simpson is tired of being ordinary. The most unusual thing she has ever done is bite the dentist's fingers. So what can she do to be special? Trade names with her best friend? Eat snails and squid? When Sarah learns that her favorite Chinese restaurant might go out of business, she comes up with a plan. One that makes people want to say, "Here comes Sarah Simpson!" and saves Wongs' Restaurant, too. In quintessential Phyllis Reynolds Naylor style, this delightful story speaks straight to the heart of kids as they struggle to define themselves. From SCHOOL LIBRARY JOURNAL: Grade 2-4-Sarah Simpson's family thinks that she is extraordinary, but she feels ordinary and is anxious to find a special quality that sets her apart. This concept, by itself, is interesting and well fleshed out. At school, she tries to trick the substitute teacher by switching names with her best friend, but that doesn't solve her "problem." She tries other ideas to no avail. Her solution arrives with an opportunity to help the parents of a classmate whose restaurant isn't doing well. Much too quickly, Sarah comes up with a plan-a T-shirt advertising "Wongs' Wings," a house specialty. Appealing full-page and spot illustrations appear throughout. Readers will like the protagonist, her family, and her friends. However, the author spends so much time setting up the Simpsons that there is almost no time for the story of the Chinese restaurant and for Sarah's individuality to develop.

2006 Simply Sarah (Book 2): CUCKOO FEATHERS Sarah Simpson is her dad's "Idea Girl," but right now she doesn't have any good ideas. Nothing that will make people think she is someone special. Then she remembers something unusual going on outside her kitchen window. Two pigeons keep appearing on the ledge and pecking at the window. Sarah begins to think of them as her pigeons and names them Coo and Cuckoo. She is horrified, however, when they start to build their nest outside the neighbors' apartment next door. How could they be so disloyal? Finally Sarah gets a big idea--one that helps her get over this catastrophe! From SCHOOL LIBRARY JOURNAL; Grade 2-4-Sarah Simpson, who made her debut in Anyone Can Eat Squid! (Marshall Cavendish, 2005), is out of great ideas, despite her nickname idea girl. After observing two pigeons outside her apartment window, she decides that she is going to keep them as pets. However, when they begin spending more time on a balcony next door and start to nest, Sarah becomes jealous of the girl and boy who live there. Soon after, she and her brother befriend the children, and her concern shifts to other pigeons that are intent on taking over the nest of the first two birds. After an egg is lost, the girl comes up with a solution that saves another egg and provides a home for the aggressive creatures. Sarah is a likable character who lives in a diverse neighborhood. Both setting and plot ring true, but the chapter Making Faces, in which Sarah and her friends discover that skin colors are neither pure white nor pure black is a bit didactic. Full- and half-page pencil illustrations break up the text for children new to chapter books From BOOKLIST Gr. 3-5. Fascinated by the two pigeons roosting outside her family's apartment window, Sarah describes them to her classmates as her "pet pigeons." Coo and Cuckoo, however, abandon that perch for a flowerpot belonging to Sarah's new neighbors. Then a third pigeon in search of a perch threatens Coo, Cuckoo, and their babies. Always an "idea girl," Sarah devises a way to attract pigeons to her family's window ledge and resolve the pigeon wars. Illustrated with ink-and-wash art, this mildly amusing sequel to Anyone Can Eat Squid (2005) will connect with children who enjoy Johanna Hurwitz's urban stories for transitional readers.

2008 Simply Sarah (Book 4): EATING ENCHILADAS Sarah Simpson likes to think of ideas that are anything but ordinary. When her third-grade teacher asks each student to pick a country and give an oral report, Sarah wants her choice to be really special. Maybe she should talk about England, since England has a queen and a castle. But as she learns more, she discovers that England isn't quite as interesting as she thought. For one thing, the English speak the same language as Americans. Sarah finally thinks of a new idea when she sleeps over at her friend Mercedes' apartment and learns wonderful things about Mexico. From SCHOOL LIBRARY JOURNAL Grade 2-4--When Sarah has to give a school report on a country, she's stumped as to which one to choose. She's disappointed that she isn't from or hasn't visited anywhere else. What can she do to make her report special? She finally chooses England so at least she can dress up like a queen and wear a sparkly crown. Then Sarah is invited to a sleepover at her friend's apartment. Mercedes has recently come from Mexico, and everything in her home reflects her native land. All of a sudden, wearing a sparkly crown doesn't seem so important. Sarah chooses Mexico for her country and knows exactly what to do to make her report extra special. This early chapter book is the fourth about Sarah but can easily stand alone. The illustrations are mostly of the characters, but the backgrounds are wonderful for comparing and contrasting the girls' apartments. The story is a great example of friendship and learning new things.

DOWN THE RIVER UNTO THE SEA is another excellent private investigator novel from Walter Mosley. The plot is extremely complicated, and there are a gazillion characters to keep straight. However, main character Joe Oliver’s love for his daughter (Aja-Denise) sustains the story as surely as that love sustains Joe and keeps him alive.

In the novel, PI Joe is a disgraced former cop who’s eking out a living as a private investigator. Straight-arrow Joe was getting too close to some dirty cops’ criminal activities, so he was framed, imprisoned in solitary for 83 days, released, and booted off the force. The prison sojourn broke him; but when he receives a confessional letter from the woman who framed him, he decides to finally investigate his own case.

He does this under cover of investigating a case for a real client. The objective there is to exonerate a black man (A Free Man) who killed two cops and is awaiting execution. It’s hard to say which of the two investigations is more likely to get Joe killed. But Joe carries on with both after enlisting the aid of a truly evil psychopath (Melquarth) who thinks he owes Joe a big favor. The police corruption that Joe uncovers is truly shocking, and even puts daughter Aja in danger. Can Joe work out a solution when all seems lost?

The book is generally well-written, but a tad sloppy in places. Sometimes you need more of a reminder than the text supplies about who a previously-introduced character is. However, Joe, Aja, and Melquarth are memorable characters; the plot is a page-turner if you enjoy police procedurals; and the ending is both believable and satisfying.

My favorite cast-iron skillet is the most heavily used piece of cookware I own and I use it for a variety of things - Dutch baby, making sauces, frying eggs and sausage, and more. It's my workhorse pan. I do keep my eyes open for good cookbooks on cooking with cast iron and this one is a good one that covers a lot of ground.

The first chapter is a good introduction for the uninitiated for buying, cooking with and caring for a cast iron skillet. Every book I have on cast iron has some advice on how to care for your cast iron, and this one is no exception. However, this one is a little more straightforward and clear and gives a bit more information than I have seen collected in one place anywhere else. If you're looking for a good starting point for working with cast iron, this book provides a good one.

The next nine chapters cover all kinds of things you can make in your skillet. There are breads and biscuits, desserts, a variety of meats, vegetable dishes and a whole lot more. I am especially pleased that pizza is covered in this book - pizza is the one thing I tried and failed to make in my pan, and this book has some tested recipe that should help me work that out when I try that again (I have not yet made another attempt).

Each recipe is labeled with one or more tags to give a very quick and helpful hint on recipe characteristics, such as "vegetarian", "gluten free", and "weekday" (translation - fast/easy). The formatting is easy on the eyes, though I would make one minor adjustment here. Most recipes have a descriptive paragraph at the top that explains some detail about the recipe, and it is formatted in a soft blue font. While pleasant, I would have opted for a darker or bolder shade of blue to make it contrast better. This is certainly not a big deal and it doesn't impact my opinion of the book, bit it's a personal preference.

The recipes use easy-to-find ingredients and are written clearly so they're easy to follow. There's not much room for improvement here.

I haven't had this book very long but I am pleased with it and I look forward to working more with it. It is well written, the recipes are clear and easy and the results (so far) are good. This is a good place to jump in if you're new to working with cast iron, and it's a good expansion point if you've been around a while too. Overall, this is an easy book to recommend.

I first heard about the StoryCorps Project a few years ago and was immediately charmed by the idea of it. Two people important to one another enter a soundproof booth and spend 40 minutes as interviewer and interviewee. The interview is recorded. They are provided with suggested questions, but more often than not it seems that once the conversation gets rolling, it becomes just that - a conversation, and not so much an interview after all. Their stories unfold, and what happens is almost magical. At the end of the session, a high-quality copy of the recording is given to the participants, and another copy is sent to the Library of Congress. The whole point is to give a voice to everyone willing to sound it. A collection of some of these recordings has been compiled by Dave Isay in the amazing book Listening Is an Act of Love.

The stories shared here are conversations between husbands and wives, aunts and nephews, coworkers, friends. The stories are funny, shocking, heartwarming, and heartbreaking. I am haunted by the stories of those closely impacted by 9/11. I cried when I read a story about a daughter asking her father to remember his experiences in a Nazi concentration camp. Some of the "how we met and fell in love" stories made me chuckle. The stories included in this book are from such different people in such different walks of life, yet so many common themes arise. Everyone wants to love and be loved, everyone makes mistakes, everyone hurts.

I borrowed this book from the library and read it in one sitting. It was so moving, so profound, that I want my own copy to keep. I want to hear these voices again and again, to remind myself that we all - all of us - have a story to tell.

Everyone knows, you can't go wrong with this, or any other, BETTY CROCKER COOKBOOK. The 12th edition subtitle is "Everything You Need to Know to Cook from Scratch", and that is NOT an exaggeration. There are timetables for cooking meats; food substitution charts (e.g., 1 c. buttermilk = 1 T. lemon juice or vinegar plus enough milk to make one cup); equivalent measurement charts (e.g., 3 tsp. = 1 T.); and recipes for everything under the sun. There are plentiful mouthwatering, full-color photographs of ingredients and prepared recipes.

In this "hardcover", 5-ring binder, 12th edition, the recipes are divided up and separated by tabbed lightweight card stock pages with the following labels: Getting Started; Appetizers; Beverages; Breakfast and Brunch; Salads & Salad Dressings; Soups, Stews & Chilies; Pasta & Pizzas; Whole Grains & Rice; Vegetables, Beans & Legumes; One-Dish Dinners; Beef, Pork & Lamb; Chicken & Turkey; Fish & Shellfish; Vegetarian; Grilling & Smoking; Do It Yourself; Sauces, Seasonings & Marinades; Breads; Cookies, Bars & Candies; Cakes & Cupcakes; Pies & Tarts; and Desserts & Fruits.

"Do It Yourself" covers canning and preserving; "Vegetarian" discusses vegetarian diet and includes vegetarian recipes (e.g., "Learn to prepare tofu"). The vegetable cooking charts are in the "Vegetables, Beans & Legumes" section. In each new cookbook edition, the Betty Crocker editors update older recipes and replace older recipes with new ones, to reflect current food wisdom on what constitutes a healthy American diet (e.g., less sugar). A word of warning: If your Betty Crocker cookbook has a recipe you love, hang onto that cookbook--because the recipe may be gone from the next edition!

This looseleaf version of the cookbook has good, tight binder rings, and pages that turn smoothly and lie flat. However, the countertop footprint of the cookbook is large (10" wide and 20" long). It consumes nearly 2 feet of counter space! (Of course, individual recipe pages can be removed when they're being used.) Also, the card stock that has the separator tabs is so flimsy, the tabs were already bent when my brand-new cookbook arrived. My cookbook also has a lot of looseleaf pages that aren't cut at the bottom; they're easy to tear apart, but I shouldn't have to do this. (I hope that this is an isolated problem affecting only a few copies like mine.)

In fact, I much prefer the spiral bound BETTY CROCKER COOKBOOK, which is smaller and also has pages that lie flat. Because of the large size, the too-easily-bent tabs, and the uncut looseleaf pages, I rate this "hardcover" 12th edition of the great BETTY CROCKER COOKBOOK at 4 stars ("I like it" on the official Amazon scale).

FROM AWAY is one heck of a fine ghost story. It’s also a “coming of age” story, and generally I don’t care for these. But this novel has a unique twist—it’s the story of how an aimless young video store clerk discovers his true calling as a Medium between this world and the next. It’s also a hard-to-put-down story about deep, loving attachments—good attachments within loving families, and toxic attachments centered on or producing abused children.

The setting—a remote island in Maine where the protagonist (Sam Kehoe) and his sister (Charlotte) summered every year until their parents were killed in a collision with an 18-wheeler—is beautifully described. The title is taken from the term applied by the island’s year-round residents to the property owners who only visit in the summers. These visitors will always be “from away”, no matter how long they have been coming to the island.

The plot is difficult to describe without spoilers, so I won’t do it. Suffice it to say that this is a fast-reading, unforgettable novel about powerful natural and supernatural forces. It draws you in, and holds your attention right up to the inevitable, satisfying end.

THE WHITES is a new mystery/thriller by novelist Richard Price (writing under the pen name Harry Brandt). Not surprisingly, it's more literary than thriller--definitely not a page-turner--but it's always interesting, and comes across pretty well as a police procedural. The characters are extremely well-drawn, well-motivated, and memorable--indeed, detective Milton Ramos is the stuff of nightmares. The complex plot involving half a dozen major characters requires the reader to work a little, but there are plenty of horrendous crimes included to keep the reader reading.

Back in the day, NYPD Night Watch detective Billy Graves was one of the Wild Geese--one of a batch of rookie cops who got good results by NOT sticking strictly to the rules. Eventually the WG's were all promoted to detective, and eventually most of them moved on to new lives. Redman ran a funeral parlor; Jimmy was an itinerant building supervisor; Yasmeen headed up a university division of crimes against students; Pavlicek was a rich realtor. But the WGs still met for a monthly dinner, and each one was haunted by a personal "White"--a criminal who had committed a horrendous crime on their watch, who had never been brought to justice. The crimes had set up housekeeping in their lives--with Pavlicek forever stalking Jeffrey Bannion, Whelan forever pursuing Brian Tomassi, Redman forever watching Sweetpea Harris, Yasmeen forever tracking Eric Cortez, and Billy forever shackled to Curtis Taft.

But when the White belonging to Pavlicek, Jeffrey Bannion, is stabbed in Penn Station and bleeds out while jumping a turnstile during Billy's Night Watch shift, Billy is pulled into an investigation of all of the Whites that ultimately tests his long-held, fierce WG loyalties. In a secondary plot, Billy's family is stalked by a murderous, brutal psychopath with an ancient grudge against Billy's wife.

As improbable as the plot description may sound, this mystery/ thriller actually works. The novel is partly a police procedural, partly an exploration of workplace friendships and family relationships--and the pages abound with serpentine twists that all come out satisfactorily at the end. Because THE WHITES is interesting, but more of a literary effort than a mystery/thriller, I rate it at 4 stars ("I like it" on the official Amazon scale).

You're sure to find it in Jan Eaton's Famous Paintings in Cross Stitch. I first discovered this delightful book in the British cross stitch magazine Cross Stitch Gold, which featured a full color pattern based on Rossetti's "La Ghirlandata," and spent the next two years trying to track down a copy of this excellent book. Note to self: why is it that all decent cross stitch magazines / books are English and super-expensive?!

The book features fifteen projects based on paintings by Van Gogh (Irises), Klimpt, Mucha, Degas, Cezanna and Botticelli. Some of the projects, such as a Degas tote bag, are smaller and more manageable, while other large-scale projects such as Van Gogh's Irises and La Ghirlandata will keep you stitching for months, if not years.

I wasn't as fond of the smaller projects; a Mucha-inspired curtain border paled next to the original print it was taken from, the Japanese woodblock print seemed a bit tired, and I noticed through careful comparison that the Degas tote bag insert featured an incomplete pattern (if you compare it to the photo, you'll see an area of shading under the ballerina that is coded in the legend, but not present on the chart). Generally, charts were easy on the eye and easy to read, although as previously mentioned, I found at least one instance where the chart and final project photo differed.

Overall, if you feel like you've conquered easier projects and you're looking for something unique, try Famous Paintings In Cross Stitch for a Mona Lisa-inspired eyeglass case, delicate sachets, greeting cards and large-scale projects that your visitors will ooh and aah over.

Like many people I read this book shortly after Timothy's fatal mauling. I was expecting an academic book about bears that laid out the research findings of Timothy Treadwell. What I got was something of a cross between the horse-whisperer and that crazy woman who used to live down the street who had tea parties with her 50 stupidly named cats.

I have to admit I found the book intriguing although I was constantly feeling uneasy about what he was saying and doing. I think spreading information and love for animals, especially animals that could be at risk, is good. In the end we truly will only save what we value. But, by the end of this book I was deeply concerned about what kind of an example Timothy is giving the world. Bears, especially the coastal Browns in Katmai, are not blood thirsty killers, but the nature of bears is unpredictable, and much like people, different from individual to individual. Timothy does make this clear in his different encounters with bears.

What Timothy does not point out or even seem to consider is that historically any time bears become habituated to people, bears suffer. Timothy's close approach to bears did nothing to help the bears or bear research. At best it only boosted his celebrity. In the book, he mentions several of these irresponsible encounters, in one example he leans over to kiss a yearling bear on the nose.

I recommend reading the book, even if at times it seems like watching a train wreck. If possible, read it with Grizzly Maze by Nick Jans or Death in the Grizzly Maze by Mike Lapinski. After you realize that he embellished nearly all parts of his life; claiming to be Australian, claiming to be an orphan .... You will get the grain of salt you should take with this book.

Sisters Maddalena and Chiaretta were abandoned as young children at the Pieta foundling hospital in Venice in 1695, and Four Seasons follows their growth, both physically and musically, over the next several decades. The Pieta was a church-run orphanage that taught girls to be singers or musicians, and staged lavish concerts of religious music for Venetian nobility. The two sisters are complete opposites: Maddalena, the oldest, is quiet and dutiful, while Chiaretta is headstrong and impulsive. Chiaretta has promise as a soprano, while Maddalena tries her hand at several instruments before she falls deeply in love with the violin. Chiaretta is beautiful, and dreams of escaping the Pieta through marriage to a noble. Maddalena has no such hopes, and abandons herself in music. When "the Red Priest" Antonio Vivaldi walks into her life, she's thrown into a cycle of heartbreak and confusion that persists throughout her life. Vivaldi is under contract to produce music for the school choir and orchestra, and he finds a kindred spirit in Maddalena through her keen ear, imagination, and skill on the violin.

Vivaldi is presented as all-too-human; despite his flashes of musical genius, he's an overworked, constantly ill man who admits that joining the priesthood was a mistake. He suffers from frequent bouts of asthma and angina, is sloppy in appearance, and he seems to have no idea what an effect he has on Maddalena, who is crushed when he leaves for the first time to work on commissions in other cities.

Chiaretta has caught the eye of Claudio Morosini, a handsome young man from a powerful Venetian family that counted several doges in its ranks. The Pieta negotiages the terms of marriage with his family, and the Chiaretta is initiated into the privileged life of a Venetian wife, including her husband's dalliances with courtesans and her own taking of a lover. She constantly worries how her marriage and motherhood will affect her deep relationship with her sister.

Maddalena remains at the Pieta, working her way up the musical ranks, secretly hoping that one day Vivaldi will return and express some sort of mutual affection for her. Her life is the opposite of Chiaretta's; she finds solace in the enforced silence and takes younger girls under her wings in her own kind of mothering. There will be no marriage or romance for her, so she lives through Chiaretta's visits and reports from the outside world.

Corona does a marvelous job at bringing a decadent Venice to life, with beautiful descriptions of the finery (velvet, jewels, paintings) contrasting sharply with the austerity of the Pieta. She's clearly done her homework into period clothing, food, customs and medicines (there are several detailed descriptions of herbal asthma and healing remedies, including bleeding and cupping). Her descriptions of the music created by Maddalena and Vivaldi (yes, the title piece makes a large appearance in the last third) are stunning; I could practically hear every note played. The deep lifelong bond between the two sisters also illustrated the church-nobility dichotomy of Venice. Also, Corona's portrayal of Vivaldi is human, to the point that she even defends him against slander. He's no mad genius, but a sick and overworked man who's trapped in the wrong profession. These intertwining stories of sisterly love, platonic love, and romantic love buoy the novel along on the sweep of strings where music and love reign supreme.

There is also a glossary, a pronunciation guide, a reading guide, a music guide to pieces featured in the novel, and an interview with the author included. For the ultimate experience, read this while listening to the included Vivaldi tracklisting. Fans of historical art fiction such as [[ASIN:0812968972 The Birth of Venus: A Novel]] and [[ASIN:0812974042 In the Company of the Courtesan: A Novel]] and lovers of Baroque music will find much to enjoy here.

I originally picked up this book because I thought it would be a good resource to help me find royalty free images for a website I was putting together. I was expecting long lists of websites that I probably could have found by googling, but was too lazy to track down. But I got something completely different.

This book is a great primer for understanding copyrights and the use of the public domain. I now feel far more comfortable about locating images and text to use on my websites. I even got a lot of ideas about what I can post on my website, items I never thought of before like historical literature that has long been part of the public domain as well as recipes (I didn't know you could not copyright a basic recipe-although there are some gray areas.)

I was also interested to find out that, like many things in life, the public domain has plenty of gray areas. But this book helped a lot in finding out where the gray areas are. I used the information to find that a Robert Service poem I was going to put on line was in the public domain in the US but was copyrighted in Canada (look more gray area!)

maybe I'm a little nerdy, but once I started reading the book I couldn't stop. and every page I had another light bulb going off about another way I could use the public domain to help my website.

I recommend this book to anyone looking to use the public domain. It really opened my eyes to a world I did not even fully realize existed.

I will start by saying that this set is not quite what I was expecting. I thought these little journaling books would be devotional-style books that had room for jotting down a few thoughts. I did not realize it is designed as a full New Testament set of volumes with as much room for writing as there is for reading. It's a very nice set suitable for gifting and for journaling if that is something that you do regularly.

This is a well-thought-out product. Instead of binding a complete New Testament into a single, fat volume with all of the writing room included, the books of the New Testament are mostly broken out individually. The result is a larger number of smaller volumes that are more manageable and are easy to work with, and it does have the added benefit of being able to locate a specific location in the Scriptures at a glance if you're not totally sure of ordering.

The text is easy to read and there is plenty of room to write. Every other page is blank for writing so that you can journal on any part of the Scripture you like instead of being directed to a verse or verses that someone else thinks is important. Perhaps that's me being overly picky with other journaling books, but it is something that does annoy me somewhat.

The artwork is pretty and it gives these a very feminine touch.

This is a very nice set of journaling New Testament volumes. It has plenty of room for writing and leaves what to write about very open-ended for the user, and the artwork is attractive. The design was thought through very well and the result is a functional and giftable set of volumes for anyone who enjoys the process of journaling their thoughts on the Scriptures.

René Redzepi is a Danish chef who co-owns Noma (now Noma 2.0), which is a restaurant in Copenhagen, Denmark. He invited the author on his quest to discover the best culinary flavors throughout the world and to publish this book about the effort. These discoveries, such as the worlds best mole, came at a price. He closed Noma (1.0) in order to create pop-up Nomas in Japan, Australia, and Mexico.

Most of this culinary story takes place in Mexico, whose eatable delicacies Redzepi loves. What I learned about this quest is the difficulty of foraging and procuring ingredients to make the best and most astonishing culinary delights possible. The author is a gifted writer in being able to weave a story that is somewhat lacking in substance but which I still found to be incredibly enjoyable. It is a journey of discovery of what the natural world can offer up that will excite our palate and also about the man and his disciples that formulate these culinary creations. The difficulty in finding superb ingredients and the stress associated with their use is front and center throughout this text.

STYX AND STONE (2013): Ellie Stone is a professed modern girl in 1960s' New York City, playing by her own rules and breaking boundaries while searching for a killer among the renowned scholars in Columbia University's Italian Department. This little book presents a small collection of four of his sermons.

This is a short and fast read, but the material is on point. He sticks close to Biblical truth and he refers to Scripture often. In a lot of ways I found his teaching to be similar to that of A. W. Tozer - very approachable and friendly but not shying away from the hard truths.

DARK MATTER: A NOVEL has a great concept--what might happen if a scientist invented a "box" that allowed him to physically interact with and explore the quantum superpositions applicable to his own life? What would happen if the scientist were able to pick and choose among the alternative lives he would have led, had he made different choices at important turning points in his life (e.g., getting engaged or not, accepting a particular job or not). What would happen if his "box" would actually allow him to go back and live inside a different life that now seems preferable to his present life?

ASIDEM NOTE ON THE SCIENCE: The concept is based on the theory of quantum superpositions, which posits that a quantum system such as an atom or photon "can exist as a combination of multiple states corresponding to different possible outcomes", and that such a system remains in superposition until it interacts with or is observed by the external world, "at which time the superposition collapses into one or another of the possible definite states" (google "Schroedinger's cat" for the full discussion).

DARK MATTER is a sort of "parallel universes" novel, but it's really an exploration of quantum superpositions. The idea of the novel is terrific, but it's poorly executed. The story is told through the inner thoughts and perceptions of the main character (Jason Dessen), a small-college physics professor who is inexplicably abducted from his happy family life and thrust into one of his possible alternative lives as a highly honored internationally known physicist and brilliant researcher.

The novel just rambles along, documenting Jason's efforts to sort out all his confused thoughts and experiences, along with his efforts to find his way back to his original, idyllic life. For me, the story didn't move very far from the basic idea, so that the plot entirely lacked in substance. Jason's character is simplistic--he just wants to get home--and the characters of Daniela and Amanda aren't developed, either. The novel never caused me to engage with, or care about, any of the characters.

+++++++++SPOILER ALERT++++++++++++++
The ending seemed very contrived. I have no idea whether the concept of many coexisting, competing Jasons makes sense in quantum theory, because I know very little about quantum theory. As an ending, this idea was poorly prepared for, and didn't make a lot of sense. It seems like the engineered life swap was doomed to failure from the outset, given that it apparently generated the multiple Jasons.
+++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++

If you're interested in literary attempts to explore extremely basic principles of quantum physics, you may enjoy DARK MATTER. However, because I found the novel boring, with a flawed plot, and not particularly well written, I rate it at 2 stars ("I don't like it" on the official Amazon scale).

I have worked a lot with active noise canceling (ANC) headphones and ear buds, and I was excited to try these as Sony has really come on strong in recent years in this area. I usually do not wear ear buds, favoring full-sized over-the-ear can, but sometimes ear buds are the right answer. I am not unhappy with these.

There are two aspects of these that need discussion - the ANC function and the sound quality. I’ll cover each of these separately.

The ANC function is good but is not top-notch. That is, it’s very effective at killing off ambient sound and it allows for listening to music at lower volumes without letting in surrounding sounds like fans and air handlers in an office or road noise in a car. It is not as aggressive as some of Sony’s other offerings, but still far and away better than cheaper headphones and ear buds available.

I like the fact that I can touch one of the buds and the mode switches to allow more ambient noise through for conversation. This is a common feature for ANC phones of any type anymore, and this pair of buds implements this well.

The default sound profile is good but not perfect. The bass is good and not overdriven which is a refreshing change from most phones I have used. The midrange is a little off, with sound being a little muddy and with the slightest of distortion if you’re looking for it. The highs are not sharp and also seem a bit muted like the midrange, though it is not severe enough to write these off by any means. I have worked with ear buds that have better balanced sound profiles, but I have also heard much worse. Now, all that said, with Sony’s application it’s easy to access an equalizer to better balance the sound as desired. I have had no trouble tweaking the active profile in the equalizer to get these to sound better depending on the kind of music I’m listening to.

These are Sony’s midrange buds, and are sold at a midrange price point. If these were priced like their top-end buds I would be hesitant to recommend them. At the price point, though, they’re a good option and are better than most off-brand or cheap ear buds available.

Help arrives in the form of a grieving gay neighbor, a visiting monarch, and the dashing young lieutenant who defects from her yacht. Bittersweet and profoundly affecting, Babycakes was the first fictional work anywhere to acknowledge the arrival of AIDS.

Significant Others (1987); Tranquility reigns in the ancient redwood forest until a women-only music festival sets up camp downriver from an all-male retreat for the ruling class. Among those entangled in the ensuing mayhem are a lovesick nurseryman, a panic-stricken philanderer, and the world's most beautiful fat woman. Significant Others is Armistead Maupin's cunningly observed meditation on marriage, friendship, and sexual nostalgia. The holiday in the redwoods goes uproariously awry when the opposing sexes camp out rather too close to each other for comfort. Among those entangled in the mayhem events at Wimminwood, a lesbian music and arts festival, are DeDe Halcyon-Day, reformed debutante, and D'orothea Wilson. and their relationship; Mary Ann Singleton, her house-husband Brian Hawkins and her daughter Shawna, the child her friend Connie gave to her when she died; Michael Tolliver, who has tested HIV-positive and is taking AZT to combat the threat to his immune system; and Anna Madrigal, the transgendered landlady who still mothers her tenants at 28 Barbary Lane on Russian Hill.

Sure of You (1989); Mary Ann Singleton now a fiercely ambitious TV talk show host finds she must choose between national stardom in New York and her husband and a child in San Francisco. Caught in the middle is their longtime friend, Michael "Mouse" Tolliver, whose own future is even more uncertain. Thack & Michael are a couple and live with the reality of AIDS; Brian and Mary Ann's marriage fails; Mona visits to Lesbos. Wistful and compassionate yet subversively funny.

Michael Tolliver Lives (2007); Michael "Mouse" Tolliver, a fifty-five-year-old gardener tell his story of survival in his own words. Along the way, the reader reunites with a number of familiar faces from the old days at 28 Barbary Lane.

Mary Ann in Autumn (2010); After the intimate first-person narrative of Maupin's last novel, "Michael Tolliver Lives", "Mary Ann in Autumn" marks the author's return to the multi-character plotlines and darkly comic themes of his earlier work. Twenty years have passed since Mary Ann Singleton left her husband and child in San Francisco to pursue her dream of a television career in New York. Now, a pair of personal calamities has driven her back to the city of her youth and into the arms of her oldest friend, Michael "Mouse" Tolliver, a gay gardener happily ensconced with his much-younger husband. Mary Ann finds temporary refuge in the couple's backyard cottage, where, at the unnerving age of 57, she licks her wounds and takes stock of her mistakes. Soon, with the help of Facebook and a few old friends, she begins to reengage with life, only to confront fresh terrors when her speckled past comes back to haunt her in a way she could never have imagined. Among those caught in Mary Ann's orbit are her estranged daughter, Shawna, a popular sex blogger; Jake Greenleaf, Michael's transgendered gardening assistant; socialite DeDe Halcyon-Wilson; and the indefatigable Anna Madrigal, Mary Ann's former landlady at 28 Barbary Lane. Over three decades in the making, Armistead Maupin's legendary Tales of the City series rolls into a new age, still sassy, irreverent and curious, and still exploring the boundaries of the human experience with insight, compassion and mordant wit.

1991 and California girl Jamie is having a gay time, she is young, doing all the things she loves and counts herself lucky to be a lesbian (so I love her right away). On her way home from a fabulous women's music festival she ends up stuck in Atlanta overnight.

Carla is a bit shy and not as flamboyant as our Jamie. She too is stuck Atlanta at the airport. Jamie, in a gutsy move, makes a play for Carla. They end up going to a Melissa Etheridge concert where they are totally captivated, the music is inspiring and they have a voluptuously passionate night together. Not surprisingly the next morning Carla has left before Jamie awakes. Jamie took it harder than I would have, but she is an extrovert and was probably packing the u-haul in her mind.

The next 20 years have their highs and lows with Melissa Etheridge sort of the touchstone along the way - so much she she was almost a character, being mentioned 35 times, I thought it was kinda fun.

We find Jamie in crisis at work. 20 years ago she was a freshly minted doctor. Today she has a fiasco on her hands at work and Jamie began to irk me, she has to do it all herself, the other two physicians in her practice want to help but she turns them down flat. Finally I didn't think Jamie was lover material, she doesn't seem to need her partner of ten years yet is very happy in her relationship.

Meanwhile Carla has been smitten for the one night stand with Jamie, pining for 20 years - I tried to imagine it and I felt so sorry for her that I was kinda depressed. So I guess after the fabulous opening chapter I was disappointed what the young women let one fabulous night when they were young fill them with "what ifs" for so long. We find out Carla was pregnant and went on to marry her boyfriend.

Huge kudos to the author in that I believed every word of it. Blair has a terrific future as a writer this just wasn't the story for me.

We even have a duplicitous villein, Jamie's partner, Sheryl, a High School Principal and so deeply closeted she hassles one of her gay students - Carla's openly lesbian daughter.

Twenty years later Carla and her husband are divorcing, turns out they are both gay, so while they still love each other they are looking for more fulfillment. Jamie and Carla meet again over a job interview (although neither let on they know the other - I can see me doing the same thing - lol!). Carla is really upset that Jamie doesn't remember her, doesn't remember the evening that was so very crucial to Carla, this made me so sad that Carla put so much invested emotion on 12 hours in her life 20 years ago.

Lastly, I needed more Carla and Jamie doing lover things together - in and out of the bedroom.

So the writing was a solid "5" but the story just didn't do it more me.

[[VIDEOID:99ec24b728fa83828f854618bef8cc0]] Most of the Bluetooth speakers I have used have been smaller and more portable, designed to be on-the-go and useful when traveling or outdoors. This speaker by GGMM is also wireless and can go with you, but I personally prefer to keep it in my room above my desk where I can use it to listen to music. This is a much better speaker than most of the speakers I have used and I am very pleased with it.

This is a large speaker, bigger than most I have used and as a result it weighs more. It is encased in a leather cover and looks very upscale when compared to plastic or rubber. The controls are straightforward and easy – power on/off, set the mode between Bluetooth, WiFi and Line-in, volume up and down and finally a bass booster. On the back there is a barrel port of plugging in the speaker, a reset button that you likely will never need to use and the port for plugging in a 3.5mm plug.

The sound profile is about as close to perfect as I have seen in any speaker. The bass is on target – strong but not overdriven unless you use the bass booster. The midrange is excellent and the music sounds rich and full, not lifeless, hollow or like it’s coming from a tunnel. The highs are bright and clean but not piercing. The sound is balanced very well and I am happy.

The bass booster does exactly what you think it does – it gives the bass a kick. Even with the boost, the bass is not overpowering but it comes forward quite a bit on bass-heavy tracks. I do not use the bass boost often as I prefer the highs.

So far I have had no connection issues and the speaker connects very quickly when put in Bluetooth mode.

This is an excellent speaker – far and away better than most smaller speakers I have seen and used. It is much more expensive, but it brings to the table great sound and fine connectivity. I use this in my home office where it sits just above eye level on my desk shelf, and I use it every night for listening to music.

For those like me who didn't read volume one here is a brief synopsis: David Hockney: The Biography, 1937-1975 (April 17, 2012): Drawing on exclusive and unprecedented access to David Hockney's extensive archives, notebooks, and paintings, interviews with family, friends, and on Hockney himself, Christopher Simon Sykes provides a colorful and intimate portrait of one of the most influential artists of the twentieth century. Born in 1937, David Hockney grew up in a northern English town during the days of postwar austerity. By the time he was ten years old he knew he wanted to be an artist, and after leaving school he went on to study at Bradford Art College and later at the Royal College of Art in London. Bursting onto the scene at the Young Contemporaries exhibition, Hockney was quickly heralded as the golden boy of postwar British art and a leading proponent of pop art. It was during the swinging 60s in London that he befriended many of the seminal cultural figures of the generation and throughout these years Hockney's career grew. Always absorbed in his work, he drew, painted and etched for long hours each day, but it was a scholarship that led him to California, where he painted his iconic series of swimming pools. Since then, the most prestigious galleries across the world have devoted countless shows to his extraordinary work. In the seventies he expanded his range of projects, including set and costume design for operas and experiments with photography, lithography, and even photocopying. Most recently he has been at the forefront the art world's digital revolution, producing incredible sketches on his iPhone and iPad, and it is this progressive thinking which has highlighted his genius, vigor and versatility as an artist approaching his 75th birthday. In this, the first volume of Hockney's biography, detailing his life and work from 1937 - 1975, Sykes explores the fascinating world of the beloved and controversial artist whose career has spanned and epitomized the art movements of the last five decades.

Author Heda Margolius Kovaly, a survivor of both Auschwitz and her husband's 1952 execution via Stalinist "show trial", was indeed born "under a cruel star". Her lovely little mystery novel, INNOCENCE; OR, MURDER ON STEEP STREET, is probably best understood as a semi-autobiographical nonfiction novel, a companion to her memoirs published as [[ASIN:0841913773 Under a Cruel Star: A Life in Prague 1941-1968]].

In INNOCENCE, a young wife, Helena Novakova, is working as an usher at a Prague movie house (the Horizon) in 1952. She's a social outcast, because her husband (Karel) has been imprisoned on suspicion of spying against the state; and she, too, is suspected of spying. Both spouses are innocent, but it doesn't matter. In 1952 Prague, nearly everyone is a spy: politicians, policemen, co-workers, neighbors, close relatives; and anyone can be imprisoned on the slightest pretext.

Two murders connected with the Horizon cinema occur within a few months. The first murder, of a small boy, is solved quickly. The second murder, of a man found knifed to death in a car parked outside the cinema, is much more difficult to solve. The solution lies in the interwoven lives of Helena, Karel, the cinema's ushers and owner, the crime's investigators, the Prague politicians, and the ushers' boyfriends. (The novel includes a third murder, a political one, but that solution is obvious to the reader from the moment the murder occurs.)

The novel's ending is satisfactory, but a little confusing to a reader like myself who isn't familiar with a society in which near-universal spying is the norm. The novel is translated from the Czech, and it's a good translation, but the translation would be improved by giving the characters more distinctive, more Westernized names. I found myself constantly flipping back to clarify which characters were which, as the characters' first and last names are used interchangeably, and the Czech names are difficult: Vendys, Novakoma, Vaclav, Nedomova, Vojta, Vranova, Ladinka, Bozema, Sulcova, Novak, Koulousek, Kourimska, etc.

Because INNOCENCE is more of an autobiography than a mystery novel, and because I had so much difficulty keeping the characters' Czech names straight, I rate the book at 4 stars ("I like it" on the official Amazon scale). I first heard about Barbara Kingsolver's (author of [[ASIN:0060786507 The Poisonwood Bible: A Novel (Perennial Classics)]]) Animal, Vegetable, Miracle: A Year of Food Life on NPR, where it had been selected as a summer must-read. As someone who shops organic at local farmer markets, this book struck a chord with me on many levels and reinforced why I chose a vegetarian lifestyle. Although I'm not currently in a position to have my own garden, I support local organic Texas produce as much as possible and strive to eat in season. I've been vegetarian for years, and Animal, Vegetable, Miracle was like sitting down for a chat with a good friend over a cup of tea.

Due to modern "convenience", many of us have forgotten what real produce tastes like. Americans are notorious for not eating our vegetables (unless you count French fries and ketchup). We expect to be able to find any fruit or vegetable at any time of the year in our local grocery stores, but how many of us calculate the cost in carbon credits, pesticides, loss of habitat and deforestation that comes with it? It is such a simple gesture to buy locally from a farmers market or organic grocery store, and you're not just benefiting yourself, but helping to support the gargantuan efforts of small organic farms in your community.

Barbara and her family (husband Steven and daughters Camille and Lily) move from Tucson to rural Virginia, where their odyssey of producing all of their food begins. The family makes a vow not to buy any out-of-season, conventional produce at the grocery store. Adios, South American bananas. Farewell, raisins. The Kingsolvers will be responsible stewards of the earth, growing most of their food needs in their garden. This includes not only in-season vegetables, herbs, and fruits, but also eggs and poultry. The few things that they are unable to produce (organic grain, fair trade coffee, olive oil, spices), they attempt to buy organically, as close to home as possible. Barbara flips lustfully through seed catalogs the way some treat Victoria Secret; she makes notes on alluring new seeds and exotic varieties of produce to try (Australian blue pumpkins and ratlike French fingerling potatoes among them).

She encourages her two daughters to take part in the cooking and storing of mountains of tomatoes, zucchini, and herbs in order to store them for the long winter. Everyone pitches in at dinnertime and during holiday menus. Barbara's youngest daughter Lily becomes an entrepreneur saving up for a horse. Her product: organic eggs. She chooses various varieties of chickens to produce a rainbow of eggshell colors, as well as chickens that lay in cold weather. Her cartons of eggs go for $2.50. Barbara's husband is the bread baker, responsible for daily creations that incorporate various flours and healthful additions such as flaxseed. Family mealtime, that great vanished American ritual, has found a new home in the Kingsolvers.

Along the way, Barbara divulges fascinating insider's tips on turkey sex life, dispatching poultry from barnyard to table, locking cars to avoid unwanted zucchini deposits from neighbors, and rediscovers the spiritual joy of working the land and living off of her labors.

The book also includes numerous excellent recipes for in-season produce and impressive lists of resources, references, and organizations for further research.

My only hope is that millions of Americans read this and discover the urgency of preserving our vanishing heirloom vegetables, fruits, and livestock, and the desperate need to economically support local organic farmers.

I loved Nancy Haddock's [[ASIN:042521995X La Vida Vampire (Oldest City Vampire, Book 1)]]; the heroine Cesca is a very hip, snarky gal who loves surfing and home decorating, works as a ghost tour guide, and oh, happens to be a vampire who hates blood (it makes her queasy, and she'll only drink caramel macchiato-flavored blood from Starbloods). In "Last Vampire Standing," Cesca ends up aiding Jo-Jo, a fugitive vamp who seeks to be America's next greatest comic and also serves as Cesca's instructor for flying lessons. The original novel was snappy and funny, but "Last Vampire Standing" never gets off the ground, much like Cesca's attempts at flight.

Part of the plot is a carryover from "La Vida Vampire": Cesca's girlhood crush on Triton plays a role in "Last Vampire Standing," and Pandora the shapeshifter is back, as is Cesca's love interest, Deke Saber. Now for the bad: the numerous plot threads dangle (example: a major character makes an appearance in the first twenty pages, and isn't heard from again until Chapter 21). I just wasn't interested in the several weak side plots. The novel dragged along; sexual innuendo and bedroom romps serve as frequent page filler rather than actual action or intrigue (sort of parallel to Charlaine Harris's Southern Vampire Series' slide into Sookie's bedroom antics). I realize that this is a paranormal romance, but Cesca was an innocent, blushing vampire virgin in the first book; she seems to have been attending Kama Sutra cram sessions in the interim. We do get to see more of Cesca's psychic powers in use, but there are no other vampire powers at work (the flying lessons were a definite dud). The flashbacks to Cesca's human life were well-drawn; I would have liked to hear more historical details from early St. Augustine.

Jo-Jo is a weak, annoying character. You'd think after centuries of experience as a court jester, he'd have picked up some remotely funny one-liners, but no. He doesn't really serve much of a purpose; although he swears to serve as Cesca's protector, he's never around after getting a contract with a high-powered agent and ditching Cesca for Leno and Oprah (amazing, since the guy has ZERO talent except for the vampire novelty factor). The novel's baddies are just mere sketches, here and then gone, and the central plot point appears in one chapter and is never fully explored. There is some good material here, but it needed to be more developed (the various plots lack cohesiveness and the secondary characters are forgettable). I really wanted to like this after loving "La Vida Vampire," but it was a struggle to finish reading it.

OK, first I will point out that this is kind of a tired formula for a book. Boy or girl doesn't fit into school, finds out that they have secret powers, then finds out that not only does he have secret powers, but he is central to hidden struggle that only he can solve, But he needs a eclectic group of misfit friends to save the day. Filling in the blanks, Secret Power - Shape Shifting into Animals, Hidden Struggle - Warfare between the animal kingdoms, of which he is potentially the heir to the greatest powers ever to exist, powers that can be wielded by anyone who collects a relic and uses it to slay him with, and his eclectic friend, a dolphin shifter, a black widow shifter, a mouse, and a shady mystery shifter.

So there's that, but what makes the book great is some good writing and a lot of tension. The main character spends most of the book in the den of his enemy or his Grandfather's bird kingdom. But the tension is even more pressing in that Simon doesn't even know who his true enemy is or who he can trust. He is often forced into alliances where he cannot fully trust his allies against enemies he cannot truly right off as being in the wrong.

Throw in a few more Juvenile Lit clichés, the book takes place in a school (like Hogwarts or Camp Half Blood.) Simon's family is held captive (like nearly every book where the main character is not an orphan.) It sounds like a recipe for tedium, but this book is well written. The action is engaging, but the very best reason for giving this book five stars is that one of our kids burned through it and raved about it. And any book that engages a kid into reading is a precious thing.

TEN DEAD COMEDIANS: A MURDER MYSTERY is a reworking of Agatha Christie’s very famous murder mystery, [[ASIN:0671552228 TEN LITTLE INDIANS (aka AND THEN THERE WERE NONE)]]. Ten comedians (some still actively performing, some wealthy, some retired, some washed up) are invited to a Caribbean island by a famous comedian, Dustin Walker, who was the inspiration--in different ways--for each man or woman's own comedy routine.

When the comedians arrive, they find that Walker has committed suicide by hanging, and that the island is booby-trapped to ensure that none of them leave the island alive. The plot is sustained by the reader's curiosity as to who will be the next victim, and how that victim will die, as the comedians are picked off one by one. With each death, the victim's photo is removed from a “gallery” in the main house.

The author attempts to differentiate the comedians by their respective styles (e.g., “We Need to Talk”, “That's Racist”, blogger critic), which are based on various well-known comics. Unfortunately, the comic monologues fall flat--no surprise, really, because standup comedy and improv depend so much on timing and delivery. The characters are extremely hard to tell apart when they're interacting with one another on the island and not trying to be funny. (The exceptions are Steve Gordon and the Orange Baby Man, who are more completely fleshed out as individuals.)

It's a tribute to the strength of Christie’s concept that I stuck with this murder mystery to the end. But I only kept on reading to find out which character was the murderer behind the whole scheme, and which characters, if any, would survive. Take away Christie's idea, and there is hardly anything left to use as the basis for recommending this novel.

I fell madly in love with Rod Stewart's Great American Songbook albums, which led me to discover other classic standards by Kern, Porter, Gershwin, Berlin, and others, and I was looking for a relatively simple, yet soulful, piano adaptation for solo piano.

The portfolio contains fifteen songs from the first two albums [[ASIN:B00006JL4J It Had to Be You... The Great American Songbook]] and [[ASIN:B0000C9ZEX As Time Goes By...The Great American Songbook: Volume II]], including You Go To My Head, Time After Time, I'll Be Seeing You, As Time Goes By, For All We Know, and The Very Thought Of You. Note that these are the original versions of the songs, complete with intros that were not recorded by Rod and transcriptions in different keys, so if all you're familiar with are the CD versions, then this will be a bit of a letdown.

However, it was exactly what I was looking for; I would label this as low intermediate, with a short learning curve, and the songs are gentle, slow, romantic and jazzy, the kind of background music you'd expect in a romantic restaurant. There are no flashy pyrotechnics or harsh chords, only simple, slow melodies that evoke a simpler time. This is perfect for a beginning piano student, provided that you have a bit of patience.

Bookwise, this is bare bones, with no photos and a scant 63 pages, but if you're a fan of the Great American Songbook, this is a very doable introduction to timeless songs that our parents / grandparents grew up with.

I have a gold streak filter that I use occasionally with my main lens. This is the first blue streak filter I have used and I use it with my most versatile (and newer) lens, and so far I am pleased with it. It's a specialty filter that is useful in certain situations.

The idea behind this filter is that it has grooves in the glass that trap light and the result is a long, blue streak in the image when a light source is bright enough or is in the frame. This kind of filter is very similar to star filters that create 4-, 6- and 8-point stars, though this one creates just straight lines. When used properly this can cause some very dramatic effects in images, such as when photographing street lights or approaching cars at night.

I do need to say, though, that this kind of filter can easily be overused if not thoughtful. When used a lot, the effect can get dull and be more of an annoyance; however, when it is sparingly used it can evoke that "oh wow!" type of response for the unexpected effect.

This is a screw-on filter that will fit most standard lenses with threads. Make sure you select a filter size that is matched to your lens.

I like this lens filter and the effect it brings to the table. It is a niche product that should be used sparingly, but when used at the right time it can create an eye-popping streak effect.

THEIR LITTLE SECRET: A TOM THORNE NOVEL is a depressing book. It sort of explores the “killer couple” phenomenon, where two relatively normal people meet and spark something in each other that transforms them into co-murderers. I’m new to the “Tom Thorne” series, so I don’t know whether this one is typical; I rather suspect that it isn’t. This is the 16th series novel (for the first, see [[ASIN:B00B6U094U Sleepyhead]]).

The co-killers here (Sarah and Conrad) are (1) a crazy divorcee whose life revolves around dropping off and picking up her son (Jamie) at school; and (2) a virtuoso con man who fleeces single women out of all their money. The spark for Sarah and Conrad is an instant recognition, at their first coffee-shop meeting, that the other is NOT what he or she appears to be to other people. That, plus incredible sex.

In the novel, a woman (Philippa) throws herself in front of a train. Her act is caught on video surveillance tape, so it’s clear that she’s a suicide. But Tom Thorne suspects there is something more to her death. In following up with Philippa’s relatives, he learns that Philippa was recently victimized by a mysterious con man (yes, Conrad), and that the experience was what drove her to suicide.

Subsequently, a pair of seemingly unrelated murders (a young man in Margate, a local school teacher) come to Thorne’s attention, and little clues start to add up, leading Thorne inevitably to the killer couple. However, most of the book is devoted to the relationship between Sarah and Conrad—as it initially forms, and then as it eventually breaks down. It’s the breakdown, of course, that is the couple’s downfall.

I don’t know whether the novel accurately depicts “killer couple” psychology. It’s an interesting read, but depressing (as previously mentioned). Series readers won’t want to miss it, though, because of developments in Thorne’s ongoing relationship with his estranged partner Helen.

I selected this book with the thought of learning a bit more about the Gospel according to Luke. I have read through Luke multiple times and it seems there is always something new that jumps out, so I was hopeful that this book would reveal some new-to-me insights. However, I also had a suspicion that it would be a book that leans heavily in the reformed theology direction, which is a trait I have noticed with most books that have the word "theology" in the title or subtitle. I was right on both counts. This book is not a deep dive, but it's a heady read that will give the reader something on which to think.

This is not a big book, weighing it at just over 200 pages if you include the indices. So, it cannot provide a deep, verse-by-verse analysis of Luke, and it doesn't try to. What it does do, though, is discuss and analyze some of the big ideas and themes in Luke. In that regard this book can be viewed as an overview more than a deep dive, though the topics it covers get fairly thorough discussion.

This book is a showcase of research and cross references. Most of the time, the author quotes from the English Standard Version (ESV) which is a trusted translation; however, he uses other translations too which is a very good thing. Sometimes different translations can amplify or more clearly make a point that a single translation cannot, and the author seems to realize this. There is frequent reference to various places in Scripture, a very positive thing for a book like this.

The writing is a bit scholarly and is not going to be an easy walk through. To me it reads almost like a student's course book, and that's all right if you know that and are willing to put in the work.

There is a definite tendency toward reformed theology and that is my one complaint. It is very difficult to find a book that remains neutral in the argument between reformed and holiness ideologies. My view is relatively balanced between the two extremes, and it is frustrating for me when looking for material that doesn't lean in one direction or the other.

This is an interesting overview of Luke. It's not a deep and thorough exploration of all the nuances of this book of the Bible, and fortunately it doesn't try to. It's a heady read and is suitable for someone looking to really dig through the big themes in Luke.

EVERYDAY BREAD BAKING: FROM SIMPLE SANDWICH LOAVES TO CELEBRATORY HOLIDAY BREADS is misnamed. It is NOT about “everyday” bread baking. Instead, it is about baking bread “from scratch”, using all of the classic time-honored--and time-consuming--steps (mixing, kneading, rising, folding, baking).

The book contains “Master Recipes” for flatbread, no-knead sourdough, sweet Levain rolls, whole wheat, rustic sourdough, challah, baguette, and brioche breads. These recipes are followed by chapters of recipes for “Everyday Breads” (sandwich loaf, lemon-herb focaccia, ciabatta, tortillas, etc.); “Entertaining and Special Occasions” (cinnamon rolls, fougasse, doughnuts, etc.); and “Holidays” (cinnamon wreath, pumpkin rolls, star bread, etc.).

The author seems to really understand bread baking, and the recipes all look like they will produce excellent bread. A nice feature of the book is the “Troubleshooting Tips” that follow each Master Recipe and answer questions such as “Why did my brioche come out tasting dry?” There are also good photos of the steps involved in making the Master Recipes.

However, if l want to learn how to bake bread the old-fashioned way, I’m going to turn to a classic work like James Beard’s [[ASIN:B004JHYSAI Beard on Bread]]. Adult coloring books are currently very popular and I have seen them in all manner of stores, from large department stores to bookstores and even in discount outlets. Most of these coloring books appear to be hand-drawn graphics, highly detailed so that filling in the color on said pages takes time and thought. This coloring book is different in that the illustrations appear to be a combination of hand-drawn imagery and either clip art or computer-generated images.

As is typical with adult coloring books, this one has illustrations on one side of each page in the book. This is a smart choice as it reduces the chances of color getting transferred from one completed image to another image when coloring. It also makes it more appropriate for removing a page and displaying/mounting it when it is complete.

As I mentioned, the images in this book are partially hand-drawn and partially made of graphic images. It is obvious where this occurs as the graphic images are very symmetrical and straight where hand-drawn images have more variance in line structure and tend to vary in straightness. This is not a fault or a criticism by any means, but more of an observation. Regardless of the rendering method, these images are highly detailed and will keep most people busy for a long time. For me, one image takes days, as I can never spend a long block of time working steadily.

The images have a distinct Parisian theme. You can find images of the Eiffel Tower, buildings and other items of interest you will find in Paris. I will say that some of the images are not unique to Paris in particular and can be found elsewhere too.

Holding the pages at an angle so the light reflects off of it, it looks (and feels) like higher-grade paper, similar to what I have in a sketchbook I keep at my desk. I have not tried coloring with pens so I do not know how resistant the paper is to soaking and running, but colored pencils work great.

This is a nice coloring book. There is a lot of detail, there are many, many images to color and because of the way the images are composed it is a bit different than other adult coloring books I have seen. It's a good choice, especially if you have a soft spot for Paris.

There are all sorts of mixes available, and this book provides home-made equivalents for over 60 of them: cake mix, chili seasoning mix, brownie mix, chicken gravy mix and so many more.

Included with the mix recipes is a collection of good recipes that use those mixes. There are many recipes for cookies, soups, breads and more. I have not tried everything this book has to offer but so far all of the recipes have turned out very well. The mix recipes make a lot (for example, the brownie mix makes 15 cups), so the one possible drawback is that one needs to consider storage for the mixes made, but the cost savings and the satisfaction of having something that is absolutely home-made is worth it. If you like to cook with mixes, either for convenience or for time savings, this book is for you. It requires a little work ahead of time but the results are worth it.

The premise of this series of books is simple - each recipe has been tried and retried until an optimum is found and that’s the recipe that is presented. Sprinkled in with the recipes are a number of cooking tips, brand recommendations and more. This book mostly follows that format and it offers numerous excellent recipes. However, it can hardly be called complete.

Based on the title one would expect to find a series of in-depth discussion regarding the process of actually making pasta. In particular there should be a good deal of instruction on how to handle dough, shaping doughs, working with pasta machines and more. In this book, which is more than 400 pages, all of the discussion about actually making fresh pasta is done within the first 40 pages and the majority of that is presentation of recipes without a lot of discussion. The rest of the book merely presents recipes using various pastas. This is a huge disappointment and as such this is the first Cook’s Illustrated cookbook I have found that is not top-notch.

Not all is lost on this book, though. If you’re looking for a book that gives a lot of ideas on how to prepare pasta dishes, look no further. This book has over 30 chapters and within those there is a great breakdown of how to work with different noodle types, sauce preparations and pairings and a lot more. Roughly 12 of those chapters deal specifically with preparing different sauces and there is an amazing variety - seafood sauces, raw tomato sauces, cream sauces, butter sauces and many more. There is a chapter on making pasta soups and another for pasta salads. And there is another dozen chapters that describe how to use the various pasta types or make a specific dish type, like ravioli or lasagna.

The recipes I have tried have turned out well. I specifically tried the recipe for making homemade white wheat pasta and the recipe worked flawlessly, as one would expect from Cook’s Illustrated. Making a prepared dish from those noodles is a huge upgrade from boxed noodles, too. I cannot say I am disappointed in the recipes I have tried.

I like this book and I think it’s a good resource. However, it is by no means complete and leaves a lot to be desired if looking for recipes for homemade pasta. In this book you’ll find a precious few recipes for making pasta, but the rest of the book is a great collection of recipes for using pasta in all manner of dishes.

Every marriage has its challenges, whether it be financial strain, loss of interest, distractions or perhaps deeper issues. There are plenty of helps and other books out there to help couples work through issues and stay committed to one another. So, how is this book different, and what sets it apart?

I will start by saying that this is a book written from a Christian perspective on marriage and that it relies heavily on Biblical concepts. Chances are, if you are looking at this book you're probably already aware of this foundation and it's probably what drew you to it. If, by chance, you are not coming from a Christian background, then this book is an eye opener that will reveal what marriage really should be.

The authors approach fighting for your marriage as exactly that - a battle to be fought with outside influences and strains that could otherwise erode your marriage or cause damage. Instead of fighting each other, couples should fight as partners.

Most Christian books on marriage have one primary theme that runs through them - God is always the top priority, and from there everything else falls into place. This book is no different and the first chapter makes that very clear. One of the authors tells his story and how he came to faith in Jesus, and how he came to understand that his marriage was worth fighting for.

This book is intended to be read almost as a couple's devotional or a workbook for couples to address marital errors. It establishes Christ on the throne, how marriage is intended, how couples should work together to strengthen their commitment to God and to one another, and how to grow. Each chapter has discussion questions, an affirmation section (assurances to one another), and an action section (what to do next). It's a successful formula and it gets couples communicating.

My wife and I are excited to work through this book together. We've not gotten far into it yet but are looking forward to the journey ahead. We still have much to learn but we're committed to working together to make our marriage better, and this book is a good resource for direction.

The thing that immediately struck me about THE DIRTY SOUTH, the 18th “Charlie Parker” supernatural thriller, is the literary quality of the writing. It’s done in a run-on sentence style--which usually indicates bad writing--but the long sentences actually provide rich background and character details in an economical way. The sentences are long, the novel is long--but the plot moves forward quickly. I didn’t want to put the book down, once I started.

In contrast, the first “Charlie Parker” novel, [[ASIN:B000FCKB98 Every Dead Thing]], is a standard thriller--except for the supernatural aspects--that is written in plain, straightforward, mass paperback style. That novel’s crimes are much more graphic and brutal than the ones in THE DIRTY SOUTH, although the latest novel’s crimes are plenty graphic.

THE DIRTY SOUTH describes at least part of former NYPD detective Charlie Parker’s activities during his first absence from New York City--right after the murder of his wife and daughter, but before he caught up with their killer. (The latter events are described in Every Dead Thing.) Charlie is hunting the murderer of his family, and is out for revenge, but stops for a little while in an Arkansas backwater town to help a local cop find the person who is killing young women and leaving their bodies on display, violated by tree branches.

Because the town is in “the dirty South”, where justice takes a back seat to political expediency, the investigation is blocked at every turn by local power brokers and politicians. No one wants details about the serial murders to leak out, because the dying town is about to be invaded by, and saved by, a group of Japanese investors who will be building warehouses and creating lots of jobs.

“Charlie Parker” fans will absolutely want to read this novel. It was my introduction to the series, and it made me into a Charlie Parker fan. The novel works fine as a standalone. It includes adequate details of Charlie’s background, but goes mercifully light on the details of his wife’s and child’s murders. Series fans will no doubt welcome the brief appearance of Charlie’s friends Angel (the burglar) and Louis (the assassin) in Part 5.

The Deep South backwoods setting rings quite true to me, though I don’t have personal experience to judge it by. It did astonish me to learn that John Connolly is actually an Irish writer, because he handles U.S. settings so convincingly.

SUPERFOOD SEAGREENS is an interesting specialty cookbook that tells you everything you need to know about safely harvesting or purchasing and preparing seagreens (e.g., brown algae, kelp, wakame, Irish moss, sea lettuce). There is a lot of nutritional information about the vitamins and minerals found in seagreens, including a quick breakdown of where their calories come from.

About half the book is devoted to recipes for using seagreens in breakfast items (e.g., smoothies); snacks (e.g., seagreen guacamole); sauces (e.g., tangy spiced gravy); salads (e.g., fennel, carrot, and seagreens salad); soups (e.g., caldo verde); larger dishes (e.g., lasagna); and breads and muffins (e.g., zucchini-seagreen bread). Many of the recipes call for only small amounts of powdered or flaked seagreens, so that the seagreens are used like a spice.

The book includes quite a few attractive full-color photos of prepared dishes and ready-to-use seagreens. It is no mean feat to make kelp, nori sheets, and dried sea lettuce look like something you would want to eat!

This is a very good cookbook for anyone who is curious about seagreens and wants to try them, or who has already discovered seagreens and wants some nice new recipes.

THE HYPNOTIST: A NOVEL (JOONA LINNA) is a new translation of the first novel in Lars Kepler’s internationally best-selling Joona Linna series. (Lars Kepler is the pseudonym of a Swedish husband-and-wife writing team.) Unfortunately, it isn’t a very good translation--the grammar is correct, but the sentences are short and choppy, and the simple, limited vocabulary makes for dull reading.

It doesn't help that the story is told in short chapters (often labeled by the same day of the week and month) that recount the particular day's important happenings from different viewpoints (Erik, Simone, Joona). The shifting viewpoints make sense, because the characters are operating independently, in different locations and contexts. However, this novel structure is hard to pull off smoothly in a writer’s original language, and the format presents extra challenges for the translator. Here, the translation seems to closely follow the words of the original, with the result that the story plods mechanically along.

The story is set in motion when the obsessive Detective Joona takes over a case involving the bloody knife murders of a teacher, his wife, and his young daughter. The teacher's son (Josef) is found covered in stab wounds, barely alive. Joona persuades a medically-qualified hypnotist (Erik)--who has sworn, after a bad experience, to never hypnotize anyone again--to hypnotize the boy in order to save the life of the murdered family’s one remaining daughter (Evelyn).

Hypnosis reveals a startling, unexpected result, and the story continues with myriad unexpected plot twists. Erik’s marriage starts to fall apart; his hemophiliac son (Benjamin) is kidnapped; there's another murder by the killer of the teacher's family; various people’s faces are disfigured; a seriously disturbed, homicidal woman (Lydia) resurfaces from Erik’s past; and more. There are multiple bloody or otherwise disturbing scenes, and the novel culminates with a wildly unbelievable series of rescues.

The novel is fairly readable, and is capable of engaging the reader’s attention. However, the characters lack depth; and the plot is overloaded with far too many twisty developments. In the end, it’s a police procedural that's simply exhausting to read.
