The five steps in 5 STEPS TO A 5: AP U.S. HISTORY 2018 are (1) set up a study program, (2) take a diagnostic test to determine your test readiness, (3) develop successful strategies for answering multiple-choice, short-answer, and essay questions, (4) review the specific material you are expected to know for the United States History Advanced Placement test, and (5) take two full-length practice tests to build confidence and test skills.

There is a daunting amount of substantive review material included in this book, but of course the book is intended for use alongside a year-long high school class in AP U.S. History. The included items that strike me as most valuable, in no particular order, are:

(1) The online dashboard that tracks your progress and performance (showing strengths and weaknesses by question categories, and your scores and percentile ranking compared to other students--all of this based on your answers in practice questions and exams);

(2) The practice exams (3 in the printed book--one diagnostic and two to be taken under simulated test conditions; 3 in the online platform) with questions similar to the ones in the actual test;

(3) The copious review material (pages 71-354, organized by major historical periods in U.S. history (Settling of the Western Hemisphere; Colonial America; British Empire in America; Resistance Rebellion, and Revolution; American Revolution and the New Nation; Establishment of New Political Systems; Jeffersonian Revolution; Rise of Manufacturing and the Age of Jackson; Union Expanded and Challenged; Union Divided; Era of Reconstruction; Western Expansion and Its Impact on the American Character; America Transformed into the Industrial Giant of the World; Rise of American Imperialism; Progressive Era; United States and World War I; Beginning of Modern America: the 1920s; Great Depression and the New Deal; World War II; Origins of the Cold War; Prosperity and Anxiety: the 1950s; America in an Era of Turmoil; Decline and Rebirth; Prosperity and a New World Order; Threat of Terrorism, Increase of Presidential Power, and Economic Crisis; Contemporary America: Evaluating the “Big Themes”); and

(4) The many multiple choice review questions with the correct answers explained in detail.

If you are taking an AP exam to secure college credit for knowledge acquired in high school, then it’s extremely important to study the exam itself. As is well known, the people who write exams have personal biases (biases that they may not even be aware of) that creep into the exams and affect the determination of “correct” answers.

By studying the explanations of the correct answers in this AP world history exam prep guide, you can learn what kinds of answers are expected from you. Armed with this knowledge of the exam itself, you can fully utilize your personal knowledge of U.S. history, give the examiners the answers they want to see, and score high on the actual exam.

Anyone who reads "She's Not There" will instantly be reminded of the Madeleine McCann kidnapping in Portugal in 2007. The set-up is almost exactly the same: upscale hotel resort, upper middle class parents, child left in hotel room sleeping as parents have dinner in the hotel restaurant, child is abducted, parents are blamed without evidence, child is never found. The spin in this novel is to fast forward 15 years from a similar event, revisit all the characters, and see what effect this abduction has had on everyone involved.

The main character is Caroline Shipley, the mother whose two-year-old, Samantha, is abducted. Caroline's life has been shattered and her marriage has ended. Her other child, Michelle, a prickly pear of a daughter, is almost constantly at odds with her, and Caroline is desperate to repair that relationship. Caroline's ex-husband has some redeeming qualities but is most memorable for his philandering ways. I can't decide if Caroline's mother is a sociopath or just a narcissist: she has one decent moment in the entire book, and it comes near the end. Other characters include Peggy, the most decent and loyal character in the book, and Samantha herself, now 17, who contacts Caroline after having seen artists' renderings of what the abducted toddler might look like in the present. Once she finally shows up, Samantha is unfailingly decent, charming, and mature beyond her years.

The book is structured so that it alternates between the present and past, with some chapters taking place 15 years ago; others 6 years ago, and still others 5 years ago. With one exception, the chapters in the last 40% of the book take place in the present, and the mystery of who took Samantha and why is finally unraveled. The book is narrated from Caroline's point of view, with the exception of one chapter near the end, which switches to an omniscient point of view so that the reader can "get inside the head" of each of the main characters. This book is exceptionally fast-moving and plot-driven. I found the characters a bit one-dimensional and the dialogue unrealistic at times, but the events of the novel move along swiftly. Few will guess the outcome, but there is a lot of foreshadowing along the way, and if you review the novel a second time, you'll find it.

It is an easy read; some would call it a beach book. I recommend it for those who enjoy crime novels with a bit of family drama thrown in for good measure. "Beast" is an exotic, creative interpretation of "Beauty and the Beast." The tale begins in Persia, and our hero Prince Orasmyn has been cursed by a parsi--a fairy--for sacrificing a camel that had been defiled. Turned into a lion, he is told that his father will kill him the next day, and that the only thing that can break the curse is the love of a woman. He flees his palaces and gardens, journeying to India and eventually to France.
The rest of the tale follows the original fairytale closely, taking place in the French countryside, with gardens full of roses. But the thing that makes Napoli's version so different and such a delight is her ability to describe the exotic sights, sounds, colours, smells and tastes of Persia, the numerous Arabic and Farsi words sprinkled throughout the text, quotes from Sufi mystics and the Quaran, and Orasmyn's observations on the countries he travels through and life as a lion. This is my favourite retelling of "Beauty and the Beast" along with Robin McKinley's version.

Under Enemy Colors (2007) A sweeping novel of maritime mutiny set against the backdrop of the French Revolution. At the time of the French Revolution, one of Britain's most skillful naval officers, Charles Saunders Hayden, is a young lieutenant, the son of an English father and a French mother. His abilities and his loyalty to the king of England are beyond dispute, yet his career seems doomed by his "mixed" heritage and lack of political connections. Consequently, Hayden is assigned to an aging frigate, the Themis, under the command of Captain Josiah Hart, a man known as "Faint Hart" throughout the service. As the Themis takes to sea to harass the enemy, the disaffection of the crew begins to boil over into acts of violence, and the lieutenant finds himself caught between his superior and a crew pushed toward mutiny. A revolution at sea ensues, and Hayden is wrenchingly torn between honor and duty, as the magnificent Royal Navy engages the French in a centuries-old struggle for power.

A Battle Won (2010) Winter 1793--the Reign of Terror rips through revolutionary France, as every able-bodied man is pressed into military service. The city of Toulon has turned itself over to the British, the red ensign of Lord Admiral Hood's flagship Victory, offering a defiant symbol of protection to its people. In Plymouth, Master and Commander Charles Hayden is summoned to the Port Admiral--his orders are to return to the ill-fated frigate HMS Themis. Placed in temporary command, he is to join the escort for the last convoy of the season--braving the wintry seas to supply Hood's fleet in the Mediterranean. Hayden's uncanny knack for attracting the attention of the French navy sees the Themis thrown back into action only hours out of port. Soon Hayden's captaincy and military skills are stretched to the utmost as he finds himself at the vanguard of this brutal clash of empires.

A Ship of War (UK) / Take, Burn or Destroy (US) (2013) 1794, the height of the French Revolution--Charles Hayden sets off aboard the ill-fated HMS Themis with orders to destroy a French frigate sailing from Le Havre and to gather intelligence from a royalist spy. On discovering French plans for an imminent invasion of England, Hayden must return to Portsmouth to give warning before it's too late. But the enemy has been lying in wait for him, and so begins a dangerous chase out into the Atlantic and into the clutches of a powerful French squadron. After a thwarted attempt to masquerade as French sailors, Hayden and his officers are taken prisoner. A shipwreck following a storm and a case of mistaken identity befall Hayden and his men, as they try in desperation to escape in order to warn the Lords of the Admiralty. Failure will mean the invasion of England--and the guillotine for Hayden.

I've installed a lot of screen protector film--on cameras, cellphones, and 7" and 9" tablets--and until now I thought it would be impossible for anyone to make a screen protector for a large tablet that would go on bubble-free and also be invisible after the installation. This Moshi iVisor XT screen protector has proved me wrong.

Living in Houston, I have owned several weather radios in this price range over the years. This radio is my favorite.

I like the fact that you can re-charge it easily with AAA batteries (not included). I have found that re-charging with a hand-crank is too slow. Solar re-charging works well on most devices if you keep the device stored on a windowsill for the year so that it is fully charged during a weather event. Having the option to use three AAA batteries is great because the radio can be ready to use immediately. Another feature that I like is that no screwdriver is needed in order to open the compartment in order to change-out the batteries. This is important when evacuating and also when the power goes out.

During Hurricane Ike, I evacuated to a friend's home. The storm made landfall around midnight or so. In the dark, it is hard to find anything, so it's good to be ready before the lights go out. I can remember lying in bed alone listening to my friend's radio (not this radio) in the dark as the NOAA forecaster reported the progress of the surge up through Galveston Bay and into the bayous, lakes, and streams inland. It was so helpful to know exactly what was happening to the area in which I lived.

My friend's radio was a very expensive radio, and the main difference between her radio and this radio seems to be the reception.

Hers ran all night with no interruption with reception. With this radio, I do have to turn the radio off and then back on if I lose reception to the channel. A really expensive weather radio would probably have better reception if you want to listen non-stop.

For my needs, however, this radio is excellent and is the best that I have owned in its price range.

But instead he discovers that his father has died, his home is overrun by livestock and drunken servants, and Elizabeth, having believed Ross dead, is now engaged to his cousin. Ross must start over, building a completely new path for his life, one that takes him in exciting and unexpected directions? Also from the Publisher: Tired from a grim war in America, Ross Poldark returns to his land and his family. But the joyful he has anticipated turns sour, for his father is dead, his estate is derelict and the girl he loves is engaged to his cousin. But his sympathy for the destitute miners and farmers of the district leads him to rescue a half-starved urchin girl; from a fairground brawl and take her home - an act which alters the whole course of his life...

From the BBC - Intro Good evening, I'm Alistair Cooke. Tonight we begin a new series, called Poldark, based on the four novels of Winston Graham. It runs to sixteen episodes and I can only say that now is the time for the party to settle in to a spate of loving, dueling, poaching, smuggling, wenching, and marrying,--not to mention banking and copper mining. Copper mining plays a big part in this story because we are in the county of Cornwall in England at the end of the eighteenth century. I don't suppose today's tourists visit the copper mines, which are abandoned, but the Greeks and the Romans knew about them and at the end of the eighteenth century copper and tin were the main sources of wealth in a county that is otherwise practically treeless--barren but very beautiful. Those of you who have been there may have noticed those strange cones of pyramids on the horizon they are China Clay deposits. Maybe we should try to pin Cornwall down on the map. When I was a boy we were told that the map of Britain was that of a pig with a man on its back and it comes out very roughly like this [Cooke draws]. The trunk is England, with his very long head Scotland. The pig's face is Wales. And here what they call West Country which goes from Dorset, Somerset, Devon, and here is Cornwall the very end here is the tip of the island Lands' End. So we are in Cornwall, then, the end of the eighteenth century just at the close of the American Revolutionary War and the surrender of the British forces to George Washington and the Continental Army. The date, as any handy schoolboy will tell you, is 1783. And our hero, Captain Ross Poldark, who has been serving in George III's forces, has come home to Cornwall. He has just landed and is on his way home back to his estate, which has indifferent farming but two copper mines. It's called Nampara. During the War he has heard that his father is no longer alive, but his relatives don't know that he himself is alive. This is not surprising because during the war they didn't have any transatlantic mail service. In fact in this year of 1783, England saw its first domestic mail coach going between Bristol and London. So we open with Captain Poldark jogging home in a stagecoach to meet and amaze his friends.

This is a memoir about Cerrotti's grandmother, Hana Dubova, a Holocaust survivor. What I really love about We Share the Same Sky is the degree to which Cerrotti had access to her grandmother's journals and even to some of the people/relatives of the people who helped Hana or journeyed with her. This is also a memoir about the ten years Cerotti spent organizing family records, having them translated and following Hana's footsteps from Czechoslovakia to Denmark to Sweden and ultimately the United States. It is a love story between Cerrotti and her future husband Sergio, a Polish man she knew from England and caught up with in her travels. We Share the Same Sky is a unique take for me on a Holocaust survival story, because the Nazis allowed Hana's group of fourteen to sixteen year old Czech Zionists to leave their occupied country and travel to Denmark where they were sponsored by various families, pending a planned move to Palestine. Hana was happily settled on a Danish farm and never did go to Israel. She eventually had to leave in an overloaded boat bound for Sweden when Denmark was no longer safe for Jews under its own Nazi occupation. This is ultimately a book about relationships--- Hana's and her lost family's relationship; Hana's and Rachel's relationship; each of their relationships with the Danish farm family that fostered Hana; the Swedish fisherman that rescued the boatload of exiles from Denmark; the famous rabbi who traveled on that boat and his descendants; Hana's not so great first marriage; and Rachel's and Sergio's relationship that led to marriage and sorrow. It is a rich and loving accounting, meticulously researched and beautifully written.

Pasta is often a stand-by staple in busy households. It’s quick to prepare, cheap to keep on hand and almost always is better the second day. However, the problem is that for many homes and families, it is a tired, old crutch – plate of pasta with jarred sauce, sprinkled with cheese and served often. It’s not a bad choice, but it does get old, particularly when it comes up frequently. This book, “Simple. Elegant Pasta Dinners” aims to make pasta more interesting and memorable. It does accomplish this, often using additions that are not usually associated with pasta (at least not that I have seen before).

The author starts off with a primer on how to actually make your own pasta from scratch. It is by no means comprehensive, but it does explain how to mix the pasta dough and how to knead it into a tidy ball, complete with a pictorial walk-through at each step. If you have never made homemade pasta before, this is a good place to learn. Do note that the recipe offered uses all-purpose or “OO” flour, not semolina.

The recipes are divided up into four chapters corresponding to the seasons. This seems to be driven by the availability of ingredients based on the time of year. The vast majority of these recipes are savory dishes, though sprinkled in are a few dessert dishes here and there. You’ll find a variety of things to try – one-pot dishes, salads, reuse of leftovers, and more.

To be honest, there are several recipes in here that I personally would not try, based on the extra ingredients. For example, a couple of recipes I found call for artichokes. I don’t like artichokes (not even a little) so these are recipes I will skip. There are a number of them that are on my short list of ones to try, especially one that calls for roasted Brussels sprouts.

I would recommend actually reading the recipes through before passing judgment. One recipe title includes the expression “roasted hazelnut oil”. I had not heard of hazelnut oil and thought it would require a special trip to a high-end shop. Reading through, the recipe calls for roasted and crushed hazelnuts, and olive oil. Had I just gone based on the title I probably would have skipped this one.

Almost every recipe has a picture. It has been said that you first eat with your eyes, so this book does provide that initial “taste”.

This is one of the more unusual pasta books I have seen, read and used. It is full of very interesting ideas that are reasonably simple though at times unusual. If you’re looking for a way to vary your pasta fare, this is one book to consider.

Ever since living in Spain in 2005 and having the opportunity to visit the fabulous Art Nouveau museum Casa Lis in Salamanca and visiting Barcelona's Palau de la Musica Catalana, I've been in love with Art Nouveau, and I was looking for a way to translate that love into my favorite medium, counted cross stitch.

I was specifically looking for designs by Art Nouveau powerhouse Alphonse Mucha, but Art Nouveau Cross Stitch also offers designs by Louis Comfort Tiffany, Wiliam de Morgan, Gustav Klimt, Charles Rennie Mackintosh and others. Whether you're looking for feminine florals, bold Mackintosh roses, a stunning stained glass lake landscape (the same image featured on the recent Tiffany US postage stamp), or a brilliantly blue taste of Persia, you'll find numerous project ideas here from table mats to runners, pillows, clocks, and small motifs specially designed for napkins, greeting cards, book covers, coasters, pincushions and more. There's also a handy selection of Art Nouveau decorative borders for customizing your own projects.

The charts are in color, are very clear and it's easy to read the legends. Larger designs are presented in sections. There's also finishing instructions, and Hammet thoughtfully includes a section on basic techniques (fabrics, needles, general accessories). Many designs feature color photographs of the artwork that inspired them, and Hammet includes tidbits on various artists and on the Art Nouveau movement. Even if you're not a cross-stitcher, this is a beautiful book that offers plenty for art lovers as well as crafters.

The digital display is large enough to read from across a room. However, the display is NOT so bright that it will interfere with sleeping. The time is easy to program by sliding the “Lock” button, holding down the volume button until the correct time is displayed, and sliding the Lock button back to locked position.

Another nice feature is the battery backup. It takes two AAA batteries, and ensures that your alarm will go off on time even if you have a power outage while you’re sleeping.

POLTARNEES, BEHOLDER OF OCEAN

Toldees, Mondath, Arizim, these are the Inner Lands, the lands whose sentinels upon their borders do not behold the sea. Beyond them to the east there lies a desert, for ever untroubled by man: all yellow it is, and spotted with shadows of stones, and Death is in it, like a leopard lying in the sun. To the south they are bounded by magic, to the west by a mountain, and to the north by the voice and anger of the Polar wind. Like a great wall is the mountain to the west. It comes up out of the distance and goes down into the distance again, and it is named Poltarnees, Beholder of Ocean. To the northward red rocks, smooth and bare of soil, and without any speck of moss or herbage, slope up to the very lips of the Polar wind, and there is nothing else there by the noise of his anger. Very peaceful are the Inner Lands, and very fair are their cities, and there is no war among them, but quiet and ease. And they have no enemy but age, for thirst and fever lie sunning themselves out in the mid-desert, and never prowl into the Inner Lands. And the ghouls and ghosts, whose highway is the night, are kept in the south by the boundary of magic. And very small are all their pleasant cities, and all men are known to one another therein, and bless one another by name as they meet in the streets. And they have a broad, green way in every city that comes in out of some vale or wood or downland, and wanders in and out about the city between the houses and across the streets, and the people walk along it never at all, but every year at her appointed time Spring walks along it from the flowery lands, causing the anemone to bloom on the green way and all the early joys of hidden woods, or deep, secluded vales, or triumphant downlands, whose heads lift up so proudly, far up aloof from cities.

This well-written mystery novel picks up the "Three Pines" story in the aftermath of the disastrous factory raid chronicled in [[ASIN:0312626908 Bury Your Dead]]. The overall theme of the novel is "hope", as various continuing characters heal from recent, serious wounds (both internal and external). Chief Inspector Gamache is recovering well; Jean Guy Beauvoir, who is in constant pain, is recovering poorly. Olivier is hurting, finding himself to be almost an "outsider" in the village after his release from prison. Ruth is grieving, watching the skies daily for Rosa's return. Clara is finally getting her solo show, and is at last receiving the recognition she deserves as a painter--but her success has severely wounded her 25-year marriage.

The mystery plot centers around the murder of a much-hated art critic, who was once Clara's best friend. The critic's body is discovered in Clara's garden on the morning after a party that celebrated Clara's solo show. The discovery ruins what should have been "Clara's day" to bask in the glow of wildly favorable critical reviews. Inspector Gamache, who has attended both the show and the party as Clara's friend, is in Three Pines, and immediately takes over the murder investigation.

In Clara's extraordinary painting of the Virgin Mary (with Ruth as her model), a dot of white paint in the Virgin's eye conveys the idea of "hope"--unless the effect is merely a meaningless "trick of the light". The novel's theme of "hope" is further carried out, as new characters appear in the context of Alcoholics' Anonymous. The healing process required of recovering alcoholics plays a significant role in the events leading up to the murder. But Gamache, proceeding in his usual compassionate, stolid, careful fashion, eventually uncovers the well-hidden identity of the murderer, as well as the murderer's motives.

As is always the case with Louise Penny mysteries, A TRICK OF THE LIGHT is a thoroughly enjoyable read. The plot is well constructed and believable, the characterization is excellent, and the writing is smooth and skilled. Penny also displays again her considerable gift for describing scenes and artwork, so that the reader "sees" them as if looking at a photograph.

Inspector Gamache fans will not want to miss this latest chapter in the ongoing story. However, readers new to the series should read [[ASIN:B003STCQHK The Brutal Telling]] and [[ASIN:0312626908 Bury Your Dead]] first, as this is not a standalone mystery novel. Because of this, and the rather leisurely, drawn-out plot, I give this novel 4 stars.

As a longtime fan of Persian and Indian cuisines, I was intrigued when I saw my friend Marlene Spieler mention Niloufer Mavalvala's "The Art of Parsi Cooking." Despite my familiarity with Persian and some regional Indian cuisines, I was not familiar with Parsi culture. The Parsi are followers of the Prophet Zarathushtra. The Parsi (from the word "Pars," Iran), are Zoroastrians who migrated to India between the 8th to 10th centuries, and later their descendants who settled around the globe. Parsi cooking was largely shaped by Iran and India, and you'll find that both cultures feature prominently in Parsi dishes, from dry fruit and nuts (Shirini) lending sweetness to more pungent ginger, garlic, chilies and spices from India. The trinity of tikhu-khatu-mithu (spicy-sour-sweet) forms the underpinnings of Parsi cuisine.

The included dishes in "The Art of Parsi Cooking" are arranged by course, from appetizers such as scrambled eggs with spices and prawns in spices and beloved side dishes like eggs on potatoes, okra or tomatoes and fish with green chutney in banana leaves to main dishes like shrimp coconut curry and rice, chicken curry with vegetable palau, Sunday lamb roast, and chicken almond and yogurt curry. And of course, what meal is complete without a spot of dessert? You'll find the famous Parsi wedding dish of  Lagan nu Custard and almond and rice pudding to Parsi kulfi (burnt milk ice-cream with pistachio and almond) and ravo (semolina and egg pudding). Teatime snacks also offer a nice light pick-me-up, including butter biscuits, cake, and sweet pancakes. A discussion of spice blends is also included. Best of all, many of the spices and ingredients should be readily available in your local supermarket or Amazon (I've tried to cook from some "authentic" Indian cookbooks where I couldn't locate any of the regional veggies or obscure ingredients, so this is a huge relief!).

Each beautifully illustrated recipe comes with helpful tips, and I love that the book was printed with large, bold font for ingredients, making it easy to see and cook from. I loved the brown rice recipe; not to be confused with whole grain rice, this is basmati rice that gets its color from caramelized onions and is delicately spiced with cinnamon, cloves, peppercorn, and cardamom. The baked goods were also a fascinating and delicious departure from more syrupy, often-too-sweet Indian desserts such as gulab jamun; I loved the light, semolina-enhanced kumas and the delicately-spiced butter cookies.

As we move into fall and winter's chill, I look forward to cooking my way through more of these delicious, warming dishes that have sustained generations of Parsi cooks and families.

Author Lucy Main Tweet is a former "fashion leader" for Talbots, Evan Picone, J. Crew, and Bernard Chaus; during her professional career, her passion was needlepoint. When she left the fashion industry in 2008, she accepted her mother's suggestion, and took up knitting. Thus, by her own admission, she is a "novice knitter". Her lack of knitting experience really shows in KNITOLOGIE: CREATING PERSONAL HEIRLOOM KNITS.

As a novice knitter, Tweet got bored with casting on, knitting, purling, and casting off. So she decided to make a scarf, using these basic skills, that would be personalized with her own initials. As a result, the bulk of KNITOLOGIE consists of giant knitting stitch grids (not standard knitting charts), with numbered rows, that graph a design for each letter of the alphabet. In the accompanying photos, the letters are usually made in reverse stockinette on a stockinette background. (But of course they can be knit in stockinette on a reverse stockinette background; or all in stockinette or reverse stockinette if you use two colors of yarn.)

The remainder of the book consists of extremely simple patterns for square pillows, mittens, mitts, rectangular scarves, and baby caps--all of which use one or more letters from the alphabet grids. Brand-new knitters may find the alphabet and patterns useful, but they will have to look elsewhere for even the most basic how-to-knit instructions.

KNITOLOGIE is a beautifully designed book, expensively produced with lovely color photographs. It even has a ribbon bookmark--with a cardboard "swatch" square to weight it down--attached to the inside back cover. (Be careful when you open the book, or the ribbon will tear the book's back endpaper.) However, the book's production values do not make up for the lack of useful knitting content.

When I purchased this book, I expected a book with an assortment of knitted alphabets, possibly accompanied by a text discussing how to design attractive knitted monograms. (Such a book would be a welcome addition to my knitting book collection.) However, KNITOLOGIE has only one block-letter alphabet--and that alphabet is one that could be designed by anyone with a pad of graph paper.

As a hardcover, coffee-table-sized, 160-page book, KNITOLOGIE is probably priced reasonably at slightly under $22. But KNITOLOGIE should have been published, if at all, as an inexpensive leaflet or paperback for novice knitters like the author. Because the book is overproduced (and consequently overpriced considering the actual knitting content), I rate it at 2 stars ("I don't like it" on the official Amazon scale). For now, the Internet is still the best source for knitted alphabets to be used for personalizing your hand-knitted garments and accessories.

The author delves into the family history of Mimi and Don Galvin from Colorado who have 12 children (10 boys and 8 girls). Six of the boys develop schizophrenia.

This book is a combination of a riveting yet sad story and the researchers' need to determine the "why" behind the disease. Research into this disease has spanned from believing this mental illness is the result of a domineering mother (nuture) to genetic and now to epigentic (meaning genetic expression as a result of being turned on by environment and other non-genetic influences).

There are several things I learned in this text besides the family story and the search for a cure. 

- First, ignoring a problem is never a good strategy. Perhaps if the family did not keep secrets and instead discussed what was happening to the boys, a better solution could have resulted. 

- Second, I feel that there are major potential cures that never happen not because the science does not exist but because our society is governed by the need to make money. There were three times I felt the researchers mentioned in this book were close to isolating the cause or coming up with a solution for this awful disease. For instance, I wonder what discoveries could have been made had Lynn DeLisi who was studying the genetics of the disease had not had her family research project canceled by Pfizer. What would have happened if the natural substance called anabaseine that mimicked the function of nicotine and seemed to help those with the disease had its patent purchased instead of the pharmaceutical companies trying to create their own substance? Also, would they have been successful in developing a helpful pill if those same companies did not allow the marketing team in big pharma to dictate the dosage of pills they were trying to create. This resulted in a failed attempt at creating a useful substance due to the dosing requirements. The marketing department rules how pharmaceuticals make drugs because one dose per day sells better than many doses per day.

In summary, the dynamics of a family relationship is a profound hallmark of this book as is the research into of schizophrenia that remains a mystery as of today. This book is a well-researched and fascinating read.

There are a number of reasons that people choose to follow a vegan diet, among them including the health benefits of a plant-based diet, animal cruelty concerns and also just plain moral objections to animal-based foods. Regardless of the reasons, there is a need for resources for vegans to prepare good foods at home which is much cheaper that eating out at specialty restaurants. This book is one of many available for vegan cuisine and like most DK books I have seen it’s a good one. Interestingly, there are provisions made for non-vegan diners on many of the recipes included therein.

Full disclosure: I am not a vegan or even a vegetarian, I am a full-fledged meat eater. However, I recognize the healthy side of eating vegan and vegetarian dishes and I am not unwilling to forego meats, eggs, cheese and even fish. Some vegan dishes can actually be better-tasting than their non-vegan equivalents.

The first section of this book deals with a lot of basic information that many new to a vegan diet will find very interesting and informative. It’s not a simple “this is why you should eat a vegan diet” type of presentation, either – instead, this section discusses how to make substitutions for non-vegan ingredients, how to balance the diet, how the body uses different vitamin types an a lot more. For many this might be a review, but for others it very well may be a real eye-opener to the benefits of a healthy lifestyle. It avoids getting into philosophical discussion about why one lifestyle is better than another.

After all the introductory material and information, the book presents nine chapters of recipes broken down by type: Breakfast/Brunch, Snacks Foods, Soups/Stews, Burgers/Sandwiches/Wraps, Pasta, Grains, Salads/Side Dishes, One-Pot Meals and finally Desserts. The breakdown is logical and things are easy to find. The index at the back makes finding recipes easy and it is well organized (not all cookbooks are so lucky).

Almost every recipe has a full-color picture included which makes finding something that not only sounds interesting but looks good very simple to find. I especially like the section on soups and stews and have found several recipes to try in there. One recipe in particular stood out though – lentil & mushroom burgers. As odd as that may sound to a non-vegan, lentils actually make a pretty convincing substitute for ground beef (in fact, we occasionally have vegetarian tacos made with lentils in this house, and I actually prefer them to beef tacos for the better texture). That one is getting made shortly.

Where this book really shows that some serious thought went into it is in the “Flex It” tips with many of the recipes. These offer suggestions on what can be added to recipes to make them appeal more to traditional vegetarian diners, pescaterians and even meat-eaters. This makes the recipes a lot more flexible and appealing to more diners who might desire more than a straight vegan dish, without compromising the meal for the whole family. For example, one of the risotto recipes has a tip suggesting adding a little Parmesan after the fact to add cheese for the vegetarian, which can be done on a plate-by-plate basis. Another risotto recipe suggests adding a small amount of shrimp for the pescaterian, which again can be added per plate instead of to the whole dish.

Because of the willingness to make small, optional concessions to other dietary types, this book provides a great transitional path to go from most other diet types to a vegan lifestyle. For those that just have to have cheese or can’t live without just a little fish once in a while, the recipes presented herein provide a way to phase out the things that are non-vegan rather than an abrupt switch which may be distressing.

I like this book and am happy to recommend it. It presents a very good collection of well-thought-out recipes that follow a vegan lifestyle but can be tweaked and adjusted for non-vegan diners too. If you are a full-fledged vegan, you’re considering transitioning to vegan dining or you are just looking to reduce meats and dairy from your diet, this is a fine place to find some answers to questions and recipes to prepare. It’s well organized, well-thought-out and non-confrontational.

SUPERNOTES, co-authored by "Agent Kasper" and Luigi Carletti, is a "thriller based on the true story of Agent Kasper." It's well-written, but it reads more like a nonfiction memoir than a fictional thriller. Given that "Agent Kasper" is supposed to be an alias of "a top-level undercover spy who worked for both the CIA and the Italian intelligence services", the reader is probably safe in assuming that this "thriller" is, in fact, a thinly fictionalized account of an actual kidnapping and lengthy Cambodian incarceration of an Italian/American spy.

Being a news/information junkie, I found this book highly disconcerting to read. I really don't like filling my mind with suspect facts, and this book lacks an "Author's Notes" chapter--included in many historical-fact-based thrillers (e.g., [[ASIN:1250058449 The Patriot Threat: A Novel]])--to help the reader sort out fact from fiction. If the authors wanted the world to know about, and believe in, the "explosive secret" that Kasper uncovered, it might have been better for them to write an openly nonfictional account.

In this book, the Italian owner (Agent Kasper) of a Phnom Penh bar is warned by a Cambodian senator that he needs to get out of Cambodia immediately. Unfortunately, the warning comes too late, and Kasper is captured/kidnapped by military personnel at the border. His Italian family's wealth saves his life--as long as they can make payments to the captors, Kasper will be allowed to live.

Kasper is beaten and tortured, and imprisoned under the worst possible conditions. He has been working with "the Americans" to discover the source of the "supernotes" (nearly perfect forgeries of U.S. currency) that are flooding Southeast Asia. However, the Americans have callously abandoned him. Italian diplomats merely look the other way, when informed of the Cambodians' kidnapping of an Italian citizen. So it is up to Kasper's family, and the doggedly persistent lawyer that they hire, to obtain Kasper's release and his safe return to Italy.

Because SUPERNOTES isn't much of a thriller, and makes no attempt to help the reader sort fact from fiction, I rate it at a rather generous 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

Throw out what you thought you knew about flavor pairings; Luane Kohnke's "Sassy Cookies" will take your taste buds on an extraordinary flavor journey through sweet, spicy, and savory ideas inspired by Latin America, Europe, and Asia. In addition to recipes starring cayenne and cherry, chocolate and ginger, goat cheese and caramel, saffron and pistachio, and green tea and almond, you'll pick up handy tips and techniques for working with a variety of traditional doughs as well as gluten-free macarons, meringues, and cookies.

I received a galley of "Sassy Cookies" late this spring, and had the chance to make many of the recipes including the chocolate Mexican spice cookies, mocha chocolate wedding cakes, lemon yogurt squares, chocolate-ginger fudge shortbread cookies, gingerbread and pumpkin brownies, mango-coconut bars, flourless peanut butter cookies noir, black mission fig cookies, and fleur de sel cashew cookies. I loved the Asian-inspired green tea macarons and the nod to Latin America in the goat cheese and caramel-swirl brownies (I live in a city with a huge variety of Mexican and Latin American markets, so sourcing cajeta and dulce de leche is no problem!), the Italian-inspired polenta blondies, and the Eastern-inspired chai tea and chocolate butter cookies and cardamom-ginger bars.

Recipes are clearly laid out in an easy-to-read font (ingredients are handily printed in contrasting red, baker's notes are in bold), and each recipe comes with a beautiful minimalist photo starring the featured baked good front and center, oftentimes surrounded by an artful deconstruction of its ingredients.

I loved that the book includes a wide variety of baked goods, from savories that make great cocktail / appetizer nibbles (black olive bites, blue cheese and cranberry cookies, Parmesan cheese coins with mascarpone filling, savory cheddar cocktail cookies) to sandwich cookies, bar cookies, and a good number of delicious gluten-free alternatives that don't rely on specialty GF flours or starches (the peanut butter noir and fleur de sel cookies both use a base of nut butter and sugar; the meringues and macarons rely on egg whites and almond flour).

My current favorites are the addictive chocolate Mexican spice cookies (with plenty of bittersweet chocolate, dried cherries, and a hint of heat from the cayenne) modeled after Lindt's chocolate, chili, and cherry bar, and the gingerbread and pumpkin brownies, which are perfect for fall. Both received rave reviews from my testers; the next time I make the gingerbread and pumpkin brownies, I am going to add some softened cream cheese to the pumpkin filling and sprinkle some chopped crystallized ginger on top for even more of a ginger kick! The fleur de sel cashew cookies were also a hit; I sprinkled my favorite salt [[ASIN:B006DVQBBM Falksalt Crystal Flakes Natural Sea Salt Natural 4.4 Oz]] on top. These will be an occasional splurge for me, though, as the cheapest jar of organic cashew butter in my neck of the woods goes for close to fourteen dollars! I have plenty of other recipes bookmarked as well that I am eager to try.

Verdict: "Sassy Cookies" is a must-have in any baker's collection and is sure to spice up your baking!

[[VIDEOID:7df4af9f322ab66be9930e7e573597d9]] So here is what I'm looking for in a photography field guide - information that helps me when I need it in the field. I have long owned and treasured [[ASIN:0817435425 Art of Bird Photography: The Complete Guide to Professional Field Techniques (Practial Photography Books)]] and there are a few crucial pages I ended up photocopying and putting in my photograph bag. They have simple graphics for considerations you need to make when photographing white birds against a dark background or vice versa. That is the kind of information I was hoping was in this book. And to a degree it was here.

Due to the small format of the book and the very small sized text, this book should have focused on what is needed in the field. The middle of Bosque Del Apache is not the time to debate .jpeg vs RAW but it is the time to get some quick hints about capturing flight photos. Digital Photography 101 should be left to a bigger book you can enjoy at home with full sized text.

I wish that rather than discussing what to look for in a DSLR, it had an annotated checklist of what to pack for your trip. I'm not knocking the authors for their content, it is all solid, but due to the format I wish they stuck to the immediate field needs. To stereotype, Birdwatchers have aging eyes and it is a slog to read the text cover to cover due to the tiny font size. It would have been nice to find pages on those in the field needs, like those charts in Morris' book, how should I handle a backlit flight shot of a overflying eagle. How should I use fill flash to light a roosting owl. How do I use the histogram (which is covered well in this book.) Also it would be nice to have a cold weather section focusing on camera care and exposure hints to shoot in a snowy winter landscape. Well I guess there is my million dollar idea for what it's worth, a field guide focused on what you actually need when you are in the field.

What I do like is the coverage of post photography. It is complete but not exhaustive. I like that the book is full of beautiful and inspiring photographs, although the book has a European bias in photos and content. And I like the content in general, just doesn't all fit the format.

See accompanying video for details on size.

Summary

A very good book that may not be exactly what I was hoping for, but well worthwhile. Text is small enough to be a chore to read. Beautifully illustrated. With these caveats, I would recommend it.

I spent every evening over two full weeks reading this book. This is neither an easy read nor a quick one. The author believes in conservation and letting wildlife live out their lives in nature where they belong. In this text she describes her extensive personal travels to Africa (Chad, South Africa, etc.) and Asia (Loas, Thailand, Vietnam, etc.) in search of all the animals served as food and used for medicine or illegal trade. She expertly describes the plight of the abundant poached wildlife without becoming overly gruesome except in a couple of rare cases. Asians, Africans, Americans, etc. and the top echelon of society partake in Pangolin for meat and scales, elephants for ivory, rhino horn for medicine, civet for meat, bear for bile, etc. etc. Many believe with a religious ferocity that these animal parts cure various ailments. Others do not believe it but feel superior in being able to dominate an animal by hunting or just because they want to eat something exotic.

The author tries very hard to describe the complexity of why illegal animal hunting continues and she does a pretty good job. Sometimes measures taken to help an animal wind up hurting it via a bending of the rules imposed by CITES (the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora) or the regulations of a particular country. On the positive side, she also mentions the good work of a couple of sanctuaries helping to save some of these animals, but it appears to be a revolving door with no elimination in site.

Most of what is written in this book I already knew. However I did learn a few things. For instance, I thought all animal medicine was hocus-pocus but bear bile actually works. However, a synthetic form works just as well, so there is no need to use bears. It is the high concentration of ursodeoxycholic acid in the bile which may slow the progression of some diseases; however, one may get sick form the bile because it is full of other things like pus, etc. as a result of the harvesting. It never ceases to amaze me how humans can be so utterly cruel.

Overall, I am glad Rachel Love Nuwer wrote this book. It was a difficult read both due to the subject matter and also due to so many facts and places she visited that caused me to re-read passages to ensure I understood what was being said.

Like author Terry Gamble (of Proctor and Gamble lineage), I've spent nearly every summer of my life in and around Harbor Springs, Michigan, a small Northern Michigan resort community on the Little Traverse Bay. Gamble has drawn from her childhood memories spent on Harbor Point to create the lush settings for Water Dancers, using thinly veiled pseudonyms for Harbor Point (Beck's Point), Harbor Springs (Moss Village), Petoskey (Chibawasee), and Cross Village (Horseshoe Lake).
The novel's protagonist, Rachael Winnapee, is a sixteen-year old Odawa orphan from Horseshoe Lake who, since the death of her grandmother, has lived at the Indian School in Moss Village (the actual school is alongside the Holy Childhood of Jesus Catholic Church in Harbor Springs), and like many First Nations orphans, is sent to be a domestic at Beck's Point.
The novel begins in 1945. Rachael ends up serving the March family from St. Louis. The March's sons are both overseas fighting, Lip in Belgium and Woody in the Pacific Theater. When Lip is killed in battle and Woody comes home an amputee and morphine addict, it is up to Rachel to help make Woody whole. The two begin a brief, intense love affair, sealed with seashells, hidden gifts, lovemaking in dunes, shallows and empty rooms, and finally, Rachael's unwanted pregnancy.
Rachel raises her son Ben on her own, continuing to live with the midwives who delivered her child. After nine years of helping out on their farm, Rachel moves back to Horseshoe Lake with Ben. The novel fast forwards to Ben's experiences fighting in Vietnam and his difficult readjustment to civilian life, and culminates in an unexpected and explosive conclusion in which the past is confronted and old ghosts laid to rest.
Water Dancers is a multifaceted novel of healing (three of the main characters are veterans), of class and race, duty, discovering inner strength, and seeking peace. The characters are poetically and lovingly crafted, down to the most minor details. Terry Gamble's first novel deliciously brings to life the many moods of water and forest that dominate life in Northern Michigan, and for those who are familiar with Northern Michigan, like Rachael's habit of licking stones, this novel will bring you home.

This is an enlightening, entertaining, and tremendously educational book on the act of dumpster diving. John Hoffman is a true trash seeker who shows the reader how to be self-sufficient by procuring their food, clothing, information, and other material in the trash and many times bartering or selling those items at flea markets, consignment shops, etc.

He demonstrates the best diving technique, diving etiquette, what to wear when diving, how to avoid the police, how to act, what to look for, and offers up various stories on what foods to eat from the trash, how to test them, as well as dispels many myths about trash that we have in our society.

There are beliefs of his that I found hard to accept and some of which are contradictory. For example, on one hand he will test dumpster food on his animals or pets to see if they get sick or die yet on the other hand he becomes incredibly angry that people will throw out their living plants. He advocates lying on a small scale - like sending in mailers with fictitious names or information to get free products. Although he appears a little less than ethical at times, there is no question his book is valuable for the true dumpster diver and from personal experience I know he is telling the truth.

My first experience with dumpster diving for food was when I six or seven years old. I was on Mulberry Street in Newark, NJ which is an area of several blocks of meat and fruit and vegetable vendors. My parents encountered an old couple who were eating watermelon from the trash. This couple explained to my parents that they didn't have enough money to live on their Social Security check and this allowed them to eat. It was at that moment that I learned this was an option for survival. This couple was right and that food was safe because often the Mulberry Street vendors would throw bruised fruit in the trash that patrons would not buy. It was perfectly good food; although I've never eaten such stuff and hope I never will.

I also have a few friends who have found wonderful items in the trash. In fact I purchased a beautiful mirror that hangs on my wall for $20 from an "all proceeds go to the animals" yard sale where I was told it was found next to someone's trash. I knew a store manager whose store use to throw away lots of new seasonal items and bird seed that wouldn't sell. There's certainly lots of stuff to find--some good and some not so good. I have another friend whose son found lots of nice furniture sitting by the dumpster when someone was moving; I even couldn't believe it was destined for the dump when I saw the items.

I'm big on donating items I no longer want, however, many people are not and prefer instead to just throw them out. I have another friend who throws beautiful stuff in the trash. One time she had bags of clothes that I told her I would come pick up for charity. She couldn't wait the 20 minutes it would take me to get to her house and decided to throw the items in the trash while I was driving to her. I pulled two big black garbage bags full of freshly laundered and folded clothes from her trash containers. In fact, there were several pairs of jeans with the store tag still on them.

I think this book will enrage some; but in general I think it's an in-depth tome about the art and science of dumpster diving for those who live on the extremes of self-sufficiency whether they need to or not. I bet the author would be proud that I paid nothing for this text having checked it out of the library.

I believe dumpster divers are creative people and creative people never look at things the same way mainstream America does. For instance, all my life when I see a wishing well I look at it as a form of income and think to myself "what a waste of perfectly good money." I'm sure the author would agree.

This author is certainly a fellow that I think would be interesting to meet; although I would never want to eat at his dinner table--he talks a lot about the food he gets from the trash.

Anyone who has an open mind would probably find "The Art & Science of Dumpster Diving" exceptionally interesting and educational.

Even after using both MX Master 2 and 3, my favorite mouse still is the Proteus Core G502. Does that mean I don't like the Master 2 or 3? Yes and no. Yes to 2, no to 3.

I prefer wired mice (yes, I said "mice"). The additional tools I get from the software for the G502 allow me to customize the G502 far more than I can with either the Master 2 or 3 (both use the same software). With dual monitors, the G502 creates for a seamless work environment. I no longer game, and still the G502 reigns supreme in my hand.

The Master 2 I received gratis from work. It was an arduous request to grant, but eventually my employer succumbed. However, I was far from impressed. I have small-ish hands for an adult, and found the Master 2 too large for comfort. I use a hybrid claw grip, and felt the Master 2 to be a ball in my hands.

But the Master 3 is a worthy upgrade that I recommend to those who are in the similar boat as me. To me, the Master 3 leveled some of that bump; now it contours comfortably to the shape of my palm. My only qualm is the back and forward buttons. They aren't where my thumb seems to want to find them, and oftentimes I miss pressing them.

Nevertheless, this is my go-to mouse at home.

Q- see 12 camera security system is a nice way to protect a home or business from threats. Install the cameras in different sections of the home or company and then access from home, online, etc. for top level security.

This security system seems much more complicated than it really is and the reason, I think, is due to the number of cameras. Looking at all of those cameras, out of the box, is a little bit intimidating and it leads one to believe that setup will take days and even weeks to complete. But it is actually much simpler than it looks and there is no need to install all 12. Just use the number of cameras you feel is necessary and store the rest for later use.

With this security system in place, you can access the live feed through the internet and even on your mobile phone via the Q- See applications. This is great for convenience and its one of the security systems best features. Other security systems have this feature as well, so it’s nothing unique. But it is very easy to use and it lets you monitor specific places on a property, for maximum security. Wherever you might be, home or away, you can take a look at what’s going on by pulling the mobile phone from your pocket. It doesn’t get much easier than that.

The one issue I have with this system is the same one others have complained about, and that is the wires. In the modern world in which we live, we expect wireless technology more and more. This system is wired and it could present some problems as you try to tape wires and otherwise conceal them from view. If this was a wireless system and I could place the cameras anyplace I like, then I would be hard pressed to find much wrong with this product. But I know many people who would likely reject this product immediately for this reason alone.

Security is important, especially for those who live in less safe areas or who operate a small business in a vulnerable area. With Q- See watching the home or business, you can feel a little more at ease. The cameras detect motion and can quickly help you catch a person in the act of theft, trespassing, or vandalism, providing proof positive of what happened and where. Like I said, the lack of wireless technology is a problem but if you can get past that issue, you will find that this is a very good security system for home or business needs.

I was always impressed with the room filling "surround" sound of my boyfriend's two Bose wave units. In my opinion, this system delivers that same quality audio I am used to hearing.

Besides the tabletop unit, a slim remote control, demo CD, power cord, and instructions are included in the box.

PROS

- Setup is exceptionally easy.

- The sleek design has no visible buttons.

- The slim intuitive remote is operable from up to twenty feet away. It worked for me even when the unit was not within sight. The battery is included and installed. Battery replacement requires a CR2032 or DL2032 3-volt lithium button cell battery

- It has a touch top which provides the ability to tap the top center part of the console to turn the unit on or off. Of course, those with animals might find the unit being toggled on and off by their furry companions.

- There is excellent surround sound which comes through crisp and clear. The radio required optimal placement in my house in order to receive the stations without minimal static. I actually have both AM and FM antennas on order.

- It has a sleek design and beautiful espresso black color.

- It has an integrated AM/FM tuner and the front display displays the text of music playing.

- It has a CD player that also plays MP3 music files recorded on a CD-R / CD-RW discs. I played an MP3 CD fine. In my case, only the names of the songs were displayed at the beginning of each song followed by only the track for the remainder of the play. I suspect this has something to do with the way this CD was recorded. There are also different play modes available when playing an audio CD such as normal play, shuffle repeat, repeat track, etc. (NOTE: The CD player is not for use with mini-CDs.)

- There are two alarms available.

- There are 6 presets for AM and 6 presets for FM available and are simple to program.

-There is an auxiliary input to enable playback from an audio device and a headphone jack for private listening. The audio through the headphones is as crisp, clear, and smooth as without headphones.

- A demo CD is included that wonderfully demonstrates the sound range.

- The digital clock and LED display is easily readable.

- Most system settings are permanently maintained even during a power outage or if the system is unplugged with the exception that the clock time is maintained for only 48 hours in backup memory during a power outage.

- It has a sleep timer from 10 to 90 minutes. It remembers the last sleep setting that was set and increments up from that.

- I called Bose twice asking pre-purchase questions about the Bluetooth options and also about an AM antenna recommendation (the Terk AM Advantage). Each time they answered quickly and were very helpful. The number for Bose is in the comments section of this review.

CONS

- An optional $99 Bluetooth adapter needs to be purchased to wirelessly stream music, movie sound, etc. from smartphone, tablet, laptop, or other Bluetooth device. I ordered the [[ASIN:B007ZG03DG Bose Wave Bluetooth Music Adapter]] and plugged it into the Bose Link port to test their optional adapter. Adding the additional Bluetooth adapter takes away from the sleek design and increases the footprint of the unit as a result of have to attach an extra component. Since this external adapter can only pair one Bluetooth device at a time, I had to turn the Bose on, then press AUX to cycle it to Bluetooth. Once there, I pressed the 5 button to make it discoverable. Since it remembers the last device I paired, I did not have to make it discoverable again. However, if I wanted to pair a new device, I had to press the 6 key until the unit beeped (about 10 seconds) and then it would clear the Bluetooth memory and become discoverable again. One negative I did see with the external adapter is that the volume is about half that with Bluetooth enabled. What I mean by this is that a volume of 30 on the radio sounds like 15 when paired with Bluetooth. I found that I had to double the volume when using the Bose Bluetooth adapter I purchased.

- No AM or FM antenna is included. This is not a terrible CON as for most people antennas should not be needed. I live in northwestern NJ and could not receive any AM stations until I moved the unit toward the window. I went to the Bose store and the fellow there said the power cord acts as the AM antenna (the manual did not say this). He suggested I call Bose directly. When I did call, they recommended the [[ASIN:B000069EUW Terk Indoor AM Antenna ADVANTAGE]]. I also ordered a [[ASIN:B00ZXI2MJG FM Antenna Male with 3.5 Jack Adapter]] for the FM radio. I will update this review with the results of both antennas once I receive and test them.

In summary, this tabletop Bose wave music system provides premium, crisp and clear, high-performance surround sound. However, Bluetooth capability should be both integrated into the unit and standard. The absence of integrated Bluetooth with this wave system is like buying a cook pot without an attached handle and having to purchase a "detachable" handle separately. Although most people will not require an antenna for radio reception, that might be a required purchase for some. I actually had to spend $152.10 for the additional Bluetooth and the two antennas. At a minimum, most people will have to shell out $640 (with tax) just to have a Bluetooth enabled system. If antennas are also needed, the full purchase price will be about $687. If this Bose unit had integrated Bluetooth, I would have rated this five stars. Despite the lack of Bluetooth, the incredible Bose sound comes through loud and clear.

UPDATE 9/24/2015 - I received the [[ASIN:B000069EUW Terk Indoor AM Antenna ADVANTAGE]] and tried it "wirelessly" (meaning in proximity of without the wired connection) with this Bose and it did not work to improve AM reception at all when I dialed into the stations on the antenna. I also tried it wirelessly on my [[ASIN:B013G6TMUS ION Block Rocker Bluetooth Portable Speaker System IPA76C]] and on another older system I had and it also did not work. Instead I wound up wiring this to the AM ports on the back of my older system (not a Bose) and only then did this AM antenna work. Unfortunately, I found this use for this Bose because I did not see a way to "wire" it to the music system. (For those who are interested, the link to my review of this antenna is in the comments section of this review.)

UPDATE 9/25/2015 - I received the [[ASIN:B00ZXI2MJG FM Antenna Male with 3.5 Jack Adapter]] for the FM radio today and plugged it into the FM antenna port on the Bose. No matter how I manipulated this FM antenna, it did nothing to increase reception of the FM stations. Unfortunately, this antenna purchase was useless for me as well and very disappointing.

ANYTHING FOR YOU: A NOVEL (Valerie Hart) is professionally written, but it’s annoying to read. The story unfolds in two parallel plots. One plot details the detective’s murder investigation; the other (printed in italics because it’s all in flashback) describes the murderer’s background, careful planning, and motives.

At least a third of the novel is flashback, and the italics are hard to read. Also, the parallel plot structure means there are a lot of cliffhanger chapters, which require the reader to frequently switch gears between the two unfolding stories. I personally dislike this sort of novel structure, and generally read the flashback chapters sequentially. With this particular novel, it’s a bad idea to read ahead with the flashbacks, because the flashback story really spoils the investigative plot.

The gist of the novel is that an attorney is murdered in his bedroom (with a claw hammer and a knife); his wife is severely wounded (with a knife), but survives. The perp appears from the beginning to have been the black-clad person who was seen by a neighbor in his adjoining back yard shortly before the murders. The identity of the intruder is soon known--he is a recently released felon whose DNA and fingerprints are all over the murder scene. However, the perp has disappeared from sight.

The investigation is complicated by the fact that the lead detective (Valerie Hart) once nearly had a one-night stand with the murder victim. Both detective and victim were too drunk to do anything. But because the detective doesn’t take herself off the case, she ends up with lots of explaining to do to her boss and her husband. She is also pregnant, and the investigation has her thinking a lot about mother/child relationships, and about how far a mother should go to protect her child.

The conclusion of the novel is unsatisfying, because the attorney’s behavior that ultimately provoked his murder is NOT particularly believable. It is trotted out at the end of the novel without much reader preparation. None of the characters are particularly likeable, either. The plot theme itself isn’t original or new. At the end, I felt that the novel was a waste of time, since it wasn’t very entertaining.

This ELGATO THUNDERBOLT 2 DOCK allows you to use a single Thunderbolt cable to connect all of your wired peripherals (monitors, backup drives, headphones, etc.) to your Thunderbolt-capable Mac or PC. The Elgato dock (priced about $230) costs quite a bit less than the [[ASIN:B00NAWCU7G Belkin Thunderbolt 2 Express HD Dock]] (about $300), but the Belkin dock ships with a longer Thunderbolt cable (3.3 ft. instead of 1.6 ft.), and seems to be more sturdily built. Also, the Belkin dock is more attractive (to my eye), because it's designed to look like something more than just another desktop hub. The two docks have nearly identical footprints (the Elgato is about 1/2" shorter in length), and both are powered hubs.

The docks are substantially the same in type and number of ports. In front, the Elgato has one stereo headphone port (stereo output), one mono microphone port (mono input), and one USB 3.0 port. In back, the Elgato dock has two Thunderbolt 2 ports, one HDMI port, one Gigabit Ethernet port, and two USB 3.0 ports. In front, the Belkin dock has one headphone/microphone port (audio in/out), and one USB 3.0 port. In back, the Belkin dock has two Thunderbolt 2 ports, one HDMI port, one Gigabit Ethernet port, two USB 3.0 ports, and one headphone/speaker port (audio out). Both docks promise that you can daisy chain up to four additional Thunderbolt devices (five total); and that you can have dual displays if you have a Thunderbolt monitor, by using a Thunderbolt port for that monitor and the HDMI port for a second monitor.

With either dock, I can set up a desktop with all my wired peripherals, and have them instantly available to my MacBook Air (via the one Thunderbolt connection) whenever I have real work to do. I just plug the laptop into the dock--I don't have to plug each peripheral into an appropriate laptop port, because the peripherals are already plugged into the dock. If I want to travel somewhere with the MacBook Air, or just take it downstairs for checking email at breakfast, all I have to do is shut it down and disconnect the single Thunderbolt cable.

I listen to a lot of music, usually electronic music though I listen to a little of everything. I have worked with a lot of different speakers and I have gotten very sensitive to the strengths and weaknesses that speakers bring to the table. I had high hopes for this speaker – I have always had excellent results with Yahama products so I expected the same from this speaker. It has not disappointed me.

The speaker itself is about the size of a cantaloupe – not huge but not tiny either. It's the right size for a bookshelf or as part of a larger sound system.

I did not completely understand what was meant by “MusicCast” until I started working with this speaker. In short, it is a wireless speaker that communicates over a wireless network (not Bluetooth). Using an appropriate device (like an Android tablet) the speaker is easily connected to the network and the software on said computing device allows for turning the speaker on and off and for streaming music to it. My service of choice is Pandora, and I had no trouble at all streaming a channel from Pandora to this speaker. The software comes into its own when you have more than one speaker, all of which get controlled separately and can stream different music from the same source device. So, given a sufficient budget (these speakers are not cheap), you can have different music playing in different rooms, all controlled from the same device.

The application is not perfect though I have been able to do everything I want with it – play music from local storage, stream from a service, increase/decrease volume and twiddle the sound profile a bit.

The sound quality is excellent, particularly when given a little volume. The bass is solid but not overwhelming which is great – the trend of late is to overdrive the bass which drowns out the rest of the sound profile, so having the bass not overpowering the overall profile is a big plus with me. The midrange is excellent as well and the music has the right depth as a result. The highs are bright and crisp. At lower volumes, the bass washes out which is has been the case with every speaker I have used. At higher volumes, I was unable to get the speaker to distort.

I am very happy with this speaker. I primarily use with with my tablet to stream music from Pandora, though it is useful for playing music from other sources too. It is expensive, but the sound quality is definitely there. If you like the idea of being able to add multiple speakers to your sound array and you want to design your sound system from the ground up, this is a good choice.

I ordered A SHOT IN THE DARK: A CONSTABLE TWITTEN MYSTERY because a national newspaper reviewer labeled it “the funniest mystery of the year 2018”. Well, it’s written as a farce, and funny at times, but it has an unpleasant darkness underneath that destroys the humor and fun. I shouldn’t have ignored my personal rule, which is to always avoid novels that borrow their titles from other famous literary, dramatic, or comedic works (e.g., [[ASIN:6305308713 Peter Seller’s “A Shot in the Dark”]]).

In the novel, a too-clever-by-half young constable (Twitten) arrives in Brighton, where the police (Steine and Brunswick) are in total denial about the existence of crime in the seaside resort. When crimes are reported, they dismiss them as too baffling to be solved, or accept any faked evidence that will allow them to close a case.

Twitten annoys his superiors and upsets the comfortable status quo by easily solving all the outstanding cases. In the end, he is outsmarted by an equally clever Master Criminal, and the status quo is restored by (1) an unbelievable event that removes a threat to a main character; and (2) the machinations of the Master Criminal.

The novel ends with a mild cliffhanger that suggests there may be more “Inspector Twitten” novels to come. If there are, I won’t be reading them. The novel is professionally written and plotted (with elaborate plot twists), but there isn’t a single character that I really liked.

First, let me say that I had high hopes for this book. I have not read anything by Carolyn Curtis James before, but loved the premise of the book. Nothing in the description of the book prepared me for that possibility. I do not think such stories should be quieted, however, a warning to readers about such things would have been nice.
After reading the book, it seems I should have read [[ASIN:0307387097 Half the Sky: Turning Oppression into Opportunity for Women Worldwide (Vintage)]]. Carolyn Curtis James seems to reference this book in almost every chapter, telling you something else she read in that book.
This book felt very disjointed to me. Carolyn doesn't do a very good job of making clear, concise points. In fact, I had a hard time figuring out just what she was getting at constantly. I don't think the book accomplished it's purpose, which would be to "recapture God's global vision for women." There was nothing clear about what women should be doing that they are not currently. No insight into the cultural vs. Biblical tug of war we find ourselves in.
What this book did do was start an internal dialogue for me. It started me toward thinking about where women are in my own church. It prompted me to begin thinking about how I am using my gifts for the Kingdom.
I do see that half the church is left out, or sold a smaller version of the gospel. I see that women are not given the ministry opportunities within the church. I do see how the church's view of women can harm our evangelistic efforts. However, this book didn't give me anything to rectify the situation in my life or in my circle of influence. It only gave me points to begin thinking on.

Much like his groundbreaking Plenty: Vibrant Recipes from London's Ottolenghi, Jerusalem once again finds Yotam Ottolenghi (and Sami Tamimi) exploring fabulous marriages of tastes, textures and colors inspired by the Middle East. Here, Jerusalem is the backdrop for a love song to the city's cuisine. Despite the historical tension between the city's Arab and Jewish residents, there are marked similarities in their respective cuisines (cucumber and tomatoes in an Arab / Israeli salad, kebabs and kibbeh, stuffed and pickled vegetables). Centuries of Jewish immigration by various Jewish populations loan a wealth of flavor profiles unique to their respective traditions (if you're looking for kosher recipes, there are discussions on kosher cooking, but read the ingredients to make sure; the lamb meatball recipe calls for yogurt as a topping).

You'll find recipes inspired by Jerusalem's local fruits and vegetables, including the fabulous roasted sweet potatoes and fresh figs, with its hint of heat from red chile and tartness from goat's milk cheese and balsamic vinegar, roasted butternut squash and red onion with tahini and za'atar, or the Swiss chard with tahini, yogurt and buttered pine nuts. There is a whole chapter devoted to stuffed vegetables, including such gems as lamb-stuffed quince with pomegranate and cilantro, stuffed eggplant with lamb and pine nuts, and stuffed artichokes with peas and dill.

Meat plays a starring role, largely variations on chicken, lamb and the occasional veal, but you'll also find pan-fried sea bass with harissa and rose petals, olive oil-poached tuna, and salmon steaks in chraimeh sauce. Vegetarians will delight in the savory pastries; my favorite was the red pepper and baked egg galettes and the labor-intensive (but worth it) herb pie. You'll even find Georgian mainstay khachapuri enhanced with halloumi and feta.

Finally, the sweet end to the meal: like many Middle Eastern cuisines, the desserts in Jerusalem lean toward desserts soaked or brushed with sugar syrup, including sweet filo cigars, the goat-cheese-sweetened mutabbaq, semolina, coconut and marmalade cake. European influence is evident in the beautiful, insanely addictive spice cookies studded with dark chocolate, lemon zest, orange zest, and a variety of spices, which have their roots in Germany and Italy. The showstopping chocolate krantz cakes take more than a day to make, but are well worth the effort.

Recipes are given in American and metric measurements in a large, easy-to-read font (ingredients are written in bold). Each recipe has an introduction with a brief history of the dish's origin or a personal memory from Yotam (who grew up in Jewish West Jerusalem) or Sami (who grew up in Muslim East Jerusalem).

The lavish photographs of Jerusalem's Arab and Jewish markets and restaurants are as much a feast for the eyes as the gorgeous photos of recipes, whether it's a shelf of hookah pipes, a group of elderly friends playing backgammon, or yellowed family photos. Along with the recipe backstories, these candid portraits really bring the city to life.

This is a beautiful tribute to Jerusalem, a unique culinary and cultural crossroads. The focus continues the strong flavor and texture pairings in Yotam's previous cookbook Plenty: Vibrant Recipes from London's Ottolenghi, which is still a mainstay in my kitchen. The vast majority of ingredients should be easy enough to come by in a large supermarket, and the results, like Plenty, are simply amazing. Jerusalem gets my vote for top cookbook of 2012, and I don't doubt it will be nominated for the James Beard and IACP awards.

42 year Edward, from the previous book THE 600 HOURS OF EDWARD, has Asperger's syndrome. He lives in Billings, Montana on a rigid schedule that gives him the control and structure he needs to be comfortable.

* He's been downsized from his job.
* his wonderful therapist has retired (she brilliantly told him to write complaint letters but not mail them).
* His best friends (Kyle & Donna who Edward meets in book 1) have moved away.
* his nightly ritual watching Dragnet reruns (COLOR ONLY) has been disrupted.

Then Donna calls with news that her son Kyle is in trouble. Edward makes the bold decision and drives to visit them in Boise!

Kyle is no longer the awesome boy from book 1 and is now a snotty preteen.

Edward makes another bold decision and decides to take Kyle on a road trip to Colorado! To a small town where Edward remembers he once spent a summer with his now deceased father (previously he of the monthly in person meeting, the rest of the month communication is through lawyers).

They argue (in Edward's own unique way) about football and music and have the anticipated Edward daily disasters.

Sheila Renfro, an alluring and eccentric motel owner, holds the potential of a lifetime of surprises, if she has her way.

THE 600 HOURS OF EDWARD: thirty-nine-year-old with Asperger's syndrome and obsessive-compulsive disorder, Edward Stanton lives alone on a rigid schedule in the Montana town where he grew up. His carefully constructed routine includes tracking his most common waking time (7:38 a.m.), refusing to start his therapy sessions even a minute before the appointed hour (10:00 a.m.), and watching one episode of the 1960s cop show Dragnet each night (10:00 p.m.) But when a single mother and her nine-year-old son move in across the street, Edward's timetable comes undone. Over the course of a momentous 600 hours, he opens up to his new neighbors and confronts old grievances with his estranged parents. Exposed to both the joys and heartaches of friendship, Edward must ultimately decide whether to embrace the world outside his door or retreat to his solitary ways. Heartfelt and hilarious, this moving novel will appeal to fans of Daniel Keyes's classic Flowers for Algernon and to any reader who loves an underdog.
