I have gotten more into creative photography and I have enjoyed playing with lens filters like these. I have worked with star filters in the past and I thought it might be fun to experiment with this light streak filter as well. So far I have no complaints, though it is the type of filter that should be used sparingly.

This is a gold streak filter that works in the same way as star filters, only it channels light in a straight line across the frame instead of in multiple directions. That is, it can make lights look smeared as if swept from one direction in a straight line. The color of the filter lines alters the light slightly and it has a mildly warming effect.

Some thought went into this filter and it allows for turning the filter (similar to a CPL) so that it can channel light in any single direction.

As with any filter like this, it should be used sparingly. It is possible to have too much of a good thing and as such this can easily be overdone. When used properly and used infrequently it can make some very striking and impactful photos.

It seems to be well made. There are no hitches in the turn when making directional adjustments, and the glass does not rattle loosely in the metal frame. I have found no damage to the glass or metal right out of the package either.

One question that might come up is, why should you use this kind of filter then it is easy to do the same thing in software? The answer is straightforward - it's fun!

This is very much a fun and useful filter but it is a special-use thing that should be used with some restraint. It seems to be well made and it does generate the desired effects. It is not particularly expensive either which is a plus.

LIVIA LONE is an unusual thriller, built around Brazilian jiu-jitsu holds and the title character's insatiable drive (blood lust) for revenge. Livia Lone is one of the most unforgettable characters you'll ever encounter in popular fiction--she is ruthless and brutal, yet sympathetic (if not really justified in her actions) and almost forgivable.

In the novel, Livia Lone is a Seattle sex crimes detective. As a 13-year-old, Livia (Labee) was sold by her parents--along with her beloved younger sister (Nason, or "little bird")--into a Thai human trafficking network. On their way to the United States in a shipping container, Livia and Nason are horribly molested by their captors. Once in the U.S., Livia and Nason are separated, and Livia is adopted by a wealthy man whose object is grooming her as a sex slave.

Livia's story is told in alternating "Then" and "Now" chapters that chronicle her transformation from a frightened, vulnerable little girl into a vengeful self-defense expert and rogue cop obsessed with finding her sister. The story shows clearly how Brazilian jiu-jitsu can be employed to deadly effect, even by a 125-pound female. The Author's Notes at the end include links to web sites that illustrate Livia's holds.

LIVIA LONE is hard to put down. It will open your eyes to the vivid horrors of human trafficking--which still exists--if your eyes are not already open.

THE ROOM OF WHITE FIRE is a somewhat brutal and shocking, fast-reading PI procedural that is obviously inspired by accounts of the “interrogation” techniques (e.g., waterboarding) used by the CIA and the U.S. Army at Abu Ghraib Prison during the war in Iraq. These techniques were presumably based on the psychological research behind resistance-to-interrogation-and-torture training courses that are offered to agents and military personnel who are judged at risk of capture by enemy forces.

In the novel, PI Roland Ford is hired by Arcadia, a private mental hospital (a prison, really), to track down an escaped patient (Clay Hickman). Clay, an Iraq war veteran, was being treated for schizophrenia and/or severe post-traumatic-stress syndrome. Roland soon learns that Clay was on a mission “to bring white fire to Deimos”. But what is “white fire”? And what or who is “Deimos”?

Roland is intrigued by the number of persons who seem desperate to capture Clay (his wealthy parents, his treating psychologist, Arcadia’s chief of security, Arcadia’s founder/director). As he follows Clay’s trail, Roland stumbles upon a fresh murder scene, and then the stakes go way up. In the end, Roland needs help from the ragtag bunch that rents the six casitas on his Rancho de los Robles property, to narrowly avoid becoming a murder victim himself.

Knitting book collectors who love authentic Norwegian knitting patterns will definitely want to own this latest book by Annemor Sundbo. Collectors may remember Sundbo's first book, [[ASIN:8299465710 Everyday Knitting: Treasures from a Ragpile]], which recounted her experience in rescuing beautifully patterned, worn-out, handknit clothing (sweaters, socks, hand coverings, and underclothes) from bags of items arriving at her Norwegian shoddy mill for recycling into fiberfill for mattresses.

From that same shoddy-mill experience comes this fourth Sundbo book, which presents 28 patterns for traditional Norwegian mittens or gloves that use classic Norwegian folk symbols and motifs. Each pattern replicates a pair of authentic rescued mittens or gloves, and each pattern is accompanied by a thumbnail photograph of the original pair. Without the photos of the originals, a knitter might think that whimsical, seldom-seen motifs like "squirrel and hare" or "daddy longlegs" were contemporary inventions, merely "inspired by" authentic Norwegian folk designs!

In fact, there is only one modern motif included, which is used in Sundbo's charming "dancing grannies" mittens. Each pattern is illustrated by an enlarged, full-color photo, printed on glossy paper. Each pattern also includes clear and complete charts for knitting the elaborate designs in the original colors. This is a beautiful book to simply page through! At the start of each pattern, Sundbo explains the meaning of the motif or motifs used: for example, "Odin's ravens" represent "tidings and memory". The book also includes chapters on basic techniques for knitting Norwegian mittens, and on designing garments incorporating the book's traditional Norwegian motifs.

For me, a knitting history buff, this book rates an unqualified 5 stars. I also highly recommend Sundbo's second and third books, [[ASIN:8299465737 Invisible Threads in Knitting]], and [[ASIN:8299465753 Knitting in Art]].

I thoroughly enjoyed Amy Stewart's previous anecdotal nonfiction books, [[ASIN:1565126831 Wicked Plants]] and [[ASIN:1565129601 Wicked Bugs]]. However, GIRL WAITS WITH GUN--a fictionalized account of Constance Kopp's 1914-1915 ordeal involving death-threat letters and a plot to kidnap a female member of her family--makes me wish that Stewart had stuck with straight nonfiction and left historical fiction alone.

The facts of the real-life incident strike me as too thin to sustain a full-length novel. Constance's buggy was totaled by an automobile, and the automobile's owner, a wealthy silk dyer, refused to pay for the damages. Instead, the businessman and his gang of thugs harassed Constance and her family at their farm for several months (by writing threatening "Black Hand" letters, breaking into the farmhouse, and plotting to kidnap the youngest woman). Eventually, with Constance's considerable help, the unscrupulous silk dyer was arrested, tried, and convicted, and Constance was offered a deputy sheriff's job (making her one of the very first female deputy sheriffs in the U.S.).

There are some subplots involving the terrible treatment of clothing factory workers, the disappearance of evacuated children of striking factory workers, and the transport of wayward girls to private institutions where they could stay during their confinements. The subplots have predictable outcomes, and add little suspense.

Stewart is an able writer, but the story just plods along. It is told mostly chronologically, with a few flashbacks, and there is too much meaningless imagined detail. The novel is boring from the very outset. For this reason, I rate GIRL WAITS WITH GUN at 2 stars ("I don't like it" on the official Amazon scale.)

What differentiates this from just being a very good book to what I think is an excellent one, is the background of the author, James M. Stone. Not only does he have an excellent financial academic start, but then in high level government positions, to starting and managing a decent size financial (insurance) company. So, a well diversified background to write about the challenges America must face, all depending heavily on understanding finance.

He sees 5 main areas to tackle. Following each are some items covered.

1. Fiscal Balance

Fix Social Security (adjust for life expectancy), Medicare (too generous) and Government pensions (defined contribution and matches for new enrollees), eliminate home mortgage interest tax deduction, eliminate corporation debt interest tax deduction.

2. Inequality

Both income and wealth distribution need to be addressed, in tax law especially looking at tax dodging by the wealthy and corporations via trusts, etc, also favoring long term investing and reducing speculating. The author also favors an annual tax on unrealized capital gains and also repealing the "step-up" cost basis for inherited assets.

3. Education

More money into poor areas, more use of charter schools and more vocational education - better tracking of kids, also a national service program, increased early childhood education, and longer school hours.

4. Healthcare

Lots of changes here - drug negotiating and other things plus a single negotiator, tackle end of life care, single payer and regulator, reduce excessive testing, reduce overuse of specialist doctors, salary more doctors, and more use of specialized nurses and physician assistants.

5. Financial Reform

Break up big banks - basically incentivize them to break up, less bank leverage, more disclosure, less use of derivatives, hedge funds regulated like mutual funds, reduce financialization of our economy - it reduces productivity.

I recommend the book.

When detectives interview Lillian at her workplace (Tremayne's clothing store), she persuades them to let her view the actual evidence, specifically Ruby's gown. At the police station, she identifies the gown as one worn by Gertrude Michael in a movie she'd seen, "The Return of Sophie Lang". The resourceful Lillian then persuades the detectives to take her along with them to Paramount Pictures to determine whether the original gown is missing from their wardrobe department.

At Paramount, Lillian meets Edith Head, who is not yet established as an Academy-Award-Winning costume designer. Yes, Edith says, the gown belongs to Paramount. Edith recognizes Lillian's intelligence and superb fashion memory, and enlists Lillian as a sort of undercover operative. Edith skillfully steers Lillian to the right people and the right places, so that the two of them can gather the evidence needed to solve the mystery of Ruby's death and bring her murderer to justice.

Ruby is a memorable character--a hard-boiled, ambitious, street-smart woman who would do anything to succeed as a Hollywood star--and who almost did, except that she died while playing her greatest role. The characters, whether fictional or based on real people, are vivid and adequately developed. The fashion descriptions make the reader "see", and drool over, the costumes. The complicated plot twists never confuse the reader. The novel is a fast read. In sum, DESIGN FOR DYING is highly entertaining escape fiction, everything that you look for in a cozy mystery.

I selected this monitor to work on a beefy laptop I use for building Linux virtual machines and testing software, so my use case is a little different than the target audience. I have been needing a larger monitor to go with said laptop and this one seemed to be a good one. So far I am pleased with it, though I have not pushed it to its full potential.

This is a 27" display capable of 2560x1440 resolution, fast refresh rates and bright colors. In the box comes the panel itself, a stand, and a DisplayPort cable. I was a little surprised that there was no HDMI cable in the box but this is all right, I have a couple of them so I was not left wanting.

My initial testing was disastrous, though the issue proved to be a fault with the laptop, not the monitor. My laptop has an HDMI output, and it does provide enough power to let the monitor know that something is there, but it intermittently sends a signal so I was not getting a consistent display. After a couple of hours, the monitor would display nothing at all. Thinking I had a dud, I connected a different system to verify and the monitor came right up. It did the same with a second system as well. After some research I determined that the issue was the graphics card in my main laptop which has known problems with HDMI. I bought an adapter to connect to the Thunderbolt port on the laptop and everything works fine now.

The system connected to this monitor is a gaming laptop that is running Linux with VMs installed. The system properly reports the model number of the display which is a very good sign. The OS does not push the monitor like a Windows gaming system might when used for actual gaming. For me, the screen real estate is what I needed. The adapter I bought caps the resolution at 1920x1200, so I am not getting the full resolution from this monitor but it is more than enough for my purposes.

The monitor responds to signal on both HDMI ports. So far I have not had occasion to try using the DisplayPorts on the back.

The display is very bright and clear, with no dead pixels. It seems to keep up very well with the system with no apparent lag, though again I am not pushing it as hard as I could. Because of the way I have it connected I can't bump up the refresh rate though it is happy at 60Hz. It doesn't appear to flicker to my eyes (though my camera disagrees), and it does not induce headaches.

If I could make any changes at all, I would change the design of the stand/base. The base is not height-adjustible so I cannot raise or lower the monitor without getting an arm harness. That's a minor complaint and is not enough to get myself upset about but it is worth mentioning.

Admittedly I am not the typical use case for a monitor like this, but I am happy with it nonetheless and it works well for me. The issues I have had with this monitor were related to other hardware, not the monitor itself. It seems to work very well, it is bright and clear and it gives me the screen real estate that I need. The fact that the Linux system recognizes its model number is a plus - it's supported.

I selected this hub/docking station for a new laptop that did not come with an SD card reader, a tool I used almost daily with my older system. As I looked for options and features I began to realize that I can use extra ports and interfaces too, though the card reader was the main consideration. After doing a good bit of research I settled on this hub and I am very pleased with it so far.

This is a small device, about the size of a deck of playing cards. It’s shelled in an aluminum casing so it is durable enough to handle getting battered around my desk a little which is a good thing. It comes with a USB-C cable, but I have not used the included cable, opting instead to use a cable that is able to handle higher wattage and was purchased at the same time; I’ll keep the included cable as a spare.

I had no issues with connection and my Windows 11 system was able to see it and set it up automatically with no manual effort at all. It quite literally has been plug and play for me.

The card reader works flawlessly for me. I have used it with two different cards and the system sees the cards as soon as they’re inserted into the reader.

I have not tried all of the other interfaces this device offers, but I did plug an external USB drive into the hub and it worked exactly as if it was plugged into one of the onboard ports. Speeds are excellent and I have had no problems with time-outs or stalls when moving large amounts of data across the interface.

What I have not tried yet, because I haven’t had the time, is connecting to my Linux system. My Linux system has an odd issue with the HDMI port (a known hardware issue with the graphics card model), and I want to see how well this hub addresses the conversion from USB-C to HDMI. If this solves the issue with that system’s HDMI connectivity when I try it, I’ll be buying another one. Once I have tried this I will update my review. If it doesn’t work with Linux it’s okay – the product description does not mention Linux as a supported platform, so if it does happen to work it’s a bonus.

My experience with this hub/dock has been very positive and for me it has been worth the expense. It’s expensive when considering I just needed an external card reader, but when considering everything else it does it’s a good investment for my system.

I have a Dell laptop that has served me well and I also have an older Dell workstation that has been great. I had high hoped for this tower system, and unfortunately it doesn’t quite meet expectations. If you are looking for an affordable gaming system, this one will work on the lower end.

I’ll start with the positives.

It comes with a 7th-generation core i7 processor and it is definitely fast. It is not one of the low power consumption processors, so when you look at the CPU in the device manager you see 8 of them reported - this is a good thing.

Everything is integrated with this system and there are plenty of ports. You don’t need a separate graphics card (though you can add one - more on that in a minute), sound is built in, Bluetooth is built in too and it even has integrated wireless networking.

This is a very attractive system too, and it’s quiet. If you don’t like a noisy system\, this one has you covered.

It comes with 1TB storage. It’s disk-based so it’s slower than an SSD but with that amount of space you have more than enough space for most uses.

And, it’s affordable. It will not break the bank if you already have a monitor and keyboard/mouse combo.

And now for the bad news.

I am not the least bit impressed with the graphics card. With modern games the more graphics memory you have the better, and having only 2GB video RAM is not enough to get it done anymore. My son is an avid gamer and has demonstrated to me that his business-grade laptop gets better frame rates. So, we are shopping for a better and more generous graphics card.

Another area where we will be expanding is the system RAM. The RAM is DDR4 and it’s fast, but the system comes with only 8GB. Our present plan is to double it.

No documentation? I know that the trend is to not include install/recovery media, but come on - there should be more than just a quick start in the box.

This is a decent desktop system that would be find in a business environment, but it falls a little flat when it comes to gaming. It needs a better graphics card (well, at least more video RAM) and it needs more system RAM to be a respectable gaming system.

The Kitchen Ecosystem is a very different kind of cookbook, the likes of which I have never before used or seen. It emphasizes individual ingredients instead of meal types or categories of foods and while this makes sense it’s so different from “normal” cookbooks.

The basic approach and idea of this cookbook is clearly stated - there is a life cycle to a lot of the ingredients available for cooking and it is possible to get maximum use for all phases of that cycle. Some dishes call for freshly picked ingredients, straight from the garden or farmer’s market, and some call for preserved ingredients. Still others call for the leftover bits. The cookbook presents several ingredients individually and gives one or two recipes from each stage in the life cycle of that ingredient.

There are a number of ingredients that most would consider common or easily available, such as asparagus, carrots and chicken. However, there are a few that would be less likely to be available or are not as affordable such as lobster, duck and mussels.

Each ingredient covered gets its own chapter and starts with a chart showing the breakdown of recipes into their respective categories - using fresh ingredients, making preserves, using the preserves and finally using the scraps. I have not looked at every single recipe but so far have found very few that rely on odd ingredients that would otherwise make the recipe more difficult.

There are two special chapters that address preparations. The first one addresses canning and preserving and presents almost a dozen techniques for saving ingredients for later use. The second chapter presents preparation techniques and goes into some detail on making stocks, making crepes and more.

This is not the cookbook for you if you have a specific dish in mind and you want an alphabetical list of recipes or you want to leaf to a section on types of dishes (for example, desserts). With this cookbook, you start with a single ingredient and then you can find recipes based on what you have and where the ingredient is in it’s life cycle. It’s a different approach and it works. I like this cookbook and am looking forward to working with it more.

Maureen begins by introducing us to her family...her 6 siblings as well as her parents. It didn't take very long for me to form a picture in my mind of what I felt Maureen and each of her family members looked like, thanks to her description of each as well as their personalities. I've never been to Walpole, MA but had no trouble picturing in my mind and what the town looked like in the 70's throughout Maureen's childhood. I had to smile a bit when she initially mentioned Walpole prison. There was almost a bit of pride in living in the same town as the state's newest, high-tech prison. It reminded me of my own childhood and a bit of that same feeling of pride in living in the city that was then known as the 'shopping outlet capital of the world'. I got a kick out of Maureen's mother threatening to send her children to Walpole prison if they misbehaved. My own parents used to do the same thing when I was a kid and we'd drive past the prison in our town...threaten to send me there if I wasn't good.

Eventually, Maureen's parent separate, something I did not see coming at all. They seemed to have had a very good marriage. That separation came with many changes for Maureen and her siblings. Maureen's mother took to shoplifting in order to feed and clothe her family, a habit Maureen would soon pick up as well. In a time when most women stayed at home to take care of the children and the father went to work, Maureen's mother instead enrolled and graduated from nursing school so she could provide for her kids. In a touching act of love and generosity, her mother practically moved heaven and earth to give her children a swimming pool. It didn't matter that they dug most of the hole and did most of the work on their own, she wanted her kids to have a pool and they did. But changes also came to Maureen at this time. Instead of pursuing her love of swimming and remaining on the swim team or staying in cheerleading, she began to experiment with drugs. Her friends were no longer her friends. She quickly met and made new friends who shared her love of drugs. It wasn't long before Maureen was shoplifting, ditching school and her studies in favor of partying with her new group of friends and her descent into drugs quickly worsened. So did her concern for others. In time, Maureen realizes she wants her life back and must make changes in order for that to happen. Is she successful? You'll have to read the book to find out!

I'm not quite sure what was wrong with me when I initially tried to read this book but I'm glad I set it aside for awhile and then tried it again because its absolutely worth reading! Regardless of your age , I think many people will be able to relate to Maureen at times throughout this book. It caused me to remember certain incidents from my own childhood and teen years. This was quick read for me and I'm so glad I read it!

MURDER IN SAINT-GERMAIN is my first “Aimee Leduc” novel, and I suspect that it's NOT among the best in this long-running series. (It's the 17th “Aimee Leduc Investigation”; the first is [[ASIN:1616957301 Murder in the Marais]].) Aimee comes across as a dismayingly disorganized private investigator (surely she's not just inept)--her transportation is an unreliable scooter, she can't ever reach her business partner when she needs to, she takes on complex new assignments when she's already strapped for time, and she's constantly scrambling to find trustworthy caregivers for her infant daughter (Chloe).

In the novel, Aimee runs two concurrent extra investigations atop her contracted computer systems security work at the prestigious Ecole des Beaux-Arts. The first investigation begins as simple scanning of the art school’s emails on behalf of a famous professor (Jules Dechard); it eventually uncovers clandestine sexual liaisons and blackmail threats that threaten the school’s very existence. The second investigation requires locating a presumed-dead Bosnian warlord who may or may not still exist; the warlord or someone else may be plotting to murder Aimee’s extremely busy counterterrorism investigator friend (Suzanne).

Does the plot sound complicated? You bet it is. Plus Aimee herself becomes a murder suspect, gets imprisoned, constantly fends off colleague’s entreaties to visit her dying former mentor (Morbier), and tries to handle her former husband's suspicious insistence on babysitting Chloe.

The investigations are resolved by novel’s end, but the story nevertheless ends with a significant cliffhanger involving Aimee’s back story. This was annoying, even for someone like myself who was ignorant of the back story. The Paris setting is described with considerable detail, and is probably accurate. However, I found the plot to be impossibly cluttered, and I never could warm to Aimee (who carries wigs and other silly disguises around for use at a moment’s notice).

Series fans will of course want to read this book for the information about Aimee's ongoing personal and work relationships.

When I see the color I think more of girls than boys, to be honest, though it is certainly not feminine. The font used it easy to read and the color scheme is easy on the eyes - black, blue and orange. Interestingly, this is not a red-letter Bible which was a mild surprise.

Aside from the formatting and cover, what makes this particular Bible stand out is the chapter introductions and the additional content that is scattered through the volume. The book introductions are written on an easy-to-understand level that should work for most pre-teens, neither too scholarly nor too watered down. There's a good breakdown of factual information too - who wrote it, when it was written, where it was written, who was involved, purpose and even more. At the bottom of the page of the introduction is a time line as well, giving some relevance in relation to other events.

All through this Bible there are questions and answers for the reader. An example is at the beginning of Daniel, and one question asked there is "Why did Daniel and his friends not want to eat the food provided by the king?" It's a good question, and the answer provided is very clear, understandable and worded in such a way to make it within reach of the target age group.

Of course, this is a full ESV Bible.

I really like this Bible. It is designed for younger readers (pre-teens specifically) and it is within reach of that age group. The designers and editors did a good job in putting this together. If you have a young person who is looking for a step past a beginner's Bible and wants to dig a little deeper and still have the full text of the Bible, this is a great choice.

A quick glance at MODERN KNITS, VINTAGE STYLE gives a totally wrong impression: that this is another spotty collection of "modernized" vintage knitting patterns updated for available yarns and sizing. To the contrary, MODERN KNITS, VINTAGE STYLE is a book of brand-new, modern patterns--some by well-known, currently active designers--that are merely "inspired" by vintage patterns. The book's overall layout (which places the old vintage pattern photos and drawings on right-hand pages, instead of the full-color photos of the modern patterns) is completely misleading, and the subtitle ("classic designs from the golden age of knitting") is simply wrong.

The modern designs are somewhat uneven in quality, but there is one dazzler that justifies the book's purchase price: Franklin Habit's "Jacqueline Bouvier Stole". The vintage inspiration for this beauty is a strange net stole with bouquets of artificial flowers attached at the ends. However, the real inspiration is Jacqueline Bouvier Kennedy's bouquet-covered wedding veil and dress. Franklin has translated Jacqueline's bouquets into eyelet lace patterns that make for a truly "inspired" modern stole.

Other particularly attractive patterns include Anna Bell's "Cherry Short-Sleeve Cardigan" (with overall simple lace pattern and drawstring waist), Susan Pierce Lawrence's "Branching Out Scarf" (a simple but lovely lace design using mohair yarn that bears no resemblance whatever to the clumsy vintage scarf), Elanor Lynn's "Pennant Pleated Skirt" (fitted through waist and hips with skirt falling in easy "pleats", and with an added pennant stitch pattern), Betty Christiansen's "Charming Shoulderette" (a thoroughly modern shrug with ribbed three-quarter sleeves), and Kristin Spurkland's "Nordic Pullover" (a short-sleeved pullover with allover Fair Isle pattern that sheds the overly fancy, bulky long sleeves of the original design). All of these designs incorporate considerable modern improvements over the classic designs that inspired them. Other well-known designers who contributed designs to this book include Lily Chin, Annie Modesitt, Teva Durham, and Jennifer Hansen.

For knitters who are primarily interested in vintage knitted fashion and knitting history, rather than knitting patterns, a very good recent book is [[ASIN:1600597130 Vintage Fashion: Knitwear: Collecting and Wearing Designer Classics]].

Mary Lee Settle brings a sparkling sense of wit and passion to this memoir of her journeys through central and southern Spain. Our intrepid traveler made her journey alone, rented a car and drove herself across Spain, not able to speak Spanish. Even more amazing is that she did so at the ripe young age of eighty-two years old!

Spanish Recognitions is generally a pleasant read, although it loses steam in an anticlimactic finale. Settle begins her journey in Spain's capital, Madrid, winds through Castilla (Avila, Tordesillas, Zamora, Salamanca) and into southern Spain (Extremadura and Andalusia). Nary a mention is made of the architectural gems of Barcelona, the quest for an independent Basque country, or the lush green hills and Celtic legacy of Galicia, where bagpipes are the instrument de rigueur.

What Settle brings with her is a keen sense of living history, a touch of the supernatural (one of her visits to a Templar ruin hints at a credibility-straining otherworldly encounter), and decades of traveling experience. She respects Spanish culture and customs, and weaves seamlessly between important (often violent) battles from Spain's past and their effects on the present. Snippets of Spanish legend and folktale round out her explorations of archeological ruins and restoration projects.

Nearly 100 pages are devoted to the Islamic presence in Spain. North African Muslims (Moors) invaded Spain in 711 CE and retained power over a gradually shrinking Spanish kingdom until Ferdinand and Isabel conquered their last remaining stronghold, Granada, in 1492, followed by the expulsion of all Jews and Muslims that same year. This had severe repercussions for Spain, as talented doctors, bankers, craftsmen and scholars were lost and libraries of Arabic texts on medicine and learning, very advanced for their time, were burned during the Inquisition. Settle hints at how the Moorish kingdom was torn apart not by Christian soldiers and mercenaries, but by rival Islamic rulers and increasingly extremist fundamentalists who felt that certain rulers were engaging in un-Islamic behaviors. There is even a mention of Osama Bin Laden, who cited the theft of Al-Andalus (Andalusia) by the Christians in an early videotaped tirade.

The weakest part of the book is by far the final few chapters, which take some of the power away from the excellent musings on Islamic Spain's past glories. There is a sudden, jarring transition away from Granada to theories on Atlantis, of all things. But overall, Settle brings a joyful freshness to a much-written-about destination, with a child's sense of wonder and a love of exploring off the beaten bath. She makes long-lost footnotes of Spanish history come alive in a way that few writers are able to accomplish, and fans of Michener's [[ASIN:0449207331 Iberia]] will most likely enjoy Spanish Recognitions, as will most anyone who's had the good fortune to travel in Spain.

I was looking for a book that would help me lay out a course toward achieving a fairly reasonable dream. What I got was a book that had me look very realistically at that dream and see how likely it was that I would achieve it. I turned out alright, but I have to admit I have a few questions that I could not answer as strongly as I should.

The book is not intentionally unsupportive, but it does lay out a few facts and questions that can point toward potential difficulties in reaching your dream. The good news is that if you "fail" the test questions, it does show you where you need to be to achieve your dream. But it also does explain the possibility that your dream may not be achievable or may be misguided. For me, my dream is definitely not achievable without a little more sacrifice and motivation but ultimately well within my abilities, control, and passions.

The book also spends time questioning if this dream is really what you want. It has a strong message throughout that pursuing your dreams and passions is a great way to happiness and satisfaction. To get there though you need to be picking the right dream. I tested myself on this and was surprised to find that what I saw as the end products do not seem to be my biggest aspiration, but rather the process to that end. I had never written down what my dream was in specific details before, but after doing that, the simple end goal is the smallest part of my dream.

There is some self help-type babble and quotes to help motivate, but the core message of the book is aligning yourself up with your real dreams and realistically evaluating where you are on the path to achieving it. I really feel closer to achieving my goal now that I have a much clearer vision of what I want. And I'm happy that my dream passed the test (with room for improvement!)

NICEVILLE is a small-town bank robbery caper novel, but has a unique and very dark twist. To wit: Niceville isn't an ordinary small town, but has an extremely serious supernatural problem. Niceville's residents and visitors sometimes vanish unexpectedly, and may reappear days later in sealed tombs or in hospital corridors. Or they may simply vanish, leaving behind only a menacing dark stain on a hardwood floor. Niceville's problem seems to relate to nearby Crater Sink, the proverbial bottomless pit, filled with black water, that was avoided by native American Indians who wove legends around it. But Niceville's problem also seems to involve mirrors--especially one particularly cursed and clouded antique mirror.

The bank robbers, as well as some of the victimized bank patrons, are brutal men. Early on, there is a graphic scene of the robbers' getaway--aided by a merciless roadside-sniper member of the gang--that nearly made me stop reading. But I was already caught up in the page-turning plot, and I ended up loving the book. There's a lot of black humor interspersed with the supernatural and bad-guy happenings, when the bank robbers' plans start to go wrong, and the local law enforcement officials start to make some progress solving the robbery. The worst characters mostly come to fitting (and highly unusual) bad ends, which adds to the reader's enjoyment.

Probably my favorite part of the book was the descriptive, tongue-in-cheek chapter headings--for example, "Delia Cotton's Afternoon Was Hard to Explain", and "Merle Zane Meets the Woman in the Forest". These headings kept me reading, because they foreshadowed what was to come without actually giving away the weird twists. The headings also made it easy to remember earlier events (and to reread key chapters as needed).

This book is very difficult to describe, but if you enjoyed the TV series "Supernatural", you will almost certainly enjoy this book. I can hardly wait to read the next Carsten Stroud novel in this vein, although the very singular and entertaining NICEVILLE is an extremely hard act to follow.

Other than croissants I have done very little French-style baking before receiving this book. The first chapter of this book covers some of the basics that will be needed later. These include cremes, pastes and light doughs on which some of the other recipes rely. Each of these is presented in step-by-step form complete with pictures that illustrate what happens at each step. Very few other recipes in the book have this level of detail.

The rest of the recipes are broken up into logical chapters that include cookies, custards, yeasted pastries, tarts, cakes and more. The average chapter has 6-8 recipes, and all of these are very easy to follow and produce good results (well, the ones I have tried have turned out well, anyway).

A small detail that I think is important – the dry ingredients are measured not only by volume but also by mass. Because the mass can be used instead of using volume, results can be very consistent (meaning, small variations can be avoided due to settling or measurement method).

This is a beginner’s book on French baking. It does not cover everything but it presents some important basics and it allows the rank beginner to produce reliable results.

Now an enterprising band of retirees has resolved to show it's never too late to start afresh, and open a restaurant. Snapping up a local property and throwing themselves into preparations, Theresa, Carol, William and Benjamin's plans are proceeding unnervingly well. But when Theresa encounters a mysterious intruder, she begins to wonder what secrets the building is concealing. Meanwhile Sally, an actress who fled the stage to live in quiet anonymity, has decided not to be involved. She's far too busy anyway, shepherding around a gaggle of A-listers including a suave Russian with a super-yacht and a penchant for her company. As the razzmatazz of Cannes Film Festival penetrates Bellevue-Sur-Mer, its inhabitants become entangled in a complex pattern of love triangles and conflicting business interests, and something starts to feel distinctly oeuf. I have been learning to draw and I have always liked the anime style of artwork so this book seemed like a good fit for me as a continuance of my learning. It seems to be a good book, but it is a little beyond my ability and I would hesitate to call it a beginner book.

Most courses on face portrait artwork and body drawing start with a more detailed description of not only what to do but how to get it done, with step by step instructions on how to iteratively draw a head, adding detail and eventually having a complete face. Bodies usually start with a sketch of a stick figure, adding shapes and contours until the body is viable and clear. In this specific book , much of that detailed walk-though is skipped and what is given is a very abbreviated speed-run through the process. That's fine if you are already skilled at drawing faces and people, but it's a harder sell when you're a beginner.

Once through the introduction, what comes next in this book reminds me a lot of a supply store where you buy pieces and parts. The author presents a number of different eye shapes and styles, hair styles and more. I like this approach; it makes visualizing what you want to draw a little easier as you can select one of these, one of those, and combine it with that over there and end up with a viable final drawing. Again, though, this is presented with less instruction on how to actually draw these parts.

The largest part of the book is an art gallery of sorts, presenting numerous finished characters with complete bios. There are a few intermediate drawing with each to get started but still nothing complete that would allow a less skilled artist get from start to finish without a lot of experimentation and frustration.

One thing that jumps out at me is the frequent reference to very specific brands of paper, markers, pencils and more. I get that the author likes specific things, but this comes across more as a sponsored marketing tactic rather than honest endorsement of a favorite product.

This is not a bad book and I like it. I would hesitate to call it a book that is suited to beginner, though. It skips past a lot of basic drawing concepts that one would expect, making some assumptions that the reader already has a basic understanding of how to draw faces and bodies.

THE FIRE THIEF (A DARK PARADISE MYSTERY) gets so caught up in wordy descriptions of (1) Maui’s beautiful settings, and (2) Hawaii’s spiritual traditions, it is a very tedious novel to read. The barely-there mystery plot isn’t capable of sustaining the novel. The author has great credentials as a travel writer--so the details about the setting and people ring true--but the author lacks the storyteller’s gift.

In the novel, a teenaged surfer’s body is found floating in a Maui cove. It looks like a surfing accident where the surfer hit his head on undersea lava rocks. But that doesn’t explain the shark’s tooth in his head wound, or the coroner’s finding that the surfer was dead before he went into the water.

Detective Kali Mahoe, the police chief’s niece, must investigate and find the murderer. Kali is on the path to becoming a spiritual leader, a kahu. She suspects a ritual murder, in part because of recent sightings of a noppero-bo, a malicious, faceless spirit. Kali must use both logic and her knowledge of Hawaiian legends to solve the mystery.

This is apparently the first novel in a planned series. It is more of a cozy mystery than a police procedural, because of its emphasis on the locale and the characters’ backgrounds and ruminations. As much as I generally enjoy both cozy mysteries and mysteries set in exotic locations (e.g., Hawaii, South Africa, Italy), I’ll be passing on the rest of this series.

LAST HOPE ISLAND: BRITAIN, OCCUPIED EUROPE, AND THE BROTHERHOOD THAT HELPED TURN THE TIDE OF WAR tells the neglected story of how London operated as a haven for the monarchs, governments, and armed forces of Czechoslovakia, Poland, Norway, Holland, Belgium, and Luxembourg, after these countries were conquered and occupied by Hitler's forces at the beginning of WWII. The book chronicles how these exiled governments, "in the dark years of 1940 and 1941, arguably saved Britain from defeat and, in the latter part of the war, proved of immense benefit to the overall Allied victory."

The book recounts the contributions of many larger-than-life exiles--monarchs, scientists, spies, saboteurs (e.g., King Haakon VII of Norway, the Earl of Suffolk, code-breaker Marian Rejewski, war journalist Willy Brandt)--and includes their portrait photographs in many cases.

The writing is superb; the book is a masterful work of contemporary history. The story of the unfolding events fully comes to life--with all the excitement naturally arising from narrow escapes, and from bold actions taken when outcomes were unknown. The book is thoroughly researched and footnoted, but the narrative is presented seamlessIy--so much so, you almost forget you are reading a nonfiction book about WWII history. Kudos to author Lynne Olson!

Angels are currently hot stuff in YA...just look at the success of [[ASIN:1416989420 Hush, Hush]] and [[ASIN:0385739133 Fallen]], or even earlier works like [[ASIN:1842556290 Angel]]. "Halo" is the first in a trilogy, to be followed by "Hades" and "Heaven." Unlike the "bad boy" fallen angel stories that are currently all the rage, "Halo" features a trio of squeaky-clean messengers: the archangel Gabriel, seraph Ivy, and Bethany, the youngest of the trio. Each has a special talent; Gabriel is a warrior, Ivy a healer, and Bethany has yet to discover her powers. The three are living in a house in Venus Cove, where they've been sent to counteract the dark forces at work.

Bethany is enrolled in the local Catholic high school, where she soon falls in with Molly and her crowd, and more importantly, Xavier, the school captain. Xavier has it all: he's handsome, athletic, and most importantly, Catholic. He volunteers at soup kitchens and nursing homes in his spare time. The two begin a whirlwind romance at the risk of heavenly interception. Beth becomes so wrapped up in Xavier that she starts to shirk her community service duties. Meanwhile, transfer student Jake is a charming rebel with a dark streak...

At nearly 500 pages, "Halo" reads fairly quickly for its length, but there's a lack of depth. The author has a habit of overloading descriptive adjectives into a sentence, which affected the flow and, considering the level of Bethany's reflections, the vocabulary level seemed too elevated to ring true (I expect that's because of the author's young age, and that her style will become more streamlined as she continues to write). The few descriptions of heaven seemed hastily drawn, as do Gabriel and Ivy, who conveniently appear when neccessary and come across as flat, when I would have liked to hear more about Bethany's life before coming to Venus Cove.

Much of Bethany's story is taken up by trying to fit in at school (no "modern technology" is allowed at home, so she's never seen a cell phone and doesn't know about Facebook), or her all-consuming love affair (we're constantly reminded how Xavier is gorgeous, perfect, etc., and she wallows in despair during his absences). Despite being an angel, she obsesses over prom dresses just as much as the next mere mortal (and is just as susceptible to human foibles involving alcohol at parties). She's clueless about s-e-x, too, and solicits advice from dubious sources at school.

But "Halo" isn't all squeaky clean, even if Xavier believes in "saving yourself until marriage," the angelic trio volunteers at soup kitchens and tries to bring people back to the church, and Gabriel counsels Molly to love her body the way it is instead of crash dieting. There's some pretty graphic violence, but it's starkly at odds with the Catholic messages running throughout the book. The "evil" ringleader was apparent fairly early on, which kind of ruined the suspense.

Despite the length of the book, there were several subplots that could have been more fully developed, such as Alice's story (Bethany adopts Alice's dog Phantom early on). My main issue was that the Catholic themes seemed rather forcefully inserted at times (the dinner table discussion at Xavier's, for example), and that Bethany is so busy being human that there is precious little time devoted to hearing about the heavenly Kingdom; the brief descriptions that are there feel abstract and vague. And several other minor quibbles will probably be corrected in the final print run, including numerous misspelled words that were distracting. Verdict: fans of "Hush, Hush" and "Fallen" will enjoy "Halo."

The mystery only deepens from there, as Stevens and Carla Windermere, his partner in the new joint BCA–FBI violent crime task force, find themselves on the trail of a massive international kidnapping and prostitution operation. Book #3 [[ASIN:0399165525 Kill Fee (A Stevens and Windermere Novel)]] The billionaire picked a heck of a way to die. The events of that sunny springtime day will lead Stevens and Windermere across the country, down countless blind alleys, and finally to a very flourishing twenty-first century enterprise: a high-tech murder-for-hire social media website. Book #1 [[ASIN:0399157891 The Professionals (A Stevens and Windermere Novel)]] Four friends, recent college graduates, caught in a terrible job market, joke about turning to kidnapping to survive. Inspired by the life of a great French chef (Alexis Soyer), THE DEVIL'S FEAST (A Blake and Avery Novel) is an excellent historical mystery. The fictional Chef Alexis Soyer is a highly memorable character, and apparently his flamboyant persona closely resembles that of the real Chef Soyer. The book includes a lot of fascinating detail about the real Chef Soyer's revolutionary kitchen equipment and projects to feed the poor in soup kitchens.

The third "Blake and Avery" novel (the first is [[ASIN:0399171673 The Strangler Vine]]), THE DEVIL'S FEAST works fine as a standalone. Set in the world of London's 19th-century men-only political clubs, it continues Matty's story from the previous novel, as she is now working in Chef Soyer's kitchen at the Whig-dominated Reform Club (originally established by the Liberals).

Captain Avery, a committed Tory, doesn't want to be seen at the Reform, but goes to visit Matty. She introduces him to Chef, who invites him to a private dinner that evening. When a gentleman is poisoned by arsenic at the dinner, Avery ends up being commissioned by the Reform Club to find out what happened. (Of course it turns out to be murder.) Avery is in over his head--because Blake is unavailable, having vanished from the Marshalsea (debtors' prison)--but he forges ahead valiantly, and eventually pulls off a successful investigation.

The plot is extremely complicated, but always interesting. The book paints a realistic picture of the times, and of Chef Soyer's kitchen. The actual events are total fiction, but they might have happened--and that's what I like to see in historical mystery novels.

But even such mouth-watering offerings as “Creamy Green Peppercorn Pan Sauce” or “Sour Cream and Caramelized Sweet Onion Sauce” or “Smoked Tomato and Marcona Almond Romesco” aren’t enough to convert this gastronomically impoverished cook.

For me, the trouble with sauces is threefold: (1) the impossibility of getting enough decent drippings for a tasty, non-oily pan sauce; (2) the best sauces use a lot of steps and ingredients; and (3) cooking down always takes forever. This book doesn’t solve these problems—it is really intended for cooks who are already skilled at making delicate sauces, and who think that sauces are worth all the extra effort.

That said, this is a terrific sauce recipe book. All of the sauces look gorgeous in the photos, and all of the recipes read “scrumptious”. An excellent extra feature is “The Sauce Table” at the beginning—it consists of an easy-to-read chart that shows which kinds of food (poultry, meat, fish, vegetables and pasta, desserts, dipping) each included sauce will complement or can be used for.

Electronic devices need protection. Considering the money invested in their purchase, all electronics could use some protection, but this fact is even truer for laptops because they cost more. The Thule Case Logic Gauntlet is specifically made for this purpose and it is just large enough to hold your Macbook Air and keep it safe.

The Thule Case Logic Gauntlet Air Sleeve is nothing more than a simple case/sleeve to hold your Macbook and certain other electronics and it is designed to seal out water and keep the inner contents safe from the elements. The foam construction is tough enough to cushion any blow and the vinyl lining on the inside is nice because it makes your electronic investment slide in and out with ease. From a construction standpoint, the sleeve is a good one and I feel confident knowing my electronic device is safe from harm.

One thing to keep in mind with this sleeve is that it has no additional pockets for storage. It is truly nothing more than a sleeve and while this fact should be obvious, many might purchase this expecting it to be more like a laptop bag with extra compartments. With this protector, you get nothing more than a place to insert your Mac and a Velcro- fastened flap to seal the deal. Another thing to think about is the size. This sleeve is intended to hold a 13 inch Mac tightly and securely. You can use it for other things, like regular pc's, but if they are any larger, there is a good chance they will not fit inside.

Electronics and other devices are costly and they need to be protected from bumps, drops, and weather. With the Thule Case Logic Gauntlet, you get a good sleeve for exactly that and while I agree that the price is somewhat high, this is a stylish sleeve and it does a good job protecting your Mac or other electronics from harm.

THE WEDDING GUEST: AN ALEX DELAWARE NOVEL is one of the best of the “Alex Delaware” series. The premise is quite fresh and intriguing--how do you solve a crime when the hard-to-identify victim turns out to have been living entirely “off the grid”? How do you find a killer with a motive for murder, when the victim has no driver’s license, no fixed address, no cell phone number, and no social media presence?

In the novel, a bridesmaid finds an expensively dressed young woman dead in a bathroom at a “Saints and Sinners” wedding reception. To carry out the theme, the reception was being held at the site of a former strip joint, an incredibly sleazy one at that. Problem is, no one (not the bride, the groom, the bridesmaids, the groomsmen, or the wedding guests) has any idea who the victim is. But she was definitely murdered--strangled after being drugged with a syringe of fentanyl.

Eventually, a manager of the former strip joint is able to identify the victim as a one-time, very short-term, employee. But the ID doesn’t help the investigation, because there is no recent trace of where the woman was living, of her recent associates, or of what she was doing to support herself. And why was she even attending the wedding of a pair of strangers?

The novel isn’t particularly fast-moving, which is typical of the “Alex Delaware” novels. However, the investigation is consistently interesting, and the conclusion is satisfying.

It's a little hard for me to accept that New Watch means the end of new books about Anton Gorodetsky. New Watch has the same structure as most of the Watch books, with the story split into three main sections. And like its predecessors, when New Watch ends, it doesn't feel like the end so much as a pause and an acknowledgment that life goes on.

Magic continues to play an odd role in the story, both as its center and fading into the periphery. From his humble beginnings in Night Watch, Anton Gorodetsky has become a High Magician, and an important man within the Night Watch, an organization dedicated to policing the works of the Others. But Anton rarely uses magic, except for the most trivial of things (though he finds it more of a challenge to give it up for a day than he had thought). Magic is the means by which Lukyanenko examines the philosophies of selfishness and altruism, of predestination and free will.

New Watch's plot centers around prophecies and the relation to the rest of magic. Anton's chance encounter with a young, overweight boy named Kesha at an airport reveals Kesha to be a powerful prophet. Anton is drawn into protecting him even as he has to ask whether saving the boy would be worth risking his life and the lives of all of Night Watch against a terrible opponent, who has been branded the Tiger.

Anton continues to investigate prophecies to learn more of the Tiger, taking him to England and Taiwan, and resulting in the return of Arina. As the story reaches its third act, Anton must decide whether he listens to all the prophecies that he has gathered (and which appear to relate to one another), knowing that if he does, he will have to decide whether to set them into motion.

A final note: the translation by Andrew Bromfield was top-notch. The flavor of the novel felt strongly Russian, without any awkwardness coming across in bringing New Watch into English.

I've had WD drives for decades, and the only issues I ever had were with WD Green and Black drives. Red, Red Plus, and Red Pro work where they're intended to work, as they're intended to work. Blue are to be used in a PC with one or two drives that sees daily use. That's daily, not 24/365. Not in an array. Each level of Red drive is intended for arrays of different numbers of drives. They are not quiet desktop drives. You really want them somewhere other than next to where you sit.

More importantly than all that, carefully check prices in several places. Don't pay the absurd prices that some people want after buying their stock at retail price. They'll go back down. WD will make more.

Normally when I think of smoothies I think of ice and fruit, and often milk, blended and poured in a glass. I had not even considered the idea of a smoothie bowl, and this has opened my eyes to something new. It’s a very interesting collection of recipes that has some great ideas in it for those looking for healthy variety.

What struck me about this book, and is something not immediately evident until you dig in, is that a good many of the recipes are vegan which is good news for those that follow a vegan diet and don’t wish to make concessions. The recipes call for almond milk, coconut milk and the like, and these are all fine substitutes for regular milk in recipes like these (to be fair, these types of milks are not universal substitutes and don’t work everywhere, but they do here). A few recipes call for things like honey, which can be worked around if desired by using golden syrup or corn syrup though these will change the flavors. Some recipes use yogurt which makes them difficult to convert.

There is a wide variety in this book! The sectional organization alone reveals a lot about what’s inside: “Fresh ‘N Fruity” which focuses on, well, fruit, “Super Bowls” which is a collection of smoothies with special ingredients (like bee pollen), “Sneaky Little Veggies” which uses vegetables, “We All Scream for Nice Cream” which is more dessert-oriented and finally “Toppings are Everything” which emphasizes the toppings.

I can’t see myself eating nothing but smoothies but from time to time they’re a nice treat, and this book brings a good spin on smoothies that has a little something for everyone. If you are a vegetarian, this whole book is a good resource if you’re into smoothies; if you’re a vegan in particular, a large percentage of this book is a good fit.

I wanted to give up SO many times, and the fact that I actually made it all the way through (ok, with some ~serious~ skimming near the end, I confess) deserves some kind of recognition! How did I do it? When exactly did I start caring about the characters in the book? Did I ever really care at all? The book is about two priests - or pastors, or rectors, I'm still not sure - they are husband and wife. They are Episcopalian, I got that much. There was a lot of discussion of things I need to look up in order to properly understand: the Advent, the Eucharist, and many more such capitalized Episcopalian rites. I mean no disrespect, in fact, I was quite intrigued. As a convert to my religion, I appreciate how unusual religious observances can appear to the un(religiously)educated eye. Anyway, the wife is in charge of a congregation high in the mountains of North Carolina, the husband is the chaplain and acting headmaster at the town's alternative boarding school for wayward youth. He is about 20 years older than her and suffers from terrible bouts of depression. They are both orphans - he since being abandoned as a child, she since the death of her mother when she was 6 and her father when she was in her 20's. They are at best both damaged property.

There are some odd elements sprinkled into this book, which is largely a quiet, slow, microscopic evaluation of their religious training and beliefs, as well as their lives together. First, the book takes place at the close of 1999, and a major plot point is a discussion of the Millenium and the varying beliefs and odd behavior of people in their attempt to understand Y2K. There are also two characters introduced midway through the book - the 16yr Chase, a miscreant from the school, and Tony, a mysterious traveling monk. I think it may have been the injection of these two more interesting characters that saved me from closing down completely on the humdrum husband and wife.

The "pros" of this book are few, and would have been much more valuable if I had enjoyed the story more: there are only about 3 or 4 obscenities, and only a couple of vaguely referenced examples of sexual content. There is one uncomfortable discussion about self-flagellation, but in the context of the story, it fits. I should be shouting "hurrahs" for finding such a *clean* book. If only it weren't so dull! Ack!!

One of the recurring themes in the New Testament, and in particular the 4 Gospel books, was the hypocrisy of the Pharisees, the religious leaders at the time who knew the Scriptures but largely misunderstood them and favored earthly recognition over spiritual health. So wrapped up in their rules and regulations in the pursuit of what they believed to be right - and looking righteous in front of other men - that they missed the point. The modern church is full of the Christian equivalent of the Pharisees, to the point that there are some very unhealthy congregations filled with people there for entirely the wrong reasons. In this small book, the author sheds some light on this problem and offers some generalized solutions. Much of this has been said elsewhere, though, so I would hesitate to call this new material.

This is a small and fast read, being just about 100 pages in length.

The author breaks down the material into 5 basic chapters: “Bewared of the Leaven”, “Pharisees and Revelation”, “Pharisees and Redemption”, “Pharisees and Regeneration”, and “Pharisees and God”. Though each chapter addresses a different aspect of the Pharisees’ behavior and thought, each is rooted back to the same base subjects: the Pharisees were more concerned about keeping up appearances than actually understanding the Scriptures and behaving (and believing) accordingly. From there, parallels are drawn between the Pharisees of 2,000 years ago professing Christians of today, who often have the same root problem.

Much of this has been said before, in different forms, both in written form and from the pulpits on Sunday mornings by faithful pastors seeking to bring the problem to light. It is nice to have it all in one place together, though.

The writing is good and the author uses a good bit of Scripture to back up his points. I like the fact that author does not write down to his audience like lecturing children nor does he write as if the audience is filled with doctoral candidates.

This is a good book that sheds some light on an important problem that is present in modern churches but is centuries old. It is well written and a fast read.

If you’ve mastered pie crust, then pie really is “easy as pie”. This book, THE PERFECT PIE: YOUR ULTIMATE GUIDE TO CLASSIC AND MODERN PIES, TARTS, GALLETTES, AND MORE will guide you to pie crust mastery--or you can take the easy way out (as I do) and use commercial pie crust from your grocery store’s cold case (e.g., [[ASIN:B003D1Z2E2 Pillsbury Pie Crusts]]). Whichever approach you use, this book will provide lots of different--but fairly complicated--fillings for you.

This is actually a technical cookbook for moderately advanced pie-makers, rather than a book for cooks who just want to bake pies that will please the family. I really like the explanations of “Why This Recipe Works” that appear at the beginning of many recipes. For example, the book explains that the filling in a “Skillet Apple Pie” (a recipe for a top-crust-only “pie” that begins on the stovetop and finishes in the oven) can be saucier than the filling in a double-crust pie because you don’t have to worry about a bottom crust’s becoming soggy.

I’m NOT a fan of the “Classic” pie recipes, which add steps or non-classic ingredients to basic apple, blueberry, and pumpkin pies. For example, apple pie uses Golden Delicious (horrors!) apples combined with Granny Smith (just okay) apples; and cooks and cools the filling before adding it to the crust. (My Midwestern mother’s apple pie is hard to beat--it’s made with Jonathan, MacIntosh, Gravenstein, or other firm, tart-sweet apples that are tossed with cinnamon and sugar, then added to a double crust, and baked.)

The “Classic” blueberry pie recipe adds a Granny Smith apple; the pumpkin pie recipe adds canned sweet potatoes and maple syrup, and even prebakes the crust. These recipes aren’t really classics, and I question whether they’re worth the extra trouble.

Sadly, there is no recipe at all for plain peach pie, which is one of the world’s great pleasures. Peaches are used in tarts and “Peach Slab Pie”. The “Why This Recipe Works” section for “Peach Slab Pie” says that double-crust peach pies need precooked fruit and multiple thickeners “to prevent a soupy mess”, and this has NOT been true in my experience. Simple peach pie recipes may come out a little soupy, but they’re delicious and definitely NOT a mess.

Of particular value are the many recipes for custard, cream, and curd pies (e.g., banana cream, lemon meringue, black bottom). The section on regional pies (e.g., “New England Mince Pie”, “Southern Praline Pecan Pie”) is also interesting. However, after reading the fruit pie recipes, I wonder whether these recipes will also be overly complicated for family cooks.

Like most specialty pie-making books, this book shows you how to create a variety of crust-edge designs (braided, crimped, cutout, fork-crimped, rope, scalloped-spoon), and top-crust designs (lattice, cutout, braided strips, free-form lattice, free-form shapes, herringbone).

A more unusual feature is the entire section on “Pie and Tart Doughs”. This includes recipes for chocolate, herb, nut, vegan, gluten-free, cookie-crust, and other pie doughs.

The book has many, many beautiful illustrations of finished pies--all of coffee-table-book quality. Many procedures (e.g., removing the seeds from vanilla bean pods, making and rolling slab pie dough) are clearly explained with step-by-step photos. The book also includes a few pages on troubleshooting pie problems (e.g., crust edges brown too quickly), and it is well-indexed.

This book will make a nice gift for a dedicated pie maker or cookbook collector. However, it won’t replace my go-to family-pie-making books, [[ASIN:1118432169 Betty Crocker’s Big Book of Pies and Tarts]], and [[ASIN:0470485531 Pillsbury’s Easy As Pie]].

BOYS AMONG MEN is a must-read for high school basketball players who are thinking of entering the NBA draft as soon as possible (one year removed from high school under the rule instituted in 2005). By telling the stories of the trailblazing NBA stars who successfully skipped college basketball (e.g., Kevin Garnett, Kobe Bryant), author Jonathan Abrams makes it clear how hard it is for any athlete to make the transition directly from high school player to professional player.

What the NBA prep-to-pro successes had in common was an incredible work ethic and devotion to improving their basketball skills, as well as coaches and teams that were committed to allowing their immature high-schoolers time to develop and to grow into their bodies. What the NBA prep-to-pro failures had in common were raw basketball skills that suffered from lack of college coaching, too much money to spend, and too little personal development before their short-term contracts expired.

The book is also a must-read for serious NBA history fans, because of the detailed accounts of the intense scouting and recruiting of the early prep-to-pro successes, and of the behind-the-scenes draft-pick talks among college and pro coaches, owners, managers, and players' agents. (There is one particularly interesting to me segment on how Nike came to acquire Michael Jordan for the wildly successful "Air Jordan" line of shoes.)

The book is surprisingly easy to read, considering the wealth of factual detail it contains (gathered from many, many firsthand interviews) about the prep-to-pro players, the history of the NBA, and the development of certain NBA franchises from about 1995 to the present day. However, the text is often weighed down by the sheer quantity of names. An enormous number of people were involved in the decision-making that swirled around the key NBA players featured in the book, and it's difficult to keep track of who all the people are, unless you're already familiar with a lot of NBA history. For this reason, BOYS AMONG MEN isn't a good choice for a casual NBA fan like myself, and I rate it at 4 stars ("I like it" on the official Amazon scale).

If you love 'Twas the Night Before Christmas (by Clement Clarke Moore), and also love to knit, then you'll probably love this book as much as I do. The classic poem is reprinted and illustrated by full-color, cartoon-style drawings; and full-color photographs of the knitted figures (in poses) are superimposed on the drawings to help tell the story. The book is delightful to look at, even if you never actually knit the projects.

Patterns are included for ten three-dimensional toy projects: (1) Santa; (2) Santa's reindeer; (3) Santa's bag of toys and gifts (including a candy cane, wrapped presents, a tiny doll, a tiny teddy bear); (4) the crescent moon wrapped in a scarf; (5) a father in nightcap and striped nightshirt; (6)-(7) a mother and daughter in pink nightdresses; (8) a baby in a knitted-in turquoise body suit; (9) red Christmas stockings (one life-size, one miniature); and (10) a charming 10-1/2" diameter Christmas wreath (decorated with attached flowers and an attached simple dove ornament). The book's cover photo, which shows Santa and his reindeer, gives you an idea of what the projects look like.

There are basic, easy-to-follow instructions for knitting, shaping, joining, and embroidering the figures. The figures are stuffed with ordinary fiberfill; the wreath calls for a base ring fashioned from foamboard. The patterns are written for DK yarn, and are mostly knit on size 2/3 needles. The author recommends using yarn that contains at least 20 percent wool, because cotton and acrylic yarns aren't stretchy enough to produce the best results. The figures use small amounts of yarn. For example, Santa needs 1 oz. (90 yards) of red yarn; 1/2 oz. (44 yards) each of cream yarn and beige yarn; and small amounts of black, mauve, fluffy white, white mohair, and green yarn (for, respectively, Santa's belt, boots, "fur" trim on jacket and hat, beard, and mittens).

I saw a review of "Sacré Blues" in a Canadian newspaper (I don't remember which one) and decided that, since I was in Québec and frankly quite clueless regarding many aspects of Québec history and culture, I picked up a copy at an Archambault in Sainte-Foy. I had resolved to put it away for the return train trip to Toronto, but I started reading a little bit each night. At some points in the book I was laughing out loud so much my neighbours must have wondered about my sanity.
I spent a month in Québec and plan to return often, and "Sacré Blues" helped me to understand some of the issues in modern Québec. I have taken a Québécois civilisation course, but there are many topics in the book that elaborated on things we had touched on in class, such as Québécois winters, language, popular culture, famous people, the strange and fascinating addiction to cholesterol-laden food (poutine! May Wests! Pepsi!), tabloid newspapers, politics, the Floribécois (retired Québécois who migrate in droves to Florida every winter), Céline Dion, and much, much more.
Grescoe writes with tongue-in-cheek humour that sometimes amounts to laugh-out-loud guffawing, such as the Québec Language Police...something that I evidence firsthand. Some of the topics seemed to go on for much too long, but generally the book is funny and informative, sort of a mini-introduction to Québec. Very well written, with a glossary of terms and famous Québécois, important dates, and cultural notes.

I have had this book for a few months and it has become one of my very favorite books on bread. I spend a lot of time working on bread and I am always looking for good books on the subject, so when I found this book I was quite taken with it. The more I use it, the more I like it.

Ever since picking up a copy of Reinhart's "Bread Baker's Apprentice" I have been sold on the idea of slower rise times and the use of starters (biga, poolish, etc.) to make bread, and the result has been a very significant improvement in the quality of the bread I make. Glezer's collection of formulas very much subscribe to this mindset and as a result my portfolio of breads has expanded. In my personal opinion, Glezer's writing style is somewhat more personal and warm than that of Reinhart, though it is a matter of personal preference. Both are excellent. The point is simply that Glezer's collection relies heavily on slow rise, starter-based breads.

There are no failures in this collection. Each formula is concise, clear, and makes a beautiful resulting loaf that is guaranteed to impress even the most discerning of bread critics, both visually and on the palate.

In addition to a fabulous collection of formulas, Glezer includes quite a bit of history and storytelling in her book. There is enough in here that the book might easily be considered more of a coffee-table tome than something to be used in the kitchen. Furthermore, there are pictures and lots of them. This book is beautiful in its layout and structure, becoming glamorous in its presentation without being pretentious.

For excellent loaves that require some time to make, good reading and a better appreciation for superb bread and bread baking, this book is a must-have.

COLLECTING THE DEAD: A NOVEL introduces a fascinating new “detective”—Magnus Craig, aka “Steps”, of the fictional FBI Special Tracking Unit. Steps is renowned as a “man-tracker”, and has been dubbed “the Human Bloodhound” by the national news media. He is so successful at tracking down missing persons and murderers, he and his partner (FBI Special Agent Jimmy Donovan) are in constant demand from law enforcement. At a moment’s notice, they fly all over the country in their private jet, to visit crime scenes that range from apparently undisturbed to incredibly bloody.

But Steps is a fraud. He isn’t a man-tracker at all--though he plays the part most convincingly by examining imaginary bent leaves, minute traces of blood, and the like, whenever he’s hunting a person. What Steps really does, is hunt with his unique, extraordinary gift. Because of the gift, he sees the “shine” left behind by each and every human who has been physically present at a crime scene. The “shine” is a glowing, colored aura—and he can separate the “shine” left by his target from the “shine” of other people at the scene, because the colors of “shine” vary in accordance with the good or evil nature of individual human beings.

In the novel, Steps is called out to track a serial killer (the sad-faced killer) who kidnaps young brunette women and leaves their bodies posed along park trails near Redding, California. The crime scenes are all covered with the killer’s “shine”, in brilliant amaranth and textured rust. The story is about how Steps manages to find and assemble the clues--through tracking the killer’s “shine”--in order to capture the killer and bring him to justice. The novel’s title, “Collecting the Dead”, is taken from Steps’ habit of keeping one photograph of each murder victim in a black-covered photo album, so that he’ll never forget that true evil exists.

I’ve read quite a few novels that used characters who could see other people’s colored auras, but COLLECTING THE DEAD is the first one that has gotten this concept right. The plot is believable, and the tracking concept is worked out so that it isn’t just a gimmick, but constitutes a genuine part of the plot. The characters of Steps, Jimmy, and their assistant Diane are fairly well-developed, too.

I loved this book, and can’t wait for the next one—which I believe will happen, because Steps hasn’t yet nailed his evil nemesis “Leonardo”!

I have always liked Lonely Planet books, and I was excited to take a good look at this one. It’s basically a ready-made bucket list for the traveler, though there is one aspect of the book that I think detracts from it – there is built-in obsolescence in some of the materials.

This book is a traveler’s dream guidebook. It presents a wealth of really wonderful destinations with full-color pictures and explains a bit about each place it presents. If you like to travel and like to see some truly beautiful and/or breathtaking places, this book is absolutely for you. Some of the places are very much man-made, such as the pyraminds in Egypt, while others are purely natural like locations in Norway where seeing the Aurora Borealis is ideal. This is not a regional book, either – it covers the globe.

Included in the book for each location are suggestions of places to stay and places to eat, with approximate cost. This is a nice addition that makes planning a lot simpler, but the issue here is that the prices are subject to change over time, and hotels and restaurants can change names or even go out of business. This means that over time this book will still be useful for finding really amazing places to go but will get progressively less useful in planning lodging and eating.

This is a really nice book and I am very pleased with it, but there is built-in obsolescence in the lodging and dining suggestions. If nothing else, this book needs a year in the title to establish relevance of such supporting information. Regardless, this is a traveler’s dream book for finding truly amazing places to visit.
